t: Alert List — Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms category
sl: SFC · Alert List — Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms category (2026)
s: This is the SFC's running public register of entities it has flagged as suspicious, captured on the snapshot date. It groups names into categories such as suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms, fake regulators, unlicensed firms and phishing attempts. Rows are added and removed continuously, so the file is a point-in-time capture rather than a fixed publication. Most listed names have no formal enforcement outcome attached; inclusion just signals the SFC has received complaints or spotted impersonation activity. The virtual-asset sub-list is dominated by copycat sites impersonating licensed exchange brand names.
w: Useful as one input to sanctions/fraud screening of counterparties and customer-named platforms, but it changes daily and carries no due-process explanation, so it cannot be the sole basis for a due-diligence decision.
k: The register sorts flagged names into several buckets, including one specifically for suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms.
Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms heading
Recent virtual-asset entries are dominated by look-alike domains copying a licensed platform's brand name, suggesting active phishing/impersonation campaigns rather than new unlicensed exchanges.
Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms table, entries dated Jul-Sep 2026
A separate 'unlicensed entities' bucket includes at least one digital-token-related fund/issuance name.
Unlicensed entities table, 'Vajra Fund / Vajra Issuance Limited' row
The page states each name is described only under headings such as 'type' and 'add date'; no reasoning or evidence is published alongside a listing.
table column headers throughout
rg: Skim only the virtual-asset and unlicensed-entities sections; skip the phishing/scam-website tables, which are generic and not VA-specific.

t: HKIB Annual Banking Conference: Bank of Tomorrow: Transform to Excellence – Regulatory Update by HKMA
sl: HKMA · HKIB Annual Banking Conference: Bank of Tomorrow: Transform to… (2026)
s: This is Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's slide deck for a 25 September 2026 regulatory keynote, structured around four themes: governing agentic AI, engineering technology resilience, building trusted tokenisation, and fostering data excellence. On tokenisation, it presents the Supervisory Incubator for DLT as the launchpad for business-model transformation and raises the open question of which roles banks can play as trusted intermediaries alongside smart contracts and AI agents. On resilience, it reports a first Quantum Preparedness Index score of 2.3/10 with a target of full sectoral readiness by 2030, and reports GenAI Sandbox++ growth to 36 use cases across 30 institutions and 27 tech partners.
w: Signals HKMA's current supervisory priorities on AI governance, quantum-readiness timelines and tokenisation roles for banks, ahead of formal circulars; the accountability principle ('delegating authority does not delegate accountability') is directly relevant to any bank deploying agentic AI in digital-asset workflows.
k: The deck sets out an AI action spectrum from 'Assist' (retrieve information) through 'Recommend' and 'Decide' to 'Act' (carrying out actions using approved tools), and makes clear that handing authority to AI systems doesn't hand off accountability too -- the Board and senior management stay answerable throughout the whole action chain.
slide 5 & 7

The GenAI Sandbox programme grew across three cohorts: the 2024 first cohort of GenAI Sandbox (10 banks, 4 tech partners, 15 use cases), the 2025 second cohort of GenAI Sandbox (20 banks, 14 tech partners, 27 use cases), and the 2026 first cohort of the renamed GenAI Sandbox++ (30 financial institutions, 27 tech partners, 36 use cases), reflecting a shift toward cross-sector agentic AI end-to-end processes.
slide 6

HKMA's first Quantum Preparedness Index (QPI) score is 2.3 out of 10, with banks that have transition plans reporting an expected implementation time of 5.6 years, against an HKMA objective of full sectoral readiness by 2030.
slide 11

Banks should secure their own and critical service providers' cyber fundamentals, and frontier AI-driven cyber risks should not be underestimated even as cyber risk management fundamentals remain the 'gold standard'.
slide 10
The Supervisory Incubator for DLT is presented as a 'launchpad' enabling real-value, real-transaction business-model transformation trials for banks.
slide 14

The deck poses an open question on 'who is authorised to move value' in a tokenised ecosystem involving smart contract guardrails, trusted transaction rails and AI agents -- framing potential bank roles as still under exploration.
slide 15

Data Excellence is framed around a 'GRID' model: Granularity, Reliability, Ingenuity, Discoverability, with Granular Data Reporting (GDR) 3.0 aimed at moving from aggregated template-based reporting to data-point-centric submissions ('report once, use multiple').
slide 17-18
95% fintech adoption was reported among surveyed banks, but 41% cited high-quality data as an adoption challenge.
slide 17
rg: Slide deck with minimal running text; review slides 5-7 (AI governance/accountability), 10-11 (cyber/quantum) and 14-15 (tokenisation) which carry the substantive content; slides 1-4 and 16-19 are largely agenda/branding.

t: Review of the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners
sl: HKMA · Review of the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners (2026)
s: The HKMA reviewed the ECF, the bank staff qualification framework launched in 2014 with ten workstreams including Compliance, Fintech, AML/CFT and Cybersecurity. It proposes five changes: a single common Core Level for all practitioners, one consolidated Professional Level qualification per workstream, shorter experience requirements, the ability to keep certificates after changing roles if continuing training is met, and fewer overlapping qualifications. Industry feedback gathered through HKAB and HKIB committees was broadly supportive but stressed smooth transition. A three-phase roadmap runs from mid-2028 to 2030, with HKIB to set transition arrangements and courses and the HKMA to issue new ECF guidance. Specific competency standards will be revised in a later phase.
w: Relevant to planning qualifications for digital asset compliance staff: the separate Fintech/DLT certificates will be merged and certificates will become portable. No near-term compliance obligation arises.
k: The review follows the August 2025 'Capacity Building for Future Banking, 2026-2030' study and its ASCEND action plan.
Executive summary, p.5
Core Level becomes one common, non-workstream module; completing it also gives HKIB Certified Banker Stage I.
Enhancement 2, pp.6, 16
Each of the ten workstreams (including Fintech and Compliance) will have one consolidated Professional Level qualification.
Enhancements 1 and 5, pp.6-7, 19
Experience: one year at an AI in Hong Kong for Core; three years for Professional, at least two in the workstream.
Enhancement 3, p.18
Holders may keep certificates after moving roles, provided they meet continuing professional development (CPD) requirements.
Enhancement 4, p.18
Direct entry to the Professional Level without first taking Core will be allowed.
Figure 3, p.8; Box 1, p.21
Today the Fintech workstream alone has six separate qualifications, including one on distributed ledger technology.
Figure 4, p.14
Implementation is phased from mid-2028 to 2030: HKIB transition arrangements and new courses, and new HKMA ECF guidance.
Section 4, Figure 5, p.23
rg: Read the executive summary (pp.5-8) and roadmap (p.23); skip methodology.

t: The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address
sl: Government · The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address (2026)
s: This is the Chief Executive's annual policy speech to the legislature, setting government priorities across many areas. Within the finance chapter, it lists a cluster of digital-asset initiatives that regulators and market bodies are pursuing over the coming years. These include a test of putting Exchange Fund Bills on a distributed ledger, a new digital-asset settlement platform at the clearing house CMU OmniClear, wider bond tokenisation work, and a blockchain-based tokenisation platform at the exchange operator. It also flags planned moves to widen virtual-asset licensing coverage, let licensed trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and expand tokenised bank deposits and a wholesale digital-currency settlement pilot. A separate customs-led programme will build systems to analyse digital-asset transactions for anti-money-laundering purposes by 2029.
w: None of this creates a binding rule yet -- it is a statement of government direction, so no immediate compliance action is required. It does flag several workstreams a compliance head should put on a watchlist: wider virtual-asset licensing and stablecoin trading permissions for licensed venues, a new SFC custody surveillance system that will touch custodians the bank may rely on, and the central bank's own tokenised-deposit and wholesale digital-currency pilots that the bank's treasury or product teams may be asked to join.
k: The central bank will trial running Exchange Fund Bills on distributed-ledger technology by the end of the year, aimed at letting banks manage these instruments around the clock.
para 35(ii)
A cross-agency group will start a second round of legal review on how distributed-ledger technology can be used in capital markets, working with the finance bureau.
para 35(iii)
The clearing entity CMU OmniClear will stand up a new digital-asset platform this year to handle issuance and settlement of digital bonds in one place.
para 35(iv)
The stock exchange operator is building a blockchain platform covering several asset types, already used for carbon credits, and will add tokenised commodity warehouse receipts next year.
para 46(v)
The securities regulator will widen virtual-asset licensing coverage and put out clearer rules so virtual-asset firms know what compliance is expected of them.
para 49(i)
The securities regulator will update its rules for tokenised investment products so licensed venues can offer tokenised gold and similar real-world assets, plus new product types.
para 49(ii)
The securities regulator plans to let licensed virtual-asset trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and let those tokens be used to settle tokenised money-market funds.
para 49(iii)
The central bank intends to add round-the-clock settlement using a wholesale digital-currency pilot (EnsembleTX) by roughly year-end, and keep looking for new uses of tokenised bank deposits.
para 50

The securities regulator will begin operating a system to watch over digital-asset custody arrangements sometime in the year's second half, and will switch on a separate big-data surveillance tool for market abuse and money laundering in 2027.
para 51(iii)
The central bank will keep testing new uses for tokenised deposits, including a Mainland trade-finance pilot meant to finish transactions before year-end.
para 99

Customs authorities plan a second phase, targeted for 2029, of two new systems -- one to analyse digital-asset transactions and one for anti-money-laundering analytics -- feeding into a wider financial-crime data platform.
Annex (I) New Indicators, item 209
rg: Read paragraphs 34-52 (pp.22-28, the fintech and capital-markets tokenisation measures) and Annex (I) New Indicators, item 209 (p.112, the AML digital-asset analytics system); skip the remaining roughly 370 paragraphs on national security, housing, healthcare and other non-financial topics.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
sl: HKMA · Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) (2026)
s: This is the central bank's standing web page pulling together its whole central-bank digital currency workstream. It walks through the wholesale line of work, starting with an early proof of concept in 2017 and running through joint cross-border trials with Thailand, a wider multi-country bridge project, and a tokenised-deposit initiative called Project Ensemble. It then covers a separate retail-facing strand, exploring a possible Hong Kong dollar digital currency for individuals and firms, including two rounds of public feedback and two pilot phases. The page states plainly that the authority has not yet decided whether or when to launch a retail digital currency and will instead put its near-term effort into the wholesale, institutional side. It links out to the underlying reports, whitepapers and pilot summaries that give the detail behind each project name.
w: This page is the compliance head's map of every named HKMA digital-money initiative the bank may be asked to join or reference, and it confirms there is still no live retail digital Hong Kong dollar and no firm launch date, so no new consumer-facing obligations arise from it yet. It does flag that tokenised deposits and cross-border wholesale settlement are the areas moving fastest, which is where the bank's treasury and payments teams are most likely to be approached next.
k: The authority is putting near-term priority on a digital currency built for banks and other institutions rather than one for consumers, while keeping the option open to extend it to retail use later.
para 1 (e-HKD for financial institutions intro)

The wholesale work began in 2017 as a proof of concept with the three banknote-issuing banks, then extended cross-border with Thailand, and later added mainland China, the UAE and the BIS innovation arm under the name mBridge.
Project Inthanon-LionRock / Project mBridge sections

A newer strand, Project Ensemble, launched in 2024 to build shared settlement rails for tokenised bank deposits and other tokenised assets, and moved from a sandbox into a live pilot called Ensemble TX with named participating banks.
Project Ensemble / Ensemble TX sections

An architecture community of market participants was set up in 2024 to help agree common technical standards so that tokenised deposits, tokenised assets and any future digital Hong Kong dollar can work together.
Project Ensemble Architecture Community section

On the retail side, two rounds of market feedback and two pilot phases with industry (2023 and 2025 reports) were completed before the authority concluded that, for now, the bigger near-term value lies in the wholesale space rather than a retail digital Hong Kong dollar.
e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 / Phase 2 sections

No decision has been taken on whether, or when, a retail digital Hong Kong dollar would actually be launched; preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork is being completed instead, expected by the first half of 2026.
'Policy Stance and Three-Rail Approach' section

The authority also ran two earlier joint research projects on a possible retail digital currency with the Bank for International Settlements and other central banks, one on a two-tier prototype and one on giving private firms direct access to a central-bank ledger.
'Collaborative Projects' section (Project Aurum, Project Sela)
rg: Read the wholesale and retail section headers and their opening paragraphs first; skip the speech and press-release listings and the academic expert-group member table at the bottom, which are not substantive.

t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Mitigating risks in receiving deposits through simplified eDDA arrangements
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Mitigating… (2026)
s: The SFC highlights risks in licensed firms' use of simplified Electronic Direct Debit Authorisation (eDDA) arrangements - where the firm, as payee, initiates a client's bank debit setup based on client-provided pre-authorisation rather than the client initiating it via their own bank - for receiving client trading-account deposits. Key risks are impersonation/unauthorised eDDA setup using stolen bank details, and financial exposure from indemnities the firm gives its bank against claims from fraudulent or erroneous setups. The circular requires firms to review their simplified-eDDA arrangements, assess risk, and implement mitigation measures before processing new setup requests, including verifying bank account ownership (e.g. via a one-off small-value transfer) and verifying identification information consistency, declining/withholding processing on unresolved red flags (e.g. deposits immediately converted to virtual assets and withdrawn), imposing transaction limits or withholding periods, and disclosing eDDA settings to clients with their consent. Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to alternative deposit arrangements.
w: This circular binds SFC-licensed corporations and VASPs as eDDA payees, not the bank as the account-holding institution, but a compliance head should treat its red-flag list -- especially rapid VA conversion after a new eDDA setup -- as a template for the bank's own deposit-fraud monitoring, since the bank's customer accounts are the ones being debited.
k: Under simplified eDDA, the licensed firm (as payee) initiates the setup request based on client-provided pre-authorisation and bank details, rather than the client initiating via their own bank (standard eDDA); firms bear primary responsibility for ensuring proper authorisation where the payer bank does not require account-owner confirmation.
paras 2-6
Firms may be required to indemnify their bank against losses from fraudulent or erroneous eDDA setup requests/deposits.
para 5

Before processing new simplified eDDA setup requests, firms should ascertain bank account ownership - via assessing the payer bank's authentication process, or via a one-off small-value transfer verified against the account holder's name - and verify identification information consistency with firm records.
para 10

Firms should decline/withhold processing where verification cannot be satisfied or red flags are detected, including repeated setup failures, frequent/large deposits without rationale, deposits inconsistent with client profile, new eDDA setup followed by whitelisting a new VA wallet address (or vice versa), or deposits quickly converted to virtual assets and withdrawn.
para 11

Suspicious transactions must be promptly investigated and, where warranted, reported to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit or Anti-Deception Coordination Centre (HKPF), and notified to the SFC per Code of Conduct para 12.5 / VATP Guidelines para 16.7 where applicable.
para 11, footnotes 7-8

Clients onboarded via 'online onboarding using a designated bank account in Hong Kong' should not have their initial deposit accepted via simplified eDDA unless the firm can confirm the account owner has given their consent to that setup.
para 10, footnote 5
Firms should consider supplementary measures such as transaction amount/frequency limits, withholding periods after deposits, and step-up authentication.
para 12
Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to other ways of taking deposits, such as standard eDDA or bank transfers.
para 13
Firms should disclose eDDA settings (limits, expiry) to clients, obtain consent, and remind clients to monitor their linked bank accounts for irregularities.
paras 14-15
rg: Read paras 1-6 for the mechanism and risk, then paras 9-13 (the operative risk-assessment and mitigation requirements) as the core compliance content; paras 14-17 are disclosure/administrative wrap-up.

t: Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2026)
s: This is a one-page HKMA summary flyer for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy for issuing bonds on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in Hong Kong; it states it is for reference only and points to a separate full Guideline for binding terms. A bond meeting only the basic conditions (issued in Hong Kong, plus either genuine local DLT-team presence or issuance on the CMU's own DLT platform) qualifies for a half grant of up to HK$1.25 million, covering half of eligible costs. Meeting four extra conditions as well — an independent DLT platform provider, a minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, at least five unrelated investors at issuance, and a listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP) — raises the cap to a full HK$2.5 million grant. Eligible costs named are Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, listing, arranger and audit fees, plus CMU lodging and clearing fees.
w: A bank arranging, underwriting or issuing tokenised/digital bonds in Hong Kong can weigh this cost subsidy in DLT-platform and listing-venue choices, but compliance must still check the full Guideline (not captured in this text) for binding eligibility and application terms before relying on the flyer's figures.
k: The scheme reimburses half of eligible issuance costs, capped at HK$1.25 million, once only the basic conditions are met.
p.1 (flyer text, left column)
A higher cap of HK$2.5 million applies only if the basic conditions and all four additional conditions are satisfied.
p.1 (flyer text, right column)
One basic condition is that the bond is issued in Hong Kong.
p.1, 'Basic Requirements' (a)
The other basic condition, met either way, is that the DLT development/operations team has a real Hong Kong footprint, or the bond runs on the CMU's own DLT platform.
p.1, 'Basic Requirements' (b)
An additional condition requires the DLT platform provider to be unrelated to (not an associate of) the bond issuer.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (a)
Another additional condition sets a minimum issuance size of HK$1 billion equivalent.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (b)
A further additional condition requires at least five investors at issuance who are not connected to the issuer or the DLT platform provider.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (c)
The last additional condition requires listing either on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform.
p.1, 'Additional Requirements' (d)
Costs the grant can reimburse span Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, arranger and audit fees, exchange/VATP listing fees, and CMU fees for lodging and clearing the bond.
p.1, 'Eligible Expenses'
rg: The whole one-page flyer is short enough to read in full; do not treat it as the authoritative source — the linked full Guideline (not in this text) governs actual applications.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 17-19 June 2026
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2026)
s: This is a routine SFC anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) relay of the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 19 June 2026 statements. It covers the Call for Action list (countermeasures against North Korea and Iran; extra due diligence for Myanmar) and the Increased Monitoring list (Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq added; Algeria and Namibia removed). It also relays selected results from the FATF Plenary of 17-19 June 2026: a new report on public/private information-sharing partnerships, a public consultation on cross-border payment transparency guidance under Recommendation 16 (closing 21 August 2026), a report on terrorist financing through social media, messaging, and streaming platforms, a coming report on underground banking and hawala misuse, and the seventh targeted update on how FATF's virtual asset and Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) standards are being applied, plus a new targeted report on money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk in decentralised finance (DeFi) platforms. Licensed corporations, VASPs, and associated entities are reminded to apply enhanced due diligence and the special high-risk-jurisdiction rules in the AML Guideline.
w: Most of this is a routine jurisdictional-risk update for AML/CFT screening, but the item on the coming FATF virtual asset and DeFi reports flags future SFC or HKMA guidance that a bank's digital-asset AML program should watch for.
k: FATF calls for countermeasures against North Korea and Iran, and for due diligence proportionate to risk in Myanmar's case (in place since October 2022, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by October 2026).
section (1)
FATF's Increased Monitoring list was updated: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq were added; Algeria and Namibia were removed.
section (2)

Firms are reminded to pay particular attention and take extra care with business relationships and transactions tied to higher-risk jurisdictions, applying the special high-risk rules under paragraphs 4.9 and 4.13 of the AML Guideline.
final substantive para, footnote 10

The FATF Plenary (17-19 June 2026) approved a seventh targeted update on how its virtual asset and VASP standards are being applied, plus a new targeted report on DeFi platforms' money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk, both due to be published later.
section (3)(e)
A public consultation on new guidance for cross-border payment transparency under Recommendation 16 closes on 21 August 2026.
section (3)(b)
rg: This is a routine FATF list relay - the jurisdiction lists (sections 1-2) can be skimmed for country names/changes; section (3)(e) on the VA/VASP and DeFi FATF reports is the only forward-looking item of note for digital-asset purposes.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - EvergreenHub: Navigating Bond Tokenisation  Digital Bond Knowledge Repository
sl: HKMA · EvergreenHub: Navigating Bond Tokenisation  Digital Bond Knowledge Repository (2026)
s: EvergreenHub is HKMA's reference repository on Project Evergreen and Hong Kong's tokenised bond market. It recounts three Government tokenised green bond issuances (Feb 2023 proof-of-concept, Feb 2024 first multi-currency digital bond, Nov 2025 record HK$10bn issuance integrating e-CNY/e-HKD settlement) and lists ongoing HKMA efforts: consistent tokenised government bond supply, financial infrastructure interoperability, the Tokenised Bond Expert Group, the DLT legal-framework review with FSTB, and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (a subsidy of up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance).
w: Central reference hub for any bank considering acting as arranger, dealer or DLT platform provider on a tokenised bond in Hong Kong, including the DBGS subsidy scheme and links to the underlying HKMA 'Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong' report (separately registered, id a0b44be27c40) that sets out the legal deal-structuring analysis.
k: The Government's first tokenised green bond (February 2023) proved compatibility with Hong Kong's legal/regulatory framework, completed a full bond lifecycle on DLT (issuance to redemption) and shortened primary settlement from typical T+5 to T+1.
'Feb 2023' section
The second issuance, in February 2024, broke new ground as the world's first digital bond spanning multiple currencies (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR), worth around HK$6 billion equivalent.
'Feb 2024' section

The third issuance (November 2025) set a new record, raising more than HK$10 billion across four currency tranches, with over HK$130 billion in subscriptions, stretched tenor out to five years, and became the first to settle via tokenised central bank money (e-HKD/e-CNY) for its HKD and RMB tranches.
'Nov 2025' section
The HKMA's Digital Bond Grant Scheme pays up to HK$2.5 million per qualifying digital bond issued in Hong Kong (see separate registry entry for the Guideline, id 5a0563de8142).
'Digital Bond Grant Scheme' section
HKMA is exploring legal framework enhancements for DLT adoption in the fixed income market jointly with FSTB (see the related 29 June 2026 press release, id 279f10054c6e).
'Continue to scale tokenisation' section
rg: Read the three issuance summaries (2023/2024/2025) and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme paragraph; the page's substantial site-navigation boilerplate and long video/podcast list can be skipped.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers (2026)
s: This is the HKMA's standing web page for the stablecoin issuer licensing regime, which took effect on 1 August 2025 under the Stablecoins Ordinance. It links to the licensee register, the Explanatory Note on licensing, the Supervisory Guideline, the AML/CFT Guideline, and the full history of discussion papers, consultations and conclusions that preceded the regime. It also lists related press releases and speeches, including confirmation that the first licences were granted on 10 April 2026. The page is a navigation hub rather than a source of new obligations in itself.
w: This page is the fastest way for compliance to confirm who currently holds a Hong Kong stablecoin issuer licence and to reach the current versions of the binding guidelines, which matters both for a bank's own potential issuance plans and for due diligence on any stablecoin issuer counterparty.
k: Issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin has been a licensable activity in Hong Kong since 1 August 2025, when the Stablecoins Ordinance regime started operating.
body text, p.1
The page hosts the Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers, which the public can check for who currently holds a licence.
'Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
Firms interested in applying are told to read the Explanatory Note and are invited to contact HKMA early for informal discussion before applying.
'Licensing for Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
HKMA has published a general supervisory guideline and a dedicated AML/CFT guideline setting out its regulatory expectations for licensees.
'Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1
The first stablecoin issuer licences were announced as granted on 10 April 2026, roughly eight months after the regime began.
press release list entry '10 Apr 2026', p.1

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Complaints about Licensed Stablecoin Issuers

t: Circular to licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers Implementing (i) robust authentication methods to reduce and mitigate hacking risks from phishing attacks and (ii) adequate monitoring and surveillance measures to identify suspicious activities
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers Implementing (i) robust authentication… (2026)
s: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs (currently meaning VATPs) to adopt phishing-resistant authentication (passkeys or robust device binding) for client login and device registration, and to implement effective monitoring/surveillance to detect suspicious account activity, following large-scale SMS phishing campaigns in 2025 that used man-in-the-middle attacks to intercept OTPs. OTP (email/SMS) is explicitly no longer considered phishing-resistant and should not be used for login/device-binding authentication. Firms are expected to implement robust authentication solutions no later than 8 July 2027 (12 months from the circular date), with large internet brokers expected to implement immediately; other expected enhancements (monitoring, client awareness) should be made immediately or as soon as practicable. Clients generally may not bind more than three passkeys/devices without additional assessment. Senior management — the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight together with the MIC-IT — is accountable, and firms failing to prevent large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident will be held accountable by the SFC for client losses. An Appendix gives detailed acceptable authentication examples including passkeys and device-binding verification methods.
w: This is a direct, dated cyber-governance expectation for the bank's SFC-licensed corporation or VASP entity: named senior managers are accountable, OTP should be phased out as a login factor, and the SFC has stated it will hold the firm liable for client losses from hacking if controls are inadequate.
k: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs to adopt robust, phishing-resistant authentication for client login and device binding, and to implement effective monitoring/surveillance for suspicious activity.
para 1
The SFC regards OTP (whether by email or SMS) as falling short of a phishing-resistant authentication method, and says firms should not rely on it for login or device-binding steps.
para 7
Passkeys (FIDO-certified, public-key based) and robustly-verified device binding are the two acceptable authentication methods described; existing bound devices need not be re-registered.
paras 5, 8
Generally, firms shouldn't let clients register above three passkeys, or above three devices, unless they've done extra checks for the request.
para 10
Session idle timeout should generally be limited to within 30 minutes and clients should not be allowed to disable session timeout, absent justified and monitored exceptions.
para 11

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to alert clients right away about successful logins and other high-risk account activity -- logins from new devices, device binding, or passkey creation/revocation -- using more than one communication channel.
para 13
Internet brokers and VASPs should report hacking incidents to the SFC immediately and conduct root cause analysis with remedial action.
para 18

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to implement robust authentication solutions as soon as practicable and no later than 8 July 2027 (12 months from the circular); large internet brokers are expected to implement immediately.
para 21(c)
Firms unable to meet the 12-month implementation deadline should immediately notify their case officer-in-charge.
para 23

Senior management -- in particular the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight, together with the MIC-IT -- bears ultimate responsibility for overseeing these safeguards and keeping client accounts properly protected.
para 24

If a firm doesn't put in place sufficient controls to stop, catch and halt large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident, the SFC will hold that firm accountable for the resulting client losses.
para 25
rg: Read paras 1-3 (background/2025 phishing incidents), paras 21-25 (implementation timeline and management accountability) as most consequential; the Appendix's passkey/device-binding examples (paras 1-6) are useful implementation reference but can be skimmed once the two acceptable methods are understood.

t: HKMC's HK$12 billion inaugural public digital bond issuance
sl: Other · HKMC's HK$12 billion inaugural public digital bond issuance (2026)
s: Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation (HKMC) announced pricing of its first-ever digital bond issuance, worth about HK$12 billion in total, split into three tranches: a 2-year piece of HK$6 billion, a 5-year piece of HK$2.5 billion, and a 3-year CNH tranche of CNH 3 billion. t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Enhanced cybersecurity measures to address evolving risks arising from artificial intelligence-enabled cyberattacks
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Enhanced… (2026)
s: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, licensed VATPs and associated entities (licensed firms) to heightened cyberattack risk from frontier AI models, which can identify and chain vulnerabilities, execute multi-step autonomous attacks, and lower the barrier for phishing, social engineering and deepfake impersonation. It reminds firms that senior leaders — the Manager-in-Charge of IT among them — carry ultimate responsibility for cybersecurity risk, and sets out five areas firms should review and strengthen: patching/vulnerability management, access and privilege controls (zero-trust design), detection and monitoring, third-party supply chain risk management, and incident response/recovery. Firms using AI language models must also apply the core principles from the SFC's November 2024 generative-AI circular and comply with notification requirements for high-risk AI use cases under the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules. An Appendix gives non-exhaustive illustrative examples of controls for each of the five areas.
w: Addressed to LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs (not RIs), so it does not bind the bank directly, but its AI-enabled cyberattack guidance is a useful benchmark for the bank's own cybersecurity framework and a diligence reference when assessing a VATP counterparty's resilience.
k: Senior management -- including the MIC-IT -- bears ultimate responsibility for handling the firm's cybersecurity risk; the MIC-IT should make sure changes to the cybersecurity framework get properly reviewed, approved and rolled out promptly.
para 3
Licensed firms should assess preparedness for AI-enabled cyberattacks and address vulnerabilities, seeking IT security expert advice as necessary.
para 3

Firms should maintain an accurate, up-to-date technology asset inventory identifying externally exposed and business-critical components, updated enough for same-day prioritisation when new vulnerabilities emerge.
para 6

Firms should enforce least-privilege/zero-trust access design, treat external/untrusted inputs (apps, emails, documents, webpages) as potentially adversarial, and require maker-checker sign-off before carrying out high-impact actions.
paras 10-11

Firms using AI language models (internal, group, third-party or open-source) should ensure associated cyber risks (adversarial attacks, data leakage, system prompt override) are addressed per the November 2024 generative-AI circular; those deploying such models for high-risk use cases must also meet the notification duties set out in the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules.
para 8, footnotes 3-5
Firms should strengthen third-party supply-chain risk governance, including initial/ongoing assessment of third-party service providers for AI-enabled cyberattack risk.
para 13
Firms should establish escalation/reporting mechanisms and pre-planned containment/exploit-interruption strategies, since AI-enabled attacks may outpace traditional detection-and-response.
para 15
LCs engaged in electronic trading and VATPs must back up their business records along with client and transaction data at least once a day.
para 17, footnote 8
Firms are required to give the SFC prompt notice of any material cybersecurity incident or attack, per Code of Conduct para 12.5(e) and VATP Guidelines paras 16.7(b)-(c).
para 18
The circular's Appendix sets out illustrative, non-exhaustive control measures for the five areas; firms should scale measures to their nature, scale, complexity and risk exposure.
para 3-19 framing; Appendix text not captured in the fetched source

t: Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Digital Finance Summit 2026
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Digital Finance Summit 2026 (2026)
s: In this policy-framing keynote, the HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset -- speculative crypto-assets (SFC's remit), tokenised real-world assets, and 'tokenised money' (CBDCs, tokenised bank deposits, stablecoins) -- and sets out three HKMA responsibilities: providing central bank money in new forms, setting guardrails for private-sector innovation, and building interoperable common infrastructure. It reviews a decade of HKMA digital-money work (e-HKD/mBridge, tokenised green bonds, the Stablecoins Ordinance and the April 2026 first two stablecoin licences, and Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX), and previews an upcoming Ensemble Use Case Report and Ensemble Taxonomy. It states HKMA now prioritises wholesale e-HKD over retail, and flags 'digital twin' reconciliation burden and platform fragmentation as the two main remaining structural challenges to tokenisation.
w: This is HKMA's clearest recent statement of its three-part regulatory philosophy for digital money and its confirmation that wholesale e-HKD, not retail, is now the near-term priority -- directly shaping how a bank should sequence its own tokenised-deposit, stablecoin and CBDC-interoperability roadmap and Project Ensemble engagement.
k: HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset: (1) speculative crypto-assets like Bitcoin, regulated by the SFC for investor protection/market integrity; (2) tokenisation of real-world assets (bonds, funds, receivables), a market-infrastructure question; and (3) 'tokenised money' (CBDCs, tokenised commercial bank deposits, stablecoins), which are new means of payment, not investment instruments.
'The Digital Finance Landscape' section

HKMA defines three responsibilities in digital finance: providing central bank money in new forms to anchor trust and singleness of money; setting guardrails for responsible private-sector innovation; and building common, interoperable infrastructure as a public good.
'The Role for Central Banking Institution' section

Now that Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme is done, HKMA judges that wholesale use cases matter more right now than retail ones for e-HKD, given how developed Hong Kong's retail payments already are.
'A Decade of Progress' section

The Government's third tokenised green bond issuance, in November 2025, raised roughly HK$10 billion in total across four currencies, drawing subscriptions above HK$130 billion, and was the world's first digital bond to use tokenised central bank money (e-HKD and e-CNY) for settlement.
'A Decade of Progress' section

HKMA confirms the April 2026 grant of stablecoin issuer licences to two entities and states it expects regulated stablecoins to launch in Hong Kong within the next few months, while keeping the licensing threshold high and the number of additional licences very limited.
'A Decade of Progress' section

In November 2025, Project Ensemble entered its pilot phase for real-value transactions, branded 'Ensemble TX,' allowing participating banks to settle tokenised assets against tokenised deposits on a delivery-versus-payment (DvP) basis.
'The third area—infrastructure' section
HKMA will soon publish an Ensemble Use Case Report and an Ensemble Taxonomy -- a common set of terms built jointly with the Ensemble Architectural Community -- to support interoperability standards.
'The Road Ahead' section

Most tokenised assets today follow a 'digital twin' model (off-chain register remains primary, token is a mirrored claim), which delivers efficiency gains but relocates rather than eliminates reconciliation burden; the end-state goal is 'digitally native' issuance where the token itself is the primary ownership record.
'The Road Ahead' section
The immediate next step for Ensemble TX is to extend it to support settlement of tokenised deposits in central bank digital currency, enabling continuous 24/7 settlement.
'The Road Ahead' section, closing paragraphs

Ensemble TX's initial infrastructure is built on the Ensemble Interoperability Layer, drawing on Hong Kong's existing RTGS system for interbank settlement, and is described as a pragmatic first step rather than the end-state architecture.
'The Road Ahead' section
rg: Read 'The Digital Finance Landscape' and 'The Role for Central Banking Institution' sections first for the policy taxonomy, then 'A Decade of Progress' for concrete milestones and 'The Road Ahead' for the digital-twin/fragmentation challenges; the speech has no page/paragraph numbering.

t: Circular on provision of Relevant Stablecoin service by virtual asset trading platforms and licensed corporations
sl: SFC · provision of Relevant Stablecoin service by virtual asset trading… (2026)
s: This SFC circular clarifies how the VATP Guidelines and the Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset activities apply to 'Relevant Stablecoins' - specified stablecoins under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer and authorised under that licence. Because Relevant Stablecoins are already subject to HKMA reserve-backing and redemption oversight, the SFC removes or relaxes several VATP/intermediary requirements that otherwise apply to virtual assets generally: the liquidity/index requirements for retail-tradable tokens, the client virtual-asset-knowledge assessment (for Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients), and inclusion of Relevant Stablecoin holdings in a client's virtual asset exposure limit. Suitability requirements still apply when a VATP or LC solicits or recommends a Relevant Stablecoin. The circular also permits licensed corporations to partner directly with HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers (not only VATPs) and to hold client Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts at the issuer itself, and removes the prior requirement that retail VA dealing go only through an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition. Revised VATP licensing conditions and updated Appendix 6/7 terms and conditions (clean and tracked-changes versions) are attached.
w: This directly shapes how the bank, as a Registered Institution, can onboard, disclose, and distribute HKMA-licensed Relevant Stablecoins -- including a new option to custody them directly at the issuer -- while confirming suitability rules still apply whenever the bank solicits or recommends one.
k: Relevant Stablecoins are specified stablecoins under s.4 of the Stablecoins Ordinance issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer and authorised under that licence; the circular does not apply to other stablecoins.
para 2
The retail-tradability liquidity and index requirements (VATP Guidelines paras 7.7-7.8; Joint Circular paras 20(a)(iv) and 28) need not be applied to Relevant Stablecoins.
para 4
VATPs and LCs must disclose material information on a Relevant Stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements.
para 5

VA-knowledge assessment is not required for clients who are provided Relevant-Stablecoin-only services, but firms must still assess a non-Relevant-Stablecoin-only client's VA knowledge even if that client ends up trading only Relevant Stablecoins.
para 6, footnote 7
Client holdings of Relevant Stablecoins need not be counted toward the client's virtual asset exposure limit.
para 7

A Relevant Stablecoin is treated as a non-complex product, but if a VATP/LC solicits or recommends one, ordinary suitability requirements apply and commission rebates must not be the primary basis for the recommendation.
para 8
Licensed corporations may now partner directly with an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer (not only a VATP) to provide dealing services in that issuer's Relevant Stablecoin.
para 9
Joint Circular paragraph 20(a)(iii), which required retail VA dealing via an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition, is removed.
para 10, footnote 11

Licensed corporations may now hold clients' Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts maintained with the relevant HKMA-licensed issuer itself (which provides custody with client-asset segregation), not only with VATPs or authorized financial institutions.
para 11

VATPs and LCs don't need the SFC's prior written approval to admit a Relevant Stablecoin for trading, but they must give the SFC written notice ahead of time whenever they plan to admit, suspend or remove one.
para 12
Firms must review and update internal policies, procedures and disclosures to comply with the circular.
para 13

Revised VATP licensing condition removes the 12-month track record requirement for Relevant Stablecoins and disapplies VATP Guidelines paras 7.7(b), 7.8 and 16.4 to them; para 9.4 is disapplied where a licensee serves Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients.
Appendix 1, amended licensing condition

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2026)
s: This May 2026 consolidated text sets the conditions the SFC imposes (in consultation with the HKMA for banks) on firms that broker or advise on VAs. Part I covers introducing clients and dealing through omnibus accounts, and Part II covers advice. The May 2026 edits add HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers alongside SFC-licensed platforms as permitted venues for licensed stablecoins, and create lighter paths for 'stablecoin-only' clients: no VA knowledge test, no VA exposure limit, no generic VA risk warnings, and suitability based on the client's use case. It also embeds VA financing as defined in the SFC's 11 February 2026 circular, with statement, record and custody provisions for VA collateral. Other rules such as client identity, contract notes, custody through segregated accounts, staking, record keeping and reporting of material breaches continue.

t: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
sl: HKMA/SFC · Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions… (2026)
s: These May 2026 terms apply to an LC or RI managing a fund or discretionary account that meets the VA 'de minimis threshold': a stated VA objective, or an intention to hold 10% or more of gross asset value in VAs. They cover custody of fund assets (independent custodian or self-custody, due diligence on custodians, custody agreements and disclosure), valuation, record keeping, audits, investor disclosures and reporting to the SFC and, for banks, the HKMA. Schedules add discretionary-account rules, counterparty and cyber risk controls and example risk disclosures. The May 2026 edits carve out licensed stablecoins: where the VA portion is only such coins, generic VA risk examples and the knowledge test for discretionary clients fall away, and the retail liquidity test does not apply to them. The companion circular also says an RI whose portfolios hold licensed stablecoins but no other VAs does not need Type 9 registration.
w: If the bank's private banking or asset management runs VA-exposed portfolios above the threshold, these terms apply through its registration and require HKMA reporting. The stablecoin carve-outs let cash-management style mandates in licensed stablecoins run with lighter onboarding.
