t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2026)
s: This revised SFC circular (superseding the 7 April 2025 version) sets the requirements under which the SFC will authorise public investment funds with more than 10% NAV exposure to virtual assets (VA Funds) under ss.104-105 of the SFO, including VA-related activities such as staking these funds may undertake. It does not apply to exposure to Relevant Stablecoins or tokenised deposits, which are instead covered by FAQs on the UT Code. Requirements cover eligible management companies, eligible underlying VA (must be accessible to Hong Kong public on SFC-licensed VATPs), investment strategy limits (no leverage, VA futures only on conventional regulated exchanges), transaction/custody channels (SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs), custody standards (cold storage, segregation, key management), valuation methodology, and disclosure obligations. Funds seeking more than 10% VA exposure, or wishing to engage in staking or other VA-related activities, require prior SFC consultation and approval.
w: As the current, in-force circular, this directly governs the custody and transaction-channel standards a bank AI must meet to provide VA custody to an SFC-authorised fund, and confirms stablecoin/tokenised-deposit fund exposure is regulated separately from this >10% NAV VA-fund framework.
k: Circular governs SFC authorisation of public funds with VA exposure exceeding 10% of NAV under ss.104-105 SFO.
para 1
Requirements do not apply to fund exposure to Relevant Stablecoins (HKMA-licensed, SO-authorised) or tokenised deposits; see UT Code FAQs Q20G instead.
para 2
This is a revised circular, superseding the earlier Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets, which was issued on 7 April 2025.
para 3
VA Funds are limited to investing in VA tokens -- whether directly, or indirectly through exposure -- that Hong Kong residents can already trade on SFC-licensed VATPs.
para 11
At the fund level, VA Funds are not permitted to take on leveraged exposure to VA.
para 15
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must be through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying authorized institutions (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs).
para 17

Custody should be delegated only to an SFC-licensed VATP, a qualifying AI/subsidiary meeting HKMA VA custody standards, or another SFC-acceptable entity; should use cold-wallet storage predominantly, minimise hot-wallet holdings, and secure seeds/private keys in Hong Kong with restricted access, anti-collusion measures (e.g. multi-sig, key sharding) and backups.
paras 20-21
Valuation of spot VA should use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms via a reputable benchmark index provider.
para 22
Offering documents/KFS should disclose VA exposure investment limits and key risks (price, custody, cybersecurity, fork risk for spot; roll cost/operational risk for futures).
paras 24-25

Under the ASPIRe roadmap, the SFC may let VA Funds take part in staking and other VA-linked activities via SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs, subject to guiding principles on investment consistency, internal controls, due diligence, disclosure, investor notice, and reporting of VA committed to such activities.
para 28
Funds seeking >10% VA exposure, existing funds moving to >10%, or funds wanting to engage in staking/other VA activities require prior SFC consultation and approval.
para 31
Recognised Jurisdiction Schemes (incl. UCITS) and mutual-recognition-of-funds arrangements are generally exempt from these requirements, except the prior consultation/approval requirement.
para 30, footnote 1
rg: Read paras 1-3 for scope/supersession, then paras 17-21 (custody/transactions) and para 28 (staking) as the most operationally significant sections for a bank; paras 22-27 (valuation, disclosure, distribution) are more standard fund-governance detail.

t: Updated Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · Updated Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial… (2026)
s: This Annex lists 26 expectations for banks and their local subsidiaries that hold digital assets for clients, grouped under governance, segregation, safeguarding, outsourcing, disclosure, records, ongoing monitoring and staking. Compared with the 2024 version it adds detailed wallet-operation controls: cold-wallet whitelists with system checks on every transfer, no smart contracts in cold wallets on public chains, dedicated signing devices, air-gapped integrity checks, anti-blind-signing, code-management segregation of duties and 24/7 security monitoring. The fixed 50%/100% insurance or compensation footnote is gone; instead the bank is liable for losses attributable to it and must hold adequate financial resources, which may include insurance. The 98% cold-storage rule for VAs and the Hong Kong key-location rule stay, with a new carve-out letting an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer, with HKMA consent, hold keys for its own coins in Hong Kong or another accepted location. A licensed stablecoin issuer is added as a permitted custody delegate, third-party transfers are allowed for payments and settlement where controls exist, and the separate AML section of 2024 no longer appears.
w: This is the paragraph list HKMA will test custody against. Compliance needs a line-by-line gap analysis, especially for the new wallet-operation controls in paras 10-11 and 23-25, the move from a fixed insurance percentage to liability plus adequate financial resources, and any plan to use a licensed stablecoin issuer as custodian.
k: Scope: client-held crypto-based assets (VAs, tokenised securities, other tokenised assets) at AIs and local AIs' subsidiaries; limited purpose tokens and proprietary holdings excluded. Banks that also deal in the VAs must also follow the dealing rules, e.g. on third-party transfers.
Preamble and footnotes 1-5, p.1
Before launch, run a full risk assessment and set policies and controls; board and senior management oversee risk before and after launch.
para 1, p.1
Resource the business with skilled people; train staff at the outset and continuously, with in-depth training for transaction signers on verification and handling exceptions (signer training is new).
paras 2-3, p.2
Set written roles, responsibilities and reporting lines, and manage conflicts of interest across the bank and affiliates.
para 4, p.2
Maintain contingency and disaster recovery plans and now also run drills for emergency and business continuity scenarios.
para 5, p.2
Keep client assets in segregated client accounts and wallet addresses, apart from the bank's own, so creditors cannot reach them in insolvency or resolution.
para 6 and footnote 6, p.2
Do not transfer title to, lend, pledge or encumber client assets except for settlement or fees owed, with prior explicit written client consent, or where law requires.
para 7, p.3
Controls may be risk-based by network type; new text notes permissioned tokens with smart-contract access controls may allow recovery of lost assets.
para 9, p.3
Written procedures should cover access authorisation plus detection of intrusion into critical wallet infrastructure (cold vault, signing devices, databases, production binaries, code repositories).
para 10, first bullet, p.4
New: system-enforced controls should block unauthorised cold-wallet transfers, using whitelists with tight oversight of changes and systematic verification of each transaction.
para 10, second bullet, p.4
New: procedures for handling security alerts and incidents by severity level with matching response protocols.
para 10, fourth bullet, p.4
For client VAs the para 11 controls are generally required; for other digital assets a risk-based approach is allowed, with extra caution for permissionless tokens on public permissionless chains.
para 11 (chapeau), p.4
rg: Read paras 10-11 (safeguarding controls, pp.3-7) and 14-17 (outsourcing, pp.8-9) first, then 23-25 (monitoring). Paras 1-7 and 20-22 largely repeat the 2024 text.

t: Guidance on Offering of Financing for Virtual Asset Dealing, Shared Order Book, and Client Virtual Asset Withdrawals
sl: HKMA · Guidance on Offering of Financing for Virtual Asset Dealing,… (2026)
s: A 27 May 2026 HKMA letter to all registered institutions setting the standards under which RIs may offer margin financing for VA dealing, give clients agency access to a VATP's shared order book, and permit client VA withdrawals. It largely extends to RIs the standards the SFC set for licensed VA brokers on 11 February 2026. Eligible VA financing collateral is capped to bitcoin, ether and HKMA-licensed stablecoins with prudent haircuts, and such loans get no capital credit for the VA collateral itself under the Banking (Capital) Rules.
w: Sets the precise conditions, collateral list, haircuts and controls a bank must have in place to lawfully offer VA-backed margin lending, and confirms such exposures earn the bank no capital relief for the VA collateral itself.
k: Before the SFC's 11 Feb 2026 circular, licensed corporations and RIs were barred from providing any financing for clients to buy VA, under paragraph 4.3 of the omnibus-account Terms and Conditions.
Background, p.1-2

That SFC circular now lets VA brokers under omnibus-account arrangements with SFC-licensed VATPs offer margin financing for VA dealing to clients with strong credit profiles and sufficient collateral.
Background, p.2
HKMA is letting RIs providing VA dealing services offer the same kind of VA financing, provided they meet standards equivalent to those the SFC set for VA brokers.
HKMA's guidance for RIs, p.2
VA financing may only be extended to a margin client based on the client's financial capability and on securities and/or VA collateral the client has posted.
para (1), p.2
Only the RI's existing securities margin-financing clients are eligible for VA financing.
para (2), p.2
An RI is not expected to raise a client's credit limit just because VA financing is now offered, and should factor in the price volatility of non-fiat assets when assessing financial capability.

Where a client's VA holdings feed into that assessment, the RI's assessment should weigh VA quality/volatility/price-gap risk, valuation and liquidity sustainability, digital-asset sector concentration (including operator/treasury-company shares), asset-specific risk such as infrastructure failure, correlation with equities in stress, likely deterioration of repayment ability, and (for corporates) related-party VA exposure.

The circular notes VAs have a limited track record through systemic shocks, can fall sharply within a day or across days, tend to move together across the VA sector in stress, and that leverage from margin lending or derivatives can amplify losses.
para (3), p.3
An RI should carefully consider whether relying on VA as loan collateral is prudent at all, given these risks.
para (4), p.3
Eligible VA collateral is limited to bitcoin, ether, and stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance ('Relevant Stablecoins'), with a prudent haircut applied.
A minimum 60% haircut applies to the market value of bitcoin and ether collateral; HKMA can revise this haircut later, giving RIs prior notice.
footnote 5 and para (4), p.4

An RI relying on VA collateral should document its risk-assessment methodology in its margin lending policy, set and monitor acceptable credit exposure accordingly, and keep the operational capability to track VA collateral volatility in real time and act promptly.
rg: Read the whole letter; it is short (6 pages). Pay particular attention to paras (3)-(9) on the financing/collateral controls.

t: Updated Guidance on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
sl: HKMA · Updated Guidance on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital… (2026)
s: The HKMA tells all authorized institutions (AIs, i.e. banks) that it has refreshed its expectations for holding digital assets on behalf of clients. The review reflects market and technology change and the start of the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). The refreshed standards sit in an Annex and allow arrangements proportionate to each asset's features and risks. They cover assets received as a virtual asset (VA) intermediary, through tokenised product distribution, or in a standalone custody business, and also reach subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks. Banks planning to start must discuss with the HKMA first; banks already active must review and upgrade their controls. The letter replaces the February 2024 circular.
w: Custody is now judged against the May 2026 Annex. Compliance should run a gap review of existing custody (including subsidiaries) and ensure any new custody line is pre-discussed with the HKMA before launch.
k: 'Digital assets' covers crypto-based assets such as VAs, tokenised securities and other tokenised assets, and also the keys, seeds and backups used to access them.
footnote 1, p.1
Limited purpose digital tokens and the bank's or its group's own (proprietary) holdings are out of scope.
footnote 1, p.1
The standards apply whatever the route by which the bank came to hold the client assets: VA intermediary business, tokenised product distribution, or pure custody.
Meeting the Annex does not displace other applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
p.2, second paragraph
The circular covers AIs and the subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs that do custody; the local parent should ensure those subsidiaries comply.
p.2, third paragraph
A bank (or local bank's subsidiary) that intends to offer custody should talk to the HKMA beforehand and show it meets the standards to the HKMA's satisfaction.
'Implementation', p.2
A bank already providing custody should review and revise its systems and controls to meet the latest Annex standards.
'Implementation', p.2
The 20 February 2024 custody circular is superseded.
'Implementation', p.2
The letter points to the joint HKMA-SFC VA circulars and the 27 May 2026 RI stablecoin circular as related guidance for VA intermediary activity.
footnote 2, p.2
rg: Read footnote 1 (scope) and the 'Implementation' section on p.2; the Annex carries the detail.

t: Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory… (2026)
s: This paper finalises how Hong Kong will licence virtual asset (VA) advisory services (modelled on Type 4) and VA management/discretionary services (modelled on Type 9). Both regimes are activity-based and technology-neutral: they catch AI-generated advice, robo-advisers and copy-trading, and they capture the substance of an activity regardless of labels like 'education'. VA management has no de minimis threshold — any discretionary VA exposure triggers licensing. VA management firms may appoint SFC- or overseas-regulated custodians of their choice for private funds (no mandatory SFC-custodian-only rule), though self-custody of hard-to-place tokens will be subject to new SFC-prescribed safeguards. No deeming/grandfathering will be offered when the regimes commence, though an expedited track exists for firms already vetted. A single bill covering dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This settles the two remaining pieces of Hong Kong's VA-intermediary framework relevant to any bank providing digital-asset advice or discretionary management: the no-de-minimis rule means even a token amount of client VA exposure triggers licensing, and the confirmation that private-fund custodians need not be SFC-regulated gives more counterparty flexibility than the parallel dealing-services regime.
k: VA advisory and VA management licensing look to the substance of the activity, not its label — content marketed as 'education', 'research' or 'trading signals' is regulated if it in substance advises on acquiring or disposing of VAs.
paras 6, 8

Both regimes are technology-neutral: providing an algorithm or AI language model that generates VA advice, or a robo-adviser that makes discretionary VA investment decisions, counts as providing the regulated service.
paras 9, 40

Advising on tokenised securities, or on derivatives/structured products referencing VAs, generally falls under existing SFO licences (Type 4/5/11) rather than the new VA advisory regime, since the statutory VA definition excludes securities and futures contracts.
paras 11-12

Advising on a client's combined VA-and-securities portfolio is not treated as wholly incidental to a Type 4 securities licence — a separate VA advisory licence is still required for the VA component even if delivered alongside securities advice.
para 21

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes, having observed undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs; a dedicated consultation may follow.
para 18

VA advisory service providers get a tiered capital baseline: HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital, matching Type 4 treatment; dual Type 4/VA-advisory licensees are not subject to double capital requirements.
paras 25-26
VA management has no de minimis threshold — any portfolio with discretionary VA exposure, however small, requires a licence, matching the 'no de minimis' approach under Type 9.
para 32
A VA management licensee that deals in VAs solely to service its own fund management (e.g. converting subscription proceeds to VAs) is exempt from also needing a separate VA dealing licence.
para 38

Private VA fund managers retain flexibility to appoint any qualified custodian globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for the funds they manage, mirroring existing Type 9 treatment; the SFC will however prescribe specific safeguards where a manager self-custodies tokens lacking any supporting custodian.
paras 56-57

No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will be offered; both regimes take full effect on the commencement date, with an expedited approval track for firms already assessed by SFC or HKMA, and existing RA9 managers below the old VA de minimis threshold must either seek a licence or wind down their VA management activity in an orderly way by commencement.

The VA dealing, advisory and management regimes will operate as standalone AMLO licensing regimes that replace the current practice of imposing VA-related terms and conditions on SFO licensees under the Joint Circular; existing Joint Circular requirements become the new regimes' baseline.
para 62
Both regimes prohibit actively marketing VA advisory or management services to the Hong Kong public from anywhere in the world without an SFC licence or registration.
para 70
rg: Read paras 1-52 (Sections A-D) for scope, technology-neutrality and capital rules; read paras 53-57 (custody, Question 7) closely if the bank runs or advises VA funds; skim licensing fees and skip the respondent annex.

t: Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
sl: FSTB/SFC · Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2026)
s: FSTB and SFC conclude the further consultation (closed January 2026) on separate AMLO licensing regimes for VA advisory services (modelled on SFO Type 4) and VA management services (modelled on SFO Type 9). The scope is technology-neutral, covering AI/algorithm-driven advice and discretionary robo-management, and excludes advice or management confined to tokenised securities (which stays under the SFO). No de minimis threshold applies to VA management. Private funds managing VAs will retain flexibility to appoint qualified custodians globally rather than being restricted to SFC-regulated VA custodians, though the SFC plans to set strict rules for VA management firms that hold client tokens themselves because no qualified custodian is available. No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will be given; a bill is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.
w: This finalises the scope, exemptions and custody flexibility for any bank-affiliated VA advisory or fund/portfolio management activity, including the important carve-out that Relevant Stablecoins dealt in by SFC-licensed intermediaries don't need separate VA licences, and that private VA funds are not forced into SFC-regulated custodians only.
k: VA advisory services scope covers giving advice, or issuing analyses/reports, on whether, which, when or on what terms VAs should be acquired or disposed of; the assessment turns on substance, not labels like 'educational content' or 'trading signals'.

Mirror/copy trading that provides trading signals for others to replicate constitutes VA advisory; if execution is also provided, that constitutes VA dealing, and if trades are executed on a discretionary basis, that also involves VA management.
para 8, p.5

Technology tools (algorithms, AI language models) that generate specific VA recommendations for others' use amount to VA advisory services; tools that merely filter factual information for self-directed research do not.
para 9-10, p.5

Advice on a client's portfolio comprising both VAs and securities is not treated as 'wholly incidental' to RA4 (securities advisory) -- VA advice requires a separate VA advisory licence even when given concurrently with securities advice.
para 21, p.7-8

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes, citing concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs.
para 18, p.6-7
No de minimis threshold will apply to VA management -- any entity managing a portfolio with any VA exposure needs a licence or registration, mirroring the VA dealing/custodian regimes' approach.
Where a VA management licensee deals in VAs purely to support its VA management work (for example, turning subscribed VAs into cash before investing), it will not also need a VA dealing licence.
para 38, p.11

SFC-licensed or registered intermediaries dealing in 'Relevant Stablecoins' (specified stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers) will be exempt from needing separate VA service provider licences for those SFO activities.
para 39, p.11

Private funds retain flexibility to appoint qualified VA custodians globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for VAs held by the funds, mirroring existing RA9 treatment; however, the SFC intends to impose strict conditions where a VA management service provider holds client tokens itself because no qualified custodian exists for them.

Financial resources requirements for VA advisory and VA management providers mirror RA4/RA9: HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital; dual RA4/RA9-and-VA licensees are not subject to double capital requirements but must meet the highest applicable requirement.

There will be no deeming or grandfathering for firms already providing VA advisory or VA management services; both new regimes become fully effective on the statute's commencement date, though the timing of commencement will factor in transition needs.

The VA Dealing, VA Advisory and VA Management Regimes will run as standalone regimes under the AMLO, taking over from today's approach of attaching terms and conditions to SFO licences for intermediaries under the Joint Circular; those existing requirements will become the regimes' baseline.
rg: Read Section A (VA Advisory scope, p.4-8) and Section C (VA Management scope, p.9-12) for the definitional boundaries, then the custody discussion under Question 7 (para 53-57, p.13-14) and the transitional/other-comments sections (p.15-18); skip the Annex list of respondents (p.19-20).

t: FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset advisory and management regimes
sl: FSTB · FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset advisory… (2026)
s: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB), together with the SFC, issued their conclusions on the plan to license providers of virtual asset (VA) advisory and VA management services, after getting broad support across 51 responses. Following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, the new regimes will be aligned respectively with Type 4, which covers advising on securities, and Type 9, which covers asset management, regulated activities under the SFO. The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO, aiming to bring a bill to the Legislative Council (LegCo) in 2026. Together with the already-concluded VA dealing and custodian regimes, this completes the planned set of new VA intermediary licences envisioned in the FSTB's Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025), covering VA trading platforms, stablecoin issuers, dealing, custody, advisory, and management.
w: This confirms the scope (matching Type 4 and Type 9 rules) of the coming VA advisory and management licensing regimes, headed for a 2026 bill. The bank's licensed representative (RI) arm should track this and think about talking to the SFC early if it advises on or manages VA portfolios.
k: 51 responses came in from a wide range of stakeholders on the further consultation for the VA advisory and management regimes, with broad market support.
Note 2, p.1

The VA advisory regime will align with Type 4 (advising on securities), and the VA management regime with Type 9 (asset management) -- both regulated-activity categories under the SFO -- following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.
para 2, p.1
The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO (Cap. 615) for these new regimes, aiming to bring a bill to LegCo in 2026.
para 3, p.1

This wraps up the fourth and final piece of a set of new VA intermediary regimes (dealing, custody, advisory, management), which together with the existing VATP and stablecoin issuer licences are meant to cover the key parts of Hong Kong's digital asset ecosystem under Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025).
paras 4-5, p.1
Firms already offering, or planning to offer, VA advisory and management services are strongly urged to start talking with the SFC well before they apply.
para 6, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full for the policy conclusion; the detailed consultation conclusions paper (with the Annex list of 51 respondents) is referenced but not included in this document.

t: FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals for regulating virtual asset advisory and management services
sl: FSTB/SFC · FSTB and SFC publish consultation conclusions on legislative proposals… (2026)
s: FSTB and the SFC published the conclusions of the one-month consultation on licensing regimes for virtual asset (VA) advisory and VA management service providers, modelled respectively on the Type 4 and Type 9 regimes under the Securities and Futures Ordinance. Of 51 submissions, most supported the proposals. Officials frame this as completing the legal-framework coverage across the full digital-asset value chain — trading platforms, stablecoin issuers, and the now-finalised dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes — with a single bill targeted for the Legislative Council within the year. The operative detail is in the companion consultation-conclusions paper, summarised separately.
w: This confirms the government is now finalising all four new VA intermediary licensing tracks together in one bill, so a bank offering or planning to offer VA advice or discretionary VA management should treat this timeline as the point to firm up its licensing strategy.
k: 51 submissions were received on the further consultation covering VA advisory and VA management services, most supporting the proposed regimes.
para 2 (main text)
The VA advisory regime will track the scope of Type 4 (advising on securities) and the VA management regime will track Type 9 (asset management) under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
para 3 (main text)

Officials describe the dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes together as completing coverage of the key nodes of Hong Kong's digital-asset ecosystem, alongside the existing VATP and stablecoin issuer licensing regimes.
para 4 (main text)
A single bill covering the VA dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes is targeted for introduction into the Legislative Council within the year.
para 5 (main text)
rg: Read this press release for headline dates; the companion consultation-conclusions paper (registry id 01c5c5c4045f) has the operative scope and requirements detail.

t: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026
sl: LegCo · Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common… (2026)
s: This bill amends the Inland Revenue Ordinance to insert a new Part 8B creating Hong Kong's CARF reporting regime and to update the Common Reporting Standard rules. It defines Hong Kong Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (HKRCASPs), sets nexus, due-diligence, registration and reporting duties, and creates new offences and penalties, including a financial-penalty alternative to prosecution.
w: This is the actual legal text underlying the IRD's CARF summary; compliance should use it (not just the webpage) to confirm exact offence thresholds, the 'reasonable excuse' defence, and that outsourcing to a service provider does not remove the bank's own liability.
k: Part 2 of the Ordinance (the CARF rules) starts on 1 January 2027; Part 3 (amended CRS) starts on 1 January 2028; the rest starts on gazettal.
A new Part 8B (sections 50M-50Y) sets out interpretation, nexus rules, registration duty, due diligence, and reporting duties for HKRCASPs.
Clause 3, Part 8B, p.C192 onward
An HKRCASP that fails to register, carry out due diligence, or file a return without reasonable excuse commits an offence punishable by a fine at Level 3.
New s.80R(1) and (3), p.C325
For registration, reporting, and certain notice failures, a continuing daily fine of $500 applies after conviction for each day the offence continues.
For a due-diligence breach, the court can instead fine $1,000 multiplied by the number of affected crypto-asset users and controlling persons, if that is higher than the standard fine.
A person who knowingly or recklessly gives a misleading, false or incorrect self-certification commits a separate offence with a Level 3 fine.
New s.80(2ZD)-(2ZE), p.C325
An administrative financial-penalty mechanism is created as an alternative to prosecution, with a right to make written representations and to appeal to the Board of Review.
New ss.82E-82F, p.C351-C359
Engaging a third-party service provider to carry out CARF duties does not by itself excuse an HKRCASP from an offence for failing to register, do due diligence, or report.
rg: Read Clause 1 (commencement) and new sections 50M, 50O-50R (duties) and 80R-82F (offences/penalties); skip the bilingual formatting and page-number front matter.

t: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026 to be gazetted
sl: FSTB · Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common… (2026)
s: The government announced that a bill implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and the updated Common Reporting Standard (CRS) would be gazetted 22 May 2026 and tabled for first reading in the Legislative Council on 3 June. CARF requires crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus to register with the Inland Revenue Department and comply with due diligence, filing and record-keeping duties, taking effect the year after passage. Sharing tax data automatically on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions, alongside the amended CRS, are both targeted to start in 2028.
w: Once enacted, this will impose direct crypto-asset tax-reporting registration and due-diligence duties on the bank wherever it, or an affiliate, qualifies as a crypto-asset service provider with a Hong Kong nexus, so compliance should start scoping which of the bank's digital-asset activities will trigger CARF registration ahead of the 2027 effective date.
k: The bill was to be gazetted on 22 May 2026 and introduced to the Legislative Council for first reading on 3 June 2026.
para 1 (main text)

CARF will be implemented the year following the bill (i.e. from 2027); crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus must register with the Inland Revenue Department and meet due diligence, return-filing and record-keeping duties.
para 4 (main text)

Hong Kong aims to start swapping tax data on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions automatically, and to roll out the amended Common Reporting Standard, both from 2028, depending on those jurisdictions' own readiness.
para 4 (main text)

A public consultation ran from December of the prior year to February of the Budget year, and stakeholders including the financial and crypto-asset sectors generally supported the proposals; their feedback informed the bill's drafting.
para 5 (main text)
The Inland Revenue Department will issue guidance and provide technical support to help industry adapt to the new requirements.
para 6 (main text)

t: Annex: Proposed Amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L)
sl: HKMA · Annex: Proposed Amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules (2026)
s: This annex sets out illustrative drafting for proposed BCR amendments. Most items concern CET1 capital-base deductions and Basel technical updates with no VA link. The stablecoin/crypto-relevant items would: define a new BCR category of 'other regulated financial institution' covering entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers; generally exclude such subsidiaries from an AI's consolidated capital-ratio calculation (subject to HKMA override); confirm that carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity counts as an activity ancillary to banking; add specific default-risk-exposure rules for hedged 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts'; and remove cryptoassets from the BCR's list of assets treated as low-risk 'cash items'.
w: If enacted, clarifies how the bank must capital-treat any stablecoin-issuer subsidiary (deduction rather than consolidation, generally) and confirms cryptoassets get no 'cash item' capital relief, plus specific rules for hedged crypto-derivative counterparty exposure.
k: A new BCR term, 'other regulated financial institution', would be created to cover licensed entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers, distinct from banks, insurers and securities firms.
Item 5, p.9

An AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary would generally be left out of the AI's consolidated capital-adequacy-ratio calculation, unless HKMA decides on reasonable grounds it is prudent to include it.

In deciding whether to include such a subsidiary in consolidation, HKMA may weigh the subsidiary's business/activities, its size and financial significance to the AI, the risks it poses to the AI, and any other relevant factor.

The BCR's 'financial sector entity' definition would be clarified to expressly cover activities ancillary to banking listed in the Banking Ordinance's Fourteenth Schedule; the drafters confirm carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity falls within this.
Item 7, p.11

Where an AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary has a capital shortfall it fails to fix in time, HKMA could require that shortfall to be deducted from the AI's own CET1 capital.
Item 8, p.12

A new rule would set out how to calculate default-risk exposure on 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts' when an AI hedges the counterparty credit risk with a guarantee or credit derivative, mirroring the general hedging-recognition mechanics proposed elsewhere in the annex.
Cryptoassets would be removed from the definition of 'cash item' in Part 6 of the BCR, meaning they can no longer be treated as a low-risk cash-equivalent exposure for capital purposes.
rg: Skip the general CET1/ECAI/technical-amendment items; read Items 5-9 (stablecoin-issuer subsidiary capital treatment, p.9-12), Item 19 (crypto derivative hedging, p.28-29) and Item 45 (cash-item definition, p.50-51).

t: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (2026)
s: This SFC circular (revised 20 April 2026) sets the rules for turning SFC-authorised investment products -- authorised under Part IV of the SFO for public sale in Hong Kong -- into tokenised form. Using a 'see-through' approach, SFC allows primary dealing (buying and selling units) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised products, as long as the underlying product still meets every authorisation rule, plus extra safeguards for tokenisation-specific risks: record-keeping, cybersecurity, avoiding open public blockchains, smart-contract integrity, disclosure, distributor regulation, and staff competence. Secondary trading of these tokenised products on SFC-licensed VATPs is allowed separately, under a companion circular. New tokenised products, or big changes to how tokenisation works, need SFC consultation and approval first.
w: This rule applies to the fund or product-provider entity, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution. But if the bank distributes or structures tokenised SFC-authorised products through its licensed corporation or fund arm, a compliance head must make sure smart-contract audits, staff competence, and blockchain controls are all in place, and that SFC has been consulted beforehand.
k: The SFC will permit subscription and redemption (primary dealing) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised investment products, provided the underlying product satisfies all standard authorisation rules along with extra safeguards specific to tokenisation.
para 5, p.1

Trading tokenised SFC-authorised investment products in the secondary market on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform is permitted too, provided rules on fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity, and disclosure are met, as detailed in the companion 'Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products.'
para 6, p.1
Product Providers stay fully responsible for running the tokenisation arrangement soundly and for keeping ownership records, even if parts of the work are outsourced.
para 10, p.2
Tokenised SFC-authorised investment products are not expected to be issued as bearer instruments.
para 11 and footnote 2, p.2
Product Providers should avoid open, permissionless public blockchain networks unless extra controls -- such as a permissioned token -- are added.
para 13, p.2

If SFC asks, Product Providers must show their operations are sound, get independent audit or verification of the tokenisation setup and smart-contract integrity, and obtain a satisfactory legal opinion to back their application.
paras 14-16, p.2

Offering documents must clearly explain the tokenisation setup -- including whether settlement is final off-chain or on-chain -- how tokens represent ownership, and the risks involved (cybersecurity, system outages, undiscovered technical flaws, and a changing regulatory landscape).
para 17, p.3

Anyone distributing tokenised products, including a Product Provider selling its own products, must be a regulated intermediary (an SFC-licensed corporation or registered institution) following existing conduct, onboarding, and suitability rules.
para 18, p.3
Product Providers must confirm at least one staff member has the relevant experience to run or oversee the tokenisation setup and manage the new ownership and technology risks.
para 19, p.3
New tokenised products need SFC consultation before authorisation; tokenising an existing product, or making a major change to how tokenisation works, may also need prior approval.
paras 20-21, p.3
rg: Read Section A (background, paras 2-7) for context, then Section B (paras 8-19) in full as the binding requirements; Section C (paras 20-22) covers the prior consultation/approval process. The document shows 'Amended' markers indicating this is a revised version.

t: Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products (2026)
s: This SFC circular lays out the conditions for permitting public secondary trading, on SFC-licensed VATPs, of Tokenised Products — tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, mainly open-ended funds. It should be read together with the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products and the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities. It covers on-platform trading rules, fair-pricing controls including a mandatory Price Deviation Alert measured against indicative net asset value (NAV), liquidity requirements (at least one market maker, with 3 months' notice before ending that role, and appointed SFC-licensed distributors), detailed disclosure duties in offering documents and Key Facts Statements (KFS), and prior SFC consultation or approval for new or existing tokenised products and for major changes to trading arrangements.
w: This directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution if it sells tokenised SFC-authorised funds or connects clients to secondary trading of them on VATPs. It creates Price Deviation Alert, risk-disclosure, and advance-notification duties to both SFC and, at the same time, HKMA.
k: Secondary trading of Tokenised Products can be offered to retail investors through on-platform, on-screen auto-matching trading on SFC-licensed VATPs, following the existing VATP Guidelines' trading rules and risk controls.
paras 8-9, p.2

SFC-licensed VATPs must run a Price Deviation Alert that warns investors when the trade price would move significantly away from the product's real-time or near real-time indicative NAV, plus controls such as trading bands and cooling-off periods to guard against sharp price swings and manipulation.
para 12, p.2
Product Providers should make their best effort to line up at least one market maker per Tokenised Product, and give at least 3 months' notice before ending that arrangement.
para 15(a), p.3

Distributors appointed for Tokenised Products need to hold SFC licences (as corporations or registered institutions), and normally take care of creation and redemption requests coming from third-party investors.
para 15(c), p.3

Offering documents, including the Key Facts Statement, must clearly disclose the risks of secondary trading -- liquidity, price deviation, price differences across trading channels, and reliance on the market maker -- along with how the trading channel works, market-making arrangements and incentives, and any conflicts of interest if a market maker is an affiliated entity.
para 19, p.4-5

SFC-licensed VATPs and Connecting Brokers must maintain online tools that display real-time or near-real-time indicative NAV, refreshed no less often than every 15 seconds while trading is underway, together with the last NAV, and must obtain client confirmation of understanding the risks before allowing secondary-market trades.
para 20(b)-(c), p.5

Product Providers must immediately tell SFC and investors if dealing in a Tokenised Product stops or is suspended, or if market-making activity stops, is disrupted, or is suspended -- including an assessment of the impact and a plan to fix or manage the situation.
para 22, p.5

New tokenised products need prior SFC consultation before authorisation; adding tokenisation or secondary-trading features to an existing SFC-authorised product needs both prior consultation and approval.
paras 23-24, p.5
Registered institutions doing secondary trading of Tokenised Products must also notify HKMA, following the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities.
footnote 13, p.6
rg: Read Section A (background, paras 1-6, p.1) then Section B in full (paras 7-22, p.2-6) as the operative requirements; Section C (paras 23-28, p.5-6) covers the prior consultation process, important for registered institutions needing dual SFC/HKMA notification.

t: SFC unveils new regulatory framework to allow secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · SFC unveils new regulatory framework to allow secondary trading… (2026)
s: SFC rolled out a fresh set of rules, in a same-day circular, to pilot secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised funds (mainly open-ended funds) on SFC-licensed VATPs, with over-the-counter deals looked at case by case. It builds on the tokenisation framework SFC first put in place through two circulars dated 2 November 2023. By March 2026, Hong Kong had 13 such tokenised products on the market, and their combined tokenised-class assets under management (AUM) had grown roughly seven times over within a year, reaching $10.7 billion. The plan is to let trading run around the clock, beyond normal market hours, potentially helped along by licensed stablecoins and tokenised deposits. The first products under the scheme are likely to be tokenised money-market funds.
w: This sets out a framework for VATPs and fund issuers, not a direct bank obligation, but a compliance head should track it as it shapes how the bank's tokenised fund products could achieve round-the-clock secondary trading through regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits.
k: SFC first put its tokenisation framework in place via two circulars dated 2 November 2023: the 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' and the 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities.'
Note 1, p.1

para 4, p.1

para 5 and Note 2, p.1
Trading mainly happens on SFC-licensed VATPs under this scheme, though SFC may also weigh up over-the-counter secondary-trading setups on an individual basis.
para 2, p.1
New safeguards cover fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity, and disclosure, drawing on lessons from exchange-traded fund (ETF) trading and SFC-licensed VATP systems.
para 5, p.1
The first products likely to launch under this scheme are tokenised money-market funds; SFC plans to review how things go before widening the range of products covered.

t: Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026 (English only) (with photos/video)
sl: Government · Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026… (2026)
s: The Financial Secretary set out Hong Kong's policy approach to the convergence of Web3, tokenisation and AI, reaffirming 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' and a dual regulatory mandate of prudent oversight plus market facilitation. He confirmed that two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier that month, described more than US$2 billion in tokenised green and infrastructure bonds issued to date with issuance now regularised, and referenced EnsembleTX (launched the previous November) which lets participants put tokenised deposits to work in money-market-fund dealings and treasury management. He flagged three cross-cutting risks from AI-driven Web3 activity — settlement speed keeping pace with machine-speed transactions, maintaining human control over autonomous AI agents, and keeping regulation and accountability current — and announced a new Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy that will cover the Web3/AI intersection.
w: This is a useful confirmation that only two stablecoin issuer licences existed as of the speech date, and it flags coming AI-governance expectations (predictability, traceability, human override) that compliance should anticipate extending to any AI-agent-driven digital-asset activity the bank builds or relies on.
k: Two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier in the month the speech was given (April 2026).

t: Robust development of the regulated stablecoin ecosystem in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Robust development of the regulated stablecoin ecosystem in Hong… (2026)
s: HKMA announced its first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance: Anchorpoint Financial Limited — jointly owned by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands — and HSBC. Both will initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement and other programmable use cases. HKMA received 36 first-batch applications by the 30 September 2025 deadline and assessed them mainly on risk-management capability and viable use cases. Licensees must complete technology and risk-management preparatory work before launch, expected mid-to-second-half of 2026, and will face ongoing on-site/off-site supervision. HKMA signalled the overall number of licences will remain very limited given high licensing thresholds.
w: This is the first concrete market outcome of the Stablecoins Ordinance and directly names one bank counterparty (HSBC) now licensed to issue regulated stablecoins; relevant for counterparty due diligence on any regulated-stablecoin product, payments partnership, or as a competitive-landscape reference given the very limited number of licences signalled.
k: HKMA granted the first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance to Anchorpoint Financial Limited -- owned jointly by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands -- and The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC).
para 1

HKMA received 36 applications in the first batch by the 30 September 2025 deadline, assessed chiefly on (1) applicants' risk-management capability/compliance commitment and (2) ability to propose distinct, viable use cases.
para 3-4

Both licensees plan to initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement, and other programmable use cases such as conditional payments and supply chain financing.
'Use cases and strategic priorities' section

Licensed issuers must implement robust risk-management measures covering fiat reserve asset safekeeping, price stabilisation, redemption arrangements and technology risk mitigation, plus AML controls including blockchain analytics tools and holder identity verification (directly or via reliable third parties).
'Risk management measures' section

Prior to launch, licensees must complete preparatory work including technology platform/systems testing and implementation of risk-management measures and HR arrangements; regulated stablecoins are expected to launch in mid-to-second-half of 2026.
'Follow-up work' section
Once the regulated stablecoins launch, HKMA plans continuous oversight -- a mix of site visits, remote reviews, independent assessments, and direct contact with licensees' senior leadership.

t: LCQ18: Development of digital Renminbi and stablecoins
sl: FSTB · LCQ18: Development of digital Renminbi and stablecoins (2026)
s: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Financial Secretary's Bureau gave an update on the cross-boundary e-CNY (digital Renminbi) pilot with the People's Bank of China: e-CNY wallet issuance by Mainland institutions has grown to five, 18 local banks now support top-ups via the Faster Payment System, roughly 80,000 wallets were registered as of end-January 2026, and around 5,200 local merchants now accept e-CNY. k: By the close of January 2026, roughly 80,000 e-CNY wallets tied to Hong Kong mobile numbers had been set up in total, per PBoC data.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 11-13 February 2026

s: This SFC circular relays the FATF's February 2026 statements identifying DPRK and Iran as jurisdictions subject to a call for countermeasures, and Myanmar as subject to enhanced due diligence (with countermeasures to be considered if no progress by June 2026); the updated list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea. It also flags three FATF Plenary (11-13 February 2026) outputs of particular relevance to VA-related firms: a paper on cyber-enabled fraud (published 24 February 2026), a report on offshore virtual asset service provider risks (published 11 March 2026), and a targeted report on stablecoins and unhosted wallets illicit-finance risks (published 3 March 2026).
w: The stablecoin/unhosted-wallet and offshore VASP FATF reports flagged here are directly relevant to a bank's stablecoin and VA AML risk assessments and travel-rule/unhosted-wallet controls, and the DPRK/Iran call-for-action list must feed sanctions screening for VA transactions specifically.
k: FATF reiterates calls for countermeasures against DPRK given continued AML/CFT deficiencies and proliferation financing risks linked to increased DPRK connectivity with the international financial system
FATF calls for effective countermeasures against Iran, citing non-compliant ratification of the Palermo and TF Conventions and continuing failure to address its action plan since 2016

Myanmar remains subject to a FATF call for enhanced due diligence proportionate to risk; the FATF says it will weigh countermeasures should this situation still lack meaningful improvement come June 2026.
The FATF's updated list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea

Among FATF's listed countermeasures, one option is capping or cutting off dealings and money movements -- including in virtual assets -- with persons or entities tied to the flagged jurisdiction, applied according to risk.
footnote 4, p.2

FATF approved publication of a targeted report (3 March 2026) on stablecoins and unhosted wallets, highlighting illicit finance risks from criminals' misuse of stablecoins via peer-to-peer transactions through unhosted wallets, with recommended controls
para (c), p.3

FATF approved publication of a report (11 March 2026) on understanding and mitigating risks of offshore virtual asset service providers, examining how regulatory/supervisory gaps are exploited by criminals

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future”
sl: HKMA · Opening Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future” (2026)
s: Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's opening remarks (event held 9 March 2026) frame DLT's transformative effect on bank liquidity through three concepts -- 'novel', 'smart' and 'trusted' liquidity -- and position banks as trusted intermediaries bridging traditional and digital finance. The speech announces that HKMA is issuing, the same day, a circular that asks banks to review their business models strategically in light of digital transformation (see the separate registry entry for that circular, id 3ec5b269b5dc).
w: Directly previews the HKMA circular (see 3ec5b269b5dc) requiring the bank's board to endorse a formal digital-transformation strategic business plan within six months, and frames the regulator's rationale for expecting banks to act as trusted intermediaries in tokenisation.
k: DLT is described as unlocking three new forms of liquidity: 'Novel Liquidity' (tokenising previously illiquid assets like corporate loans, carbon credits and IP), 'Smart Liquidity' (smart-contract automation compressing settlement time), and 'Trusted Liquidity' (banks as trusted intermediaries verifying underlying assets and smart contract integrity).
paras on Novel/Smart/Trusted Liquidity, p.1

The same day, HKMA is issuing a circular that calls on banks to strategically review their business models in response to digital transformation, covering product offerings, revenue models, customer engagement, risk management frameworks and operational processes.
'Call for Action' paragraph, p.1
The strategic review is meant to steer how banks navigate the next five years as DLT, AI, cloud and high-performance computing reshape business models.
'Call for Action' paragraph, p.1
rg: Read in full (short); the circular referenced (footnote 3) is the operative document and is separately registered (id 3ec5b269b5dc).

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Welcoming Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future”

From 2026, HKMA plans to onboard more banks, add use cases and enhance EnsembleTX. The speech calls on banks to take proactive steps to capture tokenisation opportunities.

EnsembleTX entered its pilot phase in November 2025, enabling market participants to conduct real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets for liquidity and investment management.

para 7, p.1

para 8, p.1

t: Strategic Review of Business Models amid Digital Transformation
sl: HKMA · Strategic Review of Business Models amid Digital Transformation (2026)
s: This HKMA circular (reference B1/15C, dated 9 March 2026, signed by Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen) tells banks to actively rethink their long-term business models in light of digitalisation, distributed ledger technology (DLT), agentic artificial intelligence (AI), and cloud or high-performance computing. It refers to the HKMA's Fintech Promotion Blueprint under 'Fintech 2030.' It asks each bank's board to oversee and approve a formal strategic business plan covering these changes within six months of the circular, optionally using the Supervisory Incubator for DLT to test new business models, and confirms banks must still discuss any new digital-asset activity with the HKMA before launching it.
w: This creates a specific, dated board-level task — a strategic plan covering DLT and digital transformation, due within six months — and restates the standing rule that any new digital-asset activity must be discussed with the HKMA first. Compliance needs to track and calendar both.
k: Digitalisation, especially the spread of distributed ledger technology (DLT), is reshaping customer expectations and the financial landscape, a shift the HKMA says agentic AI, cloud computing, and high-performance computing are speeding up.
letter body, para 2

The HKMA expects each Authorized Institution's Board of Directors to oversee and approve, within six months of the circular's date, a formal strategic business plan covering these technology shifts, spanning products, revenue models, customer engagement, risk management, and operations where relevant.
letter body, para 4
As part of that plan, a bank may choose to run small, real-world trials through the HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT to test new business models.
letter body, para 4
Some Authorized Institutions will be asked to submit their strategic business plans through the HKMA's Survey Tool.
letter body, para 4
As is already the practice, banks entering new digital-asset activities are still expected to talk through their plans with the HKMA before launching.
letter body, para 5
rg: Read the full two-page letter; it is short and entirely about the strategic business-plan expectation and DLT-related digital transformation.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain sign MOU to strengthen Shanghai-Hong Kong co-operation in digitised cargo trade and finance (with photo)

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain sign MoU to strengthen Shanghai-Hong Kong cooperation in digitised cargo trade and finance
sl: HKMA · Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Shanghai Data Bureau, and National… (2026)
s: HKMA, together with two Mainland partners -- the Shanghai Data Bureau (SDB) and NTICBC (the National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain) -- signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) aimed at deepening Shanghai-Hong Kong ties in digitised cargo trade and finance. Under the deal, the three sides will jointly look into digital-technology uses, weigh up building a cross-border platform, and, through that platform, open up cross-border financial cooperation while separately looking at electronic bills of lading (eBL) under Project Ensemble. They will also study how trade finance could move faster using cargo and trade data, linking to the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI) on one side and Cargo X on the other.

t: The 2026-27 Budget — Speech by the Financial Secretary
sl: Government · The 2026-27 Budget — Speech by the Financial Secretary (2026)
s: In the digital-asset section of the 2026-27 Budget Speech, the Financial Secretary confirmed plans to introduce a bill in 2026 licensing digital asset dealing and custodian service providers, and noted the first batch of stablecoin issuer licences would be issued the following month. The SFC will look to widen liquidity and product access for professional investors and set up an accelerator for market innovation. Separately, an Inland Revenue amendment bill will implement the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the amended Common Reporting Standard within two years. The HKMA's CMU OmniClear will launch a digital asset platform in 2026 to support digital bond issuance and settlement, alongside continued rollout of Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit pilot (EnsembleTX).
w: The speech confirms government-level timelines the bank should track against its own build plans: the dealing/custodian licensing bill, first stablecoin-issuer licences, and the CARF tax-reporting bill all land or advance in 2026, and CMU OmniClear's new digital asset platform signals where institutional tokenised-bond settlement infrastructure is heading.
k: A bill to establish licensing regimes for digital asset dealing and custodian service providers will be introduced in 2026.
para 104
The first batch of stablecoin issuer licences (under the existing licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin issuers) was due to be issued the month after the speech.
para 105

The SFC intends to broaden digital-asset market liquidity and product/service offerings for professional investors, subject to sufficient investor protection, and will set up an accelerator to speed up market innovation.
para 106
Government will issue guidelines clarifying that debenture-holder registers may be kept as a distributed ledger, to support tokenisation of bond issuance and trading.
para 107

The Government plans to bring a bill amending the Inland Revenue Ordinance to adopt the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the OECD's updated Common Reporting Standard sometime in the year's first six months, with the two-year rollout starting after that.
para 108

Project Ensemble's pilot phase, EnsembleTX (launched the previous November), lets industry participants transact in tokenised deposits and digital assets in a controlled pilot environment; the HKMA will keep upgrading it toward 24/7 settlement and cross-market interoperability standards.
para 109
