t: Public consultation on implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and amendments in relation to Common Reporting Standard launched
sl: FSTB · Public consultation on implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and… (2025)
s: The government launched a public consultation on implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and related amendments to the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) in Hong Kong, both to be enacted via changes to the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112). CARF, published by the OECD in 2023, lets partner jurisdictions automatically swap tax data on crypto-asset transactions with each other. The government plans to finish the local legislative amendments within the coming year, aiming to start CARF information exchange from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029. Proposed changes also include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and higher penalties, partly in response to an OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS framework. The consultation runs to 6 February 2026.
w: This is the launch notice for the CARF/CRS consultation (see the fuller consultation paper entry for detail); it flags the 2028 start date and the proposal for mandatory registration and higher penalties, both of which bear directly on any bank group entity that is a reporting financial institution for crypto-asset transactions.
k: The government will amend the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112) to implement the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the newly amended Common Reporting Standard.
para 4
The government targets completing the legislative amendments within the coming year, starting automatic exchange of crypto-asset tax information from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029.
para 5
Proposed amendments include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and increased penalty levels, partly to address an ongoing OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS administration.
para 6
The public consultation covers reporting procedures, record-keeping requirements, and penalties and enforcement, and closes for comments on 6 February 2026.
para 7
rg: Read paragraphs 4-7 for the substance; paragraphs 1-3 are OECD/CRS background that can be skimmed. Cross-refer to the full consultation paper (id 275d5cc93a88) for detail.

t: Implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amendments in Relation to Common Reporting Standard in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amendments in Relation… (2025)
s: This joint FSTB/Inland Revenue Department consultation paper sets out legislative proposals to bring the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and an amended Common Reporting Standard (CRS) into the Inland Revenue Ordinance. It defines who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what crypto-asset transactions must be reported, and what due diligence RCASPs must run on customers. It also proposes mandatory RCASP registration, record-keeping, enforcement powers, and a tiered penalty regime modelled on existing CRS sanctions. Separately, it proposes amending CRS itself so it also covers certain digital financial products (excluding CBDCs and specified electronic money products, which fall under CARF instead), and proposes strengthening CRS's own administrative framework (mandatory RFI registration, higher penalties) in response to an OECD peer review. It sets a phased implementation timeline running from 2027 through the first CARF information exchange in 2028 and first amended-CRS exchange in 2029, and invites comments by 6 February 2026.
w: If the bank or a group entity executes crypto-asset exchange transactions or operates a trading platform for customers, it will likely be an RCASP and face new mandatory registration, customer due diligence, and reporting duties from 2027, with real penalties for non-compliance; banks that are already CRS Reporting Financial Institutions must also plan for dual CARF/CRS reporting on the same crypto-asset disposals under the government's proposed default treatment.
k: A Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP) is any business executing crypto-asset exchange transactions or transfers for customers, or making available a trading platform (including certain decentralised platforms), and RCASPs will have to register, run customer due diligence and report transaction data to the Inland Revenue Department.

Crypto-assets that cannot be used for payment or investment, central bank digital currencies, and specified electronic money products fall outside CARF's reporting scope (though CBDCs and some e-money products fall under the amended CRS instead).
para 1.5, p.7

RCASPs must obtain customer self-certifications to determine tax residency, cross-checked against AML/KYC information; for existing customers, self-certifications must be obtained within twelve months of CARF taking effect in Hong Kong.
para 1.15 and footnote 18, p.13-14

All RCASPs with any nexus to Hong Kong must register on the IRD's CARF Portal, whether or not they have information to report, with registration proposed to run from September 2027 and be completed by end-December 2027 or end-January 2028 depending on when the nexus arose.
para 2.8 and Chapter 6 timeline, p.20 and p.48

RCASPs must keep due diligence and reporting records for at least six years, and must tell IRD within one month if the business is dissolved or terminated, with the obligation to preserve records falling on former directors if the RCASP is dissolved.

Proposed penalties for RCASP non-compliance range from a HK$10,000 fine for failing to register or file a return, up to a HK$100,000 fine plus three years' imprisonment on indictment for knowingly providing false information with intent to defraud; an administrative-penalty alternative to prosecution is also proposed.

Entities that are both RCASPs and Reporting Financial Institutions (RFIs) will, under the proposed default treatment, have to report the same crypto-asset sale/redemption proceeds under both CARF and the amended CRS, rather than being allowed to report only once.

The government proposes introducing mandatory registration and a stronger penalty regime for CRS-reporting financial institutions generally, in response to an OECD peer review finding gaps in how Hong Kong identifies reporting financial institutions and enforces the existing CRS regime.

Implementation is phased: RCASP due diligence starts January 2027, RCASP registration from September 2027, first CARF returns filed by RCASPs in June 2028, and first CARF information exchange with partner jurisdictions in September 2028; amended-CRS due diligence starts January 2028 with first exchange in September 2029.
Chapter 6 implementation table, p.44-45
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.1-4), Chapter 1 (RCASP scope, transactions, due diligence, p.5-21), the penalty and timeline sections of Chapter 2 (p.23-26) and Chapter 6's implementation table (p.44-45); Chapters 3 and 5's treaty/administrative detail and Annex C can be skimmed unless drafting a formal consultation response.

t: Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau: Fintech
sl: FSTB · Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau: Fintech (2025)
s: This is FSTB's standing overview webpage on fintech policy, last revised 5 December 2025, summarising ongoing initiatives across payments, AI, talent and cross-border cooperation, with a digital-asset section on Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX, mBridge, e-CNY, and a pointer to the October 2022 Policy Statement on the Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong. It states Hong Kong currently has 11 licensed virtual asset trading platforms, eight digital banks and four virtual insurers. It links two substantive documents as attachments: the October 2024 Policy Statement on Responsible Application of AI in the Financial Market, and the original October 2022 VA Policy Statement (see their separate entries).
w: Gives a current headline count of licensed VA trading platforms a bank's compliance team can use as a first checkpoint when counterparty due diligence starts, and confirms the 2022 VA Policy Statement remains the government's standing policy reference alongside the live EnsembleTX and mBridge initiatives.
k: As of this page's last revision, Hong Kong has 11 licensed virtual asset trading platforms, alongside eight digital banks and four virtual insurers.
Introduction section
Project Ensemble's real-value pilot phase, EnsembleTX, launched in November 2025 and will progressively extend to round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money.
Strengthening Connection and Cooperation section

The HKMA runs the Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency Bridge (mBridge) project with the Mainland, Thai, UAE and Saudi central banks/monetary authorities, and it reached Minimum Viable Product stage in June 2024.
Strengthening Connection and Cooperation section
The page still points to the Government's October 2022 Policy Statement on the Development of Virtual Assets as the standing statement of Hong Kong's VA policy approach.
Policy Statement on development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong section
rg: Read the Introduction (VA/digital bank/virtual insurer counts), the Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX and mBridge paragraphs, and the VA Policy Statement section; skip the AI, payments infrastructure and talent-scheme sections as unrelated to digital assets.

t: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework: Frequently Asked Questions (Last updated December 2025)
sl: Other · Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework: Frequently Asked Questions (2025)
s: This is the OECD's own FAQ on interpreting CARF, hosted by IRD as background reading rather than a Hong Kong-specific document. It clarifies edge cases such as branch nexus, retail payment reporting thresholds, staking/wrapped-token treatment, NFT exclusions, and how tokenised traditional financial assets are treated.
w: These OECD interpretive answers will likely shape how HK's own CARF rules are applied in practice, so compliance can use them to pressure-test edge cases (staking, tokenised securities, NFTs) even though the document itself is not a Hong Kong legal instrument.
k: A retail payment transfer above USD 50,000 made as agent for the customer must be reported as a separate 'Reportable Retail Payment Transaction' category.
Section II, Q1, p.2
Moving crypto into a staking contract and receiving a matching tokenised version back counts as a reportable exchange transaction.
Section IV, Q2, p.4-5

An NFT is excluded from reporting only if it does not represent a financial asset, is not marketed as an investment, is not an AML/KYC virtual asset under FATF rules, and has low value/trading volume (illustratively, under USD 200 and no meaningful trading).
Section IV, Q5, p.6

A tokenised traditional financial asset is NOT treated as a reportable crypto-asset if it can only be held or transferred through custodial accounts at regulated custodians, i.e. it is not truly disintermediated.
Section IV, Q6, p.6-7
rg: Skim Section headers only; read Section II Q1 (retail payments) and Section IV Q2, Q5, Q6 (staking, NFTs, tokenised assets) as the parts most relevant to a bank's product set.

t: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
sl: HKMA · CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (2025)
s: This statutory guideline sets out how the HKMA runs the Pillar 2 supervisory review process, including how it may adjust a bank's individual capital requirement above the regulatory minimum. Version 7 adds a dedicated paragraph on cryptoassets: because crypto activities and their risks are still new and evolving, the HKMA may respond to capital or risk-management shortcomings tied to crypto with capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other mitigation measures. Separately, the module's general Pillar 2 governance guidance now lists cryptoasset activity alongside securitisation as an example of a complex activity the board and senior management must understand as part of firm-wide risk oversight.
w: Compliance should flag that examiners can now raise Pillar 2 capital or impose activity limits specifically because of crypto risk-management gaps, so any internal audit or risk-management finding on crypto should be remediated before a supervisory review cycle.
k: Because crypto risks are new and still developing, the HKMA may use any of four supervisory tools where it sees capital or risk-management gaps tied to a bank's crypto activity: extra capital add-ons, requiring provisions for foreseeable and estimable crypto losses, imposing activity limits, or other mitigation measures.
para 3.6.6

The board and senior management should understand firm-wide risks from complex or new activities - crypto is now named alongside securitisation and 'originate-to-distribute' lending as an example - and should set firm-wide prudential limits consistent with the bank's risk appetite.
para 4.2.8
A dedicated SPM module, CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets, is now listed in this module's index of related modules under a new 'Cryptoassets' heading.
module index, 'Cryptoassets' heading
rg: Read para 3.6.6 (p.52-53) and para 4.2.8 (p.63) for the crypto-specific text; the rest of the module is the general Pillar 2/SRP framework and can be skimmed unless capital planning is in scope.

t: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
sl: HKMA · CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (2025)
s: CR-G-8 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.16(10) explaining how locally incorporated AIs apply the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) on single-counterparty, equity and land exposures. The crypto change is a new part of section 2.8: cryptoasset-related exposures are valued under a new Division 5A of BELR Part 7. Only crypto exposures that carry a counterparty's default risk count toward large exposure limits; pure holdings without counterparty risk are disregarded. The bank identifies counterparties as it already does for capital purposes, and valuation depends on the exposure type, its Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification and whether it sits in the banking or trading book. The rest of the module restates existing limits, board oversight and breach notification duties that apply equally to crypto-related counterparty exposures.
w: Exposures to crypto counterparties, such as a stablecoin issuer, custodian or derivative counterparty, now count toward the bank's large exposure limits under a dedicated valuation method. Compliance must make sure limit monitoring and breach notification cover these crypto-linked counterparties.
k: The module is a statutory guideline and applies to AIs incorporated in Hong Kong; overseas-incorporated AIs still report large exposures of their Hong Kong operation.
Cover (Classification; Application)
A large exposure is any exposure to one counterparty or linked group equal to or above 10% of Tier 1 capital.
para 1.1.5
The statutory ceiling on exposure to a single counterparty or linked group is 25% of Tier 1 capital; local global systemically important banks face a 15% cap toward other such groups.
Crypto-related exposures are valued under BELR Part 7 Division 5A, separately from ordinary exposures in Divisions 4 and 5.

For crypto exposures that carry counterparty default risk, the bank must first identify each counterparty or linked group, reusing the counterparty identification already done for capital, then value each under Division 5A.
para 2.8.9
Crypto exposures with no counterparty credit or default risk are ignored when measuring large exposures.
footnote 13 (Rule 48(1)(ba))
Which valuation rule applies depends on the exposure category in the Rule 2(1) definition, the asset's Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification, and banking versus trading book.
para 2.8.10 and footnote 14
Some crypto exposures borrow Division 5 methods (for example Group 1a banking book items); others reuse capital-rule figures for credit or default risk or jump-to-default amounts.
para 2.8.11 and footnotes 15-17
Because crypto markets change fast, the Monetary Authority may set a different valuation method for one or more AIs by written notice under BELR Rule 77A(2).
para 2.8.12
Any breach of statutory or HKMA-set limits should be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable, with an impact assessment and a rectification plan.
para 6.1.1
A notifiable breach must be reported in writing with details of the limit, timing, cause and remediation; suspected breaches should be flagged before the investigation ends.
Failing to meet a prescribed notification or remedial action requirement is an offence for the AI and its directors, chief executives and managers.
para 6.4.1
rg: Read paras 2.8.1 and 2.8.8-2.8.12 for the crypto valuation rules, then section 6 on breach notification. The rest restates the existing large exposure framework.

t: LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk
sl: HKMA · LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (2025)
s: LM-1 version 5 is a statutory guideline on applying the Banking (Liquidity) Rules (BLR), covering the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The crypto additions are section 5.9 and a new Annex 3. Crypto exposures generally follow the treatment of traditional exposures with equivalent economic risk, but Annex 3 sets specific rules. Only Group 1a tokenised versions of eligible assets can count as high-quality liquid assets (HQLA). Bank-issued tokenised claims can be treated as deposits, stablecoins are treated like non-HQLA debt securities, and Group 2 cryptoassets get the harshest treatment. The HKMA may impose stricter treatment for any cryptoasset with extra liquidity risk, and CBDCs are excluded.
w: If the bank issues tokenised deposits or a stablecoin, or holds either, Annex 3 sets how they hit the LCR and NSFR. The holder-identification test for tokenised deposits and the 100% outflow for issued stablecoins are the points most likely to affect product design and compliance sign-off.
k: Crypto exposures, whether assets, liabilities or contingent items, should generally be treated like traditional exposures with economically equivalent risk across LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR.
para 5.9.1
Annex 3 adds crypto-specific rules because of extra risks and thin historical data; CBDCs are outside Annex 3 and are generally treated like the issuing jurisdiction's notes and coins.

A cryptoasset can count as HQLA only if it is a Group 1a token of an eligible asset class, both the traditional and tokenised forms meet the HQLA criteria, and operational requirements are met, for example an established ledger and a deep market.
Annex 3, para 1 and footnote 95

An issuing bank may treat its tokenised claims (Group 1a, redeemable at par in fiat, backed by the bank's own balance sheet) as deposits or unsecured funding. If the bank cannot identify holders at all times, it must treat them as other unsecured wholesale funding, and they can never count as stable retail deposits.
Annex 3, para 4
Tokenised claims used mainly for payment within an operational relationship with wholesale customers follow the operational deposit treatment.
Annex 3, para 4 (fourth bullet)

A bank holding tokenised deposits issued by another AI or a regulated bank treats them like unsecured loans to financial institutions, with no inflow recognised if they cannot be redeemed within 30 days.
Annex 3, para 5
Stablecoins in this annex are Group 1b coins, plus fully collateralised Group 2 coins that fail only the redemption test because of notice periods or fixed terms.
Annex 3, para 6

A bank that issues a stablecoin redeemable within the LCR period must apply a 100% outflow rate, unless the backing assets would qualify as HQLA apart from encumbrance; the segregated backing assets count as encumbered under the NSFR.
Annex 3, para 7 (issuer bullets)

A bank holding a stablecoin treats it as non-HQLA debt: generally a 0% LCR inflow and an 85% NSFR required stable funding factor, falling to 50% if it matures within 12 months into fiat; issuer redemption options are assumed not exercised.
Annex 3, para 7 (holder bullets)
Group 1a tokens that are not HQLA follow their traditional equivalent, but any extra liquidity risk from the token form, such as delayed cash flows from the infrastructure, must be reflected.
Annex 3, para 8(a)

Other Group 2 cryptoassets held get a 100% NSFR required stable funding factor and no LCR inflow. Unsecured crypto borrowings due within the LCR period take a 100% outflow unless covered by the bank's own unencumbered stock, and crypto-denominated funding gets 0% available stable funding.
Annex 3, para 8(b)
The HKMA may impose stricter treatment where a cryptoasset carries extra liquidity or contingent risk, for example the need to support redemptions of a stablecoin the bank issues or services.
Annex 3, para 9 and footnotes 97-98
rg: Go straight to section 5.9 (p.67) and Annex 3 (pp.91-98). The rest of the module is the general liquidity framework and can be skipped for crypto purposes.

t: Code of Practice for the Purposes of Providing Guidance in Respect of the Provisions of Rules 20(4)(b), 37(2) and (3) and 41 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (Chapter 155S)
sl: HKMA · Code of Practice for the Purposes of Providing Guidance… (2025)
s: Known as the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code, this statutory code of practice interprets three specific rules under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules: how to judge whether a third-party data provider is 'competent and reliable' for valuing collective investment scheme exposures, what counts as a bank's self-use land, and when two counterparties are 'economically dependent' on each other for large-exposure grouping purposes. It took effect 1 January 2026. Despite being bundled into the November 2025 cryptoassets standard package, the code's own text contains no cryptoasset-specific rule; it appears to be a general large-exposures code amended and reissued alongside the crypto package rather than a crypto-specific instrument.
w: This code governs how the bank groups connected counterparties for its large-exposure limits generally; compliance should note it is not crypto-specific despite arriving in the crypto package, so it does not change how crypto counterparty exposures are treated beyond the ordinary economic-dependence tests.
k: To decide if a market data provider is competent and reliable for equity-exposure valuation under rule 20(4)(b), a bank should weigh the provider's market standing, financial strength, service capacity, track record, and contingency arrangements.
para 3(2)(a)-(e)

The code defines when one counterparty is 'economically dependent' on another for grouping purposes under rule 41, listing seven specific tests such as 50%+ of receipts coming from the other party or shared reliance on the same funding source.
para 6(4)(a)-(g)

A bank may rely in good faith on information a counterparty provides about its own economic dependence, as long as it does not conflict with information the bank otherwise holds, and should actively request this information during credit reviews and when granting new facilities.
para 6(2)

Where Entity A depends economically on Entity B, the bank has to fold Entity A into Entity B's linked-counterparty group; however, that does not automatically mean Entity B belongs in Entity A's group too, unless Entity B independently satisfies the grouping criteria.
para 6(5)
rg: Read paras 3 and 6 (pages 4-12) for the two live guidance items; para 5A on self-use land premises is a narrow, low-relevance point and paras 4, 5 and 7 are repealed and can be skipped.

t: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
sl: HKMA · CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (2025)
s: CR-L-5 version 3 is a statutory guideline explaining when a locally incorporated AI needs the Monetary Authority's prior written consent to buy share capital in a company worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital. The crypto change is a footnote: under BELR Rule 21(2), a cryptoasset that carries the economic substance of equity ownership counts as share capital for these rules. The module also covers exemptions (debt recovery, underwriting, insurance business, trading book below a threshold), application content, grounds for refusal, conditions, revocation and a one-month advance notice for other significant acquisitions.
w: A bank taking a stake in a digital asset business, or holding tokens that represent equity, may need prior HKMA consent at the 5% of Tier 1 level. A strategic crypto investment that changes the bank's business line may need a month's advance notice even below that level.
k: A locally incorporated AI should not acquire shares in a company worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital without the Monetary Authority's written consent; this also covers setting up a company.
para 1.1
Tokens that give the economic substance of equity ownership count as share capital for this consent regime.
para 2.1.3, footnote 1 (BELR Rule 21(2))
The 5% test uses book value at acquisition plus any unpaid amount, normally against the previous quarter-end Tier 1 figure.
Exemptions cover debt recovery, underwriting for up to seven working days, insurance business meeting set conditions, and trading book holdings whose assessment amount is below 5% of Tier 1.
para 2.2.1
The rule applies on a solo and consolidated basis, so acquisitions through a consolidated subsidiary also need consent.
para 2.3.1
AIs should approach the HKMA early and file a written notice with details such as value, capital impact, funding, business plan and the target's regulation.
para 2.5.1
Consent may be refused, conditioned or revoked if depositors' interests would be threatened; the AI gets a chance to make representations first.
AIs are expected to give at least one month's notice of other acquisitions with significant effect, such as entering a new line of business or cutting the capital ratio by around 0.5% or more.
rg: Read para 1.1, footnote 1 on page 3 and paras 2.5 and 2.9; the deemed-consent transition in 2.4 is historical.

t: Cryptoassets standard: SPM modules, code of practice, disclosure templates and tables, and banking returns
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard: SPM modules, code of practice, disclosure templates… (2025)
s: This circular is the HKMA's formal announcement that, after several rounds of industry consultation, it has finalised a package of capital, disclosure and reporting changes to implement Hong Kong's new cryptoasset prudential standard. It finalises a new SPM module (CRP-1, classification of cryptoassets) plus revisions to nine other SPM modules and a code of practice, all taking effect on 1 January 2026 alongside related Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) amendment rules. It also issues a revised disclosure package with a new crypto-specific disclosure part, and confirms new banking return templates. A six-month transitional easement lets banks with no cryptoasset exposure on 1 January 2026 keep using the old return templates until 30 June 2026.
w: This is the master document setting the effective date and transitional relief for the entire crypto capital/disclosure/reporting package; compliance needs it to plan the 1 January 2026 go-live and decide whether the bank qualifies for the six-month reporting transition.
k: Ten SPM modules/code items (listed (a) to (j)) were finalised and take effect on 1 January 2026, implementing three sets of Banking Ordinance amendment rules due to commence the same day.
p.1, 'SPM modules and code of practice'

Compared with the consultation draft, the HKMA further clarified how central bank digital currencies are treated for prudential purposes and eased the process for classifying tokenised traditional assets, both in module CRP-1.
p.2, bullet 1
The HKMA clarified that moving a position between books purely because of a cryptoasset reclassification is not treated as a book switch, so it does not trigger the usual capital surcharge in MR-1.
p.2, bullet 2
A revised standard disclosure package, including a new Part XII for cryptoasset exposures, takes effect for any reporting period ending after 1 January 2026.
p.2-3, 'Disclosure templates and tables'
Seven new or revised banking return templates, including capital adequacy, market risk/CVA, liquidity, leverage and large exposures returns, were scheduled for release in December 2025.
p.3, 'Banking returns' list (a)-(g)
Banks with no cryptoasset exposure as of 1 January 2026 may keep using the old return templates for six months, until 30 June 2026, for four of the listed returns.
p.3-4, transitional arrangement paragraph
Even banks using the transitional easement must still apply the revised completion instructions for unrelated miscellaneous changes in the capital adequacy ratio return from 1 January 2026.
p.3, footnote 4

A bank that gains cryptoasset exposure after 1 January 2026, or a transitional bank not yet ready to switch return formats, may agree a temporary alternative reporting arrangement with the HKMA covering the period 31 January to 30 June 2026.
p.4, first full paragraph
rg: Read the full four-page letter; it is short. Pay closest attention to the commencement date, the list of ten finalised modules, and the transitional-arrangement paragraphs on pages 3-4.

t: MR-1 Market Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · MR-1 Market Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-1 is the HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual module telling locally incorporated banks how to work out the capital charge for market risk. A new section 6, added for the cryptoassets standard, sets out how each of the four cryptoasset categories defined in module CRP-1 must be handled. Group 1a tokens (tokenised traditional assets) and Group 1b tokens (asset-referenced coins such as stablecoins) are mapped onto the risk factors of the asset they represent or reference, so they mostly ride on the existing framework. Group 2a tokens get their own separate risk bucket with no diversification benefit against other assets, and cannot use a bank's internal model. Group 2b tokens fall outside market-risk rules altogether and instead pick up the flat, punitive treatment set in the credit-risk rules.
w: This module tells compliance exactly how trading-book crypto and stablecoin positions must be classified and capitalised, and shows that most crypto trading exposures cost more capital than an equivalent traditional position because diversification and netting benefits are restricted or removed.
k: Before applying any market-risk method, a bank must first sort each crypto position into Group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b using module CRP-1.
para 6.1.1, footnote 79
A bank holding any cryptoasset exposure loses access to the small-portfolio (de-minimis) exemption from market-risk capital rules, even if the position is tiny.
para 6.1.1, footnote 80
For Group 1a tokens, hedging and netting against the underlying traditional asset is allowed provided both are mapped to the same risk category.
para 6.1.2
For Group 1b tokens (e.g. stablecoins), the credit risk that the redeemer or an intermediary fails to honour redemption is capitalised separately under the credit-risk rules, not under market risk.
Banks using the internal models approach cannot use it at all for Group 2a tokens; only the two standardised methods are allowed for that group.
para 6.1.9
For Group 2a tokens, positions in the same coin held on different exchanges cannot be netted against each other; long and short amounts must be kept separate.
para 6.2.6
The formula for a Group 2a token's net position only lets 65% of the smaller of the long/short side offset the larger side, so full netting is not available.
para 6.2.7
The capital charge for a Group 2a token's position risk is simply 100% of that net position, added up across all such tokens with no diversification credit.
Options on a Group 2a token must be valued with a scenario (matrix) method, moving the price and volatility by up to 100% each way; simpler option methods are banned for these tokens.
para 6.2.10

A footnote confirms that when a bank moves a position between the banking book and trading book purely because of a CRP-1 reclassification, this is not treated as a book-switch and does not trigger the usual capital surcharge for switching.
para 6.1.1, footnote 79, p.151; also para 2.1.15 with footnote 13, p.14
rg: Read section 6 (paragraphs 6.1-6.2, pages 151-160) in full; the earlier sections 1-5 are the general, non-crypto market-risk framework and can be skimmed unless a cross-reference sends you there.

t: MR-2 CVA Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · MR-2 CVA Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: MR-2 tells banks how to compute the capital charge for CVA risk, the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens before a trade settles. A new section 4 extends this to crypto derivatives and to securities-financing trades collateralised by cryptoassets. Group 1a and 1b tokens are broadly treated like the traditional asset they represent, though a bank must separately check the tokenised version for extra liquidity mismatch risk. Group 2a tokens can use most CVA methods except the advanced standardised approach. Group 2b tokens skip CVA calculation entirely and instead get the same flat, punitive capital charge used for their credit risk.
w: This module sets how much extra capital a bank's derivatives desk needs to hold against counterparty credit-spread risk on crypto trades, and flags that the harshest, 1,250% treatment applies automatically to the riskiest token category without any modelling option.
k: Derivatives and securities-financing trades on Group 1a tokens are generally capitalised the same way as trades on the underlying traditional asset.
para 4.2.1
A bank must assess the tokenised asset in its own right, not simply assume it qualifies for the same treatment as the traditional asset it copies, because liquidity can differ.
para 4.2.2

If a bank cannot get enough data to model the liquidity difference between a tokenised asset and its traditional counterpart, it must fall back to the simpler basic CVA approach rather than the standardised one.
para 4.2.2
Derivatives on Group 1b tokens (stablecoin-type instruments) follow the same CVA treatment as trades on non-tokenised assets.
para 4.2.3
For Group 2a tokens, every CVA method applies except the standardised CVA approach, which is off-limits for these instruments.
para 4.3.1
Group 2b token exposures do not get a separate CVA calculation; they instead carry the same conservative 1,250% risk weight used for their credit risk.
para 4.3.2
Securities-financing trades collateralised by Group 2b tokens only attract a CVA charge if the HKMA decides that CVA risk on those trades is material.
para 4.3.3
rg: Read section 4 (paragraphs 4.1-4.3, pages 44-46) in full; sections 1-3 cover the general, non-crypto CVA framework and can be skimmed for background only.

t: Annex 4: Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables
sl: HKMA · Annex 4: Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables (2025)
s: This is the full set of Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables that locally incorporated banks must use, updated to add a new Part XII covering cryptoasset exposures. Part XII adds Table CAEA (a narrative on the bank's crypto activities and risk approach), Template CAE1 (exposure amounts and risk-weighted assets by cryptoasset group), Template CAE2 (accounting classification of crypto holdings) and Template CAE3 (liquidity metrics for crypto exposures, for banks designated as category 1 institutions). Crypto exposures must also feed into the ordinary credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity templates elsewhere in the package, not only the dedicated crypto tables. Frequency ranges from annual (Table CAEA) to semi-annual (CAE1-3), and formats are mostly flexible rather than fixed.
w: These are the actual public disclosure formats the bank's Pillar 3 report team must build from Jan 2026 onward whenever the bank has any crypto exposure, so compliance needs to confirm finance/risk have mapped internal data to every CAE1-3 field and the CAEA narrative before the first reporting cycle.
k: Table CAEA requires an annual narrative naming the bank's crypto-related activities (holding crypto directly, trading for clients, equity stakes in crypto exchanges or fund managers, or issuing crypto liabilities), and whether the bank acts as a redemption intermediary.
Table CAEA, point (a)
The same narrative must cover how each crypto activity feeds into credit, market, operational and liquidity risk, the mitigation policies applied, and the most significant current and emerging risks.
Table CAEA, points (b),(d),(e)
For group 1 cryptoassets, the bank must explain, using public information only, how it assessed each of the four BCR classification conditions.
Table CAEA, point (f)

Template CAE1 breaks out total exposure, exposure at default, and risk-weighted assets separately for group 1a, 1b, 2a and 2b cryptoassets, split by credit risk and market risk columns, on a semi-annual basis.
Template CAE1, table and columns (a)-(f)

A bank must add extra rows for any individual stablecoin or unbacked cryptoasset that is 'material' under the template's own test - broadly, group 2 exposure ratio at or above 0.3% of the bank plus that single asset over 5% of all group 2 holdings.
Template CAE1, points to note (iii)(a)-(b)

Template CAE1 also captures how close a bank is to the group 2 (unbacked/algorithmic) cryptoasset concentration limits - it must show any exposure or RWA once the 1% of Tier 1 capital threshold is crossed, and total RWA once the 2% cap is breached.
Template CAE1, rows 6-10

The bank must separately state the total market value of client cryptoassets it holds in custody, broken down by tokenised traditional assets, stablecoins, and other crypto, as narrative accompanying CAE1.
Template CAE1, 'Accompanying narrative'

Template CAE2 shows how crypto holdings and crypto liabilities are booked on the balance sheet (cash, financial assets by measurement basis, intangibles) split again by the four crypto groups, on a semi-annual basis.
Template CAE2

Template CAE3, required semi-annually only from banks designated as category 1 liquidity institutions with crypto exposure, reports the liquidity-coverage-ratio haircuts, inflow/outflow rates and net-stable-funding factors applied to each crypto category.
Template CAE3

Group 1 and group 2 crypto exposures reported in the crypto-specific templates must also be folded into the bank's ordinary credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity disclosure templates elsewhere in the package, to avoid double-counting confusion.
Template CAE1, points to note (ii); Template CAE2, point to note (i)
rg: Read only Part XII (pages 210-219, [[page 210]]-[[page 219]] markers) plus the points-to-note; the rest of the 220-page document is unrelated Basel III disclosure templates and can be skipped.

t: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties
sl: HKMA · CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties (2025)
s: CR-G-9 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.7(3) on how locally incorporated AIs identify, limit and control exposures to connected parties under BELR Part 8. The text does not mention cryptoassets directly; it appears in the package because connected-party exposures are valued the same way as Part 7 large exposures, which now include the new crypto valuation rules. It sets the aggregate and single connected-party limits, arm's-length dealing, board oversight, independent monitoring and breach reporting.
w: If the bank's group holds crypto-related positions with an affiliate or a firm linked to its directors or controllers, those exposures fall under connected-party limits and arm's-length rules. The module itself adds no crypto-specific duty.
k: AIs should deal with connected parties at arm's length, and the same impartiality applies to non-lending dealings such as asset sales and service contracts.
Breaching a Rule 87 limit is a notifiable event; the AI must tell the Monetary Authority as soon as practicable after it knows or should know.
para 1.1.3
Connected parties include directors, credit approvers, controllers and their relatives, plus firms and unlisted companies in which they hold key roles.
para 2.1.1
The aggregate connected-party exposure ratio must not exceed 15% of Tier 1 capital; exposure to a single connected natural person is capped at the lower of HK$20 million or 5% of Tier 1.
Connected-party exposures are valued in the same way as Part 7 counterparty exposures, subject to Part 8 adjustments, and only the portion not covered by recognised credit risk mitigation counts.
para 2.3.1
The board should understand the legal limits, approve a connected-party policy and ensure systems exist to monitor and control these exposures.
A designated independent unit should monitor connected-party exposures, and internal audit should review them regularly.
Figures in the large exposures return, MA(BS)28, and the compliance certificate, MA(BS)1F(a), must be accurate, and limit breaches reported promptly.
rg: Read paras 2.2-2.3 for limits and valuation and 4.2 for reporting; the rest restates existing connected-lending controls.

t: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
sl: HKMA · CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets (2025)
s: CRP-1 is a new, non-statutory SPM guidance note (Version 1, dated 1 January 2026) that explains how AIs sort their cryptoasset exposures into prudential groups under the HKMA's implementation of the Basel cryptoasset standard. A cryptoasset reaches Group 1 only if it passes four classification conditions; Group 1a covers tokenised traditional assets and Group 1b covers stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism, while everything else falls into Group 2. Group 2 is split into Group 2a (limited hedge recognition, if three hedging recognition criteria are met) and Group 2b (no hedge recognition). The module sets extra safeguards for assets on permissionless blockchains, requires HKMA notification and agreement before any new cryptoasset can leave Group 2b, and lets the HKMA override a bank's classification. The Banking (Capital) Rules (BCR), Part 12, carry the legal requirements and prevail over the module in any conflict.
w: Every crypto or tokenised exposure the bank takes, including tokenised deposits, bonds, stablecoins and crypto ETFs, needs a documented classification, and any new asset type needs an HKMA notification and sits in punitive Group 2b until the HKMA agrees otherwise. Compliance should own the notification and evidence trail, because missing it means full-capital treatment and supervisory override.
k: CRP-1 is guidance, not statute: a new non-statutory guidance note that applies to every AI from 1 January 2026.
Cover page (Classification; Application)
The legal rules on classification conditions, initial approval and later reclassification sit in BCR Part 12. If CRP-1 and the BCR differ, the BCR wins.
para 1.1.4

A cryptoasset is a digital store of value that relies mainly on cryptography and distributed ledger technology (DLT) and can be used to pay, invest or access goods and services. Securities issued on DLT are in scope; securities on centrally run electronic registers are not.
Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) sit outside the standard and are generally treated like the fiat money of the issuing central bank.
para 1.2.3 and footnote 4
Group 1 requires all four classification conditions. Group 1a is tokenised traditional assets; Group 1b is stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism. Anything not in Group 1 is Group 2.

Group 1 assets get the same capital, liquidity and other treatment as the underlying traditional asset. The HKMA may add an infrastructure risk add-on, which starts at zero but can be raised if weaknesses are seen in the underlying technology.
para 1.3.2 and footnote 5

Group 2 covers all unbacked cryptoassets plus tokenised assets and stablecoins that fail the conditions, and attracts full capitalisation. Hedging recognition criteria split it into Group 2a (some hedging recognised) and Group 2b (none).
para 1.3.3
Look-through: funds such as Group 2b cryptoasset ETFs, entities whose value derives mainly from Group 2b assets, and equity, derivative or short positions in them are all treated as Group 2b.
para 1.3.3, footnote 6
The standard and CRP-1 took effect on 1 January 2026. Any cryptoasset exposure held before that date must sit in Group 2b until the HKMA agrees the bank's classification assessment.

Classification is a continuing duty. AIs must have policies, procedures, governance, staff and IT able to assess cryptoasset risk, and must fully document the evidence for each classification and give it to the HKMA on request.
para 2.1.1

Before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset, an AI must notify the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees any better classification. A first Bitcoin spot or derivative trade triggers notification; Bitcoin futures after existing spot exposure do not.
para 2.1.2 and footnote 7

If an agreed Group 1a, 1b or 2a asset stops meeting its conditions or criteria, the AI must drop it to Group 2b at once until it complies again. Later purchases take the last assessed classification, and moving back up from Group 2b needs HKMA agreement.
rg: Read sections 1.3-1.4 and 2.1 first (group structure, effective date, notification and reclassification process), then section 2.6 for permissionless chains and section 3 for Group 2a thresholds. Paragraphs 2.2.6-2.2.9 on reserve quality matter mainly when assessing a specific stablecoin.

t: Supporting Artificial Intelligence Adoption in AML/CFT

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Detection and prevention of potential layering activities in money laundering
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2025)
s: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities to an emerging pattern of layering activities in money laundering, characterised by frequent, swift fund/VA deposits and withdrawals with little or no trading. It sets out red flags drawn from the AML/CFT Guideline and Hong Kong Police Force intelligence, including scam-related proceeds being converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets. It reiterates regulatory expectations that firms implement robust transaction monitoring, screen VA transactions and wallet addresses, and establish bank account/wallet address registration or whitelisting mechanisms. It warns of supervisory and enforcement action, including licence conditions, suspension or revocation, for firms that fail to detect and prevent such activity.
w: This circular's AML/CFT obligations bind licensed corporations and SFC-licensed VA service providers, not the bank directly (the bank's governing text is the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline); compliance should use its layering red flags as reference indicators for the bank's own monitoring and be alert when client fund flows touch LC/VATP accounts exhibiting these patterns.
k: Licensed firms are reminded that strict AML/CFT compliance is both a legal obligation and essential to safeguarding operational and systemic integrity
para 2, p.1

Typical layering pattern: frequent, scattered small/odd-amount deposits from multiple bank accounts, later withdrawn to the client's own (sometimes different) bank accounts, with no or minimal trading, and accounts going inactive afterward
para 7, p.2
Scam proceeds are being layered through licensed firms via bank transfers, some converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets, to obscure fund flows
para 8, p.2

Licensed firms must put in place transaction-monitoring systems that are robust and effective, scaled to their transaction volume and ML/TF risk, and must apply extra vigilance when handling deposits and withdrawals.

Firms should establish a registration mechanism for client bank accounts and a whitelisting mechanism for VA wallet addresses, verifying ownership (e.g. micropayment test, message signing test) and avoiding sole reliance on client-provided documents
para 20(a), p.6

Whenever a registered bank account or whitelisted wallet address is added or replaced, senior management -- the MIC of AML/CFT, the compliance officer, or the MLRO -- should review and approve it, applying a risk-sensitive approach.
para 20(c), p.7
Clients may not share bank accounts or wallet addresses with each other, and this bar covers ones that were previously removed or replaced too, except where an account is jointly owned.
para 20(d) and fn.12, p.7
Firms should consider limiting withdrawals to the accounts/wallets from which funds/VAs were originally deposited and implementing a withdrawal holding period (e.g. one to two days)
para 23(a)-(b), p.7
VA transactions and wallet addresses should be screened using blockchain analytical tools before and, on a risk-sensitive basis, after transactions to identify illicit-linked addresses
para 17, p.5-6

SFC will not hesitate to use powers under the SFO and AMLO against firms and senior management (directors, ROs, MIC, MLRO) for AML/CFT failures, including licence conditions, business restrictions, suspension/revocation, fines and reprimands
para 25, p.8
rg: Read paras 5-23 (the red flags and expected controls); paras 1-4 and 24-26 are framing/contact boilerplate and can be skimmed.

t: HKMA announces new phase of Project Ensemble to support real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets
sl: HKMA · HKMA announces new phase of Project Ensemble to support… (2025)
s: The HKMA launched EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, moving from the proof-of-concept Ensemble Sandbox (running since August 2024) to real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. Seven named commercial banks will issue tokenised deposits to customers and settle interbank tokenised deposit transactions through EnsembleTX, alongside other named industry pioneers. The pilot's initial focus is tokenised money market fund transactions and real-time liquidity/treasury management. EnsembleTX runs throughout 2026, starting with interbank settlement via the existing HKD Real Time Gross Settlement system, before being upgraded to round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money. The SFC is a partner in the Ensemble Architecture Community.
w: Directly relevant if the bank is one of the seven named EnsembleTX participating banks or considers joining: it is now a real-value pilot, not a sandbox, so settlement obligations, liquidity risk and operational readiness for tokenised deposits become live issues rather than test exercises.
k: EnsembleTX is the new real-value pilot phase of Project Ensemble, succeeding the Ensemble Sandbox that had tested tokenised-deposit-based digital asset settlement since August 2024.
para 2
Named commercial banks in Annex A will provide tokenised deposits to Hong Kong customers and settle interbank tokenised deposit transactions in real value through EnsembleTX.
para 3
The pilot's initial use cases are tokenised money market fund transactions and real-time liquidity and treasury management.
para 3

EnsembleTX will run throughout 2026; interbank settlement starts on the existing HKD Real Time Gross Settlement system before being progressively upgraded to round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money.
para 4
The HKMA and SFC will keep working together through the Ensemble Architecture Community to extend tokenisation use cases across asset classes.
para 5
rg: Read paragraphs 2-4 for the mechanics and timeline; the two named-executive quote paragraphs (5-6) are optional colour. The Annex A/B participant lists give the named banks and other pioneers.

t: HKMA announces the new phase of Project Ensemble to support real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets

s: The HKMA announced the launch of Ensemble TX, the pilot stage of Project Ensemble, moving on from the Ensemble Sandbox's proof-of-concept work since August 2024 to real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. Ensemble TX runs throughout 2026, starting with tokenised money-market-fund transactions and real-time treasury and liquidity management; interbank settlement of tokenised deposits will initially run through the HKD Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system, gradually upgraded to support round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money. The SFC, part of the Ensemble Architecture Community, continues to work with the HKMA on this.
w: For a compliance head at a participating bank, this marks the switch from simulated to real-value tokenised-deposit transactions, so operational risk, settlement finality and RTGS integration controls now need to be live, not just tested.
k: Ensemble TX is the pilot stage moving from proof-of-concept testing, run as the Ensemble Sandbox since August 2024, to genuine real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets.

t: HKMA introduces HKEX as strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited (with photo)
sl: HKMA · HKMA introduces HKEX as strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced a deal under which Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) is to acquire a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited, the holding company the HKMA's Exchange Fund set up in October 2025 to own CMU OmniClear Limited. CMU OmniClear operates the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), Hong Kong's central securities depository system, on the HKMA's behalf. After the deal, the Exchange Fund will hold 80% and HKEX 20%. The stated goal is to grow CMU into a broader, multi-asset-class central securities depository, supporting settlement and collateral services across a wider range of asset classes. The HKMA confirmed it remains the legal owner and system operator of CMU under the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.
w: CMU underpins settlement of Hong Kong government tokenised/digital bonds and other securities a bank may custody or trade; this ownership restructuring is background context for assessing the CMU infrastructure a bank relies on, but creates no new bank obligation.
k: HKEX is acquiring a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited by subscribing for new shares; after completion the Exchange Fund will hold 80% and HKEX 20%.
para 3

CMU OmniClear Limited, which operates Hong Kong's Central Moneymarkets Unit central securities depository, was established in 2024, and its holding company CMU OmniClear Holdings was set up by the Exchange Fund in October 2025.
para 3

para 7

t: HKMA introduces HKEX as a strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited
sl: HKMA · HKMA introduces HKEX as a strategic shareholder in CMU… (2025)
s: HKMA announced that HKEX will become a strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited, buying a 20% stake through a new share subscription (the Exchange Fund keeps the other 80%), to help build up Hong Kong's central securities depository (CSD) infrastructure and its fixed income and currencies (FIC) market. CMU OmniClear Holdings was set up in October 2025 by the Exchange Fund to wholly own CMU OmniClear Limited, which runs the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) system on HKMA's behalf. As of end-September 2025, CMU held around HK$5 trillion equivalent in assets under custody. HKMA stays the owner and system operator of CMU under the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.
w: Context for a compliance head: this is a governance and equity change at CMU's holding level, with HKEX taking a 20% stake, but HKMA stays the bank's legal counterparty and system operator -- so no due-diligence action is needed.
k: HKEX is buying a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited through a new share subscription; the Exchange Fund (HKMA) keeps the other 80%.

t: HKSAR Government’s Third Digital Green Bonds Offering
sl: HKMA · HKSAR Government’s Third Digital Green Bonds Offering (2025)
s: The HKSAR Government announced pricing of its third digital green bond issuance (~HK$10 billion equivalent across HKD, RMB, USD and EUR tranches) on the HSBC Orion platform, cleared via CMU. It is the first digital bond anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money -- e-CNY and e-HKD -- into how it settles, reached a record size for a digital bond with over HK$130 billion in total subscriptions, stretched its tenor to 5 years, and used Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs) plus wider ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy coverage. It is the first issuance since the Government's Policy Statement 2.0, which commits to making tokenised Government bond issuance a regular practice.
w: Names the bank (or its peers) as direct participants -- platform provider, joint coordinators, settlement agents -- in a HK$10 billion tokenised bond issuance settling partly via tokenised central bank money, giving compliance a live template for tokenised-deposit/CBDC settlement operational and counterparty risk.
k: This is the first digital bond issuance anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD) into its settlement process, running alongside the traditional settlement rails, for the HKD and RMB tranches.
para 4, p.1
The issuance size hit a record HK$10 billion, drawing total subscriptions above HK$130 billion -- the biggest digital bond deal seen anywhere so far -- with tenor stretched to as long as 5 years.
para 5, p.1
Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs, ISO 24165) were obtained for all tranches and linked to ISINs and the issuer's LEI; ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy adoption was expanded versus the second issuance.
paras 6-7, p.1

This is the first tokenised bond issuance following the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong, which commits to regularising issuance of tokenised Government bonds.
Secretary for FS&T quote, p.1
Settlement cycle is T+1; clearing and settlement via CMU (operated by the HKMA) with linkage to Euroclear and Clearstream; governing law is Hong Kong law; listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
'Key features' table, p.1
rg: Read paragraphs 1-7 (the narrative, pp.1) plus the 'Key features' table; the extensive banker/law-firm quotes are promotional and can be skimmed.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - The HKMA Unveils “Fintech 2030” at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2025
sl: HKMA · The HKMA Unveils “Fintech 2030” at the Hong Kong… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced its 'Fintech 2030' strategy, succeeding the earlier 'Fintech 2025' plan, built around four pillars called DART: next-generation Data and payment infrastructure, an AI-for-banks strategy, technology/quantum Resilience, and Tokenisation of finance. Over 40 initiatives are planned. On tokenisation specifically, the HKMA says it will keep issuing tokenised government bonds, explore tokenising Exchange Fund papers, launch the Project Ensemble pilot for real-value transactions, and support settlement via e-HKD, tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.
w: Sets the top-level policy frame (tokenisation as one of four strategic pillars) that later HKMA circulars, the Supervisory Incubator for DLT, and Project Ensemble initiatives sit under; useful context when briefing the board on why HKMA is pushing tokenisation strategic reviews.
k: Fintech 2030 is organised around four pillars nicknamed 'DART': Data and payment infrastructure, AI (the 'AI2 Strategy' for banks), technology/quantum Resilience, and Tokenisation of finance.

t: Appendix III — Amended licensing condition permitting trust/client accounts with third-party custodians for distribution activities (to the Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms)
sl: SFC · Appendix III — Amended licensing condition permitting trust/client accounts… (2025)
s: Amended licensing condition letting a VATP depart from VATP Guidelines paragraph 10.1 (which would otherwise require client assets to be held on trust solely through the licensee's own Associated Entity), so it can hold trust/client accounts in its own name with the custodian(s) of investment products it distributes that are linked to digital assets and/or tokenised securities, subject to applicable law and regulation.
w: This amends a VATP's own licensing condition, not a bank obligation, but a compliance head structuring a distribution partnership with a VATP for the bank's tokenised products should know this narrow custody exception exists.
k: Creates an exception to VATP Guidelines para 10.1's requirement that client assets be held on trust only via the licensee's Associated Entity, for the specific purpose of distribution-related trust/client accounts held with the distributed product's own custodian.
full text, p.1

t: Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading… (2025)
s: Under Pillar P (Products) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular widens what SFC-licensed VATPs may offer: (i) drops the 12-month track-record requirement for virtual assets sold to professional investors, and for stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers sold to retail investors (though that 12-month rule still applies when other virtual assets are offered to retail clients); (ii) lets VATPs sell digital-asset-related products and tokenised securities and hold client assets in trust/client accounts with third-party custodians for that purpose; and (iii) lets VATPs' associated entities custody digital assets not traded on their own platform, subject to conditions.
w: This binds VATPs, not the bank, but it opens a new distribution channel (VATPs distributing bank-originated tokenised securities) and broadens VATP-affiliated custody scope, both relevant to a compliance head evaluating new partnership structures.
k: The 12-month track record requirement no longer applies to virtual assets (including stablecoins) offered to professional investors, nor to stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer offered to retail investors; it still applies to retail offerings of other virtual assets.
paras 5-6, p.2
VATPs must still perform reasonable due diligence on all virtual assets before admission and disclose where a professional-investor-only asset has less than a 12-month track record.
para 6(a)-(b), p.2
The 12-month track-record rule is entirely inapplicable to tokenised securities and other digital securities.
para 7, p.2

VATPs may apply to amend standard licensing conditions to explicitly permit distribution of digital asset-related products/tokenised securities, and to open trust/client accounts in the VATP's own name with the custodian of the distributed product.
para 8, p.2

VATPs (via associated entities) may now apply to provide custody services for digital assets not made available for trading on their own platform — previously disallowed under existing licensing conditions.
paras 10-11, p.3

VATPs still awaiting completion of the second-phase assessment may nonetheless be allowed to custody tokenised securities where the SFC agrees individually, but must finish that assessment before they can custody other digital assets not traded on their platform.
para 13, p.3
rg: Read the full circular (3 pages); the three numbered Appendices (I-III, attachments efa03305086f, 24f2151914e3, 611efe4064cb) give the exact amended licence-condition wording and should be read alongside for precise legal effect.

t: Appendix I — Amended licensing condition removing the 12-month track record requirement (to the Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms)
sl: SFC · Appendix I — Amended licensing condition removing the 12-month… (2025)
s: This appendix gives the exact wording of an amended licence condition that removes the 12-month track-record requirement in the trading-platform guidelines (para 7.6(c)) for (1) virtual assets that only professional investors can trade and (2) specific stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers. It also requires trading platforms to tell clients on their website and app which professional-investor-only assets lack a 12-month track record, and to give clearer risk warnings for them.

full text, p.1

t: Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms (2025)
s: Under Pillar A (Access) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular lets SFC-licensed VATP operators link their order books with affiliated overseas VA trading platform operators (OVATPs) through a 'Shared Order Book,' pooling client orders into one combined liquidity pool. It sets rules for eligible OVATPs, trading and settlement risk management (delivery-versus-payment (DVP) settlement, an Unsettled Trade Limit, a reserve fund, and compensation arrangements), preventing market misconduct, and mandatory prior written SFC approval, with detailed terms and conditions in the appendix (id fda3c03f239d).
w: This binds the affiliated VATP, not the bank directly, but a compliance head overseeing a bank-affiliated VATP group should treat these as the requirements to meet -- FATF-aligned overseas affiliate regulation, a funded Hong Kong reserve, and prior SFC approval -- before that VATP shares order-book liquidity.
k: An OVATP wanting to join a Shared Order Book should be based somewhere that belongs to the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), or to an FATF-style regional body, with rules broadly matching FATF and IOSCO recommendations for crypto/digital-asset markets on market abuse and safeguarding client assets.
para 7, p.1-2

The Shared Order Book should only take fully pre-funded orders, settled through delivery-versus-payment (DVP), with settlement happening at least once a day and during the day too, to keep unsettled exposure within a set Unsettled Trade Limit.

Platform Operators must keep a Hong Kong reserve fund, held on trust, sized at no less than the Unsettled Trade Limit, to cover client losses from failed settlements, plus insurance or compensation cover for Settlement Assets no less than required under VATP Guidelines para 10.22.
paras 16-17, p.3
Retail clients can only use a Shared Order Book if the extra cross-border risks -- including possibly weaker client protection overseas -- are clearly disclosed and the client chooses to take part.
para 25, p.4
Platform Operators should obtain prior written SFC approval before running a Shared Order Book, and conditions will be imposed through licence terms.
paras 26-27, p.4
rg: Read the main circular body (pp.1-4) for the policy rationale and headline requirements; the appended Terms and Conditions (id fda3c03f239d) contain the enforceable operative detail and should be read alongside it.

t: SFC issues new guidance for licensed virtual asset trading platforms to tap global liquidity and diversify offerings
sl: SFC · SFC issues new guidance for licensed virtual asset trading… (2025)
s: Press release summarising the same-day issuance of the two 3 November 2025 circulars: the Shared Order Book circular (Pillar A - Access) and the products/services expansion circular (Pillar P - Products). It highlights that Platform Operators may now combine orders with affiliated overseas platforms and, separately, may offer VAs without a 12-month track record to professional investors and HKMA-licensed stablecoins, plus distribute tokenised securities/digital asset investment products and offer wider custody services.
w: Convenience summary of the two substantive circulars (id f009f1a6d615 and e9cab4f52431) with no independent legal content of its own.
k: The SFC's next step is to look at letting licensed brokers route client orders into regulated overseas liquidity pools operated by the same group, before considering going any further.

Summarises that the two same-day circulars implement Pillar A (Access) and Pillar P (Products) of the ASPIRe roadmap respectively.
paras 1 and 4, p.1

t: Terms and conditions for operating a Shared Order Book (Appendix to the Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms)
sl: SFC · Terms and conditions for operating a Shared Order Book (2025)
s: These are the detailed, licence-imposed terms and conditions supporting the shared-liquidity circular. They define eligibility (the Other Virtual Asset Trading Platform (OVATP) must be a 'related corporation' under section 53ZRC of the AMLO), what Shared Order Book Rules must cover, trading operations, settlement controls (delivery-versus-payment, netting, and Unsettled Trade Limit factors), default management, compensation and reserve fund mechanics, steps to prevent market misconduct, a 7-year record-keeping duty, client disclosures, and mandatory reporting of incidents and regulatory changes to the SFC.
w: This binds VATPs that run shared order books, not the bank directly, but it sets the bar for reserve funds, record-keeping, and incident reporting that a compliance head should expect from a bank-affiliated VATP before relying on shared-liquidity arrangements.
k: The OVATP should be a 'related corporation' of the Platform Operator, as defined in section 53ZRC of the AMLO.

The reserve fund should be kept, in fiat currency unless the SFC agrees otherwise, across one or more segregated accounts at an authorized financial institution, and must be at least as large as the Unsettled Trade Limit.
paras 33-35, pp.4-5
Records must be retained for at least 7 years, enough detail to rebuild the complete history of every order, trade, settlement, surveillance alert, and incident response.
para 44, p.6

A Platform Operator should tell the SFC without delay about any actual or suspected serious breach, any regulatory action taken against the OVATP or its Designated Custodian, any serious adverse event, or any possible regulatory change that could affect them.
para 50, pp.7-8
A Platform Operator should keep a contingency plan ready to pause order matching with the OVATP and isolate its own client orders if there is a serious disruption.
para 18, p.3
rg: Read in full alongside the main circular (id f009f1a6d615); the numbered paragraphs here are the enforceable licence conditions and should be treated as the primary compliance text.

t: Appointments to Stablecoin Review Tribunal
sl: Government · Appointments to Stablecoin Review Tribunal (2025)
s: This announcement confirms that the Chief Executive appointed a Chairperson and six panel members to the Stablecoin Review Tribunal, each for a three-year term starting 1 November 2025. The Tribunal is established under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) to hear appeals against specified decisions made by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority under that Ordinance. A government spokesman described the Tribunal as a safeguard to keep the Monetary Authority's stablecoin-related regulatory decisions reasonable and fair.
w: If a bank group entity ever becomes, or deals with, a licensed stablecoin issuer and disputes an HKMA decision, this Tribunal is now operational and is the appeal route to know about.
k: The Stablecoin Review Tribunal was formally staffed with a Chairperson and six panel members, each appointed for a three-year term from 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2028.
para 2
The Tribunal's function is to review specified Hong Kong Monetary Authority decisions made under the Stablecoins Ordinance, upon receiving an appeal.
para 4
rg: The whole release is short; read in full, no skip needed.

t: HKMA completes e-HKD Pilot Programme and outlines future direction of e-HKD
sl: HKMA · HKMA completes e-HKD Pilot Programme and outlines future direction… (2025)
s: The HKMA announced the publication of the 'e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report,' presenting findings from 11 industry pilot groups and the HKMA's updated policy stance. The report compares e-HKD with tokenised deposits and finds the public sees them similarly, given trust in Hong Kong's banking system. The near-term e-HKD priority is now wholesale payments rather than retail, with policy, legal, and technical groundwork for a possible future retail use to be finished by the first half of 2026. The HKMA will also publish shared token standards for programmability, coming out of the e-HKD Industry Forum.
w: For a compliance head, this signals the HKMA's near-term e-HKD focus is wholesale, not retail, so the bank need not rush retail e-HKD readiness, though wholesale and tokenised-deposit engagement stays relevant.
k: The HKMA has concluded that the near-term priority for e-HKD is wholesale payments, such as cross-border settlement and support for the tokenisation ecosystem, rather than retail use, at this stage.

t: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report (2025)
s: The HKMA's full Phase 2 Report on the e-HKD Pilot Programme (part of Project e-HKD+), documenting 11 industry pilot groups' work grouped into three areas — tokenised-asset settlement, programmable-money use cases, and payments while offline — carried out after Phase 1 finished in October 2023. The report concludes that e-HKD and tokenised deposits deliver comparable retail benefits, that commercial banks lean slightly toward tokenised deposits (lower cost of capital, faster time-to-market, customer stickiness), and sets out key design considerations (interoperability, programmability, privacy, identity, convertibility, reliability/performance) for any future retail e-HKD. The HKMA's resulting policy stance prioritises wholesale e-HKD development, treating retail extension as a longer-term, conditional option.
w: No obligation attaches, but this informs a compliance head's input on whether the bank should prioritise tokenised-deposit infrastructure over e-HKD integration, and flags concrete constraints (privacy-cost trade-offs, throughput limits) relevant to any DLT settlement build.
k: Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking, more design flexibility with a shorter time-to-market, and stronger customer stickiness.
Executive Summary, p.2 (doc p.2)

A natively 'programmable e-HKD' with explicit spending conditions risks undermining fungibility and the 'singleness of money'; purpose-bound money (PBM)/programmable payments are preferred alternatives that preserve fungibility.
Section 4, 'Programmability', p.30 (doc p.29-30)

Privacy-enhancing technologies (ZKPs via Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved privacy with similar settlement times but increased gas fees up to 320 times versus no PETs; a tiered privacy model (basic for low-value, advanced PETs for high-value/high-risk) is recommended.
Section 4, 'Privacy', p.31, and footnote 38

Public DLTs such as Ethereum Layer 1 currently manage only roughly 15-30 transactions each second, a throughput limit for high-volume retail e-HKD use; the HKMA does not rule out public DLTs but flags a need for further optimisation.
Section 4, 'Reliability and Performance', p.33
HKMA will prioritise e-HKD development for financial institutions (wholesale); a sustainable private-sector business model for retail e-HKD has not yet been identified.
Section 5, 'Path Forward', p.34

Digital identity: pilots tested a digital identity framework using verifiable credentials (VCs) and unique identifiers (UIDs) issued by a trusted authority, cryptographically verified before each signed transaction.
Section 4, 'Identity', p.32
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.2), Section 4 Design Considerations (pp.28-33) and Section 5 Path Forward (p.34) first — these carry the policy conclusions; Section 2 (pilot structure) and Section 3 (detailed findings by theme, pp.18-27) can be skimmed for specific use-case detail as needed.
