t: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report (2025)
s: This HKMA report presents the findings of Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme, in which eleven industry pilot groups tested e-HKD and tokenised deposits across three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments. It compares e-HKD against privately-issued digital money, especially tokenised deposits, and finds banks generally prefer tokenised deposits for cost-of-capital and design-flexibility reasons. It concludes that most of the programmability and settlement benefits come from smart contracts rather than from the choice of settlement medium, and that a viable business case for a retail e-HKD has not yet emerged. The HKMA states it will prioritise e-HKD development for wholesale (interbank) use and continue preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork for a possible retail extension by the first half of 2026, without committing to launch retail e-HKD.
w: This is the HKMA's own account of why it is not yet committing to retail e-HKD, and it explains the regulator's current thinking on tokenised deposits versus CBDC -- directly relevant background for a bank's own tokenised-deposit and digital-money product strategy and for engaging with the HKMA's e-HKD Industry Forum and Supervisory Incubator for DLT.
k: Phase 2 involved eleven groups of firms trialling e-HKD and tokenised-deposit use cases in three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments.
Executive Summary, p.6

Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking, greater design flexibility, and stronger customer stickiness.
Executive Summary, p.6

The HKMA will prioritise developing e-HKD for wholesale (interbank) use and will keep preparing the policy, legal and technical groundwork to allow a possible retail extension, with that preparatory work targeted for completion in 2026 -- this is not a decision to launch retail e-HKD.
Executive Summary p.6 / Section 5 Path Forward, p.34

Gains from programmability (smart contracts) were found to come mainly from the smart-contract layer itself, not from whether the settlement medium is e-HKD or tokenised deposits -- so e-HKD offers no unique programmability advantage.
Section 3.1.2, p.20

Achieving same-day (T+0) settlement of tokenised funds requires on-chain net asset values calculated close to real time, wider native on-chain tokenisation rather than mere 'digital twins', and a major redesign of core banking infrastructure -- not just a new settlement medium.
Section 3.1.1, p.20

Privacy-enhancing technologies (zero-knowledge proofs such as Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved transaction privacy but increased gas fees by up to 320 times versus transactions without such technology, creating a cost/privacy trade-off for any future e-HKD design.
Section 4 Privacy, p.31

About 35% of surveyed respondents in one pilot said they would be less likely to use e-HKD for routine payments, citing concern about the central bank's potential access to personal and transaction data.
Section 3.2.1, p.25

For offline payments, survey data showed limited appetite: 48% of respondents said Hong Kong's existing offline payment options (used by about 98% of the population) already meet their needs, and 68% of merchants expected fees in line with current merchant fees, making cost recovery for an offline e-HKD difficult.
Section 3.1.3, p.22-23

The e-HKD Industry Forum, formed December 2024, includes a Programmability Working Group of nine firms (co-led by BOCHK, DBS and HSBC) developing common token standards, due to be published separately by the first half of 2026.
Section 2.4, p.16
The report recommends an account-based balance model over a UTXO model for any future offline e-HKD, because it needs less local device storage and simpler synchronisation.
Section 3.1.3, p.24

Design considerations flagged as critical for any retail e-HKD include interoperability across DLT networks, tiered privacy (basic privacy for low-value transactions, stronger privacy-enhancing technology for high-value/high-risk ones), a digital identity/verifiable-credential framework, and non-interest-bearing design to avoid competing with bank deposits.
Section 4, p.28-33
The report notes that if e-HKD is extended to retail, holding limits and non-interest-bearing design are being considered to reduce the risk of large-scale deposit outflow from banks during stress.
Section 3.2.3, p.26-27
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.6) and Section 5 Path Forward (p.34) first for the bottom line; skim Section 3 (Findings) for the tokenised-deposits-vs-e-HKD comparison; the glossary and pilot fact-sheet appendix (p.36-44) can be skipped.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions (Version 5 - consultation draft)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime… (2025)
s: This draft module explains, at a general level, how the HKMA supervises the capital adequacy of locally incorporated banks: solo and consolidated capital ratios, the leverage ratio, capital buffers and the risk-weighting framework. The version put out for consultation adds a new subsection setting out, in outline, how cryptoasset exposures are folded into the existing credit-risk capital-charge methodology, referencing the detailed cryptoasset capital rules set out elsewhere in the Banking (Capital) Rules.
w: This is the overview-level anchor for the bank's cryptoasset capital charge; the compliance head needs it to confirm the bank's capital model correctly separates Group 1a, 1b and 2 cryptoasset exposures and applies the right add-ons, even though the line-by-line formulas sit in the underlying capital rules and CRP-1 classification guideline.
k: A bank's capital adequacy ratio and leverage ratio must be calculated in line with the Banking (Capital) Rules, and the MA can impose bank-specific minimum ratios above the regulatory minimum
For a tokenised traditional asset (Group 1a cryptoasset) held in the banking book, the bank applies the same capital treatment as it would to the underlying asset

For a Group 1b cryptoasset (e.g. a reference-asset-backed token such as certain stablecoins) held in the banking book, the bank must separately capitalise both the credit risk of the reference asset and the credit risk of the entity performing redemption

Where only some token holders can redeem directly with the issuer, a bank that is such a member must also capitalise the risk that it may have to buy the token from non-member holders; a non-member bank must capitalise its credit risk on the members instead
Riskier tokens that do not meet the Group 1 classification tests (Group 2b cryptoassets) get a conservative capital treatment set by a separate Banking (Capital) Rules provision

Extra capital add-ons apply for Group 1b assets held in the trading book, an infrastructure-risk add-on for Group 1 assets, a further add-on for Group 2a stablecoin exposures, and a concentration add-on for global or domestic systemically important banks whose Group 2 cryptoasset exposure exceeds a prescribed limit
rg: Read section 8.7 (pages 47-49) closely; sections 1-7 and 9-15 are the pre-existing general capital-adequacy overview and only need a skim for context.

t: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2025)
s: This circular updates the original December 2023 SFC-HKMA Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset activities, easing several requirements after a market review while keeping investor protection. It lets intermediaries offer staking through segregated accounts, allows VA trades via a licensed platform's off-platform service, clarifies that VA-funded subscriptions/redemptions are not 'dealing' services, and drops certain suitability and disclosure steps for institutional and qualified corporate professional investors. Separate guidance on HKMA-licensed stablecoin activities is still to come.
w: As an RI, the bank reaches this circular through HKMA's frontline supervision; it now permits staking and simplifies VA-funded subscriptions for the bank's clients, but only inside tightly controlled, pre-notified arrangements.
k: Intermediaries -- licensed corporations and registered institutions -- can now offer staking to existing virtual-asset clients, but only via segregated accounts held at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized institution, or at that institution's subsidiary.
paras 4-5
Staking is defined as locking up a client's virtual assets in a proof-of-stake blockchain's validation process to earn and pass on rewards.
para 4

Intermediaries may now execute client virtual-asset trades through a licensed platform's off-platform trading service, after removing the earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the Terms and Conditions.
para 6

Clients paying for or receiving investment-product subscriptions/redemptions in virtual assets are not treated as using a 'dealing' service, but the intermediary must still tell the regulators in advance, hold the assets at a licensed platform or authorized institution, and apply the AML travel-rule chapter to those movements.
para 7

The net-worth suitability check for clients of VA-exposed products, and the requirement to give a VA-futures-specific risk warning, no longer apply to institutional and qualified corporate professional investors.
paras 8-9

Intermediaries must tell the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) in advance before: changing the type of clients they serve, first letting clients deposit/withdraw virtual assets, first offering staking, first allowing VA-funded subscriptions/redemptions, or making other material changes to their VA activities.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular)
sl: SFC/HKMA · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2025)
s: The full, consolidated Terms and Conditions (September 2025 version, Appendix 6) governing licensed corporations/registered institutions providing VA dealing services (via omnibus account with an SFC-licensed platform) and VA advisory services. Covers interpretation, applicable codes/guidelines, financial soundness (12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital), operational controls, market-abuse prevention, extensive client-facing duties (KYC, suitability, disclosure, contract notes/statements/receipts), custody of client assets and money, a new Part VIII on staking, record keeping, auditor reporting, conflicts of interest, and ongoing SFC/HKMA reporting obligations.
w: As the current master terms and conditions for the bank's VA dealing and advisory activities as a registered institution, this directly sets the capital buffer, segregated-custody and new staking-disclosure obligations a compliance head must have live controls for, not merely track for the future.
k: A licensed corporation must keep, in Hong Kong, liquid capital in excess of its own actual operating expenses for a rolling 12-month period, over and above the ordinary Financial Resources Rules requirement.

Client virtual assets must be held on trust in segregated 'VA Segregated Account(s)' with an SFC-licensed platform or a qualifying authorized financial institution; withdrawals must go directly to the client from that account.
Discretionary account managers may only invest less than 10% of a client's account gross asset value in virtual assets where VA trading authority is ancillary to a securities discretionary mandate.

New Part VIII (Staking): intermediaries may only stake client VAs via an SFC-licensed platform or authorized financial institution ('Staking Service Provider') that has obtained the necessary regulatory approval/discussed with HKMA, and must disclose staking risks (slashing, lock-up, validator risk) and obtain client acknowledgement.

A licensed corporation should not engage in VA market making on an execution venue (e.g. an SFC-licensed platform) through which it also provides Relevant VA Dealing services to clients — a conflicts-of-interest restriction.

Auditors must report annually on whether adequate custody control systems were in place and whether the firm complied with the Custody and Record Keeping parts and the financial soundness requirement.

Standard mandatory risk disclosures to retail clients include that VAs may not be 'property' under law, are not covered by the Investor Compensation Fund, are not legal tender, and transactions may be irreversible.
rg: Read Part VII (Custody, p.20) and the new Part VIII (Staking, p.24) closely as the most operationally significant sections for a bank; Parts I-VI (client-facing conduct rules, pp.7-19) are largely a restatement of existing Code of Conduct-style obligations mapped onto VA activities and can be skimmed once familiar with the Code of Conduct.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular, September 2025)
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2025)
s: This is the September 2025 set of licensing conditions that the SFC and HKMA impose on banks and brokers that deal in or advise on virtual assets. Part I covers two dealing models: acting purely as an introducer to an SFC-licensed trading platform, and running client trades through the firm's own omnibus account at such a platform. Part II covers advisory services. The document sets client-classification, suitability, disclosure, custody, record-keeping and reporting standards, and for the first time gives detailed conditions for staking services offered to clients.
w: These are the actual licensing conditions a bank's registered-institution business must comply with for virtual asset dealing, advisory and staking, covering custody, suitability, disclosure and reporting duties owed to both regulators.
k: A firm that only introduces clients to an SFC-licensed platform must not hold client money or virtual assets itself and must use a written client agreement describing its limited role
Part I, intro (a)-(c), p.4
A firm running an omnibus account must keep at least 12 months of operating expenses as excess liquid capital in Hong Kong, on top of the normal Financial Resources Rules
para 3.1, p.8

Retail clients may only trade virtual assets through an omnibus account at a platform that itself is allowed to serve retail investors, and only in tokens that platform makes available to retail investors
para 4.1, p.9
The firm must not offer clients any financing to buy virtual assets, and should try to stop group companies doing so too
para 4.3, p.9

Recommended virtual assets for retail clients must be liquid enough to appear in at least two independent, IOSCO-consistent market indices, and must also be tradable for retail investors on the platform used
Client virtual assets must be held on trust in a segregated account at either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution (or its subsidiary) that meets HKMA's expected custody standards
para 7.1(a), p.20

A firm may stake client virtual assets only via a Staking Service Provider that is either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution, and only once that provider holds the necessary SFC clearance or has discussed the service with the HKMA.

Clients must be told the risks specific to staking, such as slashing, lock-up delays, validator hacking and legal uncertainty over their interest in staked assets, and must sign an acknowledgement of those risks before staking (unless institutional/qualified professional investors)
Records on client virtual assets, money, orders and staking must be kept for at least seven years, with contract notes/receipts kept for at least two years
Any actual or suspected material breach of these terms must be reported to the SFC, and also to the HKMA if the firm is a registered institution, as soon as practicable

For advisory services, a firm must assess a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising, train clients lacking knowledge, and only recommend liquid, index-qualifying tokens to retail clients
Part II, paras 3.1-3.5, p.35-36
rg: Read Part I paras 4 (Operations), 6 (Dealing with clients), 7 (Custody) and 8 (Staking) closely; the Schedule 1 list of applied SFC codes and Part II (advisory) can be skimmed since they largely mirror Part I's suitability logic.

t: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: SFC/HKMA · Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2025)
s: This circular adds to the SFC and HKMA's 22 December 2023 Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset (VA)-related activities, bringing in relaxations after industry feedback. It lets intermediaries offer staking services to clients through SFC-licensed platforms or authorized financial institutions (AIs), allows trade execution through off-platform virtual asset trading platform (VATP) services, clarifies that subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets is not itself a VA dealing service, and exempts institutional or qualified corporate professional investors from certain net-worth and risk-disclosure rules. Separate guidance on activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers is promised. Updated Terms and Conditions (Appendix 6) come with this circular.
w: As an update to the Joint Circular that reaches the bank through the HKMA, this circular relaxes some rules (off-platform trading, staking) while adding new advance-notice duties for staking, VA-funded subscriptions and redemptions, and other material changes to VA-related activities.
k: Intermediaries can now offer clients staking services, but only via segregated accounts kept at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized financial institution, or at a subsidiary of a locally incorporated authorized institution.
para 5

A licensed corporation or registered institution can now route a client's virtual-asset dealing trade through an SFC-licensed platform's own off-platform trading service; the earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the prior Terms and Conditions has been dropped as a result
para 6

Clients subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets, or making in-kind subscriptions or redemptions of VA funds, are not treated as receiving VA dealing services, as long as advance notice and custody conditions are met.
para 7
The net-worth rule in paragraph 6.2 of the Joint Circular no longer applies to clients who are institutional professional investors or qualified corporate professional investors.
para 8
The requirement to give risk disclosure statements for VA futures contracts (Joint Circular paragraph 13) no longer applies to institutional or qualified corporate professional investors.
para 9

Intermediaries must tell the SFC, and the HKMA where relevant, in advance of material changes such as a client's first deposit or withdrawal, first staking service, or first subscription or redemption using VA.
para 10
Separate guidance specific to activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) will come later.
para 11
rg: Read the full 3-page body; the Appendices (Appendix A clean T&Cs, Appendix B tracked-changes T&Cs) are the detailed operative rules and should be read via the separate T&C attachment records rather than in full duplicate here.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services — tracked changes version (Appendix B to the Supplemental Joint Circular)
sl: SFC/HKMA · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2025)
s: A redline/tracked-changes rendering of the same Terms and Conditions as Appendix A (id ca4bd361b05f), showing insertions and deletions made between the original October 2023 version and the September 2025 update. The substantive changes visible are the same as described in the Supplemental Joint Circular: addition of the Staking Part, removal of the off-platform execution restriction, and related renumbering of Parts VIII-XI.
w: Useful only for compliance teams needing to see the precise wording changes versus the 2023 baseline; the substance for business purposes is fully captured by the clean Appendix A version.
k: The document is explicitly a tracked-changes comparison between the October 2023 and September 2025 versions of Appendix 6.

A new Part on Staking is inserted between the prior Custody and Record Keeping parts, shifting subsequent part numbering (old VIII Record Keeping becomes IX, etc.).

t: 2025 Policy Address
sl: Government · 2025 Policy Address (2025)
s: The Chief Executive's 2025 Policy Address is a wide-ranging annual government speech; only its digital-asset/fintech passages are captured here (paragraphs 97, 103-104, 110-111 and Annex item 22, on pages 39-43 and 97). It confirms continuation of Project Ensemble, including encouraging banks to issue tokenised deposits and settle tokenised money market funds, plus regularising government tokenised bond issuance. It confirms the government is implementing a stablecoin issuer licensing regime and is drafting legislative proposals for a new licensing regime covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers, with a bill targeted for introduction to the Legislative Council in 2026. It also notes the SFC is exploring wider digital asset products for professional investors and plans automated reporting/surveillance tools, plus a tokenised-gold investment product initiative and pilot use of tokenised deposits in commodity trade finance with Brazil's central bank.
w: This is the clearest, highest-level government confirmation that Hong Kong will pass legislation in 2026 to license digital asset dealing and custody businesses, on top of the stablecoin regime already in force; a bank's digital asset business plan and licensing roadmap should track this bill.
k: The government will support issuers in launching tokenised gold as a new investment vehicle, as part of building Hong Kong into a regional gold trading and storage hub.
para 97(iv), p.39
The HKMA will keep advancing Project Ensemble, encouraging commercial banks to issue tokenised deposits and to settle tokenised money market fund transactions using tokenised deposits.
para 103, p.40
The HKMA will help the government regularise (make routine) the issuance of tokenised government bonds, and will encourage banks to strengthen risk management via the supervisory sandbox.
para 103, p.40

The government is implementing the licensing regime for stablecoin issuers and is separately drafting legislative proposals for new licensing regimes covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers.
para 104, p.41

The SFC is looking at whether professional investors could be given access to a broader menu of digital asset products and services, conditional on adequate investor safeguards, and will bring in automated reporting and data-surveillance tools against digital asset risks.
para 104, p.41
A pilot with Banco Central do Brazil will test tokenised deposits and electronic bills of lading to support international commodity trade finance.
para 111(iii), p.43
The government commits to bringing a bill to the Legislative Council in 2026 that would set up licensing for firms dealing in digital assets and providing digital asset custody.
Annex, item 22, p.97
rg: Read only paragraphs 97(iv), 103-104 and 111(iii) on pages 39-43, plus Annex item 22 on page 97; skip the rest of this 90+ page general policy speech, which covers unrelated topics (housing, healthcare, trade, shipping, etc).

t: Supervision of regulated activities of SFC-registered authorized institutions
sl: HKMA · Supervision of regulated activities of SFC-registered authorized institutions (2025)
s: HKMA catalogue entry for the current version of SB-1, the SPM module describing how HKMA supervises the SFC-registered (Registered Institution) activities of AIs. This page only carries the listing metadata; the substantive module text is in the attachment.
w: Points to SB-1, the core module for how HKMA oversees the bank's SFC-registered activities, including virtual-asset-related activities.
k: The module is filed as 'Current' status, meaning it is the version now in force.
Status field, p.1
It is classified under supervisory-approach and securities/investment-product topics.
Topic field, p.1
This version replaces the 10 May 2024 edition of SB-1.

t: SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions (2025)
s: SB-1 sets out how HKMA supervises the day-to-day conduct of an AI's SFC-registered activities once it becomes a Registered Institution (RI). It explains HKMA's role as frontline supervisor working alongside the SFC, the mandatory appointment and registration of executive officers and relevant individuals, HKMA's tiered response to control deficiencies and misconduct, and the events an RI must proactively report — including any plan to start or change virtual-asset-related activities.
w: This is the core rulebook for how HKMA actually supervises the bank's RI status day to day, including who must be appointed, what must be pre-notified before touching virtual assets, and how the bank's people and licence can be disciplined.
k: Once an AI is registered by the SFC to carry on a regulated activity, it becomes a Registered Institution (RI), and the HKMA acts as the RI's frontline day-to-day supervisor while the SFC keeps overall regulatory responsibility and can rely on HKMA's supervision.
para 2.1.3

An RI must have a minimum of two executive officers responsible for the direct supervision of each of its regulated activities, each needing the HKMA's prior written consent, with at least one available at all times per activity.

Every 'relevant individual' who performs a regulated function for an RI must be entered in the HKMA Register before starting that work, and any change to their registered details must be notified within 7 business days.

HKMA uses a three-step, risk-based approach to deficiencies: first sharing good practice, then requiring corrective action or an independent review for control weaknesses, and finally moving to disciplinary or enforcement action where there is a prima facie case of misconduct or unfitness.
HKMA generally expects an RI to meet the same conduct standards the SFC applies to licensed corporations, and can add extra investor-protection requirements specific to the banking context.

For anti-money-laundering purposes, RIs and their AI associated entities must follow the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline for Authorized Institutions, and separately must have regard to specific parts of the SFC's own AML/CFT guideline — including its virtual-asset chapter — for definitions and provisions relevant to securities-sector business.
para 4.16.1

An RI should tell the SFC and HKMA before it starts any virtual-asset activities -- dealing, advisory or asset-management services in VA products -- or before changing how it runs those activities, including changes to the kinds of clients it serves.
para 5.6

An RI must give at least 7 business days' advance notice before ceasing a regulated activity or changing its address for carrying one on, and notify certain changes to relevant individuals' backgrounds within 7 business days of becoming aware of them.
paras 5.1, 5.5

Both HKMA and SFC can discipline a relevant individual or executive officer found guilty of misconduct or no longer fit and proper — for example by removing them from the HKMA Register or withdrawing an executive officer's consent — with a right of appeal to the Securities and Futures Appeals Tribunal.
paras 6.3, 6.7
rg: Read section 2 (HKMA/SFC framework), 4.3 (executive officers and relevant individuals), 4.16 (AML) and 5 (event reporting, especially para 5.6 on virtual assets) closely; sections 4.8-4.14 on specific product/activity codes can be skimmed unless the bank runs those specific activities.

t: LCQ10: Regulation of digital assets
sl: FSTB · LCQ10: Regulation of digital assets (2025)
s: A written Legislative Council reply clarifies who may lawfully offer a stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance, in response to concerns that virtual-asset OTC shops were exploiting grey areas. It confirms only five categories of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin: licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions (banks). Virtual-asset OTC trading institutions are not permitted offerors and cannot offer stablecoins to any investor type. It also confirms no stablecoin issuer had yet been licensed as of the reply date, and that the licensing timetable for the dealing/custodian regimes would be announced after the consultation (closed August 29, 2025) is digested.
w: This is a core compliance reference: it confirms the bank, as an authorised institution, is itself one of only five categories of entity legally permitted to offer a stablecoin, while a range of common counterparties (VA OTC shops) are explicitly barred from doing so - a fact the bank should build into its own product-distribution and counterparty-screening rules.
k: Only five types of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin: licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions
reply (1), para 2
Permitted offerors may offer a regulated (HKMA-licensed-issuer) stablecoin to both retail and professional investors, but an unregulated stablecoin may only be offered to professional investors
reply (1), para 2

Because virtual-asset OTC trading institutions do not qualify as permitted offerors, they are barred from selling any specified stablecoin to any investor type, whether or not that stablecoin is itself regulated
reply (1), para 3
As of this reply, the HKMA had not licensed any stablecoin issuer, so members of the public acquiring any stablecoin currently bear their own risk
reply (2), para 1
The FSTB and SFC are still formulating details of the dealing/custodian licensing regimes based on consultation feedback and will announce a legislative timetable in due course
reply (3), para 2
rg: Read reply (1) in full for the permitted-offeror list and OTC-shop exclusion; replies (2) and (3) are shorter status updates.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (draft V.5)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of… (2025)
s: This is a statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance, in draft form, adding a new section 5.9 and Annex 3 on cryptoassets to the HKMA's existing liquidity-risk supervision module. It tells authorized institutions how cryptoasset exposures should be folded into the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The default principle is to treat a cryptoasset the same as the traditional asset or liability it economically resembles, unless it carries extra risk from its digital form. The draft sets specific rules for three buckets: tokenised claims that are a legal claim on the bank, stablecoins, and all other cryptoassets, and reserves the HKMA's right to apply tougher treatment case by case.
w: This module is the primary rulebook compliance would use to determine how any cryptoasset custody, trading, issuance or tokenised-deposit activity affects the bank's regulatory liquidity ratios, and it directly drives the new lines in Form MA(BS)1E.
k: As a baseline, cryptoasset exposures should get the same LCR/NSFR/LMR/CFR treatment as an economically equivalent traditional exposure, because of their extra risk and limited track record.
para 5.9.1-5.9.2 (footnote 78-79 define 'cryptoasset' and 'cryptoasset exposure')

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset (HQLA) if it is a 'group 1a' tokenised version of an already-eligible traditional asset, both the token and the underlying asset meet all the usual HQLA conditions, and the token meets extra operational conditions (e.g. it lives on a well-established ledger with an active, sizable market so it can be sold quickly with little loss of value).
Annex 3, paras 1-1(b) and footnote 95

If a bank issues tokens that are a direct, par-value redeemable claim on it, backed one-to-one by a matching pool of assets, it can treat the resulting liability like ordinary deposits or unsecured funding, but only at the earliest date holders could demand redemption, and only at the favourable retail/small-business rate if the bank can always identify the token holders.
Annex 3, para 4

Stablecoins a bank issues get a 100% LCR outflow rate if redeemable within the LCR window, unless they are fully backed by HQLA-eligible assets, in which case the more favourable secured-funding outflow rates may apply instead.
Annex 3, para 7

Stablecoins a bank holds (rather than issues) are treated as ordinary non-HQLA debt securities, generally with a 0% LCR inflow rate and an 85% NSFR required-stable-funding factor, though a lower 50% factor can apply if the maturity is short and will convert to fiat within 12 months.
Annex 3, para 7

Any other cryptoasset the bank holds or has borrowed gets the harshest treatment: no LCR inflow recognition, a 100% NSFR funding requirement, and a 100% outflow rate if the bank owes the asset back to a counterparty.
Annex 3, para 8(b)

The HKMA can impose stricter LCR/NSFR treatment for a specific cryptoasset if it judges the asset carries extra liquidity risk or the bank has contingent exposure from issuing or trading it, for example if the bank might feel pressure to support redemptions to protect its reputation.
para 9 and footnote 98
The same tokenised-claim, stablecoin and 'other cryptoasset' logic carries over largely unchanged to the Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (for category 2 institutions) and the Core Funding Ratio.
paras 11-17
rg: Read section 5.9 (p.65) as the summary, then Annex 3 in full (pp.88-94); skip the unchanged core LCR/LMR mechanics elsewhere in the module.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: This draft statutory guideline adds a new section 4 on cryptoassets to the module covering credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital -- the capital a bank must hold against the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens. Derivatives and securities-financing transactions referencing tokenised traditional assets or stablecoins (groups 1a/1b) are generally treated the same as instruments on the underlying traditional asset, but a bank must still separately check the token's own liquidity behaviour rather than assuming it matches the original asset. Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives cannot use the more risk-sensitive standardised CVA approach at all, and group 2b exposures are folded into an existing, very conservative flat risk-weight treatment with no extra CVA calculation.
w: Sets the capital a derivatives or securities-financing desk must hold for counterparty credit-quality risk on any cryptoasset-referencing trade, and confirms less-standard tokens cannot use the more capital-efficient standardised method.
k: Derivatives and financing trades on group 1a tokenised assets are generally charged CVA capital the same way as trades on the non-tokenised version of the asset.
para 4.2.1

A bank must independently assess the tokenised asset itself against this module's tests -- it cannot simply assume the token qualifies for a treatment just because the underlying traditional asset does, because liquidity behaviour can differ between the two.
para 4.2.2

If there is not enough data to model how those liquidity differences affect the tokenised asset's value, the more risk-sensitive standardised CVA approach cannot be used and the basic approach applies instead.
para 4.2.2
Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives and securities-financing trades must use the basic CVA approach; the standardised approach is not permitted for them.
para 4.3.1

Group 2b cryptoasset exposures generally need no separate CVA calculation because they already carry the conservative 1,250% risk weight that covers credit, market and CVA risk together; this only changes if a fair-valued, cryptoasset-collateralised transaction's credit risk is calculated some other way, in which case the 1,250% weight is applied specifically for CVA.
rg: Read section 4 in full (pp.44-46); the rest of the module is unchanged general CVA mechanics.

t: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
sl: HKMA · CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (2025)
s: CR-L-5 explains how HKMA exercises its consent power over an AI's major acquisitions of another company's share capital under Part 3 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. The revision adds a footnote clarifying that a cryptoasset counting as equity ownership is treated the same as ordinary share capital for this consent regime.

para 1.1

para 1.1, fn.1

para 2.1.1
Certain small or deemed-consent acquisitions are exempt from needing prior consent, as set out later in the module.
Structure, ss.2.2, 2.4, p.2

t: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules and code of practice
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules… (2025)
s: This is the HKMA Banking Policy Department's covering letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (addressed to its then chairperson) opening formal industry consultation on a full package of cryptoasset-related prudential guidance: a brand-new SPM module CRP-1 on classifying cryptoassets, plus revisions to eight other modules and one code. The stated purpose is to implement, at the Hong Kong level, the Basel Committee's global standard on how banks should treat cryptoasset exposures for capital purposes, alongside related amendments to the capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules. The HKMA asked for comments within about a month and noted it sent an equivalent letter to the DTC Association the same day.
w: Gives compliance the authoritative, dated list of exactly which modules and code are in scope of the cryptoasset prudential-standard consultation, useful for tracking which drafts to monitor through to finalisation.
k: The consultation covers a brand-new module, CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets', plus revisions to eight further items: CA-D-1, CA-G-5, CR-G-8, CR-G-9, CR-L-5, LM-1, MR-1, MR-2 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code.
list of modules, p.1

The revisions implement, at the local level, the Basel Committee's global standard on prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures, alongside the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
A separate, related revision to module CA-G-1 (overview of the capital adequacy regime) is being consulted on separately, not as part of this package.
footnote 1, p.1
Comments were requested by 10 October 2025.
rg: Read in full; it is short (two pages) and is the master index for the whole consultation package.

t: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties
sl: HKMA · CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties (2025)
s: CR-G-9 sets out the systems and controls a locally incorporated AI needs to identify, measure, monitor and limit its exposures to connected parties, and the statutory cap on such exposures under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. It was reissued as part of the same crypto-standard consultation package, but the introductory and structural sections reviewed here contain no crypto-specific wording; any link to cryptoasset exposures runs through the general BELR valuation cross-references rather than dedicated crypto provisions in this module.
w: This is the general connected-lending control framework the bank already operates under; the pages available here show no dedicated crypto content, so its relevance to crypto business is indirect, through the wider large-exposure/BELR valuation changes rather than this module itself.
k: The module exists to make AIs put in place systems to identify, measure, monitor and control exposures to connected parties, including those falling under Part 8 of the BELR.
Purpose section, p.1
It applies to all locally incorporated AIs in Hong Kong.
Application section, p.1
The module covers the statutory limit on connected-party exposures, board oversight of the connected-party policy, ongoing monitoring, and financial disclosure of these exposures.
Structure, ss.2-4, p.2
This version replaces four earlier editions dating back to a 1999 circular on connected lending.
Previous guidelines superseded, p.1

t: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
sl: HKMA · CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (2025)
s: CA-G-5 explains how the HKMA runs its Pillar 2 Supervisory Review Process (SRP) to set a bank-specific capital add-on on top of the Pillar 1 minimum. The revision adds an explicit statement that, because crypto activities and their risks are still new and changing, HKMA may respond to weak crypto risk management with capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other measures, decided case by case.
w: This is the mechanism by which weaknesses in the bank's crypto risk management can translate directly into a higher firm-specific capital requirement or forced activity limits, so it links crypto operational risk straight to the capital plan.
k: Because cryptoasset activities and their risks are relatively new and still evolving, the HKMA's supervisory response to gaps in an AI's crypto capital or risk management can include capital add-ons, requiring provisions for foreseeable crypto losses, activity limits, or other mitigation steps.
para 3.6.6
The HKMA's Pillar 2 capital add-on (P2A) is meant to capture material risks not already fully covered by the Pillar 1 minimum requirement.
Structure, s.3.3-3.4, p.2
Before raising or lowering an AI's Pillar 2 capital requirement, HKMA may hold off temporarily to check whether the underlying issue is genuinely resolved or just temporary.
Extra capital is not treated as a substitute for good risk management; HKMA may instead, or in addition, require better systems and controls.
para 3.6.4
Stress tests (sensitivity tests and scenario analyses) run by the AI feed into how HKMA assesses capital adequacy under the SRP.
rg: Read para 3.6.6 (the new crypto-specific supervisory response) and the surrounding 3.6 sub-section on Pillar 2 capital setting first; the legal-framework sections (2.1-2.2) can be skimmed.

t: CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure) Rules
sl: HKMA · CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure)… (2025)
s: CA-D-1 interprets how AIs should meet the Banking (Disclosure) Rules, which implement Hong Kong's Pillar 3 public-disclosure regime. This revision adds two new items tied to the cryptoassets standard: an annual qualitative disclosure of crypto-related business that creates liquidity risk, and, for larger institutions, a semi-annual quantitative disclosure of liquidity requirements tied to crypto exposures. The rest of the module sets out general disclosure timing, review and exemption rules that already applied to AIs.
w: This creates a standing Pillar 3 reporting obligation specifically about the bank's crypto activities, with personal criminal liability for directors and managers if it is missed, so compliance needs a dedicated review-and-sign-off workflow.
k: An AI with any cryptoasset exposure must give an annual, mainly qualitative, disclosure of its crypto-related activities that create liquidity risk, using the standard table the HKMA specifies.
para 12.2.4

An AI that is a 'category 1 institution' and has cryptoasset exposures must also give a semi-annual, mostly quantitative, disclosure of the liquidity requirements tied to those exposures, using a standard template.
para 12.2.4

Quarterly disclosures are due within 8 weeks of period-end, interim (half-year) disclosures within 3 months, and annual disclosures within 4 months, generally aligned with publication of the related financial statements.
para 9.3.7 (table)
A failure to meet any disclosure requirement is a criminal offence for every director, chief executive and manager of the AI, and can also count against the bank's continuing authorization.

Before publication, the board (or a delegated committee) and senior management must have the disclosures reviewed by staff independent of those who prepared them, to check they are not false or misleading.
Disclosure statements must be lodged with the HKMA before publication and e-mailed to the HKMA's register within 3 working days after publication.
rg: Read para 12.2.4 (the new crypto disclosure items) and the section 4 penalties first; the detailed Part III templates/tables guidance can be skimmed unless preparing the actual filing.

t: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
sl: HKMA · CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (2025)
s: CR-G-8 governs how AIs measure and limit large exposures and risk concentrations. This revision inserts a dedicated set of rules, Division 5A, for valuing cryptoasset-related exposures for large-exposure purposes, separate from the general rules used for other counterparty-credit-risk and non-counterparty-credit-risk exposures.
w: This determines how much of a client's or counterparty's crypto-linked exposure counts against the bank's concentration limits, which affects how much crypto business the bank can safely do with any one counterparty.
k: Cryptoasset-related exposures are valued for large-exposure purposes under a new, separate set of rules (Division 5A of Part 7 of the BELR), rather than the general divisions used for other exposures.
Before applying the crypto valuation rules, an AI must first pin down the specific counterparty (or connected group) the exposure relates to.
para 2.8.9

Which specific rule applies to a given crypto exposure depends on how it's defined under the BELR, whether the asset is classed Group 1a/1b/2a/2b, and whether it sits in the banking book or trading book.
para 2.8.10
For some crypto exposures, the AI must reuse the valuation figure it already calculated under the Capital Rules rather than doing a separate calculation for large-exposure purposes.
para 2.8.11
Because crypto markets and technology are still evolving, HKMA can give an individual AI written instructions to use a different valuation method for its crypto exposures than the one in the rules.
para 2.8.12
rg: Read paras 2.8.8-2.8.12 (the new crypto valuation division); the surrounding general large-exposure material can be skimmed if already familiar with CR-G-8.

t: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
sl: HKMA · CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets (2025)
s: CRP-1 is a new HKMA guideline that sorts a bank's cryptoasset holdings into capital-treatment groups. Group 1 covers tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that meet strict conditions, and gets treated like the underlying traditional asset. Group 2 covers everything else and needs much heavier capital backing, with a limited sub-category (Group 2a) recognised for hedging. The module takes effect from 1 January 2026 and sits alongside the Banking (Capital) Rules, which prevail if the two conflict.
w: This module decides how much capital the bank must hold against any crypto exposure it books, and it forces a conservative default and an HKMA-notification step for anything new — both are matters compliance must build a process around before 1 January 2026.
k: Cryptoassets split into Group 1 (meets four classification conditions) and Group 2 (does not); Group 1 splits further into 1a (tokenised traditional assets) and 1b (stablecoins with an effective peg mechanism).
The rules and this module start applying from 1 January 2026.
para 1.4.1
Any cryptoasset exposure an AI already holds before that date defaults to the most conservative bucket (Group 2b) until the HKMA agrees a different classification.
para 1.4.2
Before acquiring a brand-new type of cryptoasset, an AI has to tell the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees to a better classification.
para 2.1.2
If a cryptoasset later stops meeting its group's conditions, the AI has to move it straight back to Group 2b.
para 2.1.3

For a stablecoin to qualify as Group 1b, its reserve assets must, even in stress, always be worth at least the total amount holders could redeem, must be high quality, liquid, currency-matched to the peg, and independently audited at least once a year.
A stablecoin issued under the HKMA's own stablecoin licensing regime is automatically treated as meeting the extra safeguards needed for permissionless-blockchain assets to qualify for Group 1.
para 2.6.3

To count as Group 2a (limited hedging recognition), a cryptoasset needs deep, liquid markets: average market capitalisation of at least HKD 78 billion and a 10%-trimmed average daily trading volume of at least HKD 390 million over the prior year.
para 3.1.1
AIs must keep full records of how they classified each cryptoasset and hand them to the HKMA on request.
para 2.1.1
rg: Read paras 1.3-1.4 (classification overview and effective date) and 2.2 (stablecoin redemption/reserve conditions) first; the abbreviations annex can be skipped.

t: Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (draft, consequential and other amendments)
sl: HKMA · Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (2025)
s: This is a draft update to the statutory code of practice under the Banking Ordinance that guides how AIs apply parts of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) -- large-exposure limits, connected-party rules and related concepts. Despite being bundled into the HKMA's cryptoasset prudential-standard consultation, the drafted text itself covers unrelated topics: what counts as a reliable third-party market data provider, what security is acceptable to a prudent banker (including life insurance policies), how to calculate an employee's annual salary for staff-lending limits, self-use land, and when two counterparties are treated as 'economically dependent' for large-exposure grouping. No cryptoasset-specific provision appears in the text supplied.
w: Bundled procedurally with the cryptoasset package but not itself cryptoasset-relevant; compliance can note it and deprioritise it against the LM-1/MR-1/MR-2/CRP-1 drafts.
k: A bank should judge a third-party market-data provider's reliability by its market standing, financial strength and service capacity, track record, and back-up arrangements, plus any other factor the bank considers relevant.
para 3(2), p.1

A life insurance policy can count as acceptable security if written by a Hong Kong-authorized insurer, the insurer or its parent holds at least a BBB- rating (or equivalent), and it is valued at the lower of surrender value or 75% of cash value, or a more conservative internal valuation.
para 4(3), p.6

An employee's annual salary for staff-lending-limit purposes should add basic salary, other fixed payments and benefits, and estimated performance-based pay for the year, but exclude variable bonuses and non-monetary benefits like medical insurance.
para 5(2), p.6

Two counterparties are 'economically dependent' -- and so grouped for large-exposure limits -- if, among other tests, 50% or more of one party's income or spending, or of its output, flows to or from the other, or if one has guaranteed the other's exposure to a degree that could cause its own default.
rg: Skim only; no cryptoasset content was found in the supplied text.

t: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
sl: HKMA · Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (2025)
s: This is a draft statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance for locally incorporated AIs, adding a new section 6 on cryptoasset exposures to the market-risk capital module. It tells banks how to calculate the market-risk capital charge for cryptoasset positions under each of the three approaches the module already covers: the simplified standardised approach, the full standardised approach, and internal models. Tokenised assets that mirror a traditional asset (group 1a) and stablecoins referencing traditional assets (group 1b) are generally mapped onto the same risk factors as the assets they represent, so netting and hedging against the traditional asset is allowed. A separate, harsher, standalone capital charge applies to less traditional 'group 2a' cryptoassets, and internal models cannot be used for them at all.
w: Determines how much market-risk capital a trading or dealing desk must hold against any cryptoasset position, and confirms that holding cryptoassets removes access to the small-book capital exemption.
k: A bank should follow CRP-1 (a separate module) to first classify each cryptoasset into group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b before applying this module's rules.
footnote 79

For the simplified standardised approach, a group 1 cryptoasset is converted to HKD at the current spot price and mapped to the same risk category as the traditional asset it represents; hedging and netting between a token and its underlying traditional asset is recognised for group 1a, and between a stablecoin and the asset it references for group 1b.

Under the full standardised (sensitivities-based) approach, a tokenised instrument's risk exposure must be mapped onto exactly the risk factors used for the conventional asset (or reference asset) it mirrors, applying matching sensitivities.
para 6.1.4
Internal models cannot be used at all for instruments referencing group 2 cryptoassets.
para 6.1.9

Group 2a cryptoassets (which meet a separate hedging-recognition test in CRP-1) get their own standalone capital charge under modified versions of the simplified or full standardised approach; a bank cannot net or offset a group 2a cryptoasset position across different exchanges.

For each group 2a cryptoasset, a bank works out a net long/short position and applies a capital requirement equal to the full value of that net position, but only 65% of any offsetting long-vs-short amount is recognised.
A bank with any cryptoasset exposure cannot use the small-portfolio, de-minimis exemption from market-risk capital rules that would otherwise be available.
footnote 80

Group 2b cryptoassets are not subject to a market-risk capital charge at all -- instead they get the very conservative combined credit/market/CVA-risk treatment (a 1,250% risk weight) under a different section of the capital rules.
footnote 81
rg: Read section 6 in full (pp.152-157); it is the only cryptoasset-specific material -- the rest of the module restates existing non-crypto market-risk mechanics.

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A(I): Divisions A to F and L - Market Risk Capital Charge
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A(I): Divisions A to F… (2025)
s: This part of the market-risk return covers the sensitivities-based method (Divisions A-F) and the simplified standardized approach (Division L) for trading-book positions. It adds group 2a cryptoasset (broadly, stablecoin-type) positions as a new risk bucket: banks are instructed to report the highest of three correlation-scenario capital charges for that bucket regardless of charges elsewhere, add a separate curvature-risk charge for price moves in those tokens, and, under the simplified method, report each group 2a token and its hedges on its own line.
w: This is where a bank's trading-book stablecoin-type exposure turns into a specific, separately-tracked capital charge every month, on top of whatever the bank already reports for other market risk.
k: Group 2a crypto positions form their own risk bucket, and the capital charge reported for it should be the highest of the three prescribed correlation-scenario results, kept separate from charges on other risk types.
para 18, p.10
A price-curvature-risk capital charge specific to group 2a token price movements should also be calculated and reported, on top of the correlation-scenario charge.
paras 44-47, p.10
Where a fund (CIS) exposure includes a group 2a crypto slice, that slice's capital requirement should be captured in this same section.
para 48, p.10
Under the simplified standardized approach (Division L), each group 2a token should be reported on its own line, together with its associated hedging positions.
Cryptoasset exposures more generally should also follow the Part 12 crypto rules of the Banking (Capital) Rules in addition to this form's own instructions.
paras 13, 73, 102 (recurring cross-reference)
rg: Read paras 18-19 (bucket treatment), the curvature-risk paragraphs around p.21, and Division L paras on group 2a reporting; skip the non-crypto risk-class mechanics if pressed for time.

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIa) - Return of Capital Adequacy Ratio, Part IIIa - Basic Approach to Credit Risk
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIa) - Return of Capital… (2025)
s: This draft splits the credit-risk basic-approach section of the Capital Adequacy Ratio return into two halves: a Division A1 for ordinary exposures and a brand-new Division A2 dedicated to crypto holdings. Banks using the basic approach must now separately identify holdings in government-issued, bank-issued and other-issuer group 1a tokens, plus group 1b tokens, and rank their five largest crypto positions by risk-weighted amount. It also tells banks where to instead book trading-book crypto derivative and repo-style exposures -- mostly the new market-risk return or the dedicated crypto capital form -- so nothing is counted twice. The version stamp is still a placeholder, showing the instructions had not been finalised when captured.
w: Compliance needs to confirm which legal entity in the group already holds crypto and therefore must file the new template from day one, versus which entities can rely on the six-month grace period -- getting this wrong risks a late or wrongly-formatted regulatory return.
k: A new sub-section (Division A2) is added purely for cryptoasset exposures, kept apart from the existing non-crypto exposure section (Division A1).
para 4, p.2
Government-issued, other-authorized-institution-issued and other-issuer group 1a crypto holdings each get their own reporting line, and group 1b holdings get a separate line again.
Banks should total up risk-weighted amounts per individual token and list only their five largest group-1 crypto positions by that measure.
para 47, C.3, p.17

Crypto assets held in the trading book for market-risk or repo-style purposes go to the new market-risk return (MA(BS)3A) instead, with any redemption-default risk-weighted amount routed to the dedicated crypto capital form.
para 13(b)-(c), p.4
The form and instructions still carry a placeholder issue date rather than a fixed one, showing this was an unfinalised draft when consulted on.
footer, e.g. p.1

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A - Return of Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge - General Instructions
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A - Return of Market… (2025)

The crypto-specific detail lives in the Part I and Part II division instructions, registered separately; this introduction sets the reporting basis, frequency and who must file, which apply equally to the new crypto items added elsewhere in the form.

k: The market-risk part of the return is completed monthly by each locally incorporated authorized institution, except that institutions exempted under the de-minimis criteria complete only a reduced annual set of divisions instead.
paras 1, 4, p.1

A footnote records that the standards were rolled out first as a reporting-only requirement on a quarterly basis no earlier than 1 July 2024, moving to full monthly reporting no earlier than 1 January 2025 -- a general-standard timeline, not crypto-specific.

Banks exempted from market risk under the de-minimis test still complete Divisions G to K once a year, as at end-December, purely for the HKMA to re-check their exemption status.
para 4, p.1
Part II (CVA) is filed by banks with covered transactions under section 322J of the Banking (Capital) Rules; a bank with none still files a nil return.
para 5, p.1

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIc) - Return of Capital Adequacy Ratio, Part IIIc - Internal Ratings-based Approach
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIc) - Return of Capital… (2025)
s: This part of the return covers banks that use their own internal models (the IRB approach) to measure credit risk. The draft adds a brand-new memorandum form, IRB_CRYPTO, that pulls out and separately shows the crypto slice of exposures already reported in the bank's other IRB forms. Banking-book group 1a crypto holdings are split further by the type of traditional asset that was tokenised, and group 1b holdings get their own reporting logic. Investment-fund (CIS) exposures that include crypto also get a special risk-weighting rule cross-referenced here.
w: IRB-approach banks need a new control to feed the memorandum IRB_CRYPTO form correctly from existing IRB systems, since it is an add-on reconciliation rather than a fresh data source.
k: A new memorandum form, IRB_CRYPTO, should show the crypto share of exposures already captured under the bank's other IRB forms (IRB_CSB, IRB_SLSLOT, IRB_RETAIL, IRB_CIS, IRB_OTHER).
para 29, Section C, p.8
IRB_CRYPTO covers only group 1 crypto exposures held in the banking book under the IRB approach, split into on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet amounts.
para 42, C.6, p.18

Group 1a crypto exposures should be broken down by the kind of traditional asset that was tokenised, and separately flagged if in default or subject to the 1.25 asset-value-correlation multiplier for financial-institution counterparties.
item 1, p.18
Where a fund (CIS) investment includes group 1b or group 2 crypto exposures among its underlying assets, a specific risk-weighting method applies to that crypto slice.
Non-crypto trading-book crypto derivatives and repo-style deals are again routed to the market-risk return, matching the other Part III forms.
para 24, p.6
rg: Read paras 29 and 42-52 (Section C.6) on Form IRB_CRYPTO; skip the general IRB-class tables which are largely unchanged.

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)28 - Return of Large Exposures
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)28 - Return of Large… (2025)
s: This return tracks a bank's exposure concentration to a single counterparty or group of connected counterparties under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules, filed quarterly. Its crypto-specific additions are two reporting-column clarifications: certain crypto-related exposures unconnected to counterparty credit or default risk can be left out of the exempted-exposure figure, and default-risk exposures from crypto derivatives or repo-style deals must be included in the default-risk-exposure column.
w: Large-exposure/single-counterparty-limit monitoring must now correctly fold in crypto derivative and repo-style default-risk exposures, and correctly exclude the carved-out crypto amounts, or the reported concentration figure will be wrong.
k: AIs report their large-exposure positions as at each quarter-end, with submission due within one month of quarter-end.
para 4, p.1

Crypto-related exposures that are not tied to counterparty credit or default risk do not have to be counted in the exempted-exposure-before-CRM figure, alongside similar carve-outs for commodity and foreign-currency exposures.
para 12, p.4-5

The default-risk-exposure column should include default-risk exposures arising from crypto derivative contracts or crypto securities-financing transactions, alongside conventional derivative/SFT exposures.
para 32 (renumbered 31), p.9-10
rg: Read para 12 (exemption carve-out) and para 31/32 (default-risk column); skip the general large-exposure mechanics which are unchanged.

t: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)26 - Return of Stable Funding Position of an Authorized Institution
sl: HKMA · Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)26 - Return of Stable… (2025)
s: This return measures a bank's stable-funding position: category 1 institutions report the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) quarter-end, and category 2A institutions report an average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) over the quarter. Both add new memorandum items breaking out cryptoasset-related amounts: tokenised customer claims counted as available/core stable funding, and crypto assets counted as required stable funding, cross-referencing a dedicated SPM guidance annex (LM-1, Annex 3).
w: Treasury/ALM functions get a new quarterly disclosure obligation isolating how much of the bank's funding position comes from tokenised claims or crypto assets -- a number the board and regulator can now track separately from the headline ratio.
k: Category 1 institutions calculate the NSFR on the quarter-end date, and the return as a whole is filed quarterly.
paras 2, 4, p.1-2

Category 1 institutions should additionally report the total weighted amount of tokenised customer/counterparty claims counted as available stable funding, and of cryptoassets counted as required stable funding, in new memorandum items 3(a) and 3(b).
para 14, p.5
Category 2A institutions report an average Core Funding Ratio calculated over each calendar month of the quarter.
para 14 (renumbered 15), p.5-6
Category 2A institutions should additionally report tokenised-claim and cryptoasset amounts feeding their average core funding ratio, in new memorandum items 4(a) and 4(b).
para 14 (renumbered 15) area, p.6

The completion instructions define 'cryptoasset' by cross-reference to the Banking (Capital) Rules and point banks to a dedicated annex of SPM module LM-1 for the funding treatment of crypto exposures.
footnote 7, p.5
AIs must send the HKMA the complete return, including the new crypto memorandum items, once every quarter, no later than one month after that quarter ends.
para 4 (Reporting frequency and submission timeline), p.2
rg: Read paras 12-15 for the new crypto memorandum items and para 46-49 area for filing frequency; the rest of the NSFR/CFR mechanics is largely unchanged.

t: Circular to licensed virtual asset trading platform operators on custody of virtual assets
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset trading platform operators on custody of… (2025)
s: This SFC circular sets minimum custody rules that every SFC-licensed virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) operator and its associated entities must follow, issued after overseas custody-related cyber incidents and an SFC review that found some Hong Kong operators fell short. It covers who in senior management is responsible, how cold wallets should be built and run, use of outside wallet providers, round-the-clock threat monitoring, and staff training, with sample 'good practice' examples. The rules apply immediately and will also form the baseline for the coming licensed virtual-asset custodian regime.
w: These are custody rules for trading platforms, not a direct bank duty, but a compliance head should use them as the checklist for vetting any custody partner -- offline key generation in an HSM, blocking blind signing, round-the-clock monitoring -- since they also preview the coming statutory custodian regime.
k: A platform operator should put someone in charge of custody matters -- a Responsible Officer or Manager-in-Charge -- for everything this circular covers.
Section I, para 1, p.3
Seeds and private keys should, where practical, be created offline and kept in a secure setting such as a certified hardware security module (HSM).
Section II, para 2, p.2
Cold wallets should avoid smart contracts on public blockchains, to cut down online attack routes.
Section II, para 5, p.3
Once a client withdrawal is signed, its destination address cannot be changed before it reaches the blockchain; cold-wallet transfers need whitelist controls.
Section III, paras 6 & 9, pp.3-4
Seeds and private keys should be created and kept safe on offline (air-gapped) cold-wallet devices.
Section III, para 7, p.4
Blind signing -- approving a transaction without seeing its details -- must be blocked; transaction details must be shown in readable form before anyone signs manually.
Section III, para 11 and footnote 6, p.4
Operators should set up a security operations centre or similar function that watches for threats around the clock, including holidays.
Section V, paras 18 & 24, pp.5-6
Before using an outside wallet provider, operators need to vet it, keep reviewing it, run independent code checks, and test its disaster-recovery plans.
Section IV, paras 12-17, pp.4-5
These rules apply right away and should feed into operators' annual outside compliance and technology review.
'Way forward', p.7
