t: Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This is HKMA's detailed operating rulebook for licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance, expanding on the minimum criteria in Schedule 2. It sets granular expectations for reserve asset backing, composition, segregation and disclosure; issuance, redemption and distribution controls; financial resources; a full risk management stack covering credit/liquidity/market, technology (including detailed private-key and wallet controls), operational and reputation risk; incident management, business continuity and wind-down planning; corporate governance and fitness-and-propriety; and business conduct including white papers and complaints handling. It distinguishes statutory 'must' requirements from supervisory 'should' expectations throughout, and in several places exempts a licensee that is itself an authorized institution from requirements that would otherwise apply to it.
w: This is the operating-level checklist HKMA will use to supervise any stablecoin issuer, including a bank that becomes one, and it also sets the benchmark compliance should use to assess a third-party stablecoin issuer's reserve, custody and redemption practices before the bank relies on, distributes, or accepts that coin.
k: A licensee must ensure the market value of reserve assets backing each coin type never falls below the par value of coins in circulation, using a prudent valuation approach with reconciliation, and even temporarily frozen or restricted coins must remain fully backed.

Eligible reserve assets are limited to cash, bank deposits of no more than 3 months, high-quality marketable debt securities of no more than 1 year residual maturity, overnight reverse repos collateralised by such securities, dedicated investment funds holding only such assets, or other HKMA-acceptable assets; tokenised versions of these are allowed if the issuer can show they meet the same quality bar.
Reserve assets must generally be held in the same currency as the coin they back, with cross-currency mismatches allowed only with HKMA's prior written approval.

Reserve assets must be held under an independent-legal-opinion-backed trust arrangement, safe-kept by a qualified custodian (a licensed bank or an HKMA-acceptable custodian), and the issuer stays primarily accountable for their safekeeping even if a custodian or investment manager is used.
No interest or interest-like return may be paid on coins based on holding period, par value or market value, though non-interest marketing incentives are allowed.

Issuers must submit daily internal statements on reserve composition and coin circulation to HKMA on request, report to HKMA and publish key reserve information weekly, and have an acceptable independent auditor attest to full backing at least at period-end and one random business day, filed with HKMA within one month.

Valid redemption requests must be honoured within 1 business day absent HKMA consent to a longer period, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions, and an independent legal opinion confirming holders' redemption and pro-rata claim rights must be filed with HKMA.

An issuer that engages third parties to distribute its coins must ensure they are 'permitted offerors' where they offer coins in Hong Kong, and must due-diligence and risk-assess distributors and secondary-market liquidity providers.

Customer on-boarding and account operations must use effective identity verification and (generally) two-factor authentication, with transfers restricted to pre-registered, customer-named bank accounts and wallet addresses, and controls against VPN-based location spoofing to prevent unlawful cross-border offering.

Private/seed key management must cover the full lifecycle (generation, distribution, storage, usage, backup, recovery, destruction) with elevated air-gapped, HSM-based controls and multi-party authorisation for 'Significant Seeds/Private Keys' tied to contract deployment, role/minter management, or large-scale minting/burning.
Smart contracts must be independently audited at least annually and whenever redeployed or upgraded, and each coin's token standard, ledger and full contract architecture must be documented.
A licensee needs three independent lines of defence (business units, risk/compliance, internal audit), each with adequate authority, resources and a direct Board or senior-management reporting line.
rg: Read section 2 (reserve assets) and section 3 (issuance/redemption/distribution) closely for counterparty due diligence purposes; read 6.5 (technology and key management) closely if assessing custody quality; sections 6.6-6.8, 7 and 8 can be skimmed for headings and modal verbs unless the bank itself is applying for a licence.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (2025)
s: This is HKMA's finalised, binding AML/CFT rulebook for entities licensed under the Stablecoins Ordinance to issue stablecoins, issued jointly under that Ordinance and the AMLO. It covers institutional risk assessment, AML governance (compliance officer, money laundering reporting officer, independent audit, training), detailed customer due diligence including on wallets and third-party distributors, ongoing transaction and secondary-market monitoring, a full Travel Rule regime for stablecoin transfers between institutions and to/from unhosted wallets, sanctions/terrorist-financing screening, suspicious transaction reporting, and record-keeping (generally five years). Compliance is enforced through both the Stablecoins Ordinance and the AMLO, and failures can also jeopardise a licensee's ongoing eligibility under the Ordinance's minimum criteria.
w: This is the binding, in-force AML/CFT rulebook for any bank-affiliated stablecoin issuer, and its Travel Rule, wallet-risk and screening standards are also the benchmark a compliance head should apply when assessing third-party stablecoin issuers, custodial wallet providers and distribution partners as counterparties.
k: A licensee must run an institutional money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk assessment covering customer, country, product/service and delivery-channel risk factors, approved by senior management and kept up to date.
paras 2.2-2.3
AML/CFT systems must include compliance management with a named Compliance Officer and Money Laundering Reporting Officer, an independent audit function, staff screening and ongoing training.

Customer due diligence is required before establishing a business relationship or before any occasional transaction (e.g. issuance/redemption) of HK$8,000 or more, and must identify beneficial owners holding more than 25% control.

Enhanced due diligence, including source of wealth/funds checks and senior management approval, is required for Hong Kong, non-Hong Kong and international-organisation politically exposed persons presenting higher risk.
para 4.23

For customer wallets, the issuer must confirm wallet ownership/control and, for custodial wallets, run due diligence on the custodian; for higher-risk unhosted wallets it must screen the wallet address and may apply enhanced monitoring or transaction limits.

Ongoing monitoring must cover both individual customer transactions and, more broadly, stablecoins already in circulation, using risk-based technology (e.g. blockchain analytics) to trace sources/destinations and flag illicit or sanctioned wallet addresses.

Unless a licensee can prove its screening and monitoring controls are effective against illicit use – particularly for peer-to-peer unhosted-wallet transfers – HKMA expects the identity of every stablecoin holder to be verified by the licensee, a supervised institution, or a reliable third party.
para 5.11

The Travel Rule requires an ordering institution to obtain and securely, immediately transmit originator and recipient information for stablecoin transfers of HK$8,000 or more (a reduced data set below that threshold), and a licensee must verify the identity of an originator for transfers at or above that threshold.
A licensee is barred from executing stablecoin transfers where the counterparty institution is a shell bank or a shell virtual-asset service provider.
para 6.39

For transfers to or from unhosted wallets of the licensee's own customers, the licensee must still collect originator/recipient details from that customer, though peer-to-peer transfers between unhosted wallets of non-customers are exempt from this specific requirement (ongoing circulation monitoring still applies).
A licensee must screen customers and beneficial owners against terrorist/sanctions databases at both issuance and redemption, and screen all parties to a stablecoin transfer before executing it.
para 7.5

Suspicious transaction reports must be filed with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit as soon as reasonably practicable once knowledge or suspicion arises, and 'tipping off' a customer about a report (even one raised only internally) is a separate offence.
paras 8.1-8.2
rg: For a compliance head, focus on Chapters 4 (CDD, especially wallet risk paras 4.33-4.40), 6 (stablecoin transfers/Travel Rule) and 7-9 (sanctions, STR, record-keeping); Chapter 3's generic governance content overlaps with standard AML guidelines and can be skimmed.

t: LCQ10: Promoting virtual asset development
sl: FSTB · LCQ10: Promoting virtual asset development (2025)
s: A written Legislative Council reply reviews progress across virtual-asset licensing, tokenisation and AML cooperation, in response to questions about licensing speed and international competition. It confirms 11 VATPs are licensed with 9 more applications pending, and describes the SFC's swift licensing process (introduced June 2024, expanded January 2025). It notes SFC circulars from November 2023 on tokenised securities, the 2024 authorisation of a retail tokenised gold product, and the first-in-Asia-Pacific authorisation of three retail tokenised money market funds in Q1 2025, which had grown to over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025. It also summarises Hong Kong's FATF standing and international AML cooperation channels.
w: Confirms two SFC circulars (November 2023) that already govern intermediaries handling tokenised securities and tokenised SFC-authorised products - directly relevant if the bank distributes or advises on tokenised funds or securities today.
k: As of early July 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 digital-asset trading platforms and was processing nine further applications
reply (1), para 2

The SFC issued a 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities' and a 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' in November 2023 to guide intermediaries on tokenisation risks
reply (2), para 2
In 2024 the SFC authorised Hong Kong's first retail tokenised investment product, a gold token offering fractional ownership of physical gold
reply (2), para 3
In Q1 2025 the SFC authorised three retail tokenised money market funds, the first in the Asia-Pacific region, which held over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025
reply (2), para 3
Hong Kong's AML/CFT regime is recognised by FATF as overall compliant and effective, and Hong Kong participates in FATF's Virtual Assets Contact Group
reply (3), para 2
rg: Read replies (1) and (2) for licensing progress and tokenisation circulars; reply (3) on AML cooperation can be skimmed.

t: Implementation of regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers
sl: HKMA · Implementation of regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers (2025)
s: HKMA press release announcing that as the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers took effect on 1 August 2025, it published the finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and accompanying consultation conclusions, the finalised AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and its consultation conclusions, plus two Explanatory Notes covering licensing/application procedures and transitional arrangements for pre-existing issuers. The attached Supervisory Guideline sets detailed ongoing requirements on reserve assets, issuance/redemption/distribution, financial resources, risk management (including extensive technology/private-key controls), corporate governance and business conduct. The AML/CFT Guideline sets customer due diligence, wallet risk management, the HKD8,000 Travel Rule threshold, sanctions screening, STR and five-year record-keeping requirements. The Explanatory Notes define scope terms (stablecoin, regulated stablecoin activity, permitted offeror), the application process and minimum criteria, and the three-month/six-month/closing-down transitional timeline for issuers operating before 1 August 2025. As of the press release date no licence had yet been issued.
w: Brings the Stablecoins Ordinance regime into effect and sets the application timetable; directly relevant if the bank is a market participant handling or considering issuing licensed stablecoins, and it sets the register the bank should check when doing counterparty due diligence on any stablecoin issuer.
k: The regulatory regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect on 1 August 2025, together with the finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and the AML/CFT Guideline, both gazetted the same day.
para 1 (main press release)
Parties interested in applying for a licence were encouraged to contact HKMA by 31 August 2025; those wanting to be considered early were asked to submit applications by 30 September 2025.
paras 5-6
It is an offence under the SO to falsely claim to be a licensee or an applicant; as of the press release date no licence had been issued.
paras 7-8

A licensee must keep the reserve assets' market value at or above the par value of all outstanding specified stablecoins in circulation, including any that are frozen or blacklisted, at every point in time; holding some excess collateral as a cushion is expected.
Supervisory Guideline paras 2.2.1-2.2.3

Reserve assets are restricted to a defined 'eligible assets' list (cash, short-term bank deposits, qualifying marketable debt securities, overnight reverse repos, dedicated investment funds, or HKMA-acceptable equivalents); tokenised representations of eligible assets can qualify if the licensee demonstrates no added technology/operational risk.
Supervisory Guideline para 2.3.1-2.3.2

Reserve assets must be held via effective trust arrangements (independent trustee or declaration of trust), segregated from the licensee's own assets and protected from other creditors, with an independent legal opinion on effectiveness submitted to HKMA.
Supervisory Guideline paras 2.5.1-2.5.2

Valid redemption requests must be honoured, generally within one business day, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions; any delay beyond one business day requires the Monetary Authority's prior written consent.
Supervisory Guideline paras 3.3.3, 6.8.21

A licensee must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up share capital (or an HKMA-approved equivalent amount of financial resources), reserved solely for its stablecoin business and off-limits for transactions with related parties.
Supervisory Guideline para 5.1.1; Explanatory Note on Licensing para 3.3.2

For Significant Seeds/Private Keys -- those tied to smart-contract deployment or upgrades, role management, or large-scale minting/burning -- the licensee must create, keep and use them inside an air-gapped setup physically in Hong Kong (or another HKMA-acceptable location), never on a system connected to the internet; a cloud-based HSM will not usually meet this bar.
Supervisory Guideline para 6.5.7(iv), (vii); Consultation Conclusions para 2.6.3

The HKMA generally wants at least a third of the Board to be independent non-executive directors (INEDs), though this expectation is waived where the licensee is itself a bank (an authorized institution), which instead follows the Banking Ordinance.
Supervisory Guideline para 7.1.3

For stablecoin transfers (the Travel Rule), the HKD8,000 threshold determines the scope of required originator/recipient data and identity verification; transfers to/from unhosted wallets of non-customer holders are exempt from the transfer-specific data requirements but still subject to ongoing circulation monitoring.
AML/CFT Guideline paras 6.5-6.6, 6.41-6.42

Unless a licensee can demonstrate to HKMA's satisfaction that risk-mitigating measures are effective, the identity of every individual stablecoin holder (including non-customers) must be verified by the licensee, a supervised FI/VASP, or a reliable third party — a notably stricter default than typical VA intermediary AML regimes.
AML/CFT Guideline para 5.11
rg: Read the main press release in full (short), then the Supervisory Guideline sections 1-5 (reserve assets, issuance/redemption, financial resources) and 6.5 (technology/key management) closely; AML/CFT Guideline chapters 4-6 (CDD, wallets, Travel Rule) and 9 (record-keeping) are the operational core. The two Consultation Conclusions documents mainly repeat the finalised Guidelines as annexes — skim only the Q&A sections (paras 2.x) for HKMA's interpretive clarifications, not the annexes.

page body

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on The Steadfast and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on The Steadfast and Sustainable Development of… (2025)
s: HKMA's Chief Executive pushes back on what he calls overhyped and speculative market enthusiasm for stablecoins, noting many prospective applicants he has met lack concrete use cases or technical capability, and reiterating that only a handful of licences will be issued. He confirms HKMA consulted the market on both the supervision and AML/CFT implementation guidelines and was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the final rules to include tighter AML requirements than the consultation drafts. He also announces that an Explanatory Note on the licence application process would follow the next week.
w: Signals that the final AML/CFT and supervision guidelines would be stricter on AML than the May 2025 consultation drafts, and confirms the exact date from which offering an unlicensed stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors becomes illegal – both directly relevant to any group entity distributing or dealing in stablecoins.
k: Many of the dozens of institutions that approached HKMA about stablecoin issuance had only conceptual proposals lacking concrete use cases, implementation plans or risk-management competence.
para 2
HKMA reiterates that only a handful of stablecoin issuer licences would be granted, meaning most applicants will be disappointed.
para 3

The Stablecoins Ordinance commencement on 1 August 2025 would make it illegal to offer any unlicensed fiat-referenced stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors or to actively market such an unlicensed coin to the Hong Kong public.
para 3

HKMA had consulted the market on both the supervision guideline and the AML/CFT guideline following passage of the Stablecoins Bill and was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the AML requirements in the final version to be stricter than in the consultation draft.
para 4 (Guarding Against Financial Risks section)
An Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers, covering how HKMA would accept and process applications, was announced for release the following week.
final paragraph

t: Gazettal of banking amendment rules to implement Basel cryptoassets standard
sl: HKMA · Gazettal of banking amendment rules to implement Basel cryptoassets… (2025)
s: The government gazetted three sets of amendment rules - to the Banking (Capital) Rules, Banking (Disclosure) Rules, and Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules - implementing the Basel Committee's prudential standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures. The rules take effect January 1, 2026, in line with the Basel Committee's global timetable, and also make other alignment amendments informed by industry feedback. They were tabled at LegCo on July 16, 2025.
w: This is a direct, binding prudential obligation for the bank as an authorised institution: capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules for cryptoasset exposures took effect 1 January 2026 and have applied since then; risk and finance teams should confirm their calculations and disclosures are already compliant.
k: Three amendment rules sets implement Basel Committee capital, disclosure and exposure-limit standards for banks' cryptoasset exposures
para 1, p.1
The amendment rules take effect on January 1, 2026, matching the Basel Committee's implementation timeline
para 2 and closing para, p.1
rg: Read in full; short notice, but confirms a hard compliance deadline for the bank's prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures.

t: Gazettal of rules: cryptoassets standard and other updates
sl: HKMA · Gazettal of rules: cryptoassets standard and other updates (2025)
s: This HKMA circular to all authorized institutions announces that the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025 were gazetted on 11 July 2025. These rules put in place the Basel Committee's prudential standard for cryptoasset exposures, plus related changes to disclosure and exposure limits, along with some other minor alignment changes. LegCo was due to receive these rules on 16 July 2025 for negative vetting, and, assuming that stage cleared, the rules were expected to start applying on 1 January 2026, in step with the Basel Committee's timeline.
w: This marked the formal legal milestone when the crypto capital, disclosure, and exposure-limit rules moved from consultation to gazetted subsidiary legislation, with a 1 January 2026 start date that has since arrived and passed -- the rules are now in force and banks should already be running the associated reporting and disclosure processes.
k: Three amendment rules were gazetted on 11 July 2025: the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
bullet list, p.1
The amendments mainly bring in the Basel Committee's capital standard for cryptoasset exposures, along with its related disclosure and exposure-limit requirements.

The rules were scheduled for tabling before LegCo on 16 July 2025, to start the negative-vetting process.
para 3, p.1
If that vetting process went through, the rules were expected to take effect on 1 January 2026, matching the Basel Committee's timeline.
para 3, p.1

t: SFC convenes second Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting

t: LCQ5: Promoting development of stablecoins
sl: FSTB · LCQ5: Promoting development of stablecoins (2025)
s: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury describes government plans to grow stablecoin use cases, attract global issuers, and consider offshore renminbi stablecoins. It confirms the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox (opened early 2024) is not a prerequisite for licensing, and that applicants with cross-border use cases must show a comprehensive compliance plan and confirm their business partners hold necessary regulatory approvals in relevant jurisdictions. It also notes the licensing regime allows pegs to different fiat currencies, not only the Hong Kong dollar.

t: Fintech Adoption: Progress and Future Directions
sl: HKMA · Fintech Adoption: Progress and Future Directions (2025)
s: This HKMA report presents results of a January 2025 Tech Maturity Stock-take covering 56 submissions from 58 authorized institutions, benchmarked against a 2022 baseline. It measures adoption of Regtech, Wealthtech, Greentech, Insurtech, artificial intelligence and distributed ledger technology, identifies implementation cost, novel-technology risk and integration as the top adoption challenges, and sets out HKMA's next-phase promotion plan built around AI, DLT and high-performance computing, underpinned by data excellence and cyber resilience. DLT-specific detail is limited to adoption statistics and general commentary; it is not a rulebook.
w: Gives a compliance head sector-wide DLT adoption benchmarks and HKMA's stated forward priorities (risk management and systems integration for tokenisation), useful for internal business cases but not itself a source of obligations.
k: DLT adoption among surveyed authorized institutions rose from 30% in 2022 to 45% in 2025, with many institutions moving from exploratory pilots to operational use.
One financial institution highlighted in the report uses DLT to provide tokenisation, issuance, distribution and custody services across the digital asset lifecycle.

HKMA's next-phase Fintech promotion names DLT as one of three priority technology enablers (with AI and high-performance computing), with a focus on risk management, resilient operations and systems integration as tokenisation initiatives are explored.
Top adoption challenges cited by authorized institutions include implementation cost (75%), risk of novel technology (73%) and integration with existing systems (71%).
rg: Skim Key Observations 1-2 (pp.10-14) for DLT/AI adoption figures and the Way Forward section (pp.19-22) for HKMA's stated priorities; detailed Regtech/Wealthtech figures are not digital-asset relevant.

t: Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This note explains how HKMA will license stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). It defines a 'stablecoin', a 'specified stablecoin' (currently only fiat-referenced coins), and when issuing or offering one counts as a regulated activity requiring a licence. It walks through the minimum licensing criteria in Schedule 2 - corporate status, capital, reserve asset segregation and backing, redemption rights, fitness of directors and managers, risk management, AML/CFT, disclosure via a white paper, complaint handling, a ban on paying interest, and recovery/wind-down planning. It also sets out the application process, HKMA's supervisory powers over a troubled licensee, and the grounds and process for licence revocation or suspension.
w: This is the master rulebook for anyone the bank might deal with as a stablecoin issuer, and for the bank itself if it or an affiliate ever considers issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin under its own AI status. It sets the baseline the bank's due diligence on any stablecoin counterparty should be checked against, especially reserve segregation, redemption rights, and permitted-offeror status.
k: A stablecoin is a cryptographically secured digital value token that acts as a medium of exchange or store of value, is transferable electronically, runs on a distributed ledger, and claims to hold a stable value against one or more assets; central bank money, securities, SVF float and bank deposits are carved out.
Only 'specified stablecoins' - currently those referencing one or more official currencies (fiat-referenced stablecoins) - fall inside the licensing perimeter for now.

Issuing a specified stablecoin in Hong Kong, or issuing one anywhere that is pegged even partly to the Hong Kong dollar, is a regulated activity requiring a licence, and doing so without one, or holding oneself out as doing so, is an offence.

A licensee may only let a defined list of 'permitted offerors' distribute its coins - itself, an authorized institution, an SVF licensee, an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or an SFC Type 1 licensed corporation.
An applicant must be either a Hong Kong-incorporated company or an authorized institution; other foreign entities must set up a local subsidiary to apply.
Non-bank applicants need at least HKD25 million in paid-up capital or MA-approved equivalent financial resources, which cannot be used for dealings with related parties.

Reserve assets backing each type of coin must be segregated, held under a trust arrangement backed by independent legal opinion, kept in an amount whose value never falls below the circulating coins' par value, with a buffer for risk, audited regularly by an independent auditor, and disclosed to the public.
Holders have a right to redeem at par, normally processed within one business day, and licensees must publicly disclose fees, conditions, mechanics and timing of redemption.

Chief executives, directors, the stablecoin manager and controllers must be fit and proper with relevant knowledge and experience; the HKMA looks for at least a third of the Board to consist of independent non-executive directors, and generally wants to give consent before they take up post (not required for an authorized institution's own appointees).

Licensees must run a full risk management programme covering governance, credit/liquidity/market risk, technology risk, operational risk, reputation risk, and incident/business continuity/exit planning.
Licensees must publish a white paper covering the issuer, the coin, reserve management, issuance/redemption mechanics, technology and risks, before offering coins to the public.
Stablecoins must not carry any interest, return or yield tied to holding period, par value or market value.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (definitions and scope) and Chapter 3 (minimum criteria, especially reserve assets 3.4 and redemption 3.5) closely; Chapters 4-7 (process, powers, revocation) can be skimmed except section headings, and Annex B's document checklist is only relevant if the bank itself applies.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the Joint FATF-MONEYVAL Plenary, 12-13 June 2025
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities -… (2025)

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in… (2025)
s: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the SFC jointly asked for public comment (due 29 August 2025) on a revised plan to license providers who 'deal' in virtual assets (VAs), replacing the narrower 2024 proposal that only covered VA over-the-counter (OTC) trading. Feedback on the earlier plan showed the industry includes far more business types than physical coin shops -- ATMs, broker-dealers, digital-only platforms, payment firms and card networks -- serving both retail and institutional clients, and flagged a need for custody rules the first proposal lacked. Under the new plan, anyone dealing in VAs as a business (buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from VA price swings) would need SFC licensing or registration, covering everything from simple conversions to complex brokerage, block trading, advice and asset management, whether done in person or online. Banks and stored value facility (SVF) operators would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, echoing how banks' securities business is already split between the two regulators; HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers dealing only in their own coin issuance and redemption would be exempt. There is no proposed transition period for existing providers -- the rules would apply fully from day one, so the paper urges firms already in the business to contact the SFC or HKMA early to avoid having to stop trading.
w: This proposal names banks directly: a bank offering VA dealing services would have to register with the SFC while the HKMA acts as its day-to-day supervisor, mirroring how bank securities business already works -- compliance should keep watching how this consultation turns into law.
k: Anyone dealing in VAs as a business -- buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from price movements -- would need an SFC licence or registration; banks and SVFs would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, which would supervise them day-to-day.
Stablecoin issuers already licensed by the HKMA would not need a separate VA dealing licence for issuing or redeeming their own coins in the primary market.
para 1.10, p.8

The plan covers both simple conversions between VAs or between VA and cash, and more complex work such as brokerage, block trades, advice and asset management, done through shops or platforms; pure peer-to-peer trades with no middleman are excluded.
A VA dealer that lets a third party hold client VAs on its behalf must use a VA custodian licensed or registered in Hong Kong -- a topic of a separate, related consultation launched the same day.
para 2.13, p.5

Applicants other than banks must be incorporated or registered in Hong Kong, keep a permanent local office suitable for record-keeping, and name at least two officers -- SFC-approved for most firms, HKMA-approved for banks -- who are personally responsible for compliance.

Proposed capital rules for non-bank applicants: at least $5 million in paid-up share capital, up to $3 million in required liquid capital depending on the business model, plus spare liquid capital equal to at least a year's running costs.

Licences would run indefinitely until cancelled, with no transition period for firms already operating -- the rules would bind everyone once in force, so existing providers are urged to reach out to the SFC or HKMA early rather than risk having to shut down.
Firms already vetted and operating with SFC or HKMA approval -- such as existing licensed corporations, registered institutions, or licensed trading platforms -- would get a faster approval track.
Fees would mirror the existing Type 1 securities-dealing fees: currently $4,740 to apply and renew for a licensed corporation, and $23,500 to apply plus $35,000 a year for a registered institution.

Proposed penalties include up to seven years in prison and civil fines of up to $10,000,000, along with licence suspension or cancellation, reprimands and orders to fix problems -- similar to the existing trading-platform regime.
A tribunal modelled on the existing money-laundering review tribunal is proposed to hear appeals against SFC or HKMA decisions.
By end-June 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 trading platforms, with 10 more applications pending, including four operators treated as already licensed during the transition.
para 1.4, p.4
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background/scope framing, pp.1-9) and Chapter 2 (regulatory requirements, pp.10-26) in full; skip the FATF/DNFBP footnote boilerplate. The 12 consultation questions (listed at the end) map directly to each subsection and are useful as a structured checklist.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: This paper proposes a new SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset custodian services, defined as safekeeping virtual assets or the private keys that control them on a client's behalf. Banks, stored value facilities and subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks providing such services must register with the SFC, with the HKMA supervising banks and SVFs. It proposes incidental exemptions for entities whose safekeeping is merely part of another licensed activity, and a full exemption for a stablecoin issuer custodying only the stablecoins it issues. Financial-resource floors, external-assessment requirements, and sanctions mirroring the VATP regime are proposed. Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets.
w: This is the core reference for the bank's own future custody obligations if it safekeeps client digital assets or private keys, and equally sets the standard the bank must use to vet any external custodian it relies on, since regulated entities will be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered custodians.
k: Providing virtual-asset custodian services as a business - safekeeping VAs, or instruments such as private keys enabling their transfer - requires an SFC licence or registration
SFC is proposed as licensing authority and standard-setter for VA custodians; HKMA would oversee banks and SVFs directly as day-to-day supervisor of their custodian business
para 2.12(a), p.9

Regulated entities holding client VAs only incidentally to another licensed activity, and not safekeeping private keys, would be exempt; a stablecoin issuer custodying only its own issued stablecoins is fully exempt even if it holds the private keys
Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered VA custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets
Proposed minimum financial resources: HK$10 million paid-up share capital and up to HK$3 million liquid capital, benchmarked against the SFO Type 13 depositary-licence requirements
Custodians safekeeping private keys must engage an external assessor, with the SFC as a party to that engagement, before being licensed - mirroring the swift VATP licensing process
No deeming/grace arrangement is proposed; the regime becomes fully effective from the commencement date of the statutory provisions
Unlicensed provision or active marketing of custodian services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment
rg: Read Chapter 2 (pages 6-26) in full, especially the definition, exemptions and 'other regulatory requirements' sections; Chapter 1 background can be skimmed.

t: FSTB and SFC launch consultation on legislative proposals for regulating digital asset dealing and custodian services
sl: FSTB · FSTB and SFC launch consultation on legislative proposals for… (2025)
s: FSTB and SFC opened a two-month joint public consultation (to August 29, 2025) on revised legislative proposals for two new licensing regimes: digital-asset dealing services and digital-asset custodian services. Both would require licence or registration with the SFC as standard-setter, with the HKMA supervising banks and stored-value-facility licensees offering the services. Dealing covers both simple conversions and complex activities like brokerage and block trading; custody covers safekeeping of assets or of private keys enabling their transfer. No deeming arrangement is proposed, meaning the regimes take full effect from their commencement date with no automatic grace licence. Full detail is in the two attached consultation papers.
w: This is the direct precursor to the bank's own future licensing obligations for any dealing or custody activity in digital assets, and to due-diligence expectations for VATP and custodian counterparties; full substance is in the two linked consultation papers.
k: Consultation on the two licensing regimes runs from June 27 to August 29, 2025
para 1, p.1
For both regimes, the SFC will set standards and licence/register providers, while banks and stored-value-facility registrants would be supervised day-to-day by the HKMA
para 4, p.1
Dealing licensing would cover both simple conversions and complex activities such as brokerage, block trading, and advisory or asset-management activity
para 6, p.1
Custody is proposed to be defined as safekeeping digital assets, or instruments (including private keys) that enable their transfer, on behalf of clients
para 8, p.1
Both regimes are proposed to take full effect on commencement, with no deeming/grace arrangement for existing providers
para 7 and 9, p.1
rg: Read this press release for the summary, then the two consultation papers (f673ef6dcb63 dealing, 30b60438f017 custody) for the detail.

t: FSTB and SFC consult on proposed regimes to regulate virtual asset dealers and custodians
sl: FSTB/SFC · FSTB and SFC consult on proposed regimes to regulate… (2025)
s: This SFC press release announces that the FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation to introduce licensing regimes for virtual asset (VA) dealing and VA custodian service providers, one day after the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Digital Asset Development. It frames the proposals as advancing the 'Access' pillar of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap and the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, quotes SFC CEO Julia Leung and FSTB Secretary Christopher Hui, and sets a comment deadline of 29 August 2025.
w: This is a consultation announcement, not yet a rule: for a compliance head it signals that VA dealer and custodian licensing regimes are coming, worth tracking for future direct impact on the bank's own VA dealing and custody arrangements, but it creates no obligation yet.
k: FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation on licensing regimes for VA dealing and VA custodian service providers.
para 1, p.1
The consultation was launched the day after the Government released Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong (issued 26 June 2025).
quote from Christopher Hui, para 6
The two proposed regimes are positioned as advancing 'Access', one of the five pillars of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap issued 19 February 2025.
Note 1
Comments on the consultation are invited by 29 August 2025.
para 5
rg: Short press release; read in full (2-3 minutes) as context for the companion consultation paper (25CP7); skip nothing.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: This joint FSTB/SFC consultation paper proposes a new licensing/registration regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong, extending the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle already applied to VA trading platforms (VATPs). It defines VA custodian service as, by way of business, safekeeping VAs or instruments enabling their transfer (e.g. private keys) on behalf of clients, proposes SFC as licensing authority (HKMA as frontline regulator for banks/SVFs), sets eligibility, fit-and-proper, financial resources ($10m paid-up capital), individual licensing, and prohibition/sanctions provisions modelled on the VATP regime, and seeks views via 17 questions with comments due by 29 August 2025.
w: This directly affects the bank's operating model: any group entity -- the bank itself, a locally incorporated subsidiary, or an associated entity -- that safekeeps client private keys will need a new SFC/HKMA licence with no automatic transitional relief, requiring an entity-mapping exercise now.
k: VA custodian service is defined as, by way of business, safekeeping VAs or instruments enabling transfer of VAs (including private keys) on behalf of clients; self-custody by the client is excluded.

SFC will be the licensing/registration authority and standard setter for VA custodians; HKMA is the frontline regulator for banks and SVFs providing VA custody, and VA custodians that are subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks are regulated by the SFC.
para 2.12(a)

Associated entities of SFC-licensed VATPs currently providing custody by safekeeping private keys will need to obtain a separate VA custodian service licence under the new regime if they wish to continue.
para 2.21(a)

A licence or registration will also be needed by banks, by subsidiaries of a locally incorporated bank, and by SVFs, wherever they themselves hold the private keys (or similar instruments) that let client VAs be moved -- even where that happens as part of VA dealing or acting as depositary for a fund.
para 2.21(b)

A stablecoin issuer licensed by the HKMA that only custodies the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempted from the VA custodian licensing regime, even though it safekeeps private keys, because it is already subject to HKMA supervision.
para 2.19

An incidental exemption is proposed for SFC/HKMA regulated entities where safekeeping of client VAs is wholly incidental to their principal licensed/registered business, provided they do not safekeep the private keys themselves.
para 2.19

Except for banks and SVFs, an applicant must either be locally incorporated and physically based in Hong Kong, or be a company formed elsewhere but registered here under the Companies Ordinance; it must also name at least two responsible officers (for the SFC) or executive officers (for the HKMA).

Non-bank licensees would need baseline financial resources -- proposed at a minimum of HK$10 million in paid-up share capital, plus minimum liquid capital of up to HK$3 million depending on the business model -- modelled on the existing Type 13 (depositary) requirements.
para 2.39(a)

No grandfathering is planned for firms already providing VA custodian services -- the licensing regime is meant to apply in full from the day the relevant statutory provisions commence -- so firms are encouraged to approach the SFC or HKMA early (e.g. before applying) to avoid having to halt their business.
para 2.41

VA custodians safekeeping private keys will be required to engage an external assessor for an external assessment of systems and controls before licensing/registration, mirroring the VATP process, with the SFC party to the engagement.
para 2.42

Unlicensed provision, holding out, or active marketing of VA custodian services is proposed to be a criminal offence: on conviction on indictment, a fine of $5 million and imprisonment for 7 years; knowingly advertising an unlicensed provider's services carries a level 5 fine ($50,000) and 6 months' imprisonment.
para 2.51(a)-(b)

Custody technology/security requirements (private key management, cybersecurity, business continuity, storage ratios) will be aligned with existing VATP custody requirements and made subject to a further, separate public consultation, alongside SFC exploration of a 'dynamic approach' to custody technologies and storage ratios per the ASPIRe roadmap.
para 2.38
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background, paras 1.1-1.10) then Chapter 2's Scope of Regulation, Definition and Coverage, Eligibility, and Other Regulatory Requirements sections (paras 2.12-2.44); the 17 consultation questions and footnote cross-references can be skimmed after the corresponding substantive paragraph.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in… (2025)
s: This is the full consultation paper on a proposed SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset dealing services, replacing the narrower 2024 OTC-shop proposal after feedback showed dealing activity is far more varied. Banks and stored-value-facility licensees must register with the SFC (in consultation with the HKMA), which remains their frontline supervisor. Licensees must hold client virtual assets with a licensed custodian, and meet financial-resource, AML/CFT, risk-management, conduct and record-keeping requirements. Stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers are expected to be an eligible traded asset for retail clients. The paper proposes no deeming arrangement, and heavy sanctions including fines up to HK$10 million and imprisonment up to ten years for fraud-related offences.
w: This paper sets out in detail how the bank itself would become a registered digital-asset dealer under HKMA frontline supervision, including the mandatory-custodian rule and proposed financial-resource floors, and gives compliance the specific consultation questions worth a formal bank response.
k: Any person carrying on a business of dealing in virtual assets in Hong Kong, including simple conversions and complex brokerage/block-trading/advisory/asset-management activity, needs an SFC licence or registration
Banks and stored value facilities must register with the SFC for virtual-asset dealing activity, with the HKMA as frontline regulator, similar to the existing model for banks' securities business
para 1.10, p.8

A licensed stablecoin issuer conducting only primary-market offering or redemption of the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempt from the dealing licence, since it is already supervised by the HKMA
para 1.10, p.8
Licensees or registrants must hold client virtual assets with a licensed or registered virtual-asset custodian in Hong Kong
para 2.13 and 2.23, p.13 and 17
For retail clients, tradable virtual assets are expected to broadly follow VATP practice, including large-cap tokens meeting index criteria and stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers
Minimum financial resource requirements proposed: HK$5 million paid-up share capital, up to HK$3 million liquid capital, plus 12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital
No deeming/grace licence is proposed - the regime takes full effect on the commencement date of the statutory provisions
Operating without a licence while dealing or actively marketing dealing services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment
Fraudulent or deceptive behaviour in virtual-asset transactions carries a fine of HK$10 million and up to ten years' imprisonment on indictment
rg: Read Chapter 2 (pages 10-25) in full for the substantive regime; Chapter 1 background (pages 2-9) can be skimmed for context on the prior 2024 consultation.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
sl: FSTB/SFC · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset… (2025)
s: Joint FSTB/SFC consultation document proposing a new statutory licensing regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong, applying the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle. It explains the current patchwork of custody requirements (VATP associated entities, SFC/HKMA rules for intermediaries and funds) and proposes bringing standalone VA custodian services within a dedicated licensing/registration framework subject to AML/CFT and other regulatory requirements. Comments were invited by 29 August 2025.
w: Directly implicates the bank both as an eligible VA custodian for other intermediaries' clients today and as a prospective SFC registrant (HKMA-supervised) for its own VA custody business under the proposed new licensing regime.
k: Government's October 2022 Policy Statement committed to a comprehensive digital-asset regulatory framework under 'same activity, same risks, same regulation'; a second Policy Statement was promulgated 26 June 2025.
para 1.2, p.2
As of end-June 2025, SFC had formally licensed 11 VATPs, with 10 applicants (including 4 deemed-to-be-licensed) pending.

VATPs are currently required to provide custody through wholly-owned associated-entity subsidiaries; SFC-licensed intermediaries dealing in VAs must custody client VAs with SFC-licensed VATPs, banks, or subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks.
Consultation responses were due by 29 August 2025; the FSTB/SFC may reproduce and publish submissions and contributor names unless anonymity is expressly requested.
Foreword paras 2-4, p.1
Growth drivers cited for a dedicated VA custodian licensing regime include the proposed VA dealing (OTC) licensing regime and growth of VA funds such as SFC-authorised spot VA ETFs.
rg: Read Chapter 1 (Introduction/Background, pp.1-5) in full for the policy rationale; the remaining chapters (not captured in this excerpt beyond p.5) set out the detailed licensing proposal and should be read for implementation specifics before drafting any custody licensing strategy.

t: Second policy statement on development of digital assets issued to scale Hong Kong to new heights of global digital asset leadership
sl: Government · Second policy statement on development of digital assets issued… (2025)
s: The government issued Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets, building on its October 2022 statement. It sets out the 'LEAP' framework: legal and regulatory streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development. It confirms the SFC will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers, and that FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review of tokenisation covering bonds and other real-world assets. Full detail, including HKMA's role supervising banks in dealing/custodian activities, is in the attached Annex (package: a29b51bffc6b).
w: This press release is the headline announcement of the framework that leads directly to the bank's future dealing/custodian obligations; the substantive detail compliance needs is in the attached Annex.
k: The Policy Statement 2.0 organises initiatives under the LEAP framework: legal streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development
para 2, p.1

The SFC will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers, while FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review to facilitate tokenisation of real-world assets and financial instruments.
para 3, p.1
The FSTB and SFC would launch public consultations shortly on licensing regimes for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers
final para, p.1
rg: Read this press release for the headline, then read the Annex (id a29b51bffc6b) for the substance.

t: Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets… (2025)
s: This is the full annex of Policy Statement 2.0. It replaces the term 'virtual assets' with 'digital assets' in government usage and sets out the LEAP framework covering four areas: unifying licensing for digital-asset exchanges, stablecoin issuers, dealing and custodian providers under SFC leadership; regularising tokenised government bond issuance and clarifying stamp duty treatment for tokenised ETFs; supporting stablecoin payment use cases and inviting proposals to test licensed stablecoins in government payments; and expanding talent and cross-border cooperation. It confirms tax concessions for privately-offered funds will be extended to specified digital assets from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
w: This is the core policy document compliance should treat as the source of upcoming licensing structure: it confirms SFC-led licensing with HKMA as bank supervisor for both dealing and custody, which frames every subsequent consultation and future obligation for the bank's digital-asset business.
k: The government will use 'Digital Assets' instead of 'Virtual Assets' going forward, to better match international usage
footnote 1, p.1
SFC will be the lead authority for licensing digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers, while HKMA will be the frontline regulator supervising banks conducting those activities
FSTB and HKMA will lead a legal and regulatory review of tokenisation, starting with the bond market and covering settlement, registration and record requirements
para 9, p.4

para 11, p.5

para 14, p.6

para 15, p.6

t: Consultation on revised disclosure templates and tables |  | Annex 1: Standard disclosure templates and tables for making disclosure under the BDR
sl: HKMA · Consultation on revised disclosure templates and tables (2025)
s: The HKMA wrote to industry on 25 June 2025 to consult on revised standard Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables under the Banking (Disclosure) Rules (BDR). This annex adds a new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures, comprising Table CAEA (qualitative disclosure on an AI's cryptoasset activities, risk profile and classification approach) and Templates CAE1 (cryptoasset exposures and RWAs), CAE2 (accounting classification) and CAE3 (liquidity requirements, category 1 institutions only). CAE1 requires disclosure, by cryptoasset group (1a/1b/2a/2b), of credit-risk exposure/EAD/RWA and market-risk long/short exposure/RWA, a total row, and rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds; group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures must also be folded into the general disclosure templates that cover equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package. Comments were due 25 July 2025.
w: This is separate from the internal prudential returns: it is what the bank must publish externally about its crypto exposures under Pillar 3, so compliance/disclosure teams (not just regulatory reporting) need to build a public-facing crypto disclosure process alongside the internal MA(BS) returns.
k: A new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures, is added to the standard public disclosure package, comprising Table CAEA and Templates CAE1, CAE2 and CAE3.
Part XII contents listing, p.9; substantive Part XII section, pp.99-108

Table CAEA requires an AI to describe its cryptoasset-related business activities, how each translates into its risk profile, the scope of its cryptoasset reporting, its most significant current and emerging cryptoasset risks, and (for group 1 cryptoassets) its approach to assessing each of the four BCR section 361 classification conditions.
Table CAEA, pp.99-100

Template CAE1 requires, for each cryptoasset group (1a, 1b, 2a and 2b), disclosure of total credit-risk exposure, exposure/EAD and RWA, plus market-risk long and short exposure and RWA, a total row, and separate rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds.
Template CAE1, rows 1-10, pp.101-104

Beyond the dedicated Part XII templates, an AI must also fold its group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures into the general disclosure templates covering the equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package -- for example, Template OV1's row 5c (cryptoasset credit-risk RWA under BCR section 376) and row 8a (RWA for the group 2b cryptoasset derivative-contract method).
Template CAE1 Points to note item 2, p.103; cross-referenced rows in Template OV1, p.10
rg: Go straight to Part XII / Template CAE1 (around p.363-373); the rest of the annex covers unrelated Pillar 3 templates that can be skipped for crypto purposes.

t: Robust and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Robust and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins (2025)
s: HKMA's Chief Executive uses this commentary to set expectations around the newly-passed Stablecoins Ordinance, confirming it would take effect on 1 August 2025 after which HKMA would begin accepting licence applications, and describing stablecoins as a payment instrument rather than an investment. He signals that only a small number of licences would be granted at first, that use-case viability and operational readiness would be scrutinised heavily, and that participation in HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox does not guarantee a licence. The piece references the FSB's 2023 global crypto-asset framework as a basis for Hong Kong's approach and notes HKMA's coordinating role in the FSB's review of how that framework is being implemented worldwide.
w: Confirms the licensing regime's go-live date and signals a deliberately restrictive, high-bar initial licensing approach, which a compliance head should factor into any group decision about applying for a stablecoin issuer licence or partnering with an applicant.
k: The Stablecoins Ordinance was expected to commence on 1 August 2025, after which HKMA would start accepting stablecoin issuer licence applications.
para 1
HKMA describes stablecoins as a payment instrument, not an investment or speculative asset, and groups them with CBDC and tokenised deposits as alternative emerging payment options.
para 5

Hong Kong's regulatory approach draws on the Financial Stability Board's 2023 global regulatory framework for crypto-asset activities, and HKMA was coordinating the FSB's review of that framework's global implementation.
para 6-7
HKMA expects to grant only a small number of licences initially, and applicants must demonstrate viable use cases and prudent, sustainable operating capability.
para 10 (Licensing regime section)

Applicants need to show capability across reserve-asset management, price stabilisation, redemption, technology security, risk management and AML, and cross-border applicants must show their partners hold the necessary regulatory approvals.
para 11
Participation in the Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox is not a precondition for, or guarantee of, obtaining a licence.
para 13 (Licensing regime section)
rg: Read in full; short piece with no boilerplate to skip.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)26 Part I

Two new memorandum items are added: one for reporting category 1 institutions, capturing the total weighted amount of cryptoassets already reported elsewhere in the return as required stable funding for the NSFR calculation; and a parallel one for reporting category 2A institutions, capturing the equivalent amount as required core funding for the CFR calculation.

k: Item 3(b) captures the total weighted amount of cryptoassets already reported under Part 2 as required stable funding, for reporting category 1 institutions' NSFR calculation.
item 3(b) (per companion explanatory notes)
Item 4(b) captures the total weighted amount of cryptoassets already reported under Part 3 as required core funding, for reporting category 2A institutions' CFR calculation.
item 4(b) (per companion explanatory notes)

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Explanatory notes : MA(BS)28
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: Despite being issued as part of the cryptoassets standard consultation package, this document has no cryptoasset content. It proposes adding one more exemption option to the pull-down menu in Part IV, column 11 of the Return of Large Exposures (MA(BS)28), so that banks can select rule 48(1)(ma) of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules, an exemption clause that took effect 1 January 2025 but was left out of the MA(BS)28 template in the last round of amendments. As an interim fix, banks with exposures under that rule are told to use the rule 48(1)(g) option instead until the revised template is in place.
w: Not a crypto item -- it is an administrative fix to the large exposures exemption pull-down menu. Compliance should note the interim workaround (use rule 48(1)(g)) for any exposures actually exempt under rule 48(1)(ma) until the template catches up.
k: A new pull-down option, rule 48(1)(ma) of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules, is being added to Part IV, column 11 (provisions under which exemption is granted) of MA(BS)28.
Part IV (11), p.1

footnote 1, p.1
Pending the updated template, a bank with exposures reportable under rule 48(1)(ma) should, for now, report them in Part IV using the rule 48(1)(g) option as a stand-in.
footnote 1, p.1

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)3a Part I
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This draft template revises Part I of MA(BS)3A, the return of market risk and credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital charge. It adds group 2a cryptoassets (broadly, unbacked crypto held for trading, treated similarly to equities/commodities under market risk rules) as a new separate risk class within the sensitivities-based method (SBM), with its own capital charge line, and adds an infrastructure risk add-on line for group 1 cryptoasset exposures. A new Division L introduces the simplified standardised approach (SSTM) treatment for group 2a cryptoasset exposures, split between non-option and scenario-approach exposures.
w: Trading desks holding unbacked (group 2a) cryptoassets will generate a new, dedicated market-risk capital charge, and any group 1 crypto exposure carries its own infrastructure risk add-on under the market risk return as well as under credit risk -- both need to be captured without double-counting.
k: Group 2a cryptoassets are introduced as a new, separate risk class under the sensitivities-based method (SBM) for market risk capital.
Division A item 4, p.1
A dedicated SBM capital charge line is added for group 2a cryptoasset exposures.
Division B.8 item 4, p.2
An infrastructure risk add-on line for group 1 cryptoasset exposures is added to the market risk return, separate from the credit risk version in MA(BS)3.
Division A item 5, p.1 (recurs in Division E and F, pp.3-4)

A new Division L, SSTM Approach - Group 2a Cryptoasset Exposures, is added for banks using the simplified standardised approach, split into non-option exposures (L.1) and exposures captured under the scenario approach (L.2).
Division L, p.5
rg: Focus on the group 2a SBM capital charge items (p.2), the infrastructure risk add-on line, and Division L (p.9); skip unrelated existing market-risk items.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Explanatory notes : MA(BS)3 Part I
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: These notes explain how the new crypto memorandum item in MA(BS)3 Part I is built. They set out that item 2.5 (the crypto add-on feeding the capital ratio) is the sum of five specific Part IIIf components -- the group 1 infrastructure risk add-on (banking book), redemption-risk add-ons for group 1b and stablecoin-related group 2a exposures in the trading book, the group 2b risk-weighted amount, and the G-SIB/D-SIB group 2 concentration add-on -- and describe the equivalent build-up for the output floor calculation in Division B, including the separate treatment for exposures booked in the trading book under the STC approach.
w: This is the definitive map of exactly which crypto add-on components (from Part IIIf and MA(BS)3A) roll up into the bank's capital ratio and output floor -- essential for capital management to build a complete, auditable crypto capital-impact model.
k: The crypto add-on in item 2.5 equals the sum of: the group 1 infrastructure risk add-on for banking-book exposures; redemption-risk add-ons for group 1b and stablecoin-linked group 2a trading-book exposures; the group 2b risk-weighted amount; and the G-SIB/D-SIB group 2 concentration add-on.
note on item 2.5, p.1

Item 2.7 (total risk-weighted amount for the CAR calculation) is the sum of items 2.1 through 2.6, meaning the crypto add-on in item 2.5 directly raises the bank's total RWA and therefore lowers its capital ratio, all else equal.
note on item 2.7, p.1

For institutions subject to the output floor, item 1(i)(e) of Division B aggregates the STC-approach redemption-risk add-ons for trading-book group 1b and stablecoin-linked group 2a exposures, the banking-book group 1 infrastructure add-on, the group 2b risk-weighted amount, and the G-SIB/D-SIB concentration add-on.
note on item 1(i)(e), p.1

Items 1(ii)(c) and 2(ii)(d) each capture, on its own line, the infrastructure risk add-on that applies to Group 1 crypto exposures held in the trading book, sourced from the market risk return MA(BS)3A Part I.
note on items 1(ii)(c) and 2(ii)(d), p.1
rg: Read in full; two pages, entirely about how the crypto add-ons flow up into the CAR and output floor calculations.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Explanatory notes : MA(BS)3a Part I

w: Explains the calculation mechanics behind the new group 2a market-risk capital charge -- relevant for validating trading-desk capital calculations once the rule is live.
k: Each bucket and correlation scenario gets its own calculation of the SBM delta, vega and curvature capital charge tied to price movements in Group 2a cryptoassets, following Basel provision CP24.01 paragraphs 87 and 90.

reference to CP 24.01, p.1

A separate item aggregates the capital charges for other risk classes (e.g. general interest rate risk, GIRR) arising from group 2a cryptoasset exposures; the infrastructure risk add-on itself is a different, group 1 (not group 2a) item appearing in the STM, IMA and SSTM divisions.
note on Division B.8 item 3 (GIRR); infrastructure risk add-on notes on items 5/8/6, p.1-2

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | CIs: MA(BS)27 Cls
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This draft revises the completion instructions for MA(BS)27, the return of leverage ratio, so that cryptoasset exposures are correctly folded into the leverage ratio exposure measure. It provides that cryptoassets are included at their financial-reporting value, following the accounting treatment of exposures with similar characteristics; that off-balance sheet crypto items use the standard credit conversion factors; and it sets out specific rules for how crypto derivative contracts (across groups 1a, 1b, 2a and 2b) should be measured for leverage ratio purposes, generally by mapping to the treatment of the underlying traditional asset or, for group 2a/2b, using a modified SA-CCR approach with the multiplier fixed at one.
w: Leverage ratio is a binding backstop constraint for many banks, and this confirms crypto exposures (including derivatives) are pulled fully into the exposure measure with no multiplier relief -- a capital-planning point treasury and capital management need to model ahead of go-live.
k: Cryptoassets are included in the leverage ratio exposure measure at their financial-reporting value, based on the accounting treatment of exposures with similar characteristics.
para 6.5, p.10
Where a cryptoasset exposure is off-balance sheet, the standard credit conversion factors (CCFs) under paragraph 10.4 apply to calculate its leverage exposure measure.
para 6.5, p.11

For Group 1a or Group 1b cryptoasset derivative contracts, the exposure measure treats the derivative as if it referenced whatever traditional asset (or basket of traditional assets) the cryptoasset is built on.
para 10.2(ca)(i), p.20

For group 2a cryptoasset derivative contracts under the modified SA-CCR approach, the potential future exposure (PFE) is calculated under the BCR's group 2a cryptoasset derivative contracts asset class, but with the multiplier fixed at one rather than allowed to float.
para 10.2(ca)(ii), p.20
For group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts, the exposure measure uses the modified SA-CCR approach under BCR section 377, again with the multiplier fixed at one.
para 10.2(ca)(iii), p.20
rg: Read para 6.5 (p.10-11) on the general treatment and para 10.2(ca) (p.20) on crypto derivative contracts; the rest of the CIs are largely unchanged leverage ratio mechanics.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Explanatory notes : MA(BS)3 Part IIIa

s: These explanatory notes go with the draft MA(BS)3 Part IIIa return template. They walk through how to fill in the new Division A2, which covers cryptoasset risk-weighted amounts under the Basic (BSC) credit-risk approach. They confirm Division A2 is entirely new, and explain how to group a bank's crypto exposures by individual token for the top-five ranking, how to treat off-balance-sheet crypto commitments like forward purchases, and how crypto derivatives and secured-financing exposures map onto the new lines.
w: This is the practical guide the bank's regulatory reporting team will use to fill in the new crypto lines correctly -- including how to total exposures for the top-five list, and how derivatives and collateral fit in.
k: Division A2 is described as a completely new section added just to capture cryptoasset exposures reported under the BSC approach.
footnote 2

items 3a-3e

item on off-balance sheet exposures
For crypto derivative contracts, the risk-weighted amount is worked out based on which group -- 1a, 1b, or 2a -- the underlying cryptoasset belongs to.
explanatory note on derivative contracts
Separate guidance covers secured financing deals where group 1a cryptoassets are pledged as collateral, whether received or delivered, since only group 1a currently counts as recognised collateral.
note on SFT collateral

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)3 Part IIIc
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This draft template covers Part IIIc of MA(BS)3, the credit-risk risk-weighted asset calculation for banks using the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach. Unlike Parts IIIa and IIIb, crypto content here sits in an entirely new memorandum form, called Division B or Form IRB_CRYPTO, alongside -- not inside -- the main IRB sections. It mirrors the group 1a/1b split, top-five-by-risk-weighted-amount reporting, and crypto derivative and collateral treatment seen in the other approaches, adapted for IRB mechanics such as mapping to loss-given-default subclasses.
w: For banks on the IRB approach, crypto exposures come through a completely separate memorandum form (IRB_CRYPTO), not folded into the main IRB sections -- compliance needs to make sure this extra form is built into the IRB reporting process, not just the main capital adequacy ratio (CAR) return.
k: A brand-new memorandum items section, called Division B or Form IRB_CRYPTO, is added just for cryptoasset exposures reported under the IRB approach.

sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This draft return template covers Part IIIb of form MA(BS)3, which banks use to calculate credit-risk-weighted assets under the Standardised (STC) approach. As with the earlier Part IIIa template, a new Division A2 is added for cryptoasset risk-weighted amounts. This version adds extra detail not in the basic (BSC) version, including a line for group 1a cryptoassets that count as recognised collateral under the simple approach, and a note on how group 1b cryptoassets backed by a pool of traditional assets should be treated when outside parties can also redeem from that pool. The rest -- top five crypto exposures, crypto derivatives, and group 2b bilateral default-risk exposures -- follows the same structure as Part IIIa.
w: Banks on the Standardised credit-risk approach need the same crypto classification and top-five tracking as basic-approach banks, plus extra checks on collateral eligibility and pooled redemption that only apply here -- relevant to how the bank writes its recognised-collateral policy for tokenised assets.
k: A new Division A2 for cryptoasset risk-weighted amounts is added under the STC approach, following the same layout as the basic version but with STC-specific exposure classes.

t: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This is the HKMA's cover letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks, and in similar terms to the Deposit-Taking Company (DTC) Association, opening a 13 June to 11 July 2025 industry consultation on revised return templates. This follows the earlier statutory consultation on draft rules applying the Basel cryptoasset prudential standard, plus other minor updates. Seven returns are touched, covering capital, funding and exposure reporting: the Leverage Ratio return (MA(BS)27), the Large Exposures return (MA(BS)28), the Capital Adequacy Ratio return (MA(BS)3), the Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge return (MA(BS)3A), the Liquidity Position return (MA(BS)1E), the Certificate of Compliance return (MA(BS)1F), and the Stable Funding Position return (MA(BS)26). Where a template's layout stays the same, only explanatory notes or completion instructions are being issued. It asks for industry feedback by 11 July 2025 and notes the templates are preliminary, meant to help banks start building their systems.
w: This is the roadmap letter for the whole package. It tells compliance exactly which seven returns will carry new crypto reporting fields, confirms the templates were still preliminary as of June 2025, and gives the comment deadline, useful for checking whether the bank's own feedback was picked up in later versions.
k: This consultation follows an earlier statutory consultation on draft rules applying the Basel Committee's standard for how banks should treat cryptoasset exposures for prudential purposes, plus other minor updates.

t: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)3 Part IIIa
sl: HKMA · Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return… (2025)
s: This is the draft revised template for Part IIIa of the capital adequacy return MA(BS)3, which covers credit risk risk-weighted assets under the Basic Approach (BSC) for banks using that approach. The consultation adds a wholly new Division A2, Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures, alongside the existing Division A1 for non-crypto exposure classes. The new division splits crypto holdings into group 1a (e.g. tokenised traditional assets issued by government or deposit-taking issuers), group 1b (e.g. certain stablecoin-type exposures) and reports the bank's top five individual crypto exposures by risk-weighted amount, plus separate lines for crypto derivative contracts and secured-lending exposures involving crypto collateral. It was open for comment from 13 June to 11 July 2025.
w: Any bank on the Basic (BSC) credit-risk approach that holds tokenised assets or stablecoin-type exposures will need to classify each one into group 1a/1b, track its top five crypto exposures by risk-weighted amount, and separately capture crypto derivatives and crypto-collateralised financing on the quarterly CAR return once the rule takes effect.
k: A new Division A2, Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures, is inserted into Part IIIa alongside the existing Division A1 for other exposure classes.
