s: This is one part of a package the HKMA sent for comment on 13 June 2025, covering draft completion instructions for Part II (Capital Base) of the capital adequacy ratio return MA(BS)3. It sits inside a wider industry consultation on rules to bring the Basel cryptoasset prudential standard, plus other housekeeping changes, into Hong Kong bank capital reporting. The main change here is a narrow one: it tells banks that a new defined term, cryptoasset exposure, is being added to the Banking (Capital) Rules, and that such exposures held as intangible assets must be carved out of the generic other intangible assets capital deduction line. Comments were due by 11 July 2025. The rest of the Part II template and instructions are unchanged from the June 2024 version.
w: This confirms that once the crypto capital rules commence, any bank-held crypto asset booked as an intangible must be pulled out of the ordinary intangibles capital deduction and tracked separately -- a small but concrete change to the CET1 deduction mechanics compliance needs to test for.
k: A new defined term, cryptoasset exposure, is being added to section 2(1) of the Banking (Capital) Rules by the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
item 24, footnote 4, p.8
Cryptoasset exposures that are booked as intangible assets under accounting standards must now be excluded when a bank fills in the other intangible assets line.
Part II, item (f)(vi) 24, p.8
Industry members had until 11 July 2025 to send comments on this draft to the HKMA.
cover catalogue page, Consultation Close Date

t: Stablecoins Ordinance to commence operation on August 1, 2025
sl: Government · Stablecoins Ordinance to commence operation on August 1, 2025 (2025)
s: The government published a Gazette notice setting 1 August 2025 as the date the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) -- which licenses stablecoin activities -- takes effect. A second notice names professional investors as a class who may still be offered a specified stablecoin issued by an unlicensed person, relying on section 9(2)(b)(iii) of the Ordinance. Separately, the HKMA opened a consultation on the detailed regulatory requirements, including anti-money-laundering rules. Both notices were due before LegCo on 11 June for negative vetting.
w: This fixes the exact date the stablecoin licensing regime became binding law, and confirms an unlicensed issuer's stablecoin can still lawfully reach professional (but not retail) investors, which matters for the bank's private banking and institutional client segments.
k: The Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) commenced operation on August 1, 2025, as fixed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury's commencement notice
para 1 and 3, p.1
A specified stablecoin issued by a person without a section 15 licence may still be offered to professional investors, as defined under the Securities and Futures Ordinance
para 4, p.1
The HKMA launched a consultation on detailed regulatory requirements for the regime, including anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing provisions
para 6, p.1
rg: Read in full; short and gives the exact commencement date and the professional-investor carve-out.

t: Consultation Paper on the Proposed AML/CFT Requirements for Regulated Stablecoin Activities
sl: HKMA · Consultation Paper on the Proposed AML/CFT Requirements for Regulated… (2025)
s: HKMA's consultation paper explains, at a policy level, the proposed anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing rules that will apply to entities it licenses to issue stablecoins under the new Stablecoins Ordinance. It covers customer checks on issuance and redemption, extra controls where customers use unhosted (self-custody) wallets, the Travel Rule for stablecoin transfers, and ongoing monitoring of stablecoins once in circulation. It also flags that HKMA is separately drafting supplementary AML guidance for other digital-asset activities such as custody, referencing the securities regulator's existing rules to keep requirements consistent across regulators. The detailed rules were to be finalised in a companion draft Guideline; comments closed 30 June 2025.
w: Sets out the AML expectations HKMA planned to impose on any stablecoin-issuer entity within the bank's group, and foreshadows a related supplementary guideline on custody and other digital-asset activities that would apply more broadly across the bank; largely superseded once the final Guideline was published in August 2025.
k: The paper should be read together with the Stablecoins Ordinance and a parallel draft supervisory Guideline; the Legislative Council enacted the Stablecoins Bill on 21 May 2025.
A licensed issuer must run customer checks before issuing or redeeming stablecoins for any transaction of HK$8,000 or more.

Issuers should work out whether a customer's wallet is custodial or unhosted, confirm the customer controls it, and run due diligence on the institution behind a custodial wallet before issuing stablecoins to it.
Where a customer uses an unhosted wallet, the proposal adds extra controls: closer monitoring of those transfers, sending coins only to wallets assessed as reliable, and possible transaction limits.
para 3.2.4
The Travel Rule under AMLO Schedule 2 section 13A applies to stablecoin transfers, and an issuer may act as ordering, intermediary or beneficiary institution depending on its business model.
Issuers are expected to keep monitoring stablecoins after they are issued, using blockchain analytics to trace transactions and to blacklist or whitelist wallet addresses as needed.
para 3.6.2

HKMA is drafting separate supplementary AML guidance covering other digital-asset activities, such as custody services and stablecoin offering by banks and other licensees, drawing on the securities regulator's existing rules for consistency.
para 4.1
rg: Read sections 2 (background/scope) and 3 (proposed requirements) in full; section 5 (next steps) is procedural only.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (2025)
s: This is a draft AML/CFT guideline the HKMA circulated for consultation in May 2025, meant for entities that hold a licence under Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance to issue fiat-backed stablecoins. It largely mirrors the structure of existing AML rulebooks: risk assessment, governance and staff training, customer checks on stablecoin holders, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reporting and record-keeping. Its distinctive chapter applies a travel-rule-style regime to stablecoin transfers, requiring issuers to capture and pass on sender and receiver details above a threshold. The draft was still unnumbered as a Cap.[-] ordinance at the time of publication, confirming it was published ahead of the underlying law being finalised. It has not yet been confirmed as the final in-force text.
w: This shows the AML/CFT standard the bank should expect any stablecoin issuer it deals with, invests reserve assets alongside, or offers as a product to hold once licensed, and its travel-rule and counterparty-vetting provisions closely track the SFC's VATP guideline, so a bank can largely reuse existing crypto AML controls when assessing stablecoin-issuer counterparties.
k: The guideline would bind anyone holding a stablecoin-issuer licence, covering how they manage laundering and terror-financing risk from issuing, redeeming and otherwise handling their stablecoins.
A licensee must appoint both a Compliance Officer and a Money Laundering Reporting Officer, which can be the same person for a smaller issuer.
An independent audit function with a direct line to senior management and the board must review the issuer's AML controls.
para 3.6
Before transferring stablecoins worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending institution must record sender and receiver identity details and pass them to the receiving institution securely and immediately.
A licensee must vet a stablecoin transfer counterparty's ML/TF risk before dealing with it, similar to the counterparty checks other AML guidelines apply to crypto exchanges.
Filing a suspicious transaction report does not close the matter -- the issuer must still review the relationship and may need to freeze or burn the stablecoins involved.
para 8.6
Records of customer checks and stablecoin transaction data must be retained for at least five years after the transaction, even if the relationship has since ended.
para 9.3

If a licensee sets up branches or subsidiaries outside Hong Kong, it must apply group-wide AML standards and, where local law blocks the stricter of the two rule sets, tell the HKMA and take extra risk-mitigating steps.
rg: Read the introduction (Ch.1) for scope and legal basis, then Chapter 6 for the stablecoin travel-rule mechanics; the customer due diligence chapter (Ch.4) largely repeats standard AML identification requirements and can be skimmed.

t: Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
sl: HKMA · Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (2025)
s: This consultation-stage HKMA guideline spells out, in detail, what a licensed stablecoin issuer must do under the Stablecoins Ordinance to keep its licence: how reserve assets are chosen, valued, segregated and disclosed; how issuance and same-day redemption must work; minimum capital; detailed risk-management expectations including token, wallet/private-key, cybersecurity and third-party controls; incident, business-continuity and wind-down planning; and corporate-governance and fitness-and-propriety standards for directors and managers. It uses 'must' for statutory duties lifted from the Ordinance and 'should' for HKMA's own supervisory expectations layered on top. The consultation closed 30 June 2025; a finalised version was expected to follow.
w: This is the core prudential and operational rulebook a bank's stablecoin-issuer subsidiary (or an authorized institution issuing directly) would have to meet, and it is also the reference standard a compliance head should use when assessing any third-party stablecoin issuer the bank deals with as a counterparty, custodian or distributor.
k: An issuer must at all times hold reserve assets whose market value is at least equal to the face value of stablecoins in circulation, with extra buffer (over-collateralisation) built in to cover market-price swings.
para 2.1.1

Reserve assets are limited to short-dated bank deposits, high-quality marketable government/public-sector debt, overnight reverse repos and dedicated investment funds holding those instruments, or other assets HKMA accepts.
para 2.2.1

Reserve assets must be held in the same currency the stablecoin references, segregated from the issuer's own assets and protected from the issuer's other creditors, normally via an independent trustee or trust declaration.
An issuer must not pay interest or interest-like returns to stablecoin holders; any yield on reserve assets belongs to the issuer.
para 2.5.1
Reserve composition and value must be disclosed daily internally and normally reported to HKMA and the public weekly, with regular independent attestation of full backing.
Valid redemption requests must be honoured within one business day without unreasonable fees or conditions, unless HKMA has given prior written consent to a longer period.
para 3.2.3

An issuer must obtain HKMA's consent before conducting any business beyond its licensed stablecoin activity, and must show that other business will not put its stablecoin operations or customers at risk (does not apply to an issuer that is itself an authorized institution).
A non-bank issuer must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up capital (or an HKMA-approved equivalent).
para 5.1.1
Issuers should run three lines of defence (business units, risk/compliance, internal audit) with the risk function reporting directly to the board.

Detailed technology-risk rules require documenting token standards and smart-contract architecture, and multi-signature or similar controls so no single person can unilaterally mint, burn, freeze or blacklist tokens.

'Significant' private keys (governing contract upgrades, role changes or large mint/burn operations) must be generated and stored offline in an air-gapped, Hong Kong-based (or HKMA-accepted) environment with elevated physical security.
paras 6.5.8(ii),(iv)
Smart contracts must be independently audited by a qualified third party at least annually and on every deployment or upgrade.
para 6.5.5
rg: For a compliance head, prioritise sections 2 (reserve assets), 3 (redemption), 6.5 (technology/key management), 6.6 (third-party risk), 6.8 (incident/exit) and 7 (governance); the glossary (section 9) is reference-only.

t: Government welcomes passage of Stablecoins Bill
sl: Government · Government welcomes passage of Stablecoins Bill (2025)
s: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime under the Monetary Authority for anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, or issuing one pegged to the Hong Kong dollar from anywhere. Licensees must meet requirements on reserve-asset management, client-asset segregation, at-par redemption, anti-money-laundering controls, risk management, disclosure and fitness. Only licensed issuers may offer a stablecoin to retail investors, and only advertisements for licensed issuance are allowed, including during a planned six-month grace period. The press release confirms further consultation on detailed rules and previews upcoming OTC/custodian consultations and the second policy statement.

k: Anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, or a Hong Kong dollar-pegged one anywhere, will need a licence from the Monetary Authority once the Ordinance takes effect

Only specified licensed institutions may offer a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, and only a licensed issuer's stablecoin may be offered to a retail investor

During the six-month non-contravention (grace) period, only advertisements for licensed stablecoin issuance are permitted
para 3, p.1

t: Government welcomes passage of the Stablecoins Bill
sl: HKMA · Government welcomes passage of the Stablecoins Bill (2025)
s: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers in Hong Kong. Under the resulting Stablecoins Ordinance, anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or an FRS claiming to hold a stable value referenced to HKD anywhere in the world, needs a licence from the Monetary Authority (MA). Only specific licensed institutions may offer an FRS, and only a licensed issuer's coin may go to retail investors; at all times, including the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed. The Government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian services, and publish a second virtual-asset policy paper.
w: As the law bringing in Hong Kong's stablecoin regime, this directly obliges a compliance head to make sure the bank only markets or offers MA-licensed FRS coins, including HKD-referenced coins issued anywhere in the world, right from the start of the transition period.
k: Under the Ordinance, anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or an FRS claiming stable value referenced to HKD anywhere in the world, needs a Monetary Authority licence.
para 2

Licensees must meet requirements on managing and redeeming reserve assets (keeping them separate, using a solid stabilisation method, redeeming at par value on reasonable terms), AML/CFT, risk management, disclosure and audits, and being fit and proper.

Only institutions holding the right licence may issue an FRS here in Hong Kong, and only that licensed issuer's FRS is allowed to reach retail investors.
para 3
At all times, even during the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed, aimed at stopping fraud and scams.
para 3
The Ordinance was due to take effect later in 2025, with a transition arrangement giving industry time to apply for licences and sort out their business.
para 5
The Government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset OTC trading and custodian services, and publish a second policy paper on virtual-asset development.
para 6

t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2025)
s: This circular sets the rules SFC uses to authorise investment funds that put more than 10% of net asset value (NAV) into virtual assets (VA Funds), for public sale in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It replaces the 22 December 2023 circular. VA Funds can get direct (spot) or indirect (for example, futures or exchange-traded products) exposure to virtual assets. They must only invest in VA tokens that Hong Kong's public can already trade through SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs). They cannot use fund-level leverage, and any spot VA trading or custody must go through an SFC-licensed VATP or an authorized institution (AI) that meets HKMA's virtual-asset custody standards. Custody rules require segregated holdings, mostly cold-wallet storage, and Hong Kong-based, access-restricted storage of seeds and keys. New under this version: VA Funds may now stake or do other VA-related activities under the ASPIRe roadmap, as long as they follow guiding principles -- fitting the fund's investment strategy, having strong internal controls, doing due diligence on counterparties, and giving specific disclosures in offering documents and reports. Funds wanting more than 10% VA exposure, or wanting to stake, must first consult SFC and get its approval.
w: This rule applies to SFC-authorised fund providers and trustees, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution (AI). It matters to a compliance head because if the bank's AI or a subsidiary provides VA custody to one of these funds, it must meet the HKMA custody standard referenced here -- and staking is now allowed for funds.
k: SFC-authorised VA Funds are limited to holding, whether directly or through another vehicle, VA tokens that Hong Kong retail investors can already trade on an SFC-licensed VATP.
para 10, p.2
At fund level, SFC-authorised VA Funds should carry no leveraged exposure to VA.
para 14, p.2
Transactions and acquisitions of spot VA should be conducted through an SFC-licensed VATP, or through an AI (or a locally incorporated AI's subsidiary) that meets HKMA's regulatory requirements.
para 16, p.2

The trustee or custodian should only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or a qualifying AI (or its subsidiary) that meets HKMA's expected VA custody standards. VA holdings should be kept segregated, mostly stored in cold wallets, with seeds and keys kept securely in Hong Kong, access restricted, generated non-deterministically, protected by multi-signature (multi-sig) controls, and properly backed up.

A fund's offering documents, including the KFS (product key facts statements), must spell out VA exposure limits and the key risks -- price, custody, cybersecurity and fork risk for spot VA; roll costs and operational risks for VA futures.

VA Funds may now stake and do other VA-related activities -- newly allowed under the ASPIRe roadmap's Pillar P -- provided the management company follows guiding principles: fitting the fund's goals, implementing robust internal controls over risk and conflicts, proper custody, due diligence on counterparties, disclosing VA amounts used in offering documents, and telling investors about material changes.
para 27, p.4-5
Funds wanting VA exposure above 10% of NAV (whether new or existing), or wanting to stake or do VA-related activities, must first consult SFC and get its approval.
para 30, p.5
rg: Read paragraphs 6-27 (Requirements section) in full; paragraphs 1-5 are background/history.

t: SFC sets out staking guidance for licensed virtual asset trading platforms and authorised virtual asset funds
sl: SFC · SFC sets out staking guidance for licensed virtual asset… (2025)
s: The SFC published two linked pieces of staking guidance: a circular letting licensed virtual-asset trading platforms offer staking services under risk-management and disclosure conditions, and an updated circular letting SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds stake holdings through licensed platforms and authorised institutions, within a cap meant to manage liquidity risk. The SFC framed staking as part of its ASPIRe roadmap to widen the range of products and services on offer.
w: This lets licensed trading platforms and authorised funds offer staking; the bank itself has no direct duty here, but if it distributes such funds or refers clients to platforms offering staking, compliance should confirm those counterparties meet the asset-protection and disclosure standards this guidance sets.
k: SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds may only stake their holdings through licensed trading platforms and authorised institutions, and only up to a cap set to manage liquidity risk.
para 4
The guidance is presented as advancing the 'Products' part of the ASPIRe roadmap, which aims to broaden what platforms can offer.
para 2
Trading platforms should maintain measures to prevent errors in staking services, safeguard staked client assets, and ensure proper disclosure of the risks staked assets may carry.
para 3
rg: Short summary; read companion circulars 50bf95ba3143 (VATP staking) and 353535602a83 (VA Fund staking) for full operative requirements.

t: Provision of Staking Services for Virtual Assets from Custodial Services
sl: HKMA · Provision of Staking Services for Virtual Assets from Custodial… (2025)
s: This 7 April 2025 circular sets the HKMA's expected standards for authorized institutions (and subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs) that offer staking of virtual assets from their custodial services to clients. Staking here means locking client virtual assets so a validator can take part in a proof-of-stake blockchain, in exchange for rewards distributed back to the client. The circular covers internal controls, required client disclosures, and due diligence over the blockchain protocols and third-party providers used, and asks banks to discuss implementation with the HKMA in advance.
w: This is the current, in-force operating standard a bank must satisfy before or while offering custodial staking to clients, covering key-control, disclosure and third-party due-diligence expectations, plus a clear signal to talk to the HKMA before launch.
k: This circular covers authorized institutions themselves, plus any subsidiary of a locally incorporated AI, when either offers staking as part of its custodial services for clients; the parent AI must make sure such a subsidiary's conduct, practices and controls also comply.
A bank should maintain possession or control of everything needed to unstake client virtual assets, such as withdrawal keys and any pre-signed exit instructions.
p.2, section A

A bank should maintain policies to catch errors or misconduct in its staking service, keep staked client assets adequately safeguarded, and have internal controls for operational risk and conflicts of interest.
p.2, section A

A bank should disclose to clients which tokens it stakes, any third parties involved, fees, activation and minimum lock-up periods, how rewards are paid, the unstaking process and its length, uptime performance, what happens during outages, and its custodial arrangements.
p.2, section B

A bank should disclose the extra risks clients face from staking - including slashing (a validator penalty that can reduce staked assets), lock-up risk, blockchain bugs, hacking, validator inactivity, and legal uncertainty over a client's rights in staked assets - and how losses from these would be handled.
p.2, section B

Before it offers staking on a given blockchain protocol, a bank needs to carry out thorough due diligence and confirm its controls, technology and infrastructure can handle that protocol and manage the associated risks.
p.2-3, section C

Where staking is outsourced to a third-party provider, the bank should perform proper due diligence and ongoing monitoring, including checking the provider's track record, technology infrastructure, risk mitigation and security controls.
p.3, section C
Before rolling out staking services, AIs should have suitable policies, procedures, systems and controls in place, and should talk to the HKMA about their plans beforehand.
p.3, Implementation
rg: Read the whole circular (three pages); sections A-C set the substantive standards, the closing Implementation paragraph sets the expectation of prior HKMA discussion.

t: Circular on staking services provided by virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · staking services provided by virtual asset trading platforms (2025)
s: This circular allows SFC-licensed VATPs to provide staking services to clients (previously prohibited under VATP Guidelines para 7.26(b), which barred VATPs from generating returns on client VAs) by modifying VATP licence conditions, subject to the SFC's prior written approval and detailed 'Terms and conditions for providing staking services' (attached Appendix). VATPs must maintain possession/control of withdrawal mediums (no third-party custody of staked assets), implement whitelisting and verification controls, disclose staking terms/risks (slashing, lock-up, technical, hacking, inactivity, legal uncertainty risk), conduct due diligence on blockchain protocols and third-party validators, retain records for at least 7 years, and obtain SFC approval before including any protocol for retail clients (notification only for professional-investor-only staking).
w: This circular binds VATPs, not the bank, but a compliance head assessing a VATP partner's staking offering should use it as the checklist: no third-party custody of staked assets, mandatory risk disclosure, and SFC approval before retail-client protocols go live.
k: A VATP and its associated entities must keep hold of, or control, every means by which a client's staked VAs could be withdrawn (for instance, the withdrawal address's private key and any pre-signed voluntary exit message) -- they cannot leave that custody to an outside service provider.
para 6, p.1; Terms and conditions para 4, p.1

VATPs should implement systematic whitelist controls ensuring staking withdrawal addresses are limited to designated whitelisted addresses managed by the client cold wallet private key, and independently verify staking instructions before broadcast.
Terms and conditions para 6(b), p.2

VATPs should disclose on website/app: specific VAs staked, third parties involved, fees, minimum lock-up periods, unstaking process/length, outage/business-resumption arrangements, custodial arrangements, and risks (slashing, lock-up, technical/bug, hacking, inactivity, legal uncertainty).
circular para 9-10, p.2; Terms and conditions para 12, p.3-4
Except for institutional/qualified corporate professional investors, VATPs should obtain a client acknowledgement confirming understanding of staking risks before providing staking services.
Terms and conditions para 13, p.4

VATPs should obtain SFC prior written approval before including any blockchain protocol for retail-client staking, or terminating retail staking services; for professional-investor-only staking, advance written notification to the SFC suffices.
Terms and conditions para 23-24, p.6
Records relating to staking services (staked assets, validators, wallet addresses, dates, returns, protocol-selection rationale) should be retained for not less than 7 years.
Terms and conditions para 10, p.3

VATPs should exercise due skill, care and diligence selecting blockchain protocols and third-party validators, including reviewing smart contract audits, validator track record, security controls, financial soundness, and insurance for slashing risk.
Terms and conditions para 14-19, p.4-6
rg: Read the 3-page cover circular for the policy shift and background, then the 6-page Appendix (Terms and conditions) for the full operative requirements — both are needed as the circular incorporates the Appendix by reference.

t: The Hong Kong Fintech Ecosystem Report

s: Produced by Invest Hong Kong with the FinTech Association of Hong Kong and HKUST Business School, this market report profiles Hong Kong's fintech sector generally, with a timeline of policy milestones (including VATP licensing, stablecoin sandbox, Project Ensemble and spot crypto ETFs) and survey statistics on 130 Hong Kong fintech firms. It is descriptive market research aimed at investors and entrepreneurs, not a regulator publication, and contains no supervisory requirements.
w: A useful, dated market snapshot of Hong Kong's digital-asset ecosystem size and the regulatory milestone timeline, but produced by a market-research consortium rather than a regulator, so it should be treated as background context rather than an authoritative source for compliance decisions.
k: The digital asset and cryptocurrency sub-sector grew by nearly 30% from 2022 to 2024, and 111 digital-asset/cryptocurrency companies were counted in Hong Kong by mid-2024, alongside 175 blockchain application/software firms.

t: Research Paper on Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector
sl: HKMA · Research Paper on Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial… (2025)
s: On 19 March 2025 the HKMA sent all authorized institutions a circular sharing a research paper on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in finance, prepared as part of its "All banks go Fintech" initiative. The letter itself is administrative: it introduces the paper's coverage of ten real-world DLT adoption cases and analysis of risks and mitigation, encourages banks to review it and use the HKMA's DLT Supervisory Incubator, and gives contact points for follow-up. The substantive research content is in the attached study, recorded separately.
w: Signals that HKMA is actively encouraging DLT adoption and offers a low-friction sandbox route (the Supervisory Incubator); useful context when a business line proposes a DLT pilot, but this letter creates no binding obligation itself.
k: The research paper is issued under the HKMA's "All banks go Fintech" initiative within its Fintech 2025 strategy, with DLT identified as a key focus area.
A Supervisory Incubator for DLT has been set up to help banks develop DLT solutions responsibly; banks are encouraged to use it.
The paper is based on in-depth interviews covering ten real-world DLT adoption cases and includes analysis of associated risks and mitigation recommendations.
rg: One-page transmittal letter; read the attached study (id 9c5e90c118de) for substance.

t: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector - A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
sl: HKMA · Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector - A… (2025)
s: This is a lengthy HKMA research report on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in finance, describing DLT's architecture and core features, then walking through ten real-world adoption cases (including a hypothetical e-HKD use case, HKEX's Synapse platform and a UBS tokenisation pilot) covering payments, trade settlement and digital identity. It sets out practical adoption challenges such as strategy alignment, novel operational risks and regulatory uncertainty, and gives good-practice guidance for managing risks including third-party reliance, node concentration, smart contracts, key management, cybersecurity, data privacy and interoperability. It closes with the HKMA's own initiatives (the DLT Supervisory Incubator, financial and talent support) and a comparison of how Hong Kong, Singapore, the US and UK support DLT sandboxes.
w: This is educational/good-practice material, not a binding rule; it is useful as a risk-taxonomy checklist (third-party, node concentration, smart contract, key management, cyber, data privacy, interoperability) when a business line proposes a DLT pilot, and points to the HKMA's own sandbox route for engaging supervisors early.
k: The Executive Summary describes the paper's exploration of 10 real-world DLT adoption cases across programmable payments, trade settlement and digital identity; the case studies themselves (Section 3) name platforms such as a hypothetical e-HKD use case, HKEX's Synapse and a UBS tokenisation pilot.
Section 1, p.6 (overview); Section 3, p.17-40 (case detail)

Node concentration risk arises when a party gains control of over half a DLT network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens; permissioned networks face elevated concentration risk because a fixed, known set of parties already controls validation.
Section 4.1, item 2, p.48-49

Recommended mitigations for node concentration include diversifying node-hosting providers, robust software review and stress testing, contingency plans for non-DLT fallback, and (for permissionless networks) monitoring validator concentration.
Section 4.1, item 2, p.48-49
Smart contracts carry coding-vulnerability and oracle-concentration risks, since bugs can be exploited automatically and at speed, and reliance on a single oracle creates a single point of failure.
Section 4.1, item 3, p.49-50

The paper's practical guidance for banks starting DLT projects (Figure 21) includes developing a firm-wide DLT strategy, centralising efforts with a dedicated DLT team, delivering fit-for-purpose training, developing mitigation plans for identified risks, and proactively communicating with regulators.
Section 4.2, Figure 21, p.43
The HKMA's own DLT support includes the Supervisory Incubator sandbox, alongside comparable sandbox schemes run by the SFC (Regulatory Sandbox) and the IA (Insurtech Sandbox).
Section 4, p.58-59
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.6) and the risk/mitigation guidance in Section 4 (p.41-59, especially Figure 21 on p.43 and the risk-mitigation list at p.48-53); the ten case studies (Section 3, p.17-40) and glossary/appendix (Section 6) can be skimmed or used for reference only.

t: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector: A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
sl: HKMA · Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector: A Study… (2025)
s: HKMA commissioned this study, with input from SFC, IA and the MPF Schemes Authority, after interviewing ten institutions and surveying 113 firms on their DLT projects. It builds on two earlier HKMA circulars: the April 2024 risk-management circular and the January 2025 Supervisory Incubator launch. The paper walks through ten Hong Kong pilot deployments, then sets out adoption barriers and a set of good-practice pointers banks can use when scaling DLT work. It is framed as research and guidance rather than a new binding rule, and it repeats and elaborates several expectations the 2024 circular already set.
w: Although framed as research, the paper is HKMA's fullest current public statement of what it expects banks to have in place for governance, third-party, node/smart-contract, key-custody, cyber and privacy risk when running DLT, and it largely restates the April 2024 circular. A compliance head should treat sections 4.1-4.2 as the working checklist against which examiners are likely to benchmark a bank's DLT risk framework.
k: Boards and senior management should update governance, technology-risk, business-continuity and outsourcing policies before rolling out a DLT solution, and add safeguards such as dispute handling or a loss-compensation approach where customers interact with it directly.
Section 4.2.1, p.44

A firm should keep enough in-house DLT expertise, echoing the 2024 circular; the paper suggests a centralised team (e.g. a Centre of Excellence or hub-and-spoke model) blending technologists and business staff to run this.
Section 4.2.2, p.44-45

For outsourced DLT platforms, a bank should vet vendor reliability, security and regulatory standing at every stage, put performance and data-security terms in the contract, and keep backup vendors or failover plans ready.
Section 4.2.4, item 1 (Third-Party Risks), p.48

Because control of over half a network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens can let an attacker corrupt the ledger, firms should spread node hosting across providers/locations and run software review and stress testing to cut shared points of failure.
Section 4.2.4, item 2 (Node Concentration Risk), p.48-49

Smart contracts should not be used for every process; manual override should stay possible, and firms need a governance framework covering suitability review, testing before go-live, and contingency plans if a contract misbehaves.
Section 4.2.4, item 3 (Smart Contract Risk), p.49-50
Because ledger entries are essentially irreversible, firms should build strong upfront data-validation controls, since correcting an error or fraudulent entry after the fact may not be possible.
Section 4.2.4, item 4 (Immutability Risk), p.50-51

A bank holding client private keys as custodian is expected to run tight controls: secure key generation, restricted access, proprietary cold storage, backups and an incident-response plan; the paper flags hardware security modules and multi-party-computation (MPC) wallets, which split a key into shares, as ways to cut single-key concentration risk.
Section 4.2.4, item 5 (Private Key Risk), p.51-53

DLT platforms still need ordinary cyber defences - e.g. multi-factor authentication against endpoint attacks and phishing - and firms should track emerging threats such as quantum computing and adjust response plans over time.
Section 4.2.4, item 6 (Common Cybersecurity Risks), p.53

Where a ledger's transparency would expose counterparty or transaction details a firm needs to keep confidential, it should use privacy techniques (e.g. stealth addresses, ring signatures, zero-knowledge proofs) and plan for participants who want their data removed from the network.
Section 4.2.4, item 7 (Data Privacy Risk), p.53

The paper repeats the principle that new HKMA rules for DLT-based activity will track existing rules for the equivalent traditional activity rather than create a separate regime, summarised as "same activity, same risk, same regulation".
Section 4.2.5, p.57

Whether a smart contract counts as a binding legal contract in Hong Kong still has no statutory definition; enforceability turns on ordinary contract-formation tests (agreement, consideration, certainty/completeness, intent, formalities), the same approach the paper says Singapore, the US and the UK currently take.
Section 4.2.5, sub-section 1 (Hong Kong), p.57

HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT, launched January 2025, lets a bank get HKMA feedback and run live trials on its risk controls before fully launching a DLT initiative, contactable at supervisory_incubator_DLT@hkma.gov.hk; the paper also flags the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap (Feb 2025, 12 initiatives across five pillars) as the parallel securities-side track.
Section 4.2.6, p.58-59
rg: Read pp.41-59 (adoption challenges and the six practical-guidance sub-sections, especially the risk-mitigation list at pp.48-53 and the regulatory-coordination section at pp.57-59); pp.7-40 (DLT technology primer and the ten case studies) are background and can be skimmed.

t: SFC warns public of Linkbex for suspected virtual asset-related fraud
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of Linkbex for suspected virtual asset-related… (2025)

t: CMU OmniClear and HKEX sign MOU on enhancing post-trade securities infrastructure of Hong Kong's capital markets (with photos)

t: 2025-26 Budget

It also notes the stablecoin issuer bill had already reached the legislature. Most of the 179-page document covers unrelated fiscal, tax and spending matters.

t: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Cybersecurity webinar materials
sl: SFC · licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Cybersecurity… (2025)
s: This follow-up circular attaches the slide deck from the SFC's Cybersecurity Webinar held on 17 and 19 February 2025. It covers findings from the SFC's 2023/24 thematic review of cybersecurity, real incident case studies, and new risk areas. The deck, presented by the SFC's Steve Poon and Markus Au Yeung, reports on a review of 50 licensed corporations, including on-site checks of 7 internet brokers and talks with 6 licensed corporations that operate globally. It covers cloud security, remote access, managing third-party vendors, retiring old (end-of-life) software, and phishing. Two case studies are given: a ransomware attack that started from a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server, and unauthorised trades that followed an attack on an unpatched website using unencrypted data.
w: These SFC-documented case studies — a ransomware attack through a VPN gateway, and unauthorised trades through an unpatched web app — offer lessons a bank can apply directly to its own digital-asset or brokerage cyber-risk defences. They also show real concentration risk among third-party trading-system vendors.
k: The 2023/24 thematic review looked at 50 licensed corporations, with on-site checks at 7 internet brokers and discussions with 6 licensed corporations running global operations.
deck p.5
The review looked at cloud security, controls on remote access, management of third-party vendors, handling of software that is no longer supported (end-of-life), and phishing.
deck p.5
92% of internet brokers rely on trading systems built by outside vendors. The top 5 vendors hold 70% of that market, and the single biggest vendor holds 30% — a concentration risk.
deck p.6
Mobile apps have overtaken desktop computers as the main way clients trade online: 82% used mobile and 65% used desktop in 2023/24, compared with 80% each in 2019/20.
deck p.7

Between 2021 and 2024, 8 serious cybersecurity incidents were reported to the SFC, including ransomware attacks, a vendor network breach that disrupted back-office services, and account takeovers through weaknesses in network security.
deck p.9

Case study 1: attackers used a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server to plant ransomware, which disrupted trading, settlement, and back-office systems and forced a halt to online trading and client-money processing; missing logs made it hard to find the root cause.
deck p.10

Case study 2: attackers exploited an unpatched website that carried unencrypted data and outdated (end-of-life) database software, letting them break into internal servers, alter the client database, and place unauthorised trades.
deck p.11
Lessons for licensed corporations: strengthen network security, apply software patches, control user access rights, monitor client accounts, keep audit logs, and encrypt data.
deck p.12
Cyber Defender and Scameter, both tools from the Hong Kong Police Force, were highlighted as ways to stay informed about cybersecurity threats.
circular para 3
rg: Read the 2-page cover circular, then the attached deck's case illustrations (pages 9-12) for the concrete incident lessons; earlier pages (landscape stats) are useful context but less operative.

t: LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of Web3 and Virtual Assets visits Consensus Hong Kong (with photos)
sl: LegCo · LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of… (2025)

para 1

t: SFC sets out new roadmap to develop Hong Kong as a global virtual asset hub
sl: SFC · SFC sets out new roadmap to develop Hong Kong… (2025)
s: SFC laid out 12 major initiatives under a five-pillar 'ASPIRe' roadmap -- Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure, Relationships -- to boost the security, innovation, and growth of Hong Kong's virtual asset market. Planned steps include making it easier to reach global liquidity, building adaptive compliance and product frameworks, creating new regulatory frameworks for VA over-the-counter (OTC) trading and VA custodian services, expanding VA products and services, streamlining VATP operating requirements, fighting illicit activity, educating investors, and reaching out proactively to stakeholders -- including through the newly formed Virtual Asset Consultative Panel.
w: This sets out SFC's five-pillar ASPIRe roadmap. It creates no direct obligation itself, but it's the reference plan behind later binding circulars -- on staking, dealing and custodian consultations, cybersecurity, and market-making -- and should be tracked as a preview of coming change.
k: The ASPIRe roadmap has five pillars -- Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure, Relationships -- and covers 12 major initiatives.
para 1
New regulatory frameworks will be built for virtual asset over-the-counter (OTC) services and VA custodian services, which weren't separately regulated before.
para 3
The range of VA products and services on offer will grow, and the operating rules for VA trading platforms will be simplified.
para 3
The roadmap also covers fighting illicit activity, educating investors, and reaching out to stakeholders, including through the Virtual Asset Consultative Panel.
para 3, Note 1
rg: Short press release; the referenced Appendix (not fully included in fetched text) would list the 12 initiatives in detail — treat this record as the headline announcement, not the full initiative list.

t: “A-S-P-I-Re” for a brighter future: SFC’s regulatory roadmap for Hong Kong’s virtual asset market
sl: SFC · “A-S-P-I-Re” for a brighter future: SFC’s regulatory roadmap for… (2025)
s: The SFC set out a five-pillar roadmap, named Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure and Relationships (ASPIRe), for developing Hong Kong's virtual asset regulatory regime over the coming years. It opens with market context on institutional versus retail participation, fragmented trading venues, and global regulatory convergence between traditional finance and virtual assets, then lists twelve forward-looking initiatives, including new licensing regimes for OTC trading and custody, more flexible custody and cold-storage rules, staking and lending for professional investors, and better market surveillance. Most items are described as exploratory or under development rather than final rules, so the roadmap signals direction rather than imposing immediate new obligations. It targets custody legislative preparations for completion by end-2025.
w: This roadmap previews where SFC rules for VATPs, custodians and OTC desks are heading, so a bank's compliance function can anticipate new counterparty licensing categories and start planning for potential custody, staking or product changes among the intermediaries it uses or works with.
k: The SFC will support the government's introduction of a dedicated licensing framework for virtual asset OTC trading desks, applying the same rules that already bind licensed trading platforms.
Pillar A, Initiative 1

The SFC will build a separate licensing regime for virtual asset custodians modelled on traditional custodian standards for capital, cybersecurity and asset segregation, with legislative preparation targeted for completion by end-2025.
Pillar A, Initiative 1

The SFC will explore moving away from a fixed mandatory cold-storage ratio toward outcome-based, technology-neutral custody standards backed by real-time monitoring, audits and cybersecurity controls.
Pillar S, Initiative 3

The SFC will look at professional-investor-only new token listings and virtual asset derivatives trading, at aligning margin-trading requirements with securities-market risk safeguards, and at allowing staking (under custody and operational safeguards) and professional-investor-only borrowing/lending services.
Pillar P, Initiatives 6-8

The SFC will consider straight-through regulatory reporting for digital-asset information and deploy data-driven surveillance tools such as blockchain intelligence and wallet tracing to detect illicit activity market-wide.
Pillar I, Initiative 9
The SFC will strengthen cross-agency collaboration with local regulators and law enforcement, and promote cross-border cooperation with overseas regulators.
Pillar I, Initiative 10
The SFC will consider a regulatory framework for financial influencers to address their growing role in shaping investor decisions about virtual assets.
Pillar Re, Initiative 11
rg: Read the Executive Summary for context, then Pillar A (custody/OTC licensing) and Pillar S (custody flexibility) closely as these most affect bank counterparties; Pillars P, I and Re can be skimmed for direction only, as none commit to firm rules yet.

t: Keynote Speech at ASIFMA Annual Conference

t: Letter to DTCA: Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR
sl: HKMA · Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR (2025)
s: The HKMA wrote to the Deposit-Taking Companies Association on 11 February 2025 about a second, separate set of Banking (Capital) Rules changes, unrelated in subject to the cryptoasset standard but timed to commence alongside it. The main content covers a revised capital treatment for a bank's direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing-capacity (LAC) liabilities, plus clarifying edits to existing definitions to better match the Basel framework. Comments were due by 7 March 2025, with an intended effective date of 1 January 2026, the same date as the cryptoasset capital rules.
w: Not itself a crypto rule, but it bundles into the same 1 January 2026 commencement as the cryptoasset capital package, so a bank's Basel-implementation project plan for that date needs to track both streams together.
k: The amendments mainly cover a revised capital treatment for a bank's own direct holdings of certain non-capital LAC (loss-absorbing capacity) liabilities.
Other changes are definitional or clarifying edits meant to better align the Capital Rules with the Basel framework.
The HKMA intends to implement these changes at the same time as the cryptoasset capital standard, i.e. 1 January 2026.
rg: One-page cover letter; the actual amendment text was not part of this attachment set. Note this is a near-duplicate letter to the one sent the same day to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (id 843b382f9c92).

t: Letter to HKAB: Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR
sl: HKMA · Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR (2025)

t: SFC extends swift licensing process to new virtual asset trading platform applicants
sl: SFC · SFC extends swift licensing process to new virtual asset… (2025)
s: The SFC announced that all new (non-deemed) VATP applicants can now use its swift licensing process, requiring applicants to implement policies, procedures, systems and controls before conducting a single external assessment (with the SFC as a party to the engagement). This extends the approach already used for deemed-to-be-licensed applicants. The SFC also published its on-site inspection findings the same day to clarify expected regulatory standards.
w: This does not bind the bank but signals a faster regulatory pathway now available if the bank were to sponsor or invest in a new VATP applicant, and points to the same-day inspection findings worth reviewing for expected standards.
k: All new VATP applicants can now seek licences under the swift licensing process, requiring implementation of P&P before a single external assessment, with the SFC as a party to the engagement.
para 1-2
Extension follows the effectiveness of SFC's direct engagement approach used with deemed applicants during risk-based on-site inspections.
para 3
On 18 December 2024, four VATP applicants received licences from the SFC through the original swift licensing process aimed at deemed applicants.
Note 1
The SFC published its risk-based on-site inspection findings the same day to provide clarity on expected regulatory standards.
Note 3

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Findings from inspections on deemed-to-be-licensed virtual asset trading platform applicants and expected standards of conduct for virtual asset trading platform operators
sl: SFC · licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Findings… (2025)
s: Following on-site inspections of all deemed-to-be-licensed VATP applicants (focused on cybersecurity, safeguarding of client assets, and KYC), the SFC published Appendix 1 (22 detailed 'Expected standards of conduct', labelled A-V, covering cybersecurity, client virtual asset handling/segregation, the 98/2 cold/hot wallet ratio, seed/private key storage, contingency planning, compensation arrangements, client money, and access controls) and Appendix 2 (specific deficiencies observed during inspections mapped to each standard, e.g. weak/outdated cryptographic algorithms such as AES-ECB and MD5, manual-only privileged access controls, single-staff-member security operations centres, commingling of house and client virtual assets via Ethereum token-approval mechanisms, understated hot-wallet calculations breaching the 98/2 rule, multi-signature keys held partly outside Hong Kong, and bank-account signatory authority given to non-operational personnel). All Platform Operators are told to review policies/procedures/systems and immediately rectify deficiencies.
w: Publishes SFC inspection findings showing gaps in VATP applicants' cybersecurity, client-asset safeguarding and KYC processes; compliance should factor these observations into counterparty due diligence on any VATP relationship, though the circular does not bind the bank itself.
k: Platform Operators should implement network segmentation and micro-segmentation so critical systems/sensitive data are separated from higher-hacking-risk network segments; inspections found some operators allowed direct internet access to trading/custody systems or unrestricted firewall access between DMZ and internal subnets.
Appendix 1 Std A p.1; Appendix 2 paras 1-2, p.1

Platform Operators should deploy a centralized privileged access management solution covering all levels (servers, workstations, network perimeters), with senior management approving each privileged-account use; inspections found reliance on manual controls, permanent unreviewed privileged access, and one operator where a single staff member held most administrative accounts.
Appendix 1 Std B p.1; Appendix 2 paras 3-4, p.1-2

Platform Operators should use up-to-date, strong encryption for data storage and transmission; inspections found use of outdated/weak algorithms (AES-CBC, AES-ECB, MD5 hash) and unprotected internal data traffic despite TLS 1.2/1.3 on client-facing channels.
Appendix 1 Std C p.1-2; Appendix 2 paras 5-6, p.3

98/2 Requirement: Platform Operators are required to keep at least 98% of client virtual assets in cold storage; inspections found miscalculations (wrong wallet classification, excluding pending/unverified deposits) and Large Withdrawal handling that let hot wallets exceed the 2% cap.
Appendix 1 Std I-K p.3; Appendix 2 paras 17-20, p.7-8

Seeds/private keys should be kept in Hong Kong in a secure environment (e.g. certified HSM) and cold wallets should not use smart contracts; inspections found a hot wallet with 2-of-3 multisig keys split across the US, Singapore and Hong Kong, and a cold wallet using a 3-of-4 multisig smart contract.
Appendix 1 Std L p.3-4; Appendix 2 paras 21-22, p.8

Compensation arrangements should cover 50% of cold-wallet and 100% of hot-wallet client virtual assets (Compensation Amount), with insurance sufficiency analysed including exclusions and event deductibles; some operators assumed house funds would cover deductibles without proper assessment.
Appendix 1 Std R p.5; Appendix 2 paras 33-35, p.12-13

Client money should be deposited directly into the associated entity's segregated bank account (not routed via the Platform Operator's own account first); bank account signatory authority should be limited to persons involved in day-to-day operations.
Appendix 1 Std T-U p.5-6; Appendix 2 paras 38-41, p.13-14

Platform Operators should screen and block access from Restricted Jurisdictions (sanctioned jurisdictions and jurisdictions banning VA trading) and detect VPN/proxy circumvention, with documented due diligence on screening tool accuracy; inspections found minimal testing (e.g. only 1-2 IP addresses tested) and no formal VPN follow-up procedures.
Appendix 1 Std V p.6; Appendix 2 paras 42-44, p.15
rg: Read the 1-page cover circular for context, then Appendix 1 (6 pages, standards A-V) as the operative checklist, then skim Appendix 2 (15 pages) for the real deficiency examples underlying each standard — especially cybersecurity, 98/2 custody, and client-money sections.

t: Circular to new virtual asset trading platforms seeking to be licensed – Enhanced licensing process and revamped external assessments
sl: SFC · new virtual asset trading platforms seeking to be licensed… (2025)
s: This circular sets the enhanced VATP licensing process for NEW corporations applying for a licence (as distinct from deemed applicants), effective for applications submitted after 18 December 2024, and supersedes the June 2023 Scope of External Assessment Reports. It collapses the previous first-phase and second-phase assessments into a single external assessment, performed only after the applicant deploys all systems and controls, under a tripartite agreement with the SFC and an External Assessor (EA), as a direct assurance engagement (HKSAE 3000 or equivalent, e.g. ISAE 3000) signed off by a practising CPA.
w: This binds new VATP applicants, not the bank directly, but a compliance head sponsoring or partnering with a bank-backed new VATP should understand the revised single-assessment, post-deployment sequencing when planning that entity's licensing timeline.
k: Separate first-phase and second-phase assessments are being dropped for VATPs -- going forward, new applicants complete just a single external assessment across the whole licensing process.
footnote 1, p.1
Applicants must submit a licensing application bundle via WINGS including written policies/procedures, documentation showing a suitable EA has been identified, and the EA's capability statement.
para 5, p.1

The SFC will assess the applicant's business structure, competence, and fitness and properness of the applicant and its ultimate controller(s)/owner(s), substantial shareholder(s), proposed responsible officers and Managers-in-Charge, plus the EA's capability; it may oppose the EA or return an incomplete/deficient application.
para 6, p.1-2

After acceptance, the applicant must deploy its systems and controls (market surveillance, AML/CFT and KYC tools, custody solutions) and fully adapt its policies/procedures before undergoing the external assessment.
para 7-8, p.2

The external assessment must be a direct assurance engagement (under HKSAE 3000 or an equivalent standard such as ISAE 3000), signed off by a practising certified public accountant, whose job is to opine on whether the VATP's P&P have been properly designed and put into practice in line with the VATP Guidelines and the AML/CFT Guideline.
para 14, p.2-3
The SFC will pay $1 toward the external assessment fees; the VATP applicant pays the balance of all fees, disbursements and expenses.
footnote 5, p.2
As soon as practicable, the applicant must tell the SFC and the EA about any later material change to its P&P.
para 13, p.2
Once the external assessment is done and any remaining issues (such as a capital top-up) are cleared, the SFC will issue a licence provided it considers the applicant fit and proper.
para 9, p.2
rg: Read the full 3-page circular plus 1-page Appendix flowchart; the flowchart concisely visualises the sequence from application through external assessment to licence approval.

t: Letter to DTCA: Soft consultation: prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures

Further guidance, such as FAQs or Supervisory Policy Manual modules, is expected once the rules are refined after industry comment.

t: Annex 2: Disclosure Requirements in Relation to Cryptoasset Exposures
sl: HKMA · Annex 2: Disclosure Requirements in Relation to Cryptoasset Exposures (2025)
s: This document proposes new public disclosure duties for banks holding cryptoassets, added to the Banking (Disclosure) Rules from 1 January 2026 to match the Basel Committee's cryptoasset disclosure standard. It introduces four new disclosure items: yearly qualitative disclosure of crypto activities and how the bank applied the classification rules, twice-yearly disclosure of crypto exposures and their risk-weighted amounts, twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto holdings and liabilities are treated in the accounts, and twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto positions feed into liquidity ratios for banks that must meet those ratios. It also creates a new defined term, "cryptoliability", for digital liabilities tied to a cryptoasset.
w: This sets the public reporting cadence compliance must run once the bank has any cryptoasset exposure: annual qualitative disclosure of activities and classification methodology, plus semi-annual quantitative disclosures on exposures, accounting treatment and (for larger banks) liquidity impact.
k: A new term, "cryptoliability", is added, meaning a digital liability tied to a cryptoasset; it covers a bank's own token issuance liabilities and other digital liabilities linked to cryptoassets.
Item 2(2), p.2

Each year, a bank with cryptoasset or cryptoliability exposures must publicly disclose an overview of its crypto-related business, the risks involved, its risk-management policies, and how it decided whether each Group 1 cryptoasset it holds meets the classification conditions.
new s.16ZQH, p.5-6

Twice a year, a bank must disclose an overview of its cryptoasset exposures broken down by regulatory bucket (Group 1a/1b/2a/2b) and the related risk-weighted amounts, its operational-risk policies for crypto, the market value and types of crypto it holds in custody for clients, and an explanation of any material change during the period.
new s.16ZQI, p.6-7

The twice-yearly exposure disclosure must break out material individual holdings of Group 1b, Group 2a and Group 2b cryptoassets separately, not just totals; tokenised traditional assets are excluded from this breakdown.
new s.16ZQI(2), p.7
Twice a year, a bank must disclose how it classifies and measures its cryptoasset and cryptoliability holdings for accounting purposes, with a breakdown of carrying values by regulatory bucket.
new s.16ZQJ, p.8

A bank that is a category 1 institution (subject to the full liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio rules) must twice a year disclose how its cryptoasset and cryptoliability exposures feed into those liquidity ratio calculations.
new s.16ZQK, p.9

Banks incorporated outside Hong Kong face a lighter version of these rules, limited to an overview of crypto activities that create liquidity risk and, for category 1 institutions, the classification-conditions disclosure.
new s.103(4B) and s.103AC, p.11-13
rg: Read the four new disclosure sections (16ZQH-16ZQK, p.5-9) in full; the amendments to existing sections 2, 11 and 91-105 (p.2-4, 10-14) are mostly consequential cross-referencing and can be skimmed.

t: Annex 1: Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures
sl: HKMA · Annex 1: Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures (2025)
s: This document sets out the HKMA's proposed line-by-line changes to the Banking (Capital) Rules to bring in a dedicated capital regime for banks' cryptoasset exposures, copying the Basel Committee's December 2022 standard and its July 2024 amendments, targeted for 1 January 2026. It defines a cryptoasset and a cryptoasset exposure, sorts cryptoassets into four buckets with different capital treatment, and adds new rules for classifying them, assigning them to the banking or trading book, working out risk-weighted amounts, and capping how much of a bank's capital can sit in the riskiest bucket. A bank must itself decide the bucket for each cryptoasset it holds, based on conditions it must document and that the HKMA can override.
w: This is the draft capital rulebook a bank must build systems and governance against before 1 January 2026: it fixes how every cryptoasset position gets bucketed, which bucket triggers a punitive 1,250% risk weight, and a hard portfolio limit that forces board-level notification and remediation if breached.
k: A cryptoasset is a digital token representing value that can be used for payment, investment, or to access a good or service, built mainly using cryptography together with distributed-ledger or comparable technology; a cryptoasset exposure is any on- or off-balance-sheet exposure to one that carries credit, market, valuation-adjustment, operational or liquidity risk.
Item 1, p.2-4

Cryptoassets fall into four buckets: Group 1a (a tokenised version of a traditional asset), Group 1b (a token with an effective mechanism pegging it to a traditional asset or basket, i.e. a stablecoin-type instrument), Group 2a (a liquid token with an approved derivative, ETF or ETN referencing it) and Group 2b (everything else, treated as the riskiest bucket).
Item 1, p.4-6
Tokens that run on a fully open, permissionless blockchain cannot qualify for Group 1a or Group 1b, because the HKMA judges that risk controls for such networks are not yet proven under stress.

A bank decides which bucket each cryptoasset belongs in, on an ongoing basis, against conditions the HKMA sets; it must keep records showing how it met those conditions and hand them to the HKMA on request.

The first time a bank takes on exposure to a cryptoasset it has never held before, it must tell the HKMA immediately and treat that cryptoasset as the riskiest bucket (Group 2b) until the HKMA is satisfied a better bucket applies.
The HKMA can overrule a bank's own bucket decision for any cryptoasset if it judges that prudent.

Group 1a and Group 1b tokens go in the banking or trading book depending on how the equivalent traditional asset would be booked; Group 2a tokens always go in the trading book; Group 2b tokens always go in the banking book.

For each riskiest-bucket (Group 2b) cryptoasset, a bank must apply a 1,250% risk weight to whichever is bigger: the total of its long positions or the total of its short positions in that token; this one number stands in for credit, market and valuation-adjustment risk together, so none of those are calculated separately for that token.

A bank must work out a Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio (its combined exposure to Group 2a and Group 2b tokens, divided by Tier 1 capital); a globally or domestically systemically important bank must keep this at or below 1% at all times, or below 2% if it only occasionally goes over 1%.

If a systemically important bank's Group 2 exposure ratio goes over 1%, it must tell the HKMA in writing, add extra capital using a set formula, and act quickly to get back under the 1% line; going over 2% forces the bank to hold capital as if every Group 2 token were in the riskiest bucket.

For a derivative contract on a riskiest-bucket cryptoasset, the exposure used in the capital calculation is the fair value of the underlying token grossed up for leverage, capped at the most the bank could possibly lose on the contract.
The HKMA can order a bank in writing to hold extra capital if the bank has sizeable short positions in riskiest-bucket tokens that could lose more than the standard risk weight already covers.
rg: Read Item 1 (definitions, p.2-8), Item 13.3-13.4 (classification and book assignment, p.56-63) and Items 18.4 and 20 (risk weight and exposure ratio, p.97-103) closely; skim the technical market-risk formula sections in Item 18.1-18.3 (p.89-97) unless building the trading-book model itself.

t: Circular to virtual asset trading platforms on licensing process and revamped Second-phase Assessment
sl: SFC · virtual asset trading platforms on licensing process and revamped… (2024)
s: The SFC set out its VATP licensing roadmap and a revamped Second-phase Assessment. After on-site inspections, deemed applicants receive a conditional licence requiring completion of a rectification plan plus a satisfactory independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment before operating on a restricted scope of business. VATPs must then engage an External Assessor (EA) under a tripartite agreement (SFC, VATP, EA) for the Second-phase Assessment, a direct assurance engagement (signed off by a practising CPA, per standards like HKSAE3000) assessing whether the VATP's policies, procedures, systems and controls are suitably designed and implemented against the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline. Upon satisfactory completion, the SFC uplifts the business-scope restriction.
w: This binds VATPs, not the bank directly, but sets the exact assurance bar (penetration test, custody-system binary analysis, tripartite external assessment) a compliance head should require evidence of before relying on any VATP's custody and security controls.
k: Deemed applicants are granted a conditional licence after agreeing a rectification plan with the SFC; as a licensing condition they must complete rectifications and pass an independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment before operating on a restricted scope of business.

t: LCQ15: Policy on digital assets
sl: FSTB · LCQ15: Policy on digital assets (2024)
s: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury set out the government's digital-asset policy in response to questions about a dedicated crypto commissioner and bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset. t: Guideline on the Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · Guideline on the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2024)
s: This guideline sets the eligibility and application rules for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy announced in the 2024 Policy Address to encourage tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong. It reimburses 50% of eligible expenses per issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant, basic requirements only) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant, basic plus additional requirements), capped at two issuances per issuer group. Eligibility hinges on Hong Kong nexus (lead arranger or DLT team presence, or issuance on the CMU's DLT platform) and, for the Full Grant, independence of the DLT platform provider, a HK$1 billion minimum issuance size, at least five unrelated investors, and listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP).
w: Gives a concrete cost-recovery incentive and eligibility checklist a bank's treasury, DCM or digital-assets team should use when structuring or arranging a Hong Kong digital bond issuance, and it explicitly recognises listing on SFC-licensed VATPs as a qualifying route.
k: The DBGS reimburses 50% of Eligible Expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant) for meeting Basic Requirements, or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant) for meeting Basic plus Additional Requirements.
An issuer group, counting its associates as one, can draw DBGS support for no more than two digital bond deals.

To qualify at all, the issuance must be arranged half-or-more by Hong Kong-recognised lead arrangers, and either have a DLT team with substantial Hong Kong presence or be issued using the Central Moneymarkets Unit's (CMU) own DLT platform.

For the Full Grant, the digital bond must additionally: use a DLT platform provider unrelated to the issuer; be at least HK$1 billion equivalent in size (all tranches combined); be issued to five or more unrelated investors; and be listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP).

Eligible reimbursable expenses include fees to (unrelated) DLT platform providers, Hong Kong-based arrangers, legal advisers, auditors/accountants/rating agencies, listing fees (SEHK or licensed VATPs), and CMU lodging/clearing fees.

For green, social, sustainability or transition digital bonds, the issuer must pick one source for general issuance costs -- either DBGS or GSF Grant Scheme Track I, capped at HK$2.5 million -- not both; costs of the external sustainability review sit separately under Track II, capped at HK$800,000.
Applicants may seek an optional pre-application consultation, then must submit a formal application within three months of the bond's issuance.
The scheme opened for applications on 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, and covers bonds issued on or after the 16 October 2024 Policy Address announcement.
p.1, footnote 1
The HKMA retains absolute discretion over whether eligibility requirements and terms are met and over the amount of any subsidy granted, and may adjust the scheme's design over time.
rg: Read the whole guideline (six pages); it is short and every section (Overview, Basic/Additional Requirements, Eligible Expenses, Application Process) is operationally relevant.

t: HKMA launches Digital Bond Grant Scheme
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Digital Bond Grant Scheme (2024)
s: The HKMA launched the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), announced in the 2024 Policy Address, to grow Hong Kong's digital securities market and support wider take-up of DLT-based tokenisation in capital-market issuances. Per the attached Guideline, DBGS covers 50% of eligible expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant, meeting Basic Requirements) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant, meeting Basic + Additional Requirements). Each issuer (including associates) may claim for a maximum of two issuances. Basic Requirements include Hong Kong issuance/arranger presence and either substantial Hong Kong digital-team presence or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform. Additional Requirements for the Full Grant include an independent DLT platform provider, minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, 5+ independent investors, and listing on SEHK or an SFC-licensed VATP. Applications opened 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, covering bonds issued on or after 16 October 2024.

t: Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong (2024)
s: This HKMA Quarterly Bulletin feature article, published shortly after the July 2024 consultation conclusions, gives a plain-language overview of why Hong Kong is regulating stablecoin issuers, summarising market history (DeFi Summer, TerraUSD depeg, FTX collapse), the proposed licensing requirements, and the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox launched in July 2024. It confirms the first three sandbox participants (admitted July 2024) were testing payments, supply chain and capital markets use cases, clarifies that being in the sandbox is not required before applying for a future licence, and flags a rising trend of scams falsely claiming sandbox or licensed status. It also records HKMA's intention (as of writing) to bring the stablecoin bill before the Legislative Council before 2024 was out.
w: This is a useful plain-English primer for briefing non-specialist stakeholders on why the stablecoin regime exists and how the sandbox worked, and its scam warning is a reminder to verify any counterparty's claimed sandbox or licensed status directly against HKMA's published list rather than the counterparty's own representation.
k: The article frames the regime around four requirement groups: stability of the stablecoin (full backing, investment limits, redemption), safekeeping of reserves (segregation, disclosure/reporting), governance (knowledge/experience, business restrictions, Hong Kong physical presence) and risk management (risk controls, AML/CFT).
Exhibit 2, p.4
Only stablecoins issued by licensed issuers were intended to be offerable to retail investors, restricting unlicensed issuers to non-retail distribution.

The stablecoin issuer sandbox, launched July 2024, is for testing business models and getting HKMA feedback before the regime takes legal effect; sandbox participation is explicitly not a prerequisite for a future stablecoin licence application.
The first batch of three sandbox participants (admitted July 2024) tested use cases in payments, supply chain management and capital markets applications.

Sandbox testing was deliberately limited in scope - capped user numbers and issuance size, and no handling of customer or public funds at the initial stage - with HKMA able to expand scope later by separate announcement.

HKMA flagged a rising trend of scams involving entities falsely claiming to be licensed stablecoin issuers or sandbox participants, and published a list of genuine sandbox participants on its website to counter this.
At the time of writing, HKMA intended to table the stablecoin bill in the Legislative Council before 2024 ended, en route to the regime that ultimately commenced on 1 August 2025.

t: Consultation conclusions for legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers in Hong Kong released
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Consultation conclusions for legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime… (2024)
s: FSTB and HKMA jointly released consultation conclusions on the proposed licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers, following 108 submissions during the Dec 2023-Feb 2024 consultation. Key confirmed requirements: FRS in circulation must be backed in full by reserve assets without a break at any time; reserves must generally match the referenced currency (HKD issuers may hold USD reserves with MA flexibility); reserve assets must be segregated and safeguarded via trust/custodian arrangements, generally with licensed HK banks; redemption must be fulfilled within one business day at par; interest payment to FRS users is prohibited (marketing incentives are not); minimum paid-up capital is HKD25 million or 1% of FRS in circulation, whichever is higher (reduced from the proposed 2%); non-HK incorporated issuers (other than AIs) must establish a HK subsidiary; and only that specified group of licensed entities -- FRS issuers, banks, licensed corporations and licensed VATPs -- may offer FRS to the public; a six-month non-contravention transitional period was set. The bill was to be introduced to LegCo later in 2024.
w: As the definitive blueprint later enacted as the Stablecoins Ordinance, a compliance head should use this to plan the reserve segregation, redemption-timing, no-interest and audit-attestation controls the bank would need to issue an FRS, noting the capital requirement was reduced from the original proposal.
k: The full value of FRS in circulation must be matched by reserve assets without exception, at every point in time; issuers must show the MA that measures such as over-collateralisation are in place to meet this.
para 3.2.3, p.10 (attachment 54aa01e7396e)
