Reserve assets must be segregated from the issuer's own assets, safeguarded via an effective trust arrangement (independent trustee or declaration of trust), generally safekept with licensed HK banks; draft trust deed and independent legal opinion must be submitted to HKMA for review.
Monthly attestation of reserve assets by a qualified independent auditor will be required regardless of FRS circulation size.
FRS issuers must not pay interest to FRS users (via themselves or third-party arrangements); marketing incentives remain permitted if they do not amount to interest.

Redemption requests must be fulfilled within one business day in normal circumstances, at par value in the referenced currency, without undue cost; MA prior approval needed if an issuer foresees difficulty meeting this timeframe.
FRS issuers are prohibited from conducting lending or financial intermediation activities; only activities ancillary to FRS issuance (e.g. wallet services for their own FRS) are permitted.

Non-Hong Kong incorporated companies (other than AIs incorporated outside HK) must establish a Hong Kong subsidiary to apply for a licence; key management (chief executive and alternate) must be present in Hong Kong.
The minimum paid-up share capital was set at whichever is greater of HKD25 million or 1% of FRS's circulating par value -- down from the 2% floor proposed in the consultation paper.

The public may only be offered FRS by one of the specified licensed entities: an FRS issuer holding an HKMA licence, an authorized institution, a licensed corporation, or a licensed virtual asset trading platform; none of these needs a separate MA licence to offer, but each must meet its own regime's requirements.
A six-month non-contravention (transitional) period was set for pre-existing FRS issuers.
FSTB/HKMA planned to introduce a bill into the Legislative Council later in 2024, with licensing/supervisory guidelines to follow.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2024)
s: Published jointly by FSTB and HKMA in July 2024, this paper responds to 108 submissions received on the December 2023 consultation paper and confirms the authorities will proceed with a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It keeps the core proposals (full reserve backing, redemption rights, HKMA licensing) while clarifying scope questions such as what counts as 'actively marketing' to the Hong Kong public, confirming HKD-referenced coins issued from outside Hong Kong are still caught, and stating a bill would be introduced to the Legislative Council later in 2024. It should be read alongside the original consultation paper, which it amends rather than replaces outright.
w: This document shows how the government tightened and clarified the stablecoin licensing regime after industry feedback, including confirming extraterritorial reach for HKD-pegged coins, which matters for cross-border product screening and for assessing any stablecoin counterparty's licensing status.
k: The scope was narrowed so the regime targets stablecoins run on distributed ledgers not controlled by a single party, rather than covering privately-run ledgers too.
para 1.4, p.5

Both single-currency and multi-currency referenced stablecoins stay in scope, but multi-currency issuers face requirements scaled to the added complexity of managing reserves across several currencies.

Determining whether marketing counts as 'active marketing' to the Hong Kong public will look at factors like the language used, whether the audience is Hong Kong-based, and use of a Hong Kong domain name.
An overseas entity issuing a Hong Kong dollar-referenced stablecoin still needs an HKMA licence even if it operates outside Hong Kong, because of the currency's local monetary significance.

Agents or intermediaries who market a licensed issuer's stablecoin on its behalf are not themselves treated as issuers needing a licence, but anyone promoting an unlicensed issuer's coin commits an offence.
The authorities confirmed a bill to implement the regime would be brought to the Legislative Council later in 2024, with HKMA to issue licensing and supervisory guidelines afterwards.
The six-month grace period for pre-existing issuers to apply for a licence was retained, informed partly by experience running the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox.

s: This paper sets out the FSTB's and HKMA's final policy positions on the future fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuer licensing regime, after a two-month consultation that drew 108 responses. The HKMA called this the world's first link between a real-time payment system and a central bank digital currency (CBDC). e-CNY wallets support cross-border retail spending but not transfers between individuals, and now also work in mainland pilot zones beyond the Greater Bay Area.
w: For a compliance head, this shows a cross-border e-CNY/FPS link that some retail banks already support as a top-up channel; it does not create any new compliance duty for the bank itself.
k: Hong Kong residents can open a personal (tier-4) e-CNY wallet at one of four wallet operators using only a Hong Kong mobile number.
Annex 1/2, p.1

Annex 1, p.1

t: Expanding cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Expanding cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong (2024)
s: Hong Kong widened its trial of China's digital yuan, e-CNY, in partnership with the mainland central bank. Local residents can now set up a digital yuan wallet with just a Hong Kong phone number and add funds to it through the local instant-payment rail via a set list of retail banks. The announcement calls this the world's first time an instant domestic payment system has been wired directly into a central bank's digital currency. Sending money wallet-to-wallet between individuals is still blocked, and each account has a funding ceiling.
w: If the bank is one of the 17 listed FPS top-up participants, its operations and AML teams should confirm the e-CNY top-up flow is covered by existing cross-border payment AML controls, since e-CNY is a foreign central bank's retail digital currency operating through domestic rails.
k: A Hong Kong resident can now register a basic-tier e-CNY wallet with nothing more than a local mobile number, skipping the need for a mainland bank account.

t: SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions (V.3)
sl: HKMA · SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions (2024)
s: This is the HKMA's general Supervisory Policy Manual module describing how it oversees banks that are also SFC-Registered Institutions (RIs) carrying on securities and futures regulated activities, such as dealing, advising or asset management. It is not crypto-specific: it covers registration, executive-officer appointment, the HKMA-SFC cooperation framework, on-site/off-site supervision, a three-tier escalation model for deficiencies, and the major conduct requirements (KYC, suitability, product due diligence). Its one direct link to this batch's subject is a reference, in the product-due-diligence section's list of relevant circulars, to the HKMA-SFC joint circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset-related activities.
w: Establishes the governance scaffolding (executive officer regime, HKMA-SFC supervisory cooperation, escalation ladder) that applies to any bank entity conducting virtual-asset dealing, advisory or asset-management activity as an SFC-Registered Institution, even though this module itself carries no crypto-specific rules — the VA joint circular it cross-references (indexed elsewhere in this corpus) is where the crypto-specific conduct requirements actually sit.
k: The HKMA is the day-to-day 'front line supervisor' of banks registered with the SFC (RIs), while the SFC retains ultimate regulatory responsibility, and the two regulators may rely on each other's supervision under a Memorandum of Understanding

Every RI must appoint at least two executive officers per regulated activity to directly supervise it, and at least one must be available to supervise that activity at all times; executive officers need the HKMA's written consent
para 2.2.4

The HKMA applies a three-level, risk-based supervisory escalation model: encouraging good practice, then requiring corrective action for control deficiencies (potentially including an independent review), then enforcement action where there is a prima facie case for discipline

The module's product-due-diligence guidance lists, among other relevant circulars, the HKMA-SFC 'Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities' (22 Dec 2023), covering distribution of VA-exposed investment products, VA dealing, VA asset management and VA advisory services
rg: For crypto purposes, only para 4.7 (product due diligence and its list of relevant circulars, pp.41–43) is directly on point; skim sections 1–3 for the general governance/executive-officer/escalation framework and skip the sections on corporate finance, back-office and other non-VA regulated activities.

t: HKMA establishes the Project Ensemble Architecture Community
sl: HKMA · HKMA establishes the Project Ensemble Architecture Community (2024)
s: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) set up the Project Ensemble Architecture Community. This is an industry group that will build shared standards. The standards will help wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC), tokenised money, and tokenised assets work together. The first goal is a method for banks to settle tokenised deposits with each other using wholesale CBDC. The group will also help build and run the Project Ensemble Sandbox, a test environment once aimed at a mid-2024 start. Founding members are drawn from regulators and industry: the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) on the public side, plus the CBDC Expert Group and the Hong Kong arm of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. Seven private firms round out the group — HashKey Group, Ant Digital Technologies, and Microsoft Hong Kong from tech, alongside four banks: HSBC, Hang Seng Bank, Standard Chartered Hong Kong, and Bank of China (Hong Kong).
w: This sets up an industry body, including major Hong Kong banks, to shape tokenisation compatibility rules. It creates no duty for the bank yet, but it shows where wholesale CBDC and tokenised-deposit infrastructure is heading, which the bank may need to follow later.
k: This Community will build shared industry rules so wholesale CBDC, tokenised money, and tokenised assets can work with each other.
para 2, p.1
The first goal is a way for banks to settle tokenised deposits between each other using wholesale CBDC whenever tokenised assets are traded.
para 2, p.1

t: Risk management considerations related to the use of DLT
sl: HKMA · Risk management considerations related to the use of DLT (2024)
s: This Annex lists ten non-binding supervisory considerations the HKMA applies when reviewing a bank's DLT projects, grouped under governance, application design/development, and ongoing maintenance/monitoring. Key themes are board-level ownership of DLT risk, careful choice of network type (permissioned vs permissionless), smart-contract governance and audit, legal-risk awareness around settlement finality, third-party/node-operator due diligence, interoperability, cybersecurity commensurate with traditional systems, secure private-key management, data-privacy compliance on immutable ledgers, and DLT-specific contingency planning.
w: This is the HKMA's working checklist for any bank DLT proposal — tokenised deposits, custody platforms, settlement systems — so compliance and technology teams should map each planned DLT initiative against these ten considerations before submitting it to the HKMA, since the considerations, while non-binding, are what supervisors will actually probe.
k: An AI's board and senior management bear full responsibility for DLT adoption and for managing its risks, including updating technology risk management, business continuity and outsourcing policies to reflect DLT-specific factors, and ensuring sufficient in-house DLT expertise and staff training
Annex, item 1 (Governance)
Where a DLT solution is customer-facing, the bank should review whether DLT-specific consumer education, dispute handling, redress and compensation mechanisms are needed
Annex, item 1

The choice of DLT network type (permissionless, private-permissioned, public-permissioned) directly affects security, stability, scalability and resilience, and the HKMA expects the bank to justify its choice against the application's risk profile and to have compensating controls if a higher-risk design is chosen
Annex, item 2

Permissionless networks are not necessarily the obvious pick when sensitive data needs to move across the system, though they need not be ruled out if the bank can show appropriate mitigations such as zero-knowledge proofs or hybrid on/off-chain designs
Annex, item 2

Where smart contracts are used, the bank must manage associated operational, third-party and legal risks and put in place a governance framework covering suitability assessment, due-diligence review, risk-control incorporation in design, and procedures for upgrades, with third-party audits considered before deployment
Annex, item 3

Because settlement finality and legal standing under DLT arrangements can be less clear-cut than under traditional systems, banks should identify these legal grey areas, take professional advice where needed, and build mitigations into the design process
Annex, item 4

Banks must assess whether the node operators validating a DLT network are sufficiently trustworthy, reliable and diverse, and should generally avoid using permissionless networks (where node operators may be pseudonymous) for highly critical or sensitive functions unless adequate compensating controls exist
Annex, item 5

Banks are advised to design DLT systems to interoperate with both traditional and other DLT-based systems where practicable, e.g. so a tokenised deposit is not confined to the issuing bank's own proprietary network, while ensuring interbank connections are made securely
Annex, item 6

DLT applications must have cybersecurity commensurate with traditional technology, covering DLT-specific threats (e.g. 51% attacks) as well as common threats (e.g. DDoS), with response capabilities regularly updated for emerging risks such as quantum computing
Annex, item 7

Banks acting as custodian of client digital assets should apply more rigorous private-key security procedures — secure generation, storage, backup, access controls and cold storage — cross-referencing the HKMA's separate custody circular
Annex, item 8, footnote 3

Banks must continue to comply with data privacy and protection requirements regardless of whether data sits on a centralised system or a DLT ledger, addressing DLT-specific complications such as data-retention difficulties from ledger immutability, confidentiality on transparent ledgers, and cross-border data localisation
Annex, item 9

For DLT used in critical functions, business continuity plans should include DLT-specific testing scenarios (e.g. common DLT cyberattacks, key loss/theft, forking) and backup options for temporary or permanent DLT unavailability
Annex, item 10
rg: Read all ten considerations (pp.2–6); each is short and none is boilerplate.

t: Keynote Speech at the International Conference on Central Bank Digital Currencies and Payment Systems
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at the International Conference on Central Bank… (2024)
s: A senior HKMA official set out a 'digital money framework' comprising three planned components: a possible retail central bank digital currency (CBDC), regulated stablecoins, and tokenised bank deposits, all potentially underpinned by a wholesale CBDC. The speech reviewed the HKMA's CBDC work (Project mBridge, e-HKD Pilot Programme, Project Aurum) and confirmed the HKMA had just completed its stablecoin issuer consultation and would require full reserve backing with high-quality, liquid assets. It also announced a wholesale CBDC sandbox under the newly launched Project Ensemble, aimed at exploring interbank settlement between institutions' own tokenised-asset ledgers.
w: Provides the clearest early articulation of how HKMA expects stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs to fit together, which frames how a bank should position its own tokenised-deposit and digital-asset strategy relative to the regulator's roadmap.
k: The HKMA set out a digital money framework built around three components: retail CBDC, regulated stablecoins, and tokenised bank deposits.

s: This is a think-tank paper from the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC), a government-funded advisory body, arguing that Hong Kong should keep encouraging blockchain use in business-to-business finance, separate from crypto trading. t: HKMA launches Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme
sl: HKMA · HKMA launches Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme, building on Phase 1 (completed October 2023), which studied domestic retail use cases such as programmable payments, tokenised-asset settlement and offline payments. Phase 2 will go deeper into selected Phase 1 pilots (programmability, tokenisation, atomic settlement) plus new use cases, supported by an enhanced e-HKD sandbox built on the wCBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble. Applications to participate were due by 17 May 2024.
w: Informational for a compliance head: confirms e-HKD pilot infrastructure and Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit sandbox are technically converging, useful context for the bank's digital-asset roadmap but not a source of any obligation.

t: SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform Bybit

s: The SFC warns that Bybit, which offers a wide range of derivative-like and yield crypto products across many markets, is not licensed for any regulated activity in Hong Kong. It notes that crypto-linked products of this kind can count as futures contracts or securities under Hong Kong law, so marketing or dealing in them toward Hong Kong investors needs a licence unless an exemption applies. k: No entity in the Bybit group holds an SFC licence or SFC registration for any regulated activity in Hong Kong.

t: Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox
sl: HKMA · Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox (2024)
s: The HKMA announced the launch of a sandbox for firms planning to launch stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies in Hong Kong, following a December 2023 consultation paper on a future licensing regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather feedback from participants testing stablecoin business models in a limited, risk-controlled way. Admission requires a genuine plan to issue stablecoins, a concrete testing plan, and a reasonable prospect of meeting future rules. Sandbox status is not a licence and does not guarantee a future licence; the HKMA warned the public to watch for scams using the sandbox's name.
w: Marks the start of direct HKMA engagement with prospective stablecoin issuers ahead of the eventual Stablecoins Ordinance; a bank considering issuing or partnering with a sandbox participant should check the published participant list rather than rely on a counterparty's own claims.
k: Applicants must show genuine interest in and a workable plan for launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong, a concrete sandbox participation plan, and a reasonable prospect of eventually complying with the proposed rules.
section 'Eligibility for accessing the sandbox', para 11
Sandbox testing will run on a limited scale, will not use members of the public's money at the initial stage, and the HKMA can adjust the scope as testing goes on.
section 'Testing in the sandbox', para 15
Sandbox participants who break the terms can have their participation ended by the HKMA.
para 17
Being admitted to the sandbox does not mean the HKMA or any other regulator endorses or regulates the firm; a separate licence application will still be needed once the regime is in force.
para 17
Sandbox applicants should not reveal their application before admission, and admitted participants should seek the HKMA's agreement before making public announcements about their status.
section 'Staying alert to virtual asset scams', para 21
The HKMA will post the names of sandbox participants online and update the page regularly so the public can check claims.
para 21

t: HKMA launches stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement

Admission does not amount to HKMA endorsement or a licence; a separate application will be needed once the regime is implemented.

t: HKMA launches the stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement

s: The HKMA launched a sandbox arrangement for parties with a genuine interest in launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong, tied to the ongoing consultation on the proposed stablecoin issuer regulatory regime. t: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support development of Hong Kong tokenisation market
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support development of Hong… (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) programme meant to back interbank settlement of tokenised money. The initial focus is tokenised deposits issued by commercial banks, which would use the wCBDC as a settlement foundation for tokenised asset transactions such as green bonds, carbon credits and trade documents. A wCBDC Sandbox and an industry Architecture Community, including banks and technology firms, were planned to test use cases and set standards.

k: Project Ensemble is a wholesale CBDC initiative to enable interbank settlement of tokenised money, initially focused on bank-issued tokenised deposits.

t: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support the development of the Hong Kong tokenisation market
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support the development of… (2024)
s: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) effort meant to back Hong Kong's tokenisation market. It will initially focus on tokenised deposits (a digital representation of commercial bank deposits) as the settlement asset for tokenised real-world-asset transactions (e.g. green bonds, carbon credits, aircraft, EV charging stations, e-bills of lading, treasury management). A wCBDC Sandbox is planned to launch later that year, supported by a wCBDC Architecture Community of banks, digital-asset firms, tech companies and the CBDC Expert Group. The HKMA said it may conduct a 'live' wCBDC issuance later if the sandbox garners sufficient industry interest.
w: No compliance obligation attaches yet, but a compliance head should track Project Ensemble as the origin of the tokenised-deposit infrastructure the bank may be asked to connect to, with governance and control implications once real transactions begin.
k: Project Ensemble will explore new financial market infrastructure enabling interbank settlement of tokenised money via a wholesale CBDC (wCBDC).

t: SFC reminds public VATP application period has ended under transitional arrangements
sl: SFC · SFC reminds public VATP application period has ended under… (2024)
s: The SFC reminded the public that the 29 February 2024 deadline for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) operating in Hong Kong to submit licence applications under the AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements had passed. VATPs that did not apply by that deadline must close their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024; continuing to operate unlicensed is a criminal offence. t: Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
sl: HKMA · Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets (2024)

t: Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
sl: HKMA · Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services… (2024)
s: This Annex sets the HKMA's detailed, numbered expected standards for a bank's custody of client digital assets, covering governance, segregation, safeguarding of keys, delegation/outsourcing, disclosure, record-keeping, AML/CFT and ongoing monitoring. Core requirements include client-asset segregation from the bank's own assets, board-level risk oversight before launch, a written key-management policy covering generation through destruction, a numeric cold-storage floor and insurance/compensation floors for virtual assets specifically, and strict limits on who a bank may delegate custody to. The standards are risk-based for most digital assets but become prescriptive, effectively mandatory, minimums for virtual assets.
w: These are the concrete, numeric custody minimums (98% cold storage, 50%/100% compensation cover, permitted-delegate list) that a bank's digital-asset custody build must satisfy, plus the segregation, key-management and disclosure controls an examiner will test against — this is one of the most operationally binding documents in the batch for a custody-offering bank.
k: Before launching digital asset custody, a bank must complete a comprehensive risk assessment and put in place policies and controls, with the board and senior management exercising effective oversight both before launch and on an ongoing basis
Annex, para 1

A bank must allocate adequate resourcing and expertise to custody activities and ensure staff and control-function personnel have the necessary knowledge and skills, kept current through ongoing training given the pace of change

A bank must have effective controls that cut the chance of client digital assets being lost to theft, fraud, negligence or misappropriation, and that stop access being delayed or lost

t: Sale and distribution of tokenised products
sl: HKMA · Sale and distribution of tokenised products (2024)
s: The HKMA sets out its expectation that when a bank sells a 'tokenised product' (a digital wrapper around a real-world asset, excluding securities-law-regulated tokens and stablecoins) to customers, the same consumer-protection rules that already apply to the underlying non-tokenised product apply equally to its tokenised form. Banks are expected to do enhanced due diligence on issuers and technology vendors, disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers, and put proper risk-management and custodial controls in place before launching such sales. The circular does not create a new licensing regime; it layers tokenisation-specific expectations on top of existing product rules.
w: Confirms that selling a tokenised product does not escape existing suitability, disclosure and conduct rules — compliance must extend, not replace, its existing product-governance and disclosure controls to cover tokenisation-specific risks, and must pre-clear new tokenised offerings with the HKMA.
k: The circular covers tokenised digital representations of real-world assets (e.g. structured investment products, precious metals) but does not apply to instruments already regulated under the Securities and Futures Ordinance or to stablecoins
Coverage section, footnote 1, p.1

As a general rule, the existing supervisory and investor-protection requirements for a traditional product also apply to its tokenised version, since the tokenised form carries the same terms, features and risks as the underlying asset (apart from tokenisation-specific risk)
General principle, p.1

Because tokenisation can change a product's substance (e.g. fractionalised tokenised interests may become a collective investment scheme), banks should independently evaluate the terms, features and risk of each tokenised product and use professional judgment on which legal regime applies, seeking outside advice if unsure
Before selling a tokenised product, banks should have adequate systems, controls and additional internal controls addressing the product's specific tokenisation risks

Banks should perform ongoing due diligence on the tokenised product itself, on its issuer, and on any third-party technology vendor (e.g. the tokenisation platform), including their track record and systems for managing ownership and technology risk
Section A, p.3

Due diligence should specifically cover private-key management, safeguards against theft/fraud/hacking, technology audits (including smart-contract audits where used), and contingency plans for DLT network failure or loss of private keys
Section A, p.3–4

Before offering a tokenised product, banks should disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers, including DLT network risk, cybersecurity vulnerability, transfer restrictions, smart-contract risk, legal uncertainty on ownership/settlement finality, and custodial risk, in plain, non-technical language
Section B, p.4–5

A bank issuing a tokenised product itself should apply the same due-diligence expectations to its own issuance and consider the most appropriate custodial arrangement, with extra care for permissionless public tokens
Banks providing custody of tokenised products should separately meet the HKMA's expected standards on digital asset custody (i.e. the companion custody circular)
Section D, p.6
Banks intending to engage in tokenised-product activities should discuss their plans with the HKMA in advance of launch
Implementation, p.6

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Regulate Over-the-Counter Trading of Virtual Assets
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Regulate Over-the-Counter Trading… (2024)
s: This paper proposes a new licensing regime, run by the Commissioner of Customs and Excise (CCE) rather than the SFC or HKMA, for businesses that buy and sell virtual assets for cash over the counter (OTC), including physical shops and digital platforms. Licensees would only be able to trade VA-for-money, transfer coins to wallets the customer can prove they own, and only offer tokens already tradable by retail investors on an SFC-licensed platform or stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer. Authorized institutions, licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing such services would be exempt from the new regime because they are already regulated. The paper proposes fines up to HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment for operating without a licence.
w: The bank itself would be exempt from this specific licensing regime if it provides VA OTC-type services, but its retail and private-banking teams should know that once enacted, sending client funds to an unlicensed OTC shop becomes a criminal offence for the counterparty, which is relevant to fraud-typology monitoring and customer education.
k: A VA OTC licence would be required for anyone conducting spot VA-for-money trading as a business, whether through a physical outlet, ATM, or digital platform.
para 2.6, p.6
Licensees could not offer VA-to-VA conversion trades; customers wanting that would need to use a licensed VA trading platform instead.
para 2.12, p.9
Licensees could only offer tokens that retail investors can already access via an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or stablecoins from an HKMA-licensed issuer.
Authorized institutions (banks), licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing OTC services would be exempt from the new regime, since they are already regulated by the HKMA/SFC.
Operating an unlicensed VA OTC business would be an offence carrying a fine of HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment.

CCE would gain powers to inspect premises, investigate, arrest, and impose sanctions including licence suspension or revocation, plus a proposed power to block websites of unlicensed or fraudulent operators.
Proposed transitional period is six months, during which pre-existing operators must apply for a licence within the first three months to keep operating.
rg: Read Chapter 1 (background, paras 1.1-1.6) and Chapter 2's scope, eligibility and sanctions sections (paras 2.6-2.30); the 15 consultation questions can be skimmed.

t: Cryptoasset Exposures — Consultation Paper CP 24.01
sl: HKMA · Cryptoasset Exposures — Consultation Paper CP 24.01 (2024)
s: The HKMA proposes to bring the Basel Committee's December 2022 global standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures into Hong Kong's capital, liquidity, leverage and large-exposure rules, targeting an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025. Cryptoassets are split into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins meeting four strict conditions) and Group 2 (everything else), with Group 2 subject to far more punitive treatment, including a 1,250% risk weight and, for systemically important banks, a hard cap of 1-2% of Tier 1 capital. Banks must self-classify every cryptoasset they hold on an ongoing basis, document the assessment, and tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type; the HKMA can overrule the bank's classification. The paper also sets out liquidity, leverage, large-exposure, operational-risk, disclosure and risk-governance expectations. A 2025 letter to the industry shows the HKMA has since moved to a soft consultation on draft rule text, so this paper is the original blueprint rather than the current in-force wording.
w: This is the master blueprint for how much capital, liquidity and large-exposure headroom the bank will need to hold against any cryptoasset business, and it sets a hard ceiling on speculative (Group 2) exposure for systemically important banks — compliance needs classification, documentation and pre-notification processes in place well before the rules bite, even though the exact commencement date has since moved.
k: The HKMA does not plan to bring the new capital rules into effect any earlier than 1 July 2025, with rule-gazetting and Legislative Council tabling expected in Q2 2025
para 11

Banks must continuously assess whether each cryptoasset they are exposed to meets the four classification conditions, must keep full documentation available to the HKMA on request, and must tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset
para 14
The HKMA can override a bank's own classification of a cryptoasset if it disagrees with the bank's assessment
para 15

Cryptoassets fall into two broad groups: Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and cryptoassets with an effective stabilisation mechanism, i.e. certain stablecoins) gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset; Group 2 (everything failing those tests) gets much harsher capital treatment
para 17

To qualify as Group 1, a cryptoasset must pass four cumulative tests on an ongoing basis: it must confer the same legal rights as the traditional asset or have an effective peg; all rights must be clearly and legally enforceable and transfers final; the token's network and functions must not create material added risk; and every entity performing key functions (redemption, custody, settlement) must be regulated or subject to appropriate risk standards

A stablecoin only meets condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed, and where risky must overcollateralise, the aggregate redemption value at all times including under stress, are of minimal market/credit risk, are held in matching currencies, and are independently audited at least annually with daily value and weekly composition disclosure
para 23
A cryptoasset arrangement only meets condition 2 if full redemption can happen within a five-calendar-day window from the time it is requested, at all times
para 26

A bank adopting the basic approach must risk-weight almost all Group 1a and Group 1b cryptoassets at 1,250% (i.e. hold capital equal to the exposure) and cannot use them as collateral, unless they are issued by the HKSAR Government or a designated public sector entity
paras 36, 40 n.10

Systemically important banks (G-SIBs and D-SIBs) must cap their total Group 2 cryptoasset exposure at no more than 1% of Tier 1 capital as a normal ceiling, and must never exceed 2%; breaching 1% requires prompt notification to the HKMA and rapid rectification, and any exposure above the limit is treated at the harsher Group 2b rate in the meantime
paras 130–133

A Group 2 cryptoasset defaults to the harshest (Group 2b) capital treatment unless the bank proves to the HKMA's satisfaction that it meets the Group 2a hedging-recognition tests (a regulated derivative/ETF exists, the asset is highly liquid, and sufficient price/volume data exists)
paras 68–69

Banks must maintain a monitoring framework to verify at all times that a stablecoin's peg-stabilisation mechanism is actually working, and must document the evidence used, including for newly launched coins where data is thin
para 22

Operational risk from cryptoasset activity must be captured through the standard operational-risk framework (Business Indicator and Internal Loss Multiplier); if that is insufficient the HKMA will act through the supervisory review process
para 109
rg: Read paras 1–23 (scope, timeline, classification conditions) and paras 130–145 (exposure limits, risk management, disclosure) closely; the credit/market-risk RWA mechanics in paras 31–100 can be skimmed unless the bank runs a trading desk in tokenised instruments.

t: Cryptoasset Exposures - Consultation paper | CP 24.01
sl: HKMA · Cryptoasset Exposures - Consultation paper (2024)
s: The HKMA sets out how it plans to apply the Basel Committee's global capital rules for banks' cryptoasset holdings in Hong Kong. It sorts cryptoassets into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that pass strict tests) and Group 2 (everything else, including most crypto), each with very different capital, liquidity and large-exposure treatment. It also caps how much of a systemically important bank's capital can sit in Group 2 cryptoassets. The paper invited comments by 6 May 2024 and targeted an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025.
w: This is the rulebook that will decide how expensive it is for the bank to hold, trade or provide derivatives on any cryptoasset once finalised; compliance needs to track classification of every crypto exposure now, since misclassification carries capital, liquidity and reporting consequences.
k: Cryptoassets fall into Group 1 (tokenised assets or stablecoins that meet four strict tests) or Group 2 (everything else); only Group 1 gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset.

A stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism only meets classification condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed the peg value at all times, are minimal-risk and currency-matched, and are externally audited at least annually with value disclosed daily and composition disclosed weekly; a separate condition (condition 2) requires full redeemability within five calendar days.
Banks must assess and document classification of every cryptoasset on an ongoing basis, tell the HKMA in advance before acquiring a new type, and the HKMA can override a bank's own classification.
Group 2 cryptoassets that fail hedging tests get a punitive 1,250% risk weight, meaning a bank must hold capital equal to the full value of the position.

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset if it is a Group 1a tokenised version of an asset that already qualifies, and only if the tokenised and traditional forms both meet the same eligibility tests.
para 112, p.35

Only systemically important banks (G-SIBs/D-SIBs) face a formal ceiling: Group 2 cryptoasset exposure should generally stay under 1% of Tier 1 capital and must never exceed 2%; breaches must be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable.

Banks must fold cryptoasset risk into existing risk-management frameworks (board-approved risk appetite, operational resilience per SPM OR-1/OR-2) and tell the HKMA about their actual and planned cryptoasset activities.
Banks must give qualitative and quantitative public disclosures on cryptoasset business activities, risk management and exposures, following the SPM CA-D-1 disclosure principles.
Planned local timeline: preliminary consultation in H2 2024, draft rule consultation in Q1 2025, gazetting in Q2 2025, with revised rules taking effect no earlier than 1 July 2025.
Table 1, para 11, p.6
rg: Read paras 1-20 (scope and classification conditions) and paras 129-145 (large exposures, Group 2 limit, risk management, disclosure) first; the detailed market-risk formulas in paras 71-100 can be skimmed unless the bank trades Group 2a instruments.

t: Disciplinary Proceedings at a Glance (for regulated persons under Part 5B of AMLO)
sl: SFC · Disciplinary Proceedings at a Glance (2024)
s: This SFC guide explains, in plain terms, how the SFC disciplines regulated persons (virtual asset trading platform licensees, their responsible officers, and managers) under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance. It sets out the criteria the SFC weighs before taking action and setting sanction levels, the available sanctions (up to licence revocation and fines up to HK$10 million or three times profit gained or loss avoided), and the step-by-step process from investigation through a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action, representations, a decision notice, and rights of review before the Review Tribunal and appeal to the Court of Appeal.
w: For counterparty due diligence on VATPs, this is the SFC's own roadmap of what triggers enforcement, what sanctions can follow, and how public the outcome will be; a bank should treat a VATP's history of NPDAs, decision notices or public reprimands as material to its ongoing due diligence and monitoring of that platform.
k: The SFC can only discipline 'regulated persons': licensed VATP operators, their licensed representatives, responsible officers, and individuals involved in management, including directors and those serving as Managers-in-Charge of Core Functions.

Factors the SFC weighs include the nature and seriousness of conduct, impact on market integrity or Hong Kong's reputation, losses caused, whether conduct was intentional or negligent, prior SFC guidance on the conduct, and the degree of cooperation shown.

Available sanctions include licence revocation or suspension, prohibition from applying for a licence or to be a responsible officer, a fine of up to HK$10 million or three times the gain made or loss avoided, whichever amount is larger, reprimand, and remedial action orders.
Except for a private reprimand, all SFC sanctions are announced publicly by press release.
A regulated person that receives a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action is normally given 30 days to make representations, extendable on reasonable request.

If the person does not apply for a review, the SFC's decision takes effect once the 21-day review-application window (from service of the decision notice) expires; an application for review suspends the decision until the Review Tribunal rules.
A person dissatisfied with the Review Tribunal's determination may ask for leave to bring the matter before the Court of Appeal, within a 14-day window from that determination.
rg: Read pages 3-9 (English) in full; the Chinese-language section from page 10 onward duplicates the same content and can be skipped for an English-reading audience.

rg: Skim; standard template.

t: Tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (Investment Products Division presentation, 10 January 2024)
sl: SFC · Tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (2024)
s: This SFC presentation explains its 'see-through' approach to tokenised SFC-authorised investment products: it treats them as fundamentally traditional products wrapped in tokenisation technology. It sets out extra safeguards product providers must apply for primary dealing, flags secondary trading as needing more caution, and requires prior SFC consultation for new or changed tokenised products.
w: If the bank distributes or manufactures tokenised SFC-authorised funds, this sets the disclosure, custody, staff-competence and prior-consultation checklist compliance must apply before launch, and clarifies that outsourcing tokenisation tech does not shift legal responsibility away from the manager/distributor.
k: The SFC treats tokenised products as traditional products with a technology wrapper, applying existing product rules plus extra safeguards for the new risks.
Secondary trading of tokenised fund units needs more caution than primary dealing because of 24/7 trading and market-infrastructure readiness challenges.
Product providers/fund managers must remain ultimately responsible for the tokenisation arrangement and ownership record-keeping, even if a technology provider is engaged.
Products should not use public-permissionless blockchains without extra controls, such as a permissioned token layer.

Offering documents must clearly disclose token ownership rights, whether settlement is on-chain or off-chain and final, transfer limits, smart-contract audit status, and associated cybersecurity/legal risks.

Distributors of tokenised funds must be SFC-licensed for Type 1 regulated activity, follow suitability and onboarding rules, and choose a custodial arrangement suited to the product's ownership and technology risks.

Prior consultation with the SFC is required both for new tokenised products seeking authorisation and for adding tokenisation to an existing authorised fund; adding a further, substantially similar tokenised share class to the same fund does not need fresh prior approval.
rg: Read pages 10-16 (SFC guidance section); the introduction and global-adoption comparison (pages 3-8) are useful context but not obligations.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Paper
sl: FSTB/HKMA · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2023)
s: Jointly issued by FSTB and HKMA in December 2023, this paper set out the proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS), i.e. tokens that try to hold a steady value against one or more currencies. It proposed that anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-pegged stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence. It set out detailed licensing conditions covering reserve backing, redemption rights, capital, governance and AML controls, plus who could offer FRS to the public, and HKMA's supervisory, investigation and enforcement powers. This proposal was later enacted; the analysis below reflects the original proposal stage, some of which was refined in the July 2024 conclusions paper.
w: This is the original blueprint for Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime that a bank's compliance function must map against: it shows which licensing conditions apply differently to banks (as authorized institutions) versus non-bank issuers, and sets the baseline for due-diligence questions to any stablecoin issuer counterparty.
k: Any company issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence.
A licensed FRS issuer must keep reserve assets worth at least the full value of coins in circulation at all times, and coins backed only by algorithms or arbitrage would not qualify for a licence.
Reserve assets must be held separately from the issuer's own assets, normally with a licensed bank or an HKMA-approved custodian, under a trust structure that protects holders on insolvency.

Issuers must let holders redeem coins at face value in the referenced currency promptly and without unreasonable conditions or fees, and must keep a contingency plan for orderly redemption if the issuer runs into trouble.

A minimum paid-up capital was proposed at whichever is higher of HKD 25 million or 2% of the coins in circulation, though this and three other criteria would not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions (i.e. banks).

Only licensed FRS issuers, banks, licensed securities dealers and licensed virtual asset trading platforms would be allowed to offer FRS to the Hong Kong public; unlicensed-issuer coins could only be offered to professional investors and must be clearly labelled as such.
para 7.2, p.24
HKMA would get powers to intervene in a struggling issuer's management, gather information, conduct on-site inspections, investigate suspected offences, and apply for search warrants.

Proposed criminal penalties for unlicensed issuance reached a HKD 10 million pecuniary penalty (or three times the profit/loss avoided) plus lower fines and up to seven-figure fines with prison terms for specific offences under the wider financial-crime framework the paper draws on.

Pre-existing stablecoin issuers with a real Hong Kong presence would get a 6-month grace period to keep operating, conditional on applying for a licence within the first 3 months after the regime starts; those who do not apply in time must wind down by month 4.
rg: Read the Executive Summary (paras 1-4, pp.8-9) then section 6.2 licensing criteria (pp.16-22) and section 7 on offering (p.24); skip the Foreword, Personal Information Collection Statement and repeated consultation-question call-out boxes.

t: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong (Consultation Paper)
sl: HKMA/SFC · Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin… (2023)
s: In this joint consultation paper, the FSTB and HKMA set out a detailed legislative plan for licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers, building on the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper and its January 2023 conclusions. It proposed a new stand-alone ordinance under which the Monetary Authority would licence anyone who issues an FRS from Hong Kong, issues any stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or actively promotes FRS issuance to people in Hong Kong. Licensing criteria covered full reserve backing, par-value redemption rights, restricted business scope, Hong Kong incorporation and management presence, minimum capital, disclosure (white paper), governance, risk management, audit and AML/CFT controls. It proposed that only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong, with unlicensed-issuer FRS restricted to professional investors. This 2023 consultation was the direct precursor to what became Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656); by 2026 the regime it proposed has been substantially enacted, so this paper itself is superseded as a proposal though historically important.
w: This is the founding text of Hong Kong's stablecoin licensing regime: it defines who may issue and who may offer/distribute an FRS (including that authorized institutions, licensed corporations and licensed VATPs are the permitted offering channels), sets the reserve, redemption, custody and AML standards a bank should expect of any FRS issuer it deals with, and previews the sanctions regime the MA can apply -- essential due-diligence criteria for any stablecoin custody, settlement or distribution relationship.
k: A company would need a Monetary Authority licence if it issues an FRS in Hong Kong, issues a stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or actively promotes its FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public.
para 6.1.1

An FRS issuer must ensure reserve assets are at all times at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation ('full backing'); algorithmic/arbitrage-only stabilisation would not be licensable.
para 6.2.1

Reserve assets must be high-quality, high-liquidity, generally held in the referenced currency, and segregated via an effective trust arrangement in accounts with licensed banks or MA-approved custodians, protected against theft, fraud and misappropriation.
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users any interest; income or losses on reserve assets belong to the issuer, not the holder.
para 6.2.6

FRS users have a right to redeem at par value without undue cost or unreasonable conditions, including direct redemption from the issuer if an intermediary channel becomes unavailable, backed by a contingency redemption plan.

FRS issuers may only conduct FRS issuance and closely ancillary activities (e.g. wallet services for their own FRS); lending, financial intermediation and other regulated activities (SFO, MPF, insurance) are off-limits.

Non-bank FRS issuers must be Hong Kong-incorporated with a registered office, and their chief executive, senior management and key personnel (heads of operations, IT, finance, risk, compliance, internal audit) must be based in Hong Kong; this requirement, plus restricted business scope and minimum capital, does not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions.
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital for a non-bank issuer is the higher of HK$25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation.
para 6.2.15
Issuers must publish an MA-notified white paper disclosing the stabilisation mechanism, reserves management, technology and risks, and must disclose redemption policy, fees and timeframe.

Total FRS in circulation and reserve asset value must be disclosed at least daily, reserve composition at least weekly, and an independent auditor must attest to reserve adequacy and issuer compliance at least monthly.
para 6.2.5

Only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations (holding a Type 1 licence permitted to deal in virtual assets) and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong; FRS from unlicensed issuers may only be offered to professional investors by these entities, and must be clearly labelled as not issued by a licensed issuer.
para 7.2

People who control, direct or run an FRS issuer as chief executive must meet fit-and-proper standards, and the MA's prior consent is needed for any change in ownership, controllers or senior management.
para 6.2.19, para 9.1.2
rg: Read section 6 (licensing criteria, p.16-22) and section 7 (offering, p.23) in full as the operative substance; sections 9-12 (supervisory/investigation powers, offences) are useful for context but largely procedural; skip the Personal Information Collection Statement (p.6-7).

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Stablecoins – Regulating issuers to accord protection to users
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Stablecoins – Regulating issuers to accord… (2023)
s: This is Eddie Yue's public explainer accompanying the FSTB/HKMA joint public consultation paper on a legislative proposal for regulating fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers, published the same day. It explains what stablecoins are, why unregulated stablecoin failure risks harm users and financial stability, and summarises the proposed regime at a high level: an HKMA licence requirement for FRS issuers, local incorporation and management presence, financial resources rules, an effective par-value redemption mechanism backed by high-quality liquid reserves held in proper custody, AML/CFT compliance, and a planned supervisory sandbox. It states only licensed issuers' stablecoins may be offered to retail investors. The full technical proposal is in the attached consultation paper (id 41a8fe3f0ec7).
w: This is the public-facing summary of what became Hong Kong's stablecoin licensing regime (later the Stablecoins Ordinance, Cap. 656); a bank should track this as the origin of rules on which stablecoins it may safely custody, distribute or accept from clients.
k: The HKMA proposes that any entity issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) in Hong Kong must hold an HKMA licence, be locally incorporated with local management presence, and meet financial resources requirements.
para on proposed regime
Only stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers may be offered to retail investors; unlicensed-issuer stablecoins are implicitly restricted to non-retail channels.
para on proposed regime

Licensed issuers must maintain an effective stabilisation mechanism, generally a pool of high-quality, highly liquid reserve assets in matching currencies with proper custody, so users can redeem at par.
para on proposed regime
The HKMA plans to launch a supervisory sandbox to communicate expectations to firms interested in issuing stablecoins in Hong Kong, with details to follow separately.
closing paras
rg: Read this for the plain-English framing, then go to the attached consultation paper (id 41a8fe3f0ec7) for the operative detail; skip the historical section on 1935 Hong Kong banknote silver-token redemption, which is colour only.

t: Consultation on legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers and announcement on introduction of sandbox arrangement
sl: FSTB · Consultation on legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for… (2023)
s: The FSTB and HKMA jointly launched a public consultation (27 Dec 2023 - 29 Feb 2024) on a proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) in Hong Kong, to be administered by the Monetary Authority. The consultation paper proposes a new standalone ordinance requiring FRS issuers to be licensed, sets licensing criteria (full backing, segregation, redemption at par, no interest payment, minimum capital, physical presence, disclosure), restricts who may offer FRS, and proposes MA supervisory/investigation powers, offences and a transitional arrangement. A parallel sandbox arrangement was announced for prospective issuers.
w: This consultation is not yet binding, but a compliance head should read it as the draft blueprint for the MA licence the bank would need to issue a stablecoin itself, and note AIs are proposed to be exempt from several non-prudential licensing criteria that would otherwise apply to non-bank issuers.
k: Any entity issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS issuance to the HK public would require an FRS issuer licence from the Monetary Authority
FRS reserve assets must at all times be at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation (full backing); issuers deriving value from arbitrage/algorithm would not be licensed
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users interest earned on reserve assets
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital: the higher of HKD 25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation

FRS issuer must be HK-incorporated with a registered office and key personnel based in Hong Kong; this and the business-restriction/financial-resources criteria do not apply to authorized institutions

Only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations (with Type 1 licence permitted to deal in VA) and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong or market it to the HK public; non-MA-licensed FRS may only be offered to professional investors
Proposed maximum pecuniary penalty: HKD 10,000,000 or 3x the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is higher, plus criminal offences for unlicensed issuance/marketing

Proposed transitional arrangement: regime commences 1 month after gazettal; pre-existing FRS issuers with meaningful HK presence get a 6-month non-contravention period, conditional on lodging an application with the MA during the regime's first three months
Consultation period ran from 27 December 2023 to 29 February 2024, alongside a new HKMA sandbox for prospective FRS issuers
press release para 3, 6
rg: Read the Executive Summary and section 6 (licensing criteria) first; skim the Foreword/PICS and the consultation-question call-outs, which are procedural, not substantive.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities | Appendices: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This is the full appendix set behind the 22 December 2023 joint circular. It gives the client-knowledge test criteria, the list of jurisdictions whose regulator-approved crypto funds qualify for lighter treatment, a decision flowchart for classifying crypto-linked products, a fund due-diligence checklist, model risk-disclosure wording, the current dealing/advisory licence conditions with a redline against the earlier version, and a separate standalone set of conditions for firms managing crypto-invested funds or mandates. That last piece, Appendix 7, is effectively its own rulebook for crypto fund managers covering custody, capital, valuation, record keeping and reporting, distinct from the dealing and advisory conditions covered elsewhere.
w: Appendix 7 is the operative rulebook if the bank's asset-management arm ever runs a mandate meant to hold crypto or that could cross the 10% threshold; it sets a hard capital floor, custody and insurance expectations, and a fast notification clock the bank must be able to meet. The rest of the appendices supply the working detail (due-diligence checklist, risk wording, product-classification flowchart) behind the main December 2023 circular.
k: A firm counts as a knowledgeable client if it has had crypto training, has worked with crypto, or has traded crypto before - any one of the three is enough.
Appendix 1
Twelve named jurisdictions' regulator-approved retail crypto derivative funds and exchanges qualify for the lighter selling regime; anything else defaults to the stricter complex-product path.
Appendix 2
A fund that is meant to invest in crypto, or that a manager intends to put 10% or more of its value into, makes that manager a 'Virtual Asset Fund Manager' bound by the Appendix 7 conditions.
Appendix 7, Interpretation, 'de minimis threshold'

A licensed corporation acting as such a fund manager and holding crypto for its funds shall at all times keep liquid capital of at least HK$3 million, or its variable required liquid capital if that is higher.
Appendix 7, para 3.1

The fund manager should use a custodian independent of itself, and if it self-custodies, should show the crypto is legally ring-fenced from its own assets (for example by a declared trust over the wallet and keys) and carry adequate insurance.
Appendix 7, para 4.1(a), 4.4-4.6

Choosing a third-party custodian calls for documented diligence on its crypto track record, regulatory status, asset segregation practices, and financial/insurance strength, and the manager should think about spreading assets across more than one custodian.
Appendix 7, para 4.7 and accompanying note

The fund manager should tell the SFC (and HKMA, if a registered institution) at least 7 business days before any significant change to its business, and report material non-compliance as soon as practicable.
Appendix 7, para 7.1-7.2

Fund investors should be told the fund's key crypto risks up front - for example that most trading venues and custodians are still unregulated, and that self-custody and hot-wallet use carry loss risk.
Appendix 7, Schedule 4

Appendix 6 restates the dealing/advisory licence conditions current as of this circular; Appendix 6a marks up exactly what changed from the earlier version, mainly the retail exposure-limit and knowledge-test wording.
Appendix 6a
Appendix 3's flowchart is the reference tool for working out whether a given crypto-linked product is a complex product and which selling rule therefore applies.
Appendix 3
rg: Read Appendix 7 (crypto fund-manager conditions, especially custody in section IV and reporting in section VII) closely if the bank runs or is considering any crypto-invested mandate; Appendices 1, 2 and 5 are short reference lists that can be skimmed; Appendix 6/6a largely duplicates id 8401e273511f/bc97c16bac5e's dealing conditions plus a redline.

t: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (2023)
s: This SFC circular sets out the conditions under which the SFC will authorise investment funds with more than 10% of net asset value exposed to virtual assets (VA) for public offering in Hong Kong under ss.104-105 of the SFO. It covers eligible underlying VA, investment strategy limits, transaction/custody channels, custody standards (cold storage, key management), valuation, disclosure and prior-consultation requirements. It supersedes the October 2022 VA futures ETF circular and cross-refers to the companion Joint Circular on intermediaries.
w: If the bank's RI arm manages, distributes or provides custody for SFC-authorised funds with virtual-asset exposure, this circular sets binding requirements on custody segregation, cold storage, key management, disclosure and prior SFC consultation before exceeding the 10% NAV threshold.
k: SFC-authorised VA Funds may invest more than 10% of NAV in virtual assets, directly (spot) and/or indirectly (e.g. futures, other exchange-traded products)
para 1, 5
This circular supersedes the 31 October 2022 circular on Virtual Asset Futures ETFs
para 2
Underlying VA must be limited to tokens the Hong Kong public can already access for trading on SFC-licensed VATPs
para 10
SFC-authorised VA Funds must not carry leveraged VA exposure at the level of the fund itself
para 14
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must go through SFC-licensed VATPs or HKMA-compliant AIs (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs)
para 16
Custodian may only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or an AI meeting HKMA's expected VA custody standards
para 19

Custody standard: most VA holdings must be stored in cold wallets, hot wallet amounts/duration minimised to what's needed for subscriptions/redemptions; seeds/private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, access tightly restricted, resistant to speculation/collusion (e.g. multi-sig, key sharding), and backed up
para 20(b)-(c)
Valuation of spot VA must use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms (a benchmark index from a reputable provider)
para 21
Funds seeking VA exposure above 10% of NAV (whether new or existing) require the SFC's prior consultation and sign-off
para 29
rg: Read paras 1-2 (scope/supersession) and the custody section (paras 19-20) first; skim footnotes and the disclosure/service-provider paragraphs (22-27).

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This joint SFC/HKMA circular updates the conduct rules for intermediaries doing virtual asset (VA) related distribution, dealing, advisory, and asset-management work. It treats most VA-related products as complex products that can only be sold to professional investors after a suitability check, with a VA-knowledge test required. It carves out exceptions for exchange-traded derivatives and SFC-authorised funds, limits VA dealing to omnibus accounts held with SFC-licensed VATPs, and applies RA9 terms and conditions to VA fund managers. It replaces the October 2023 and January 2022 joint circulars.
w: This is a core, directly binding circular for the bank as a Registered Institution: it sets the capital buffer, custody, VA-knowledge-test, suitability, and platform-partnering rules the bank must meet for any VA dealing, advisory, or asset-management work.
k: VA-related products are 'very likely' complex products, so -- with limited exceptions -- they should go through a suitability check and be sold only to professional investors.
para 5-6.1

Apart from institutional and qualified corporate professional investors, intermediaries should check a client's VA knowledge before any VA-related transaction (a one-off check is acceptable); if a client lacks that knowledge, the intermediary may proceed only after providing adequate training.
para 6.2

VA futures or derivative funds traded on specified exchanges, or authorised in listed jurisdictions, and SFC-authorised VA funds traded on SEHK, the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, skip the professional-investor-only and suitability rules if there's no solicitation, but still need the VA-knowledge test.
para 7, 9.1

The SFC and HKMA see a clear need to make intermediaries deal only with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms for VA dealing (via an omnibus account or introducing-agent model), and intermediaries should provide such dealing services only to clients approved for Type 1 regulated activity.
para 17-18

Under the omnibus-account terms and conditions, a licensed corporation must keep excess liquid capital in Hong Kong equal to at least 12 months of actual running costs, on a rolling basis, on top of the SF(FR) Rules requirements.
Appendix 6, Part I, III para 3.1

Client virtual assets should be held on trust in separate VA Segregated Accounts, either at an SFC-licensed platform or an HKMA-compliant authorized institution; the intermediary should not provide clients with financial accommodation (margin/leverage) to acquire virtual assets.
Appendix 6, Part I, VII para 7.1(a); IV para 4.4

Advice and recommendations offered to retail clients must be limited to large-cap VA that appear on at least two acceptable indices from two independent providers, and that are available for retail trading on SFC-licensed platforms.
para 28; Appendix 6, IV para 4.9

Asset managers count as VA fund managers under the 'de minimis threshold' -- and so must follow RA9 terms and conditions -- if the fund's stated goal is to invest in VA, or if it plans to put 10% or more of gross asset value into VA.
para 23; Appendix 7, I
Type 1 intermediaries offering VA dealing only as a side service, using their own discretion, may invest less than 10% of a client portfolio's gross asset value in virtual assets.
para 24
The transition period for intermediaries already serving non-qualified or individual professional-investor clients ended 20 January 2024.
para 30
Intermediaries are reminded to give the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) advance notice before starting or changing any VA-related activity.
para 31
rg: Read the main circular body (paras 1-31) first for the policy; then Appendix 6 Parts I-II (dealing/advisory terms and conditions) and Appendix 7 (RA9 asset management terms) for the operative conditions. Skip Appendices 1, 2, 4, 5 and the marked-up redline appendices (6a, 7a) unless comparing to the prior version.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This is the current SFC/HKMA rulebook for how banks and brokers may distribute crypto-linked investment products and offer crypto dealing, advisory and asset-management services to clients. Most crypto-linked funds and derivatives are treated as complex products that only professional investors can buy, with narrow carve-outs for exchange-listed futures ETFs and SFC-authorised funds sold under extra safeguards. Firms must test a client's crypto knowledge, size their exposure against net worth, and route any actual dealing only through SFC-licensed trading venues. It folds in seven detailed appendices covering due diligence, risk wording, and standalone conditions for dealing, advisory and fund-management activities, and replaced the two earlier joint circulars in full.
w: This is the single rulebook that currently governs a bank's crypto distribution, dealing, advisory and asset-management business in Hong Kong, so every product-shelf and onboarding decision for crypto exposure should trace back to it. It sets the boundary between what needs professional-investor-only treatment and what can go to retail, and dictates which platforms and custodians the bank may use.
k: Products whose value comes mainly from crypto - funds, ETPs, structured notes - are presumed complex and, unless specifically carved out, can only be sold to professional investors.
para 5-6.1
Before any transaction in a crypto-linked product, the firm has to run a one-off knowledge check on the client and either proceed, train the client first, or decline.
para 6.2
Exchange-listed crypto futures and SFC-approved futures ETFs escape the professional-investor-only rule when there's no solicitation, but the knowledge check still applies.
para 7, 9.1
Distributing a crypto fund the SFC hasn't authorised calls for extra due diligence on the fund manager, the fund itself, and its trading/custody counterparties, per a checklist in Appendix 4.
para 12.3

Actual dealing in crypto for clients may only run through an SFC-licensed trading venue, either as an introducer or via a shared (omnibus) account, and only for clients already approved for securities dealing.
para 17-18
Retail dealing clients need a knowledge check, a net-worth-based exposure cap that is disclosed to them, and access limited to coins the partner venue allows retail investors to trade.
para 20(a)
Client coins from dealing clients must sit in a segregated account either at the partner venue or at a bank meeting the HKMA's custody standard.
para 20(b)
A fund manager whose fund is meant to invest in crypto, or is expected to hold 10% or more of its value in crypto, must instead follow the separate fund-manager conditions in Appendix 7.
para 23
Firms already serving non-qualified and individual professional-investor dealing clients under the old rules had until 20 January 2024 to bring their systems up to the new standard.
para 30
Firms must tell the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) in advance before starting any crypto-related activity, or before materially changing one already running.
para 31
rg: Read paragraphs 1-31 in full - it is only 9 pages; do not skip section E (Implementation) at the end, which carries the transition deadline and the advance-notification duty.

t: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement… (2023)
s: The SFC warned about two entities, HongKongDAO and BitCuped, suspected of virtual-asset fraud, and said it had asked police to block their websites and issued cease-and-desist letters. BitCuped falsely named two HKEX senior figures as its chairman and CEO on its website; neither has any affiliation with the firm.

Both entities already appeared, before this warning, on the SFC's list of suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms (HongKongDAO 24 Nov 2023, BitCuped 10 Nov 2023).
Notes 1-2

t: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds
sl: SFC · SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement… (2023)
s: The SFC warns of two suspected scam operations, HongKongDAO and BitCuped. HongKongDAO sells a token and is accused of spreading false claims about holding SFC licences and bidding for a 'Hong Kong Digital Currency Exchange Licence' that does not exist. para 5

t: AN ASSESSMENT ON THE BENEFITS OF BOND TOKENISATION
sl: HKMA · AN ASSESSMENT ON THE BENEFITS OF BOND TOKENISATION (2023)
s: This is a staff research memorandum, not a policy or supervisory document, that empirically studies whether tokenised bonds deliver measurable benefits versus conventional bonds. Using data on 28 tokenised bonds issued globally since 2018 (total US$3.9bn by March 2023, about 70% from Asian issuers) matched against similar conventional bonds from the same issuers, the authors find tokenisation is associated with lower underwriting fees, lower yield spreads, tighter bid-ask spreads, and improved liquidity in the matched conventional bonds too. The paper explicitly states the views are the authors' own, not HKMA policy, and cautions the sample is still small.
w: This is HKMA staff research, not supervisory guidance, but it is the empirical basis regulators and market participants cite for tokenisation's cost/liquidity case; useful background if the bank is weighing participation in tokenised bond issuance, underwriting or custody, but creates no obligations.
k: By end-March 2023 total global tokenised bond issuance reached US$3.9 billion across 28 deals from 23 issuers since 2018, about 70% issued by Asian institutions.
Key points / Section 2
Tokenised bonds in the sample had underwriting fees averaging 0.22 percentage points of par value lower than matched conventional bonds, a 25.8% relative reduction.
Section 3a

Tokenised bonds had yield spreads averaging 0.78 percentage points lower than matched conventional bonds, a 23.9% relative reduction, i.e. investors accepted lower compensation for tokenised issuance.
Section 3a
Tokenised bonds showed bid-ask spreads 5.3% tighter than matched conventional bonds on average, rising to 10.8% tighter when the tokenised bond was open to retail investors.
Section 3b
After an issuer's tokenised bond launch, that issuer's comparable conventional bonds also saw bid-ask spreads tighten by about 8.5%, suggesting a price-discovery spillover effect.
Section 3c
The paper explicitly disclaims that findings represent HKMA views and flags the sample as still small, so results should be read with caution.
disclaimer, p.1; Section 4
rg: Read the Key Points box (p.1) and Section 3 findings (p.7-10); the Annex regression methodology (p.14-17) can be skipped by a compliance reader.

t: Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities
sl: SFC · intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities (2023)
s: The SFC sets out guidance for intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities, applying a 'same business, same risks, same rules' approach: tokenised securities remain subject to existing securities law, but intermediaries must additionally manage new ownership and technology risks from DLT use. It clarifies that tokenisation itself does not change a security's complex-product classification (a 'see-through' approach based on the underlying security) and that the prior mandatory professional-investor-only restriction from the 2019 Statement is lifted for tokenised securities that are fundamentally traditional securities. The circular formally supersedes the 2019 Security Token Offerings Statement and distinguishes 'Tokenised Securities' from broader, more bespoke 'Digital Securities' (which remain presumptively complex products).
w: This circular directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution: it sets the classification test, disclosure and prospectus obligations for any tokenised bond or fund the bank deals in, advises on, or distributes, and confirms the outdated 2019 professional-investor-only mandate no longer applies.
k: This circular formally supersedes the SFC's 29 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings
para 21
Whether a Tokenised Security is a 'complex product' is assessed via a see-through approach based on the complexity of the underlying traditional security, not the tokenisation wrapper itself
para 24

The mandatory professional-investor-only restriction previously imposed by the 2019 Statement on security tokens is no longer imposed, since Tokenised Securities are, at their core, ordinary securities carrying a tokenisation wrapper
para 26

Public offering of Tokenised Securities still requires compliance with the prospectus regime (C(WUMP)O) and Part IV SFO offers-of-investments regime, or must be restricted to professional investors / an exemption applies

t: Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2023

On virtual assets he notes the HKMA has worked with the SFC to roll out investor-protection measures so intermediaries (including banks) understand their responsibilities when distributing digital asset products.
