t: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
sl: SFC · tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (2023)
s: The SFC sets out requirements under which it would consider allowing tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products offered to the public in Hong Kong. It permits primary dealing (subscription/redemption) of tokenised authorised products where the underlying product meets all existing authorisation requirements plus additional tokenisation safeguards, while secondary trading of such tokenised products is treated with more caution and remains under SFC review. Product Providers must retain full responsibility for the tokenisation arrangement, avoid unrestricted public-permissionless blockchains, and satisfy disclosure, staff competence, and prior consultation/approval requirements.

t: Experimenting with a multi-CBDC platform for cross-border payments (Project mBridge Update)
sl: BIS · Experimenting with a multi-CBDC platform for cross-border payments (2023)
s: This is a joint BIS Innovation Hub / HKMA / three other central banks technical and governance update on Project mBridge, an experimental multi-CBDC platform for wholesale cross-border payments. It explains the goal of shortening correspondent-banking chains via direct bilateral bank-to-bank settlement in central bank money, describes the custom permissioned DLT (the 'mBridge Ledger', EVM-compatible, Dashing BFT consensus), privacy design (pseudonymous addresses, encrypted metadata), and a four-subcommittee governance structure (compliance, technology, legal, policy) under a Steering Committee. It states the platform is experimental only, with no live-value production use, and outlines a roadmap toward a Minimum Viable Product.
w: mBridge is a wholesale, central-bank-led settlement rail, not a retail product, but any Hong Kong bank with cross-border correspondent banking exposure should track it as a potential future settlement channel; KYC/AML/CFT compliance stays with participating commercial banks off-platform, which is the key point for a compliance head to note now.
k: Project mBridge aims to let central banks and commercial banks settle cross-border payments directly in central bank money (CBDC), bypassing multi-hop correspondent banking chains.
p.2, 'What is Project mBridge?'

Each central bank remains the sole issuer/redeemer of its own CBDC on the platform, and only domestic commercial banks may request issuance or redemption of their local CBDC, preserving currency sovereignty.
The platform is built on a custom permissioned, EVM-compatible DLT ('mBL') using the Dashing Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus protocol and ISO 20022-based APIs for interoperability.
p.4, 'Technology'

Privacy is implemented via pseudonymous addresses and encrypted payment metadata; only four parties can decrypt transaction details -- the two transacting commercial banks, each one's own central bank, and the central bank that issues the CBDC.
Governance runs through a Steering Committee plus four subcommittees (Compliance, Technology, Legal, Policy); banks remain responsible for KYC/AML/CFT compliance off-platform ('off-bridge').

The mBridge Platform Terms bind the administrator, each central bank, and each central bank's own commercial bank participants into a single contract; jurisdiction-specific Issuance and Redemption terms and a Platform CBDC Instrument sit alongside them.

As of the report, four central banks had founded the project and more than 25 members were observing it, with the next stage targeting evolution to a Minimum Viable Product, still explicitly experimental with no production/live-value transactions.
p.1 (footer disclaimer), p.10-11
rg: Read pages 2-3 (goals, principles) and page 8-9 (governance/legal) for the compliance-relevant framing; the technical architecture on pages 4-6 can be skimmed by a non-technical reader.

t: e-HKD Pilot Programme • Phase 1 Report
sl: HKMA · e-HKD Pilot Programme • Phase 1 Report (2023)
s: This is the HKMA's detailed writeup of the first round of its e-HKD Pilot Programme, launched in late 2022 as part of a three-rail plan toward a possible retail central bank digital currency. Sixteen firms ran fourteen pilots spanning six use-case areas -- ordinary retail payments, conditional or smart-contract payments, payments without network connectivity, bank deposits represented as digital tokens, using e-HKD to settle transactions in the Web3/crypto space, and settling other digitally-represented assets. The report walks through case studies, survey feedback, and a table contrasting e-HKD against stablecoins, stored-value wallets, and digital deposit tokens on who issues them, what backs them, how transferable they are, whether they carry deposit insurance, and how they can be redeemed. It reiterates that no call has been made on issuing an e-HKD and describes plans for a further pilot round.
w: Banks already piloting or considering digital deposit tokens should study the Table 2 comparison closely -- it is the HKMA's own framing of how such tokens differ from e-HKD and stablecoins on backing, deposit protection, and redemption, useful for internal product classification and disclosure work -- while the note that these products sat outside a settled legal framework at the time is a prompt to check how far that has since changed.
k: Sixteen firms ran 14 pilots across six use cases: fully-fledged payments, payments that are programmable, payments made offline, deposits that are tokenised, the settling of Web3 transactions, and the settling of tokenised assets.
Executive Summary, p.6

Three areas were identified where an e-HKD could bring something new: letting payments carry conditions (programmability), representing assets digitally (tokenisation), and settling transactions instantly and simultaneously (atomic settlement).
Executive Summary, p.6
Hang Seng Bank, HSBC and Visa piloted tokenised deposits with wholesale-CBDC settlement, testing on-us and cross-chain payment atomicity.
Case Study 4, p.19

A comparison table sets out that digital deposit tokens sit on a commercial bank's own balance sheet, are generally covered by the Deposit Protection Scheme unless excluded, and are repayable in ordinary currency -- unlike e-HKD (backed by the central bank's statutory authority) and stablecoins (in the table's characterisation, generally backed by assets and issued by largely unregulated private entities).
Table 2, p.29
The report cautions that, at the time of writing, neither stablecoins nor digital deposit tokens sat within a settled legal or regulatory framework in Hong Kong.
Table 2 note, p.29
The HKMA says no call has yet been made on whether, or when, an e-HKD might actually be issued.
Executive Summary, p.6
The report flags that a DLT is not a prerequisite for a CBDC, and the HKMA remains open to both DLT and non-DLT designs.
section 4.2, p.32
Fubon Bank and Ripple piloted using tokenised real-estate liens as collateral for a home equity line of credit settled in hypothetical e-HKD.
Case Study 6, p.21

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: The SFC and HKMA updated their policy on intermediaries engaging in virtual asset (VA)-related activities, covering distribution of VA-related products, VA dealing services, VA asset management, and VA advisory services. t: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
sl: HKMA/SFC · Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions… (2023)
s: Known as the RA9 Terms and Conditions, this is the clean October 2023 text of licensing conditions applied to firms whose managed fund or discretionary account either aims to invest in virtual assets, or holds 10% or more of its value in them. It covers custody of the fund's virtual assets (including standards for self-custody versus an independent custodian), segregation of client cash, record keeping, appointment and oversight of an auditor able to verify virtual-asset holdings, counterparty and cybersecurity risk management, and a duty to report material breaches or business changes to the regulators. A separate schedule adds extra rules for firms running discretionary accounts rather than pooled funds.
w: For any bank running a discretionary account or fund with material virtual-asset exposure, these terms set the actual custody, disclosure and reporting standard the SFC and HKMA hold it to; compliance needs them to build custodian due diligence, disclosure and change-notification processes.
k: The extra rules bite once a fund's stated goal is to invest in virtual assets, or once it intends to hold 10% or more of its value in them; a fund is not automatically caught just because price gains alone push it briefly above 10%, provided the firm is taking steps to bring it back down.
s.I, definitions, p.3-4

Before choosing between self-custody and an independent custodian, a firm must document its reasoning, weighing accessibility against the security of key handling and the custodian's ability to compensate for any loss.
s.IV, para 4.3, p.6-7

If a firm chooses self-custody, it must keep the custodial function independent from the fund-management function internally, and may formalise the split, for example by placing a legal declaration of trust over the fund's crypto wallet and keys.
s.IV, para 4.4-4.5, p.7

Firms must document why they picked a given independent custodian, covering its track record with virtual assets, regulatory oversight status, segregation of client assets, and insurance cover, and should prefer a custodian that is itself subject to regulatory oversight where possible.
s.IV, para 4.7 and Note, p.7-8
If more than 10% of a fund's assets sit with one custodian or in self-custody, that concentration and its risks must be disclosed to fund investors, along with any significant later changes.
s.IV, para 4.11, p.9

The fund's independent auditor must understand how it verifies the existence and ownership of virtual-asset holdings and the reasonableness of their valuation, and this information must be made available to fund investors on request.
s.IV, para 5.6, p.10-11

A firm must tell the SFC (and HKMA, for a registered institution) of any significant change to its business, giving at least 7 business days' notice before that change takes effect, and report any suspected material breach as soon as practicable.

When vetting a virtual-asset trading platform as a counterparty, a firm should weigh its track record, regulatory status, governance, custodial arrangements, market-surveillance controls, cybersecurity measures and its financial ability to cover client losses.
Schedule 3, s.B, p.19-20
rg: Read section IV (Custody, p.5-9) and section VII (Reporting, p.11-12) in full; Schedule 2 (discretionary accounts) applies only if the firm runs discretionary VA mandates rather than pooled funds, and Schedule 3 (risk controls) is a useful due-diligence checklist for vetting VA counterparties.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2023)
s: This is the full standalone conditions document referenced by the 20 October 2023 circular, split into a dealing-services part and an advisory-services part. It fixes how firms must onboard, disclose to, and safeguard assets for clients trading or being advised on crypto. It was itself superseded on 22 December 2023 by an updated version bundled in the Appendices package (id 0027a8747112), which tightened the retail exposure-limit and knowledge-test wording; the redline is in that package's Appendix 6a.
w: This was the operating rulebook a bank had to build its VA dealing and advisory controls against for about three months; it is no longer current, but its structure (onboarding tests, exposure limits, custody segregation, monthly statements) carried forward almost unchanged into the December 2023 version.
k: A firm dealing under an omnibus account structure must keep the account with a licensed venue and execute trades only if the client's balance already covers them (no running a negative balance).
Part I, para 4.1 and 4.3
Where a client has given the firm discretion to trade both securities and crypto, crypto exposure in that mandate must stay under 10% of the account's value.
Part I, para 4.8
Firms must charge fees that are transparent, fair and clearly tied to order type, trade size and coin type.
Part I, para 4.10
A monthly statement is required whenever a client had a contract note that month, a non-zero balance, or held any coins - it must reach the client within 7 business days of month end.
Part I, para 6.12(g)-(h)
Firms must tell clients how compensation would work if a partner venue is hacked or otherwise loses client coins, and how forks or airdrops on held coins will be handled.
Part I, para 7.9(c)-(d)
A licensed corporation's yearly audit must state whether it had adequate custody controls, actually complied with the custody and record rules, and stayed within the financial soundness rule.
Part I, para 9.1(a)-(c)
A firm cannot make markets in crypto on the very venue where it also deals for its own clients.
Part I, para 10.1
For advisory clients, the same virtual-asset knowledge test and liquidity screen for retail recommendations apply as on the dealing side.
Part II, para 3.1 and 3.5
rg: Read Part I sections IV, VI and VII (operations, dealing with clients, custody) closely; Part II largely cross-refers back to Part I so can be skimmed.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This joint circular sets updated ground rules for banks and brokers that sell virtual-asset investment products, run dealing, advisory or discretionary asset-management services in virtual assets, or let clients deposit and withdraw virtual assets. It replaces the January 2022 version, widening retail access under new safeguards rather than tightening the earlier professional-investor-only stance. Most such products must still be treated as complex products requiring a suitability check and a virtual-asset knowledge test, but a narrow set of exchange-traded derivative products tracked on approved exchanges is carved out of the professional-investor restriction. Firms offering dealing services may only route trades through SFC-licensed trading platforms, and any client deposits or withdrawals of virtual assets must run through segregated accounts held either with those platforms or with banks meeting HKMA's custody standards. A three-month transition period applied from the issue date for firms already serving clients under the old rules.
w: This is the core standing instrument for any AI/RI conducting virtual-asset dealing, advisory or asset-management business with clients; it sets the licensed-platform-only routing rule, the custody channel for client deposits/withdrawals, and the pre-notification duty that compliance must build into onboarding and change-management processes.
k: Firms distributing products that mainly track the value of virtual assets must treat them as complex products and apply the SFC's usual suitability checks, unless the product is one of the narrow exchange-traded derivative types carved out.
para 5

Before letting a client trade virtual-asset products, a firm must confirm the client understands the risks (a one-off knowledge test is acceptable) and has enough net worth to bear potential losses, unless the client is an institutional or qualified corporate professional investor.
para 7.2

A defined list of overseas venues qualifies as 'designated jurisdictions' for certain exchange-traded derivative funds to be offered without the professional-investor-only limit; the full list sits in Appendix 2 (separate entry, id bf255e1026f4).
para 8, footnote 10

Firms may only provide virtual-asset dealing services by routing client business through platforms licensed by the SFC, whether by introducing clients to those platforms directly or by running a pooled (omnibus) account with them.
para 16

Where a firm lets clients deposit or withdraw virtual assets, this can only happen through segregated accounts held with its partner SFC-licensed platform, or with a bank (or that bank's subsidiary) that meets HKMA's published custody standards.
para 19(b)

A firm managing a portfolio is only pulled into the extra virtual-asset rules once the fund's stated goal, or an intention to hold 10% or more of its assets, is to invest in virtual assets; a related note limits discretionary trading in virtual assets on an ancillary basis to under that 10% threshold.
para 22-23

Before recommending any specific virtual asset to a retail client, a firm must check it is highly liquid, evidenced by being included in at least two recognised market indices, and that it is actually tradeable by retail clients on the licensed platform.
para 27

Firms already offering dealing services to certain professional-investor clients before the circular's issue date get a three-month grace period to bring their systems and controls up to the new standard; new entrants must comply from day one.
para 29

A firm must tell the SFC (and HKMA, where relevant) in advance before starting, or materially changing, any dealing, advisory or asset-management activity involving virtual assets or tokenised securities.
para 30
rg: Read paragraphs 1-30 in full; the numbered footnotes carry operative definitions (e.g. 'virtual asset', 'SFC-licensed platform') that matter for scoping. The five enclosures (Appendices 1-7a) are logged as separate registry entries and should be read alongside the relevant section (dealing, advisory, or asset management) a firm is assessing.

t: Appendices 1-5 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Appendices 1-5 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual… (2023)
s: These five short appendices flesh out the main joint circular. Appendix 1 lists simple, non-exhaustive tests a firm can use to decide if a client already knows enough about virtual assets. Appendix 2 names twelve overseas markets whose exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds can be sold without the usual professional-investor-only limit. Appendix 3 is a decision flowchart for classifying a given virtual-asset product as complex or not. Appendix 4 lists the due-diligence checks a firm should run before distributing a virtual-asset fund that the SFC has not itself authorised. Appendix 5 gives model wording for the risk warnings firms must hand clients.
w: These appendices supply the working checklists (client-knowledge test, jurisdiction list, product classification, fund due diligence, risk-disclosure wording) that a bank's front line and compliance function need to actually apply the main circular's requirements day to day.
k: A client can be treated as having virtual-asset knowledge if they have taken relevant training, have related work experience, or have previously traded virtual assets or related products.
Appendix 1, p.1

Twelve markets qualify as 'designated jurisdictions' for offering certain exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds without the professional-investor-only restriction: Australia, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Taiwan (China), Thailand, the UK and the US.
Appendix 2, p.2

The Appendix 3 flowchart routes a virtual-asset product first by whether it is a derivative and whether it trades on a specified exchange, before landing on whether professional-investor-only and suitability rules apply.
Appendix 3, p.3

Before distributing an SFC-unauthorised virtual-asset fund, a firm should scrutinise the fund manager's background, internal controls, and whether portfolio management, risk, valuation and custody functions are properly segregated.
Appendix 4(A)(a)-(b), p.4
Fund due diligence should also cover the fund's custody arrangement, including how assets are split between exchanges, custodians, hot storage and cold storage.
Appendix 4(B)(d), p.5

Diligence on the fund's counterparties should check their regulatory status for custody or trading of virtual assets, their track record, IT and cybersecurity robustness, and financial soundness including insurance cover.
Appendix 4(C), p.5-6

Model risk-disclosure wording for clients must cover legal uncertainty over whether a virtual asset counts as 'property', valuation difficulty, price volatility, weak or absent regulation of most trading and custody venues, and the particular danger of loss when assets sit in a 'hot wallet'.
Appendix 5, p.7
rg: Read Appendix 4 in full if distributing unauthorised VA funds, and Appendix 5 in full for client disclosure wording; Appendices 1-3 can be skimmed once the underlying criteria are understood.

t: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
sl: HKMA/SFC · Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for… (2023)
s: This is Appendix 6a to the joint circular: the full text of the licensing and registration conditions imposed on firms that run virtual-asset dealing or advisory services, shown with tracked changes against the January 2022 version. Part I covers dealing services, split between an introducing-agent model (where the firm never holds client assets and simply refers clients to a licensed trading platform) and an omnibus-account model (where the firm pools client trades through its own account with a licensed platform). Part II covers advisory services. Both parts carry detailed rules on know-your-client checks, disclosure, custody of client virtual assets and money, record keeping, an independent auditor's opinion, anti-money-laundering controls, conflicts of interest, and a duty to report material breaches to the regulators.
w: These are the actual binding licensing/registration conditions a bank running VA dealing or advisory business signs up to; compliance needs them as the checklist for custody segregation, client disclosures, AML controls, conflict-of-interest limits, record retention and the auditor's annual sign-off.
k: Under the introducing-agent model, the firm must not relay client orders itself, and must not hold any client money or virtual assets at all; a written client agreement must spell out that the firm provides no dealing, financing, settlement or custody service.
Part I, condition (a)-(c), p.3-4

Under the omnibus-account model, a firm may only trade client virtual assets through an account it holds with an SFC-licensed platform, and retail clients may only be given access to virtual assets that platform itself makes available to retail investors.
Part I, para 4.1, p.7-8

A firm must never let clients withdraw or transfer virtual assets from its own account; clients may only deposit and withdraw fiat currency through their segregated account, never virtual assets directly.
Part I, para 4.3, p.7
A firm must not offer any financing to help a client buy virtual assets, and should try to stop other companies in its own group from doing so either.
Part I, para 4.5, p.8

Firms must hold client virtual assets on trust in a segregated account kept either with the SFC-licensed platform itself or with a bank meeting HKMA's custody standards, and access to move those assets must be tightly restricted to authorised staff.
Part I, para 7.1, p.19-20

Firms must tell clients up front how they would be compensated if the licensed platform or its affiliate were hacked or otherwise caused a loss of client virtual assets, and must notify clients promptly of events like hard forks or airdrops affecting their holdings.
Part I, para 7.9, p.24

A licensed corporation's yearly audit must include the auditor's opinion on whether its systems adequately ensured compliance with the custody and record-keeping requirements, and whether it met the minimum liquid-capital rule.
Part I, s.IX, p.28-29

Firms must build anti-money-laundering controls specifically for virtual-asset dealing, including reviewing red-flag indicators against Financial Action Task Force guidance before launching new products or technologies.
Part I, s.X, para 10.1, p.28-29
A firm may not run virtual-asset market-making activity on the same licensed platform through which it services its own clients' dealing business, to avoid a conflict of interest.
Part I, s.XI, para 10.1, p.29
Any actual or suspected material breach of these conditions must be reported to the SFC (and to HKMA for a registered institution) as soon as practicable.
Part I, s.XII, para 11.1, p.29-30

For advisory services, a firm must confirm a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising them, and when recommending a virtual asset to a retail client must confirm it is highly liquid (listed on two independent indices) and actually tradeable on a licensed platform.
Part II, s.III, para 3.1 & 3.5, p.34-35
rg: Read Part I sections IV (Operations), VII (Custody), IX (Auditors) and X (AML/CFT) in full for a bank running dealing services; read Part II section III in full for advisory services. Definitions in section I and the Schedule of cross-referenced codes can be skimmed.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities | Enclosure 2: Appendix 6
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (2023)
s: This annex was the first set of licence and registration conditions telling brokers and banks how they could deal or advise in crypto tokens. It let firms either introduce clients straight to a licensed trading venue or run client trades through one shared account at that venue. It laid down client vetting, custody, record and reporting duties for that business. A newer version issued two months later, on 22 December 2023, replaced it in full, so day-to-day compliance work should follow entries bc97c16bac5e and 0027a8747112 instead.
w: This is the version that started imposing binding custody, suitability and reporting mechanics on VA dealing and advisory business, but it has already been fully replaced. Compliance should treat this only as a historical baseline and confirm live procedures track the December 2023 package instead.
k: A firm acting purely as an introducer may only steer clients toward opening their own account at a licensed trading venue; it cannot pass on trade instructions itself or hold any of the client's coins or cash.
Part I, licensing condition (a) and (c)
Firms running trades through a shared (omnibus) account may only use venues that hold an SFC trading-platform licence, and can spread business across more than one such venue.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.1
Firms cannot lend or extend credit to clients so they can buy crypto, and should try to stop group affiliates doing the same.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.4
Coins pushed to retail clients must sit in at least two well-run market-cap indices from separate providers and be listed for retail trading on the partner venue before a firm can recommend them.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 4.9(i)-(ii) and Note 1-2
Before serving a client, the firm must check whether the client understands crypto risk; if not, it can still proceed only after giving that client proper training.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.1-6.2
Each client needs a personal crypto exposure ceiling set against their net worth, told to them, and reviewed from time to time.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.4

Clients must be warned, among other things, that coins may not count as legal property, are not covered by the Investor Compensation Fund, and that a lost or wrongly sent coin usually cannot be recovered.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 6.10(b)-(f)
Client coins must be kept on trust in a ring-fenced account, either at the partner trading venue or at a bank meeting the HKMA's custody expectations.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 7.1(a)
Any real or suspected serious breach of these conditions has to go to the SFC (and the HKMA for a registered institution) without delay.
Part I, Terms and conditions para 11.1
The advisory half of the annex mirrors the dealing rules: assess the client's crypto knowledge, size a suitable exposure, and only recommend coins that meet the same liquidity bar.
Part II, Terms and conditions para 3.1, 3.3, 3.5
rg: Skip the BRDR catalogue boilerplate in the parent page; go straight to the attachment's Part I (dealing) and Part II (advisory) terms and conditions, pages 3-32.

t: HKPF and SFC establish joint working group on VATPs
sl: SFC · HKPF and SFC establish joint working group on VATPs (2023)
s: Following a senior-level meeting on 28 September 2023, the SFC and the Hong Kong Police Force (HKPF) set up a joint working group to strengthen cooperation on watching for and investigating illegal virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) activity. It draws on three HKPF units -- the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau -- together with the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions, to share intelligence on suspicious activity, assess risk at VATPs, and coordinate investigations.
w: Background for a compliance head: confirms formal SFC-Police cooperation on investigating trading-platform fraud exists, which matters when deciding whether and how to escalate a suspicious virtual-asset counterparty, though it creates no direct duty for the bank.
k: A dedicated SFC-HKPF working group was set up after a senior meeting on 28 September 2023 to strengthen how they cooperate on spotting and investigating illegal trading-platform activity.
main text, para 1-2

The group brings together three HKPF units -- the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau -- with the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions.
main text, para 2
Its job is to share intelligence on suspicious platform activity and breaches, build a way to assess how risky a suspicious platform is, and improve coordination between investigations.
main text, para 3

t: SFC publishes lists of virtual asset trading platforms

t: Statement on JPEX
sl: SFC · Statement on JPEX (2023)
s: The SFC issues a statement responding to public interest in the JPEX virtual asset trading platform, which it says has been unregulated and under SFC scrutiny since March 2022 over suspected false representations and unlicensed activity, and was placed on the SFC Alert List in July 2022. The SFC confirms JPEX has never applied for or discussed a Hong Kong VATP licence with the SFC, contrary to claims JPEX made, and states JPEX unlawfully published confidential SFC correspondence in breach of secrecy provisions in the SFO and AMLO. The SFC says it has referred the matter to Police amid suspicion of fraud, with investigations ongoing.

t: HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela
sl: HKMA · HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela (2023)
s: The HKMA, Bank of Israel (BOI) and BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre jointly published 'Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem', launched in Tel Aviv on 12 September 2023. Sela is a proof-of-concept exploring an rCBDC architecture where a central bank operates the retail ledger and settlement directly, while a new category of intermediary — 'Access Enablers' (AEs) — provide all customer-facing services without ever holding or controlling users' rCBDC funds or needing balance-sheet liquidity, potentially justifying a lower regulatory bar and lower barriers to entry for non-bank payment providers. The project does not reflect any policy decision by HKMA on e-HKD or by BOI on the digital shekel.
w: For a compliance head this is horizon-scanning, not a rulebook: Project Sela demonstrates a possible rCBDC architecture where non-bank 'Access Enablers' could bypass bank-style regulatory requirements, worth tracking as a disintermediation risk, but it creates no HKMA obligation on banks today.

t: Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem
sl: HKMA · Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC… (2023)
s: This joint HKMA/Bank of Israel/BIS Innovation Hub report describes a proof-of-concept (PoC) for a retail central bank digital currency (rCBDC) ecosystem where the central bank operates the settlement ledger directly, while a new category of intermediary called an "Access Enabler" (AE) handles all customer-facing services (onboarding, KYC/KYB, AML/CFT screening, payment routing) without ever holding customer funds or private keys. Existing banks ("Funding Institutions") retain the role of converting deposits and cash to and from the CBDC. The report argues AEs could face a lighter prudential regime than banks (systems/controls, governance and operational capital requirements, but no client-money capital rules) since they never hold customer funds, and explains a legal analysis (based on UNIDROIT digital asset principles) concluding neither the AE nor the central bank, but the end user, legally "controls" the CBDC. It also sets out cyber-security design principles (authentication, key management via HSMs/TEEs, limiting central-ledger programmability) intended to let broader access coexist with strong security. The report is exploratory and states it does not reflect any HKMA or Bank of Israel policy decision on issuing an actual CBDC.
w: If Hong Kong eventually adopts an Access-Enabler-style rCBDC architecture, non-bank intermediaries could gain a lighter-touch route to provide customer-facing payment services on the central bank's own ledger, a potential structural competitive and disintermediation risk for banks' payments and deposit franchises that compliance should track even though this remains purely exploratory research.
k: A new intermediary type, the Access Enabler (AE), performs all customer-facing rCBDC services (onboarding, KYC/KYB, compliance, payment routing) but never holds customer funds or private keys, unlike a bank
Section 2, p.8
Funding Institutions (i.e. banks) keep the role of managing customer deposit accounts and ATMs and converting between rCBDC and bank deposits/cash
Section 2, p.8

The report proposes AEs bear AML/CFT customer due diligence and transaction-screening responsibility, relieving the central bank of that role, with detailed obligations left to individual jurisdictions
Section 3.5, p.21
Legal analysis under UNIDROIT's digital-asset control test concludes end users, not AEs or the central bank, legally control their rCBDC, since AEs cannot access private keys or move funds
Section 4.2, p.25-26
A tailored, lighter prudential regime is proposed for AEs, covering systems and controls, governance, and a minimum operational-capital buffer, rather than client-money capital requirements
Section 4.3, p.26-27

Cyber-security design deliberately restricts programmability execution to the AE layer rather than the central ledger, and relies on hardware security modules and trusted execution environments for key protection
Section 5, p.29-30
The project is explicitly exploratory and does not reflect any policy decision by HKMA on introducing e-HKD, or by Bank of Israel on a digital shekel
Introduction, footnote 5, p.5

t: A Bridge to the Future: Hong Kong Fintech Promotion Roadmap
sl: HKMA · A Bridge to the Future: Hong Kong Fintech Promotion… (2023)
s: HKMA, working with the Securities and Futures Commission and the Insurance Authority, commissioned outside consultants to review how far banks, brokers and insurers have taken up fintech, and set out a forward plan under a four-part framework it calls PACE (Propagate, Assess, Connect, Equip). The document restates known milestones such as virtual bank and virtual asset trading platform licensing rather than announcing new rules, and closes by flagging that firms still find blockchain hard to explain internally and lack a clear business case for it. t: Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong
sl: HKMA · Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong (2023)
s: A detailed HKMA report documenting the design, legal and technology choices made in Project Evergreen's inaugural tokenised government green bond, intended as a reference for market participants considering their own digital bond issuances. It covers the technology platform (private permissioned blockchains, node-hosting versus API access, data visibility choices), deal-structuring questions (whether Hong Kong securities and companies law require any particular legal form for a bond, 'native' versus 'non-native' tokenisation, on-chain versus off-chain payment, investor access via self-custody or custodians, and credit rating considerations), and forward-looking priorities such as cross-platform interoperability, using digital bonds as repo collateral, and extending tokenised bonds to retail investors.
w: This is the HKMA's own working reference on how tokenised bonds map onto existing Hong Kong securities, companies and payment law, and it sets out concrete expectations for KYC/custody roles, business-continuity planning and platform-technology risk that a bank should apply when structuring, custodying, or rating a digital bond, or when assessing a DLT platform provider as a counterparty.
k: Project Evergreen used a 'non-native' issuance: the bonds existed first as conventional book entries in the CMU's securities database, with beneficial interests then recorded on the digital platform in tokenised securities accounts, rather than being created directly on-chain.
para 26, p.11

Neither the Securities and Futures Ordinance nor the Companies Ordinance -- nor, for that matter, the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance -- prescribes a particular physical or paper form for debt securities, so a distributed ledger entry can satisfy existing Hong Kong law without new legislation for this kind of issuance.

For a Hong Kong-incorporated corporate issuer, digital bonds are treated as 'debentures' under the Companies Ordinance, which still requires a Debenture Holders Register that can be printed out in hard copy even if kept electronically.
para 28(b), p.12

The Notes were distributed only to 'professional investors' under the SFO, and the existing SFO licensing regime for regulated activities (dealing, advising, automated trading services) and securities offering rules apply to digital bond issuance and distribution in the same way as to conventional bonds.
paras 23-24, p.11

Investors can hold digital bonds either by self-custody (directly controlling their own digital wallet and, where applicable, private keys) or through a custodian; self-custody gives more control but exposes the investor to the risk of losing keys or suffering a security breach, with full responsibility on the investor.
para 42, p.15

Where investors are on-boarded directly to the DLT platform, the platform operator (and any custodian) is expected to carry out know-your-customer checks and enable AML/CFT compliance; where investors instead access the bond only through a custodian, KYC is the custodian's responsibility.
para 44, p.16

In Project Evergreen, only custodians that are CMU participants and are on-boarded to the digital platform can open tokenised securities and cash-token accounts; non-participant investors hold their interest through an off-platform custody relationship, recorded in the custodian's own books and records — structurally similar to indirect participation in a conventional clearing system like Euroclear or Clearstream.
para 45, p.16

The Notes were credit-rated on par with the Government's conventional green bonds; the report flags that digital bond ratings should factor in additional risks from largely untested DLT platform technology, and recommends a documented business continuity plan covering platform disruption, cyberattack, and database migration to an alternative platform.
paras 46-47, p.17

The digital platform used two private, permissioned blockchains (Hyperledger Besu as Layer 1, Canton as Layer 2, with Daml smart contracts) rather than a public blockchain, prioritising security and data privacy over the openness of a public chain.
para 12, p.8

Participants can access a DLT platform either by node-hosting (running their own copy of the ledger, at higher cost and higher operational/cyber-risk exposure) or via a standard API/user interface (lower technical burden); Project Evergreen participants used a graphical user interface.
paras 15-16, p.9

Payments in Project Evergreen were made on-platform using 'Cash Tokens' minted by the CMU, each representing a claim on the HKMA equal to one Hong Kong dollar, settled atomically with the transfer of tokenised securities balances (i.e., a delivery-versus-payment transaction either completes fully or not at all).

Other digital bond transactions may instead use payment tokens not issued by a central bank, which the report flags as carrying higher counterparty, credit, operational, volatility and liquidity risk than central-bank-backed cash tokens.
para 34, p.14
rg: Read Sections I (Overview), III (Deal Structuring Considerations — especially Applicability of securities regulations, Investor access and custody arrangement, and Credit rating) and IV (Unlocking the Potential of DLT) in full; Section II (Technology/Platform Design) can be skimmed for the network-type and participation-model choices unless the reader needs the technical architecture detail.

t: Report on Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong

s: The HKMA press release announcing publication of the report 'Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong' (24 August 2023), summarising the Government's inaugural tokenised green bond -- Project Evergreen (HK$800 million, February 2023, the first tokenised green bond any government worldwide has issued, using DLT for primary issuance, secondary-trading settlement and coupon payment, with maturity redemption to be tested later). t: Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices

t: Frequently Asked Questions on streamlined approach for compliance with suitability obligations when dealing with sophisticated professional investors
sl: SFC · Frequently Asked Questions on streamlined approach for compliance with… (2023)
s: A seven-question FAQ explaining how intermediaries should apply the SFC's streamlined suitability approach for sophisticated professional investors (SPIs). It covers evidencing SPI status, using a representative's investment knowledge, categorising products (with virtual assets and VA-related products as their own category), what a Product Category Information Statement should cover, setting and reviewing a streamlining threshold, monitoring compliance with that threshold including via designated sub-accounts, and handling leveraged or margin transactions under the approach.
w: Confirms that virtual assets sit in their own ring-fenced Product Category even for sophisticated clients under the lighter streamlined suitability regime, and sets concrete, auditable criteria (five trades in three years) that the bank's product-categorisation and threshold-monitoring controls must be built around.
k: An SPI's requisite knowledge or experience can be shown by qualifications, work experience, or by having executed at least five transactions in the same product category within the past three years, including via power of attorney or joint accounts.

Intermediaries should create Product Categories such as accumulators/decumulators, insurance-linked-securities funds, loss-absorption debt instruments, virtual assets, and VA-related products, keeping each separate from the others.
An SPI may specify their own streamlining threshold appropriate to their financial situation, and the intermediary is required to keep records of the rationale supporting that threshold.

Intermediaries are not expected to force-unwind a client's exposure just because it later exceeds the streamlining threshold, but may restrict further top-ups or execute new trades outside the designated account instead.

Intermediaries may execute leveraged or margin trades on behalf of an SPI using the streamlined approach, so long as these stay within the SPI's specified Product Categories and threshold, but they must put in place effective systems and controls that keep the gross leveraged exposure at or below that threshold.
rg: All three pages are relevant; read in full.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers
sl: SFC · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for… (2023)
s: This is the SFC's seventh-edition AML/CFT rulebook for licensed corporations (LCs) and SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform operators (VASPs), in force since June 2023. Most of its chapters cover generic bank-style controls: risk-based assessment, customer checks, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-report filing, record-keeping and staff training. Chapter 12 adds virtual-asset-specific rules binding on LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, including a Hong Kong version of the international travel rule that requires firms to collect and pass on sender and receiver details for crypto transfers, counterparty due-diligence duties, and extra checks for transfers to wallets not held by a regulated firm. A bank does not follow this Guideline directly for its banking business, which is governed by the HKMA's own AML/CFT Guideline; only a bank's SFC-registered institution (RI) arm is required to have regard to specific cross-referenced parts of this Guideline (the customer definition, the correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the illustrative suspicious-indicator appendix), and the bank otherwise meets this Guideline only as a due-diligence benchmark for its VATP/LC counterparties.
w: This Guideline binds the bank's SFC-licensed VATP and LC counterparties directly, and its Chapter 12 travel-rule and counterparty due-diligence content sets the benchmark a compliance head should check any such counterparty against. It does not bind the bank's own banking business directly: for the bank's own AML/CFT programme the governing text is the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline (For Authorized Institutions); the bank's RI arm is required only to 'have regard to' the customer-definition, correspondent-relationship, Chapter 12 and suspicious-indicator parts of this Guideline (para 1.6), not to comply with it as an SFC licensee would.
k: The guideline is legally grounded in the anti-money-laundering ordinance and the securities law, and a firm's failure to follow it can count as misconduct affecting its fitness to hold a licence. It applies to SFC-licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers; a bank's RI arm is required only to have regard to specific cross-referenced parts (see para 1.6: the customer definition, correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the suspicious-indicator appendix), not the whole Guideline.

Chapter 12 covers both virtual assets as legally defined and any tokens that count as securities under the securities law, and it applies to FIs that hold an SFC VASP licence, and to LCs when carrying out VA-related or ML/TF-risk-relevant business.
Before moving crypto worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending firm must capture and record both the sender's and the receiver's identifying details, including an account or wallet reference.
The sending firm has to pass that sender/receiver data on to the receiving platform securely and before or at the same time as the transfer itself.

A firm should vet any platform it transacts with on the other end of a crypto transfer, covering its licensing status, ownership, and whether its AML controls and data-security practices are adequate.
Deals with a counterparty that is a shell entity with no real presence and no group oversight are banned outright.

For transfers to or from a wallet not controlled by a regulated firm, the firm should still gather comparable sender/receiver information from its own customer and assess whether the wallet looks trustworthy before proceeding.
Firms' screening mechanisms should also cover every party in a crypto transfer against sanctions and watch lists before the transfer goes through.
para 12.8.1
Sender/receiver data collected for a crypto transfer, and records tied to occasional transactions above the threshold, must be kept for at least five years.
Deposits or withdrawals routed through a third party's crypto wallet get extra scrutiny, and firms are encouraged to pre-approve a whitelist of wallets belonging to clients or vetted third parties.
rg: Go straight to Chapter 12 (p.140-189); skim Chapters 2-9 only for cross-references Chapter 12 points to (e.g. paras 4.20 on correspondent relationships), and skip the generic securities-sector CDD detail not tied to virtual assets.

t: SFC Disciplinary Fining Guidelines (for regulated persons under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance)
sl: SFC · SFC Disciplinary Fining Guidelines (2023)
s: These guidelines, made under s.53ZSS(1) of AMLO Part 5B, explain how the SFC decides whether and how much to fine a regulated virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operator or its staff found guilty of misconduct or unfitness. The maximum fine is HK$10 million, or, if larger, three times the profit gained or the loss that was avoided, and can be assessed per affected person. The guidelines list general factors that make conduct more or less serious, then detailed specific factors the SFC will weigh, covering the nature and impact of the conduct, whether it was intentional or negligent, cooperation and self-reporting, remedial steps, prior disciplinary record, and consistency with past cases.
w: Sets out the fining framework a bank's counterparty VATPs (and any bank entity itself licensed under AMLO Part 5B) face for AML/CFT or fitness-and-properness breaches; useful benchmark when assessing enforcement risk of a VATP relationship.
k: Maximum fine under s.53ZSP(3)(c) is HK$10 million or three times the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is greater, and may be multiplied by the number of persons affected
SFC will not impose a fine where facts warrant only a public reprimand, and will publicise all fining decisions as policy
Intentional or reckless conduct, conduct damaging market integrity, or conduct facilitating money laundering/terrorist financing is treated as more serious
p.3, General considerations
Timely self-reporting to the SFC, full disclosure, cooperation and remedial action (including client compensation) are mitigating specific considerations
p.4, Specific considerations
A fine should not be set so as to place a firm or individual in financial jeopardy, save where financial distress is deliberately engineered to avoid a fine

t: Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
sl: SFC · Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (2023)
s: These are the SFC's detailed operating rules for Virtual Asset Trading Platform (VATP) Operators licensed under the Securities and Futures Ordinance and/or the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance. They cover fitness-and-properness, competence and training of staff, financial soundness, token admission, client dealing, custody of client assets, governance, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors and ongoing reporting duties. A VATP must hold client assets through a separate Associated Entity and must keep 98% of those assets in cold storage. Retail clients may only trade large-cap tokens meeting strict listing criteria. The guidelines set the baseline a bank should expect any licensed VATP counterparty in Hong Kong to meet.
w: This is the primary rulebook against which a bank must due-diligence any Hong Kong VATP it partners with, refers clients to, or banks as a customer; the cold-storage, compensation, segregation and reporting thresholds here are the benchmarks compliance should check the VATP actually meets. It also frames the SFC's expectations on suitability and disclosure that a bank distributing or facilitating access to VATP services should mirror.
k: A VATP must be either an SFC Type 1/Type 7 licensed corporation or hold an AMLO virtual asset service licence, and should keep client assets on trust for those clients, held through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity that does no other business.
para 1.1 (definitions), para 10.1

Directors, responsible officers and licensed representatives must meet fitness-and-properness and competence tests, including recognised exam papers, minimum industry experience and continuing training hours.
Part II-IV, paras 2.1, 3.16, 4.14

A VATP must at all times maintain HK$5,000,000 minimum paid-up capital and liquid capital above a required threshold, and should keep at least 12 months of operating expenses in liquid non-crypto assets in Hong Kong.
paras 6.1-6.7

A token admission and review committee, including compliance, risk and IT heads, should set and enforce criteria for listing, suspending and delisting tokens, and report to the board at least monthly.
paras 7.1-7.5

Before listing any token the platform should run documented due diligence covering the project team, legal status, liquidity, technical design and money-laundering risk, and commission an independent smart-contract audit.
Tokens offered to retail clients should not be securities (unless a prospectus is used) and should be included in at least two independent, IOSCO-aligned large-cap indices.
paras 7.7-7.8

Platforms should not offer algorithmic trading, virtual asset futures or derivatives, or financial accommodation (margin) to clients to buy tokens, or yield-generating uses of client tokens, and should not engage in proprietary trading or market making on own account.

Clients (other than professional/institutional investors) should be assessed for virtual-asset knowledge, risk profile and a personal exposure limit before trading, and complex products need extra suitability checks and warnings.

At least 98% of client virtual assets should be held in cold storage (e.g. HSM-based), with strict controls on private-key generation, multi-person access and Hong Kong-based storage of seeds and keys.
para 10.6(c), para 10.8(e)
A VATP should maintain an SFC-approved compensation arrangement (insurance, ring-fenced funds, or bank guarantee) covering 50% of cold-storage and 100% of hot/other-storage client virtual assets.

Client money should be paid into segregated accounts with a Hong Kong authorized institution (or an SFC-agreed overseas bank) within one business day and may only be used for client-authorised purposes.
The platform should run an independent market-surveillance system from a reputable provider, reviewed at least annually, and notify the SFC promptly of any suspected manipulation.
paras 8.1-8.4
rg: For a bank compliance head, prioritise Part X (Custody, p.62), Part VI (Financial Soundness, p.36), Part VII (Token admission, p.40) and Part XVI (Reporting, p.94) as the core due-diligence checklist for a VATP counterparty; the Fitness/Competence/CPT detail in Parts II-IV (p.7-35) and Schedule 4's application forms can be skimmed.

t: Circular on transitional arrangements of the new licensing regime for virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · transitional arrangements of the new licensing regime for virtual… (2023)
s: The SFC set out transition rules under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) trading non-security tokens, as the new licensing regime began on 1 June 2023. A 'non-contravention arrangement' lets VATPs already genuinely present in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 keep operating for 12 months, until 31 May 2024, without breaching licensing rules. A 'deeming arrangement' lets qualifying existing VATPs that file a complete licence application by 29 February 2024 be treated as licensed from 1 June 2024, while the SFC finishes its review. VATPs that were not doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 get none of this relief and must be licensed before starting up. Platforms trading both security and non-security tokens need licences under both the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) and the AMLO.
w: This sets the AMLO transition and deeming timetable that decides whether a VATP counterparty was legitimately operating, deemed-licensed, or required to shut down. That is essential for reviewing any VATP relationship active in 2023-2024.
k: The transition rules apply only to VATPs trading non-security tokens; there is no transition period for meeting SFO (security token) rules.
para 3
VATPs genuinely doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 may keep operating from 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2024 (a 12-month non-contravention window) without breaching AMLO licensing rules.
para 6

To count as 'genuinely present,' factors include being incorporated in Hong Kong, having a physical office, running central management from Hong Kong, having Hong Kong-based key staff, showing real trading activity, and other supporting evidence; a shell company is not enough.
para 7-8

To qualify for deeming (treated as licensed automatically from 1 June 2024), an existing VATP must file a complete WINGS application between 1 June 2023 and 29 February 2024, and meet further conditions on confirmations and evidence.
para 12

VATPs with no Hong Kong footprint before 1 June 2023 cannot use these transition rules. They must not start business or actively market to Hong Kong investors until formally licensed; doing so unlicensed is a criminal offence.
para 10
An existing VATP must submit at least two Responsible Officer (RO) applications with its licence application, and at least one RO must live in Hong Kong, to meet the minimum RO condition for deeming.
para 26
Applications filed after 29 February 2024 cannot qualify for deeming, and the SFC cannot extend this statutory deadline.
para 20
VATPs trading both security and non-security tokens should apply for licences under both the SFO and the AMLO through one combined application.
para 30-33

t: Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions)
sl: HKMA · Consultation Conclusions on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money… (2023)
s: The HKMA sets out what banks said about its draft AML/CFT Guideline changes and how it responded. The changes implement the 2022 AMLO amendments, which introduced VASP licensing and updated CDD definitions. On virtual assets, the HKMA confirms banks stay under its own Guideline rather than the SFC's, with RIs referred to the SFC text via footnote 1. It also states banks may carry out VA transfers for customers if the statutory s.13A conditions are met. Other responses cover digital ID, trust beneficiaries, former PEPs, bearer shares and applying new rules to existing customers.
w: It is the HKMA's clearest statement that a bank may execute VA transfers for customers if s.13A of Schedule 2 is satisfied. It also confirms the bank answers to the HKMA Guideline, with SFC Chapter 12 relevant only through footnote 1.
k: Following the AMLO amendments gazetted on 16 December 2022, the HKMA consulted banks from 18 January to 8 March 2023 and received comments from four industry associations.
Part I, paras 1 and 3, p.3

The SFC's AML guideline (with its new virtual asset chapter) covers SFC licensees and SFC-licensed VASPs. Banks, including RIs, keep following the HKMA Guideline; footnote 1 was updated so RIs and AI associated entities have regard to the SFC text.
Part II, para 4.2, p.7

The HKMA states the AMLO does not bar banks from carrying out VA transfers for customers, provided section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. Banks should keep following HKMA circulars of 28 January 2022 and 27 April 2023 and may raise questions with the AML & Financial Crime Risk Division.
Part II, para 4.3, p.7

Private-sector remote-onboarding tools are not 'recognised digital identification systems' under Schedule 2; iAM Smart is. Existing remote onboarding practice under earlier HKMA circulars continues to apply.
Part II, paras 1.2-1.4, pp.4-5

For trusts, where beneficiaries are a class, banks may gather enough information to identify them at payout; a new para 4.4.13 lets banks verify beneficiaries using trustee-provided information on a risk basis.
Part II, para 2.3, p.6
Senior management approval is no longer required to stop applying EDD to a former PEP, but banks need sound internal controls and oversight for that decision.
Part II, para 3.2, p.6
Updated CDD rules can be applied to existing customers through normal periodic or trigger reviews; high-risk ones (e.g. non-Hong Kong PEPs) should be updated at or before their next review.
Part II, para 6.3, p.9
The revised Guideline was to be gazetted on 25 May 2023 and take effect on 1 June 2023.
Part III, para 1, p.10
rg: Read Part II section 4 (p.7) first, then 6.3 (p.9) and Part III (p.10); sections 1-3 and 5 are background for non-VA changes.

t: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions) (Revised May 2023)
sl: HKMA · Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For… (2023)
s: This is the HKMA's binding AML/CFT rulebook for all banks (Authorized Institutions), including those registered with the SFC. The May 2023 revision came into effect on 1 June 2023 alongside the 2022 AMLO amendments that created the VASP licensing regime. Its virtual-asset content is thin and targeted: a HK$8,000 CDD trigger for occasional VA transfers, matching record-keeping, a cross-reference to s.13A of Schedule 2, correspondent-style due diligence for overseas VASPs, and a footnote pointing RIs to the SFC guideline's VA chapter. Everything else a digital-asset business line touches (risk assessment, new-product assessment, CDD/EDD, monitoring, sanctions screening, STRs, records) is governed by the generic chapters. It contains nothing specific on stablecoins, unhosted wallets or VA red flags.
w: This, not the SFC guideline, is the bank's own AML/CFT rulebook; SFC Chapter 12 reaches the bank only for its RI/associated-entity business via footnote 1. The VA-specific rules are few (HK$8,000 VA transfer trigger, s.13A cross-reference, overseas-VASP correspondent measures), so most digital-asset controls must be built from the generic risk-assessment, new-product, CDD, monitoring and record-keeping chapters.
k: The Guideline is the HKMA's AML/CFT rulebook for every Authorized Institution (AI), including AIs that are also SFC Registered Institutions (RIs). It is issued under the AML/CFT Ordinance (AMLO, Cap 615) and the Banking Ordinance, and breaches can lead to disciplinary or other action under either law.
paras 1.1, 1.3, p.3 (printed p.1)
Both 'must' and 'should' in this Guideline denote a mandatory requirement, so 'should' is not optional wording for an AI.
para 1.6, p.4 (printed p.2)

Virtual-asset (VA) cross-reference: RIs, and AIs that are associated entities of SFC licensees, must additionally have regard to the SFC's AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed VASPs, including its Chapter 12 on virtual assets. This reaches only AIs acting as RIs or associated entities; it does not import SFC Chapter 12 for a bank's general banking business.
Chapter 1, footnote 1 (to para 1.3), p.3 (printed p.1)

Non-compliance can count against the Seventh Schedule authorization criteria under the Banking Ordinance (adequate systems of control), and courts and the HKMA take the Guideline into account when judging Schedule 2 breaches.
paras 1.7-1.8, p.4 (printed p.2)

Penalties: an AI that knowingly breaches a specified AMLO provision faces up to 2 years' jail and a HK$1m fine (7 years if intent to defraud); staff and managers who cause a breach face the same; the HKMA can also impose a pecuniary penalty up to HK$10m or three times the profit gained or cost avoided, whichever is higher.
paras 1.16-1.18, p.7 (printed p.5)

Each AI should run a documented institution-wide ML/TF risk assessment covering customers, customer and operating jurisdictions, and products, services, transactions and delivery channels. Senior management approves the results, and it is refreshed at least every two years and on material trigger events.

Before launching a new product, business practice or delivery mechanism, or using a new or developing technology, the bank should first weigh the ML/TF risks involved and put mitigants in place. This is the hook for assessing any VA, tokenisation or stablecoin-related service before launch.
paras 2.10-2.11, p.12 (printed p.10)

The board (or delegated committee) and senior management must understand the bank's ML/TF risks and receive timely management information. Senior management appoints a management-level Compliance Officer (CO) and a senior Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO), normally based in Hong Kong and independent of business lines as far as size allows.
paras 3.6-3.9, pp.15-16 (printed pp.13-14)

A Hong Kong-incorporated AI should apply these standards group-wide to overseas branches and subsidiaries doing financial-institution business, apply the higher of home or host rules, and tell the HKMA if host law blocks compliance.
paras 3.15-3.19, pp.17-18 (printed pp.15-16)

The four core customer due diligence (CDD) steps are: identify and verify the customer; identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable steps to verify them (including understanding ownership and control); understand the purpose of the relationship; and verify anyone acting for the customer and their authority.
para 4.1.3, p.19 (printed p.17)

VA transfer threshold: for a walk-in (occasional) customer, an AI must complete CDD before executing a virtual asset transfer of HK$8,000 or more, whether done in one go or split into operations that appear linked. The same trigger applies to wire transfers, while other occasional transactions use HK$120,000.
para 4.2.1(b)(iii), p.20 (printed p.18)

Footnote 15 points AIs to section 13A of Schedule 2 to the AMLO for virtual asset transfers. The Guideline itself gives no further VA transfer (travel rule) detail, so the statutory text of s.13A is the operative source for a bank's VA transfer obligations.
para 4.2.1, footnotes 14-15, p.20 (printed p.18)
rg: Read fn 1 (p.3), paras 2.10-2.11 (p.12), 4.2.1-4.2.5 with fn 14-15 (pp.20-21), 8.4 (p.71) and 11.6-11.25 (pp.81-86) first; then Chapters 5 and 6 for monitoring and screening. Chapter 12 (private banking) and the PEP detail can be skimmed for VA purposes.

t: SFC concludes consultation on regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC concludes consultation on regulation of virtual asset trading… (2023)
s: The SFC released Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for VATP Operators, following 152 written submissions. A significant majority of respondents supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, subject to robust protections (suitability onboarding, governance, enhanced token due diligence, admission criteria, disclosures). The resulting Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators took effect 1 June 2023, alongside related AML/CFT guidelines and Disciplinary Fining Guidelines gazetted 25 May 2023. The SFC noted that, as of commencement, it had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors, and most platforms accessible to the public remained unregulated.
w: The retail-access decision and 1 June 2023 commencement date here bind VATPs, not the bank directly. A compliance head needs it mainly to confirm which VATP-facing instrument set (VATP Guidelines plus AML/CFT Guideline) now governs any VATP the bank refers clients to or partners with.
k: 152 written submissions were received; a significant majority supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors.
main text, para 2-3

The VATP Guidelines -- formally titled Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators -- became effective 1 June 2023. They cover keeping client assets safe in custody, keeping client assets segregated, avoiding conflicts of interest, and cybersecurity.
main text, para 4 / Note 2
Despite regime commencement on 1 June 2023, the SFC had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors, and most publicly accessible VATPs remained unregulated by the SFC.
main text, para 5

On 25 May 2023 the SFC gazetted the VATP Guidelines, the AML/CFT Guideline (for LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs), the Prevention of ML/TF Guideline for Associated Entities, and the Disciplinary Fining Guidelines, and gazetted application forms; applications opened 1 June 2023.
Note 2-3
Operators unwilling to meet SFC standards should proceed to orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.
main text, para 6
rg: Read main text in full; Notes give the exact list of gazetted instruments and dates, useful as a citation index.

t: Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
sl: SFC · Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual… (2023)
s: The SFC finalises the rulebook for platforms it licenses to trade virtual assets, after a public consultation that drew 152 submissions. It allows retail investors onto licensed platforms, subject to knowledge and risk checks, exposure limits, and a narrow list of large, index-listed tokens eligible for retail trading. It sets custody, insurance, financial soundness and cybersecurity standards for platform operators, and folds virtual-asset-specific anti-money-laundering rules, including a Travel Rule for virtual asset transfers, into the SFC's AML Guideline. The finalised texts, annexed as appendices, took effect on 1 June 2023, with a 12-month transition for firms already licensed.
w: This is the baseline SFC rulebook against which a bank's compliance function should measure any licensed virtual-asset trading platform it deals with, partners with, or (if the group runs one) operates, covering custody, capital, AML/Travel Rule and disciplinary exposure.
k: Licensed platforms may serve retail clients, but only after assessing each client's virtual-asset knowledge, risk tolerance and personal exposure limit; a client is treated as knowledgeable once they have made five or more virtual-asset trades in the prior three years.
paras 12, 18, 21; Appendix A para 9.4 Note 2
Stablecoins are not to be admitted for retail trading until Hong Kong's own stablecoin regime is in place, because the SFC sees unresolved run and redemption risk in unregulated stablecoins.
para 51

A retail-eligible token needs a track record of at least 12 months (security tokens excepted) and must appear in at least two independent large-cap indices, one of which follows IOSCO benchmark standards; the SFC will not publish its own eligible-token list.
paras 47-49; Appendix A para 7.8

Every platform must run a token admission and review committee, drawn from senior managers responsible for the core business, compliance, risk and IT lines, which sets and enforces listing and delisting criteria and reports to the board at least monthly.
Appendix A paras 7.1-7.5

Before listing any token the platform must complete due diligence covering the team, jurisdictional regulatory status, liquidity, technical security, governance and legal risk, and for retail-eligible tokens must also confirm it is not a security under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
Appendix A paras 7.6-7.7

The SFC dropped its original plan to require platforms to file a lawyer's written opinion with the SFC confirming a token is not a security, citing cost; platforms still have to satisfy themselves of this before retail listing.
para 39
Token listings need an independent smart-contract audit for security flaws, though the platform may rely on an audit the token issuer itself commissioned rather than always commissioning its own.
para 38; Appendix A para 7.10

Client virtual assets must be split 98% cold storage / up to 2% hot or other storage, held through a dedicated, wholly-owned custody subsidiary (the Associated Entity), with keys generated and kept in Hong Kong.
Appendix A para 10.6(c); para 71

Platforms need a compensation arrangement (insurance, ring-fenced funds, virtual assets, or a bank guarantee, alone or combined) covering 50% of cold-storage client holdings and 100% of hot/other-storage holdings, monitored daily against actual custodied value.
Appendix A paras 10.22-10.23

Proprietary trading in virtual assets by the platform itself stays banned, but the SFC relaxed the original blanket ban so that other group companies (affiliates) may trade or market-make, as long as it is not routed through the licensed platform.
para 84; Appendix A para 7.26
Platforms may not offer deposit-taking, lending, borrowing or yield/earn-type products alongside their trading service; their role is limited to matching client orders.
para 86; Appendix A para 7.26

A minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5 million and required liquid capital of at least HK$3 million (or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount if higher) must be maintained at all times, plus 12 months of operating expenses held in Hong Kong in liquid, non-virtual-asset form.
Appendix A paras 6.1-6.3
rg: Read the Executive summary (paras 1-7), the retail access, custody/compensation and AML/Travel Rule discussion (paras 8-119) and the Implementation timetable (paras 151-154) first; these carry the SFC's authoritative final position in plain prose. Skim or skip Appendix E (list of respondents) and the non-virtual-asset-specific chapters of the AML Guideline appendices (Appendix B/C Chapters 1-11), which restate generic AML/CFT requirements not unique to this instrument.

t: Commencement of e-HKD Pilot Programme (with photos)
sl: HKMA · Commencement of e-HKD Pilot Programme (with photos) (2023)
s: The HKMA announces the start of its e-HKD Pilot Programme, the second of three rails in its approach toward a possible retail central bank digital currency (CBDC). Sixteen firms from banking, payments and technology were selected for the first pilot round, testing six use cases: fully-fledged payments, payments that are programmable, payments made offline, deposits that are tokenised, the settling of Web3 transactions, and the settling of tokenised assets. t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening remarks at the commencement event of e-HKD Pilot Programme
sl: HKMA · Opening remarks at the commencement event of e-HKD Pilot… (2023)
s: This speech launches the e-HKD Pilot Programme, the second of three 'rails' in the HKMA's approach to a possible retail central bank digital currency. s: This is a tracked-changes copy of the AML/CFT Guideline for Authorized Institutions, showing edits from the October 2018 text to the May 2023 text. It is for reference only; the gazetted version governs. For virtual assets it shows the new HK$8,000 VA transfer CDD trigger, the s.13A cross-reference, the widened footnote 1 pointing RIs to the SFC VA chapter, and the overseas VASP correspondent extension. It is useful for seeing exactly which VA words were added in 2023.
w: Handy for gap analysis: it pinpoints each 2023 VA-related insertion in the bank rulebook. Cite the final Guideline, not this markup, for obligations.
k: Footnote 1 was widened so RIs and AI associated entities have regard to the SFC guideline now covering SFC-licensed VASPs, including its Chapter 12 on virtual assets; the draft had only referred to specific SFC paragraphs on customer definition and securities red flags.

The linked-transaction and record-retention provisions add VA transfers to the HK$8,000 bracket alongside wire transfers.
Para 11.23 extends correspondent-banking measures to correspondent-type services for VASPs outside Hong Kong; a new footnote 81 clarifies this does not apply to AMLO-defined financial institutions.

t: SFST's speech at Aspen Digital Web 3 Investment Summit (English only)
sl: Government · SFST's speech at Aspen Digital Web 3 Investment Summit (2023)
s: SFST Christopher Hui reiterates Hong Kong's Web3/VA support strategy, disclosing that over 80 VA-related companies expressed interest in Hong Kong following the October 2022 Policy Statement, with 23 confirming plans to establish a presence by end-February 2023. t: 2023-24 Budget Speech
sl: FSTB · 2023-24 Budget Speech (2023)
s: In the 2023-24 Budget Speech, the Financial Secretary sets out government support for Web3 and virtual asset (VA) development, referencing the October 2022 VA Policy Statement and announcing a new Task Force on VA development plus HK$50 million to grow the Web3 ecosystem through events and youth workshops. He also announces the government's first tokenised green bond issuance (HK$800 million), describing it as the first government-issued tokenised bond globally, and states the government will review the potential for wider use of tokenisation in the capital market. A separate paragraph on Fintech confirms ongoing e-HKD and e-CNY cross-boundary payment infrastructure work.
w: Sets the funding and policy-priority backdrop (VA Task Force, tokenisation pilots, e-HKD/e-CNY work) against which later HKMA/SFC rules in 2023-24 were issued; useful for board context on why the regime accelerated, but creates no direct bank obligations.
k: Government will allocate $50 million to expand the Web3 ecosystem via international seminars, cross-sector cooperation events and youth workshops

A Task Force on VA development will be established, led by the Financial Secretary, to recommend on sustainable VA sector development
para 57
Government issued an HK$800 million tokenised green bond, described as the first government-issued tokenised bond globally
para 59
The tokenised green bond pilot targeted institutional investors and tested compatibility of Hong Kong's legal framework and infrastructure with tokenised issuance
para 94
Government will continue testing e-HKD together with e-CNY, as infrastructure for cross-boundary payments
para 100
