t: Consultation Paper on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
sl: SFC · Consultation Paper on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual… (2023)
s: This SFC consultation paper (20 Feb 2023) proposed the regulatory requirements for VA trading platforms ahead of the AMLO VASP licensing regime commencing 1 June 2023, alongside the pre-existing SFO regime for platforms trading security tokens. It set out a draft version of Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (below, VATP Guidelines), plus a new AML/CFT Chapter 12 for platform operators, Disciplinary Fining Guidelines, and transitional arrangements (deeming and non-contravention periods) for pre-existing platforms. Central proposals included allowing retail investor access for the first time, subject to knowledge assessment, suitability, and token admission safeguards; a token due-diligence and 'eligible large-cap virtual asset' framework for retail-available tokens; 98% cold storage and detailed custody/key-management controls; a flexible compensation-arrangement requirement replacing the old insurance mandate; and a two-phase external assessor report requirement for licence applicants. The paper also proposed removing several prior SFO licensing-condition requirements (e.g., the 'security token' admission criterion, mandatory voting-rights facilitation, legal opinion for all tokens) as the regime evolved. Comments were due 31 March 2023; the finalised VATP Guidelines were subsequently issued (dated June 2023 per the draft appendix cover) and this consultation paper is now a superseded/historical proposal document, though it remains the primary explanatory source for the final Guidelines' rationale and numbering.
w: This consultation paper binds virtual asset trading platforms and SFC-licensed intermediaries, not the bank as an AI. Its lasting value for a compliance head is as the source of the custody, cold-storage and Travel Rule benchmarks to test any VATP counterparty against, while the bank's own AML/travel-rule duties are governed by the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs.
k: The AMLO VASP regime (non-security-token VA trading platforms) commenced 1 June 2023, running alongside the existing SFO regime (which already covers platforms offering at least one security token); dual licensing is required if a platform's token mix spans both.
Part I, para 1-2

The SFC proposed for the first time to allow retail investor access to licensed VA trading platforms, subject to robust investor protection measures (knowledge assessment, suitability, exposure limits).
Part III, para 27, Question 1

Under the proposed rule, a platform operator, together with its Associated Entity, should keep 98% of client virtual assets in cold wallets, with only limited, SFC-approved exceptions -- a stricter bar than the roughly 95% cold-storage benchmark cited elsewhere in the same paper for existing SFO licensees.
Appendix A (VATP Guidelines), para 10.6(c)

Seeds and private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, generated in a non-deterministic/random manner, with no single person holding the entirety of seeds/keys/backup passphrases, and distributed backups mitigating single points of failure.
Appendix A, para 10.8(a)-(e)

The prior mandatory insurance requirement (full coverage for hot storage, substantial e.g. 95% coverage for cold storage 'at all times') is replaced by a flexible SFC-approved compensation arrangement that may combine third-party insurance and/or trust-segregated own funds.
Appendix A, para 10.22; main body para 53-55

'Eligible large-cap virtual assets' for retail trading must be included in at least two 'acceptable indices' from independent index providers, with at least one index provider experienced in traditional (non-VA) financial markets.
Appendix A, para 7.6, Notes 1-3

Licensed platform operators must maintain minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5,000,000 and required liquid capital of the higher of HK$3,000,000 or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount, plus 12 months of operating expenses in liquid HK assets.
Appendix A, para 6.1-6.3
Platform operators are barred from offering, trading in, or dealing with virtual-asset futures or related derivative contracts, and from providing algorithmic trading services to clients.
Appendix A, para 7.23-7.24

Virtual asset transfers of HK$8,000 or more trigger mandatory Travel Rule originator/recipient information collection, and the ordering institution must obtain and record originator/recipient details (name, account/wallet, address or ID number) before executing the transfer; a reduced dataset applies below that threshold.
Appendix B (AML Guideline), Chapter 12, para 12.11.5-12.11.6

Transfers to/from unhosted wallets require the FI to obtain and record originator/recipient information from its own customer (since the counterparty institution cannot be relied upon), with risk-based mitigating measures such as enhanced monitoring or transaction limits.
Appendix B, Chapter 12, para 12.14.1-12.14.3

Pre-existing VA trading platforms (operating in Hong Kong with meaningful/substantial presence before 1 June 2023) had until 29 February 2024 to submit a licence application to qualify for the deeming arrangement, and could continue operating penalty-free under a non-contravention arrangement until 31 May 2024; any platform not licensed or deemed licensed by 1 June 2024 is in breach and subject to enforcement.
Part IV, para 74, 79(b), 82; Appendix E timeline

The SFC proposed to publish four public lists — licensed, deemed-licensed, closing-down, and unlicensed VA trading platforms — explicitly warning that appearance on the 'deemed licensed' list does not mean the SFC has vetted the platform's fitness and properness.
Part IV, para 86-87
rg: Read the Part I Executive Summary (p.6) and Part III retail-access/custody/insurance sections (p.10-24) first for policy rationale, then Appendix A Chapters VI, VII, X and XII (Financial Soundness, Operations, Custody, Cybersecurity, p.64-109) for the operative requirements; skim the generic AML/CFT boilerplate in Appendix B outside Chapter 12 and the fitness-and-properness/competence chapters (Appendix A Parts II-IV), which largely restate standard SFC licensing conditions.

t: SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading… (2023)
s: The SFC launched a consultation on proposed requirements for operators of centralised virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), ahead of a new licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023. The proposals are based on the SFC's existing 2019 regulatory framework for VATPs trading at least one security token, benchmarked to the standards already applied to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues. A central question is whether licensed VATPs should be permitted to serve retail investors, and if so what additional investor-protection measures (suitability, token admission) would apply. Pre-existing platforms were told to start preparing to comply; those not intending to apply should prepare for orderly closure. Comments were due 31 March 2023.
w: This consultation previews the mandatory VATP licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023; it creates no bank obligations directly, but flags that any VA-trading-platform counterparty needed to prepare for licensing or wind down.
k: A new licensing regime for centralised VATPs carrying on business in or actively marketing to Hong Kong was to take effect 1 June 2023.
para 2 (main text)

Proposed requirements are benchmarked to the existing SFO rules that apply to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues, following the SFC's 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.
main text, para 3
The SFC specifically sought views on whether to allow licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, and what extra protections (e.g. suitability in onboarding and token admission) should apply if so.
main text, para 4
Pre-existing platforms intending to apply for a licence should begin reviewing and revising systems and controls; those not applying should prepare for orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.
main text, para 6
A platform counts as 'pre-existing' if it already had a real and substantial footprint operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023.
Note 6
rg: Read the main release in full (short); skip the boilerplate Notes 1-6 except Note 6 (pre-existing definition). The attached 2019 Position Paper gives full background on custody/insurance benchmarks referenced by this consultation.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Tokenised Bond: Huge Potential to be Unlocked
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Tokenised Bond: Huge Potential to be… (2023)
s: This article by the HKMA Chief Executive marks the issuance of the world's first tokenised green bond by a government, issued by the Hong Kong Government using distributed ledger technology. It explains that HKD cash tokens, akin to wholesale CBDC, were minted by the HKMA for banks to settle the transaction on-platform, cutting settlement time from five business days to one. It flags that custody arrangements will need to be uplifted so custodians can hold digital securities on investors' behalf, and states the HKMA will publish a white paper summarising lessons learned to guide future issuers.
w: This is the HKMA's own account of a landmark tokenised bond transaction that directly foreshadows custody expectations for digital securities: the compliance head should track the promised white paper, since it will likely set out legal-certainty and custody-uplift expectations relevant to any digital-bond custody or agency role the bank takes on.
k: The Hong Kong Government's tokenised green bond is described as the world's first tokenised bond issued by a government, using distributed ledger technology (DLT).
para 1

HKD cash tokens, akin to wholesale CBDC, were created by the HKMA when banks handed over fiat cash, and used to settle the primary issuance, secondary trading, coupon payment and maturity redemption on-platform.
para on cash-token minting
Settlement time was cut from the conventional five business days (T+5) to one day, using tokenisation instead of separate bond and cash settlement channels.
para on operational improvement
Existing custody arrangements may need to be uplifted so that custodians are able to hold digital securities for investors, and banks in agency roles may take on new on-platform tasks.
para on non-technological challenges

The HKMA states it is writing a white paper summarising lessons from this issuance to guide future tokenised issuers, and will set out its thinking on providing legal certainty for digital securities created natively on DLT.
closing paragraphs

The tokenisation approach builds on Project Genesis, a 2021 proof-of-concept co-sponsored with the BIS Innovation Hub, and draws on the cash-token mechanism developed for the mBridge cross-border CBDC platform.
paras on Project Genesis and mBridge synergy
rg: Read the full article; it is short and entirely on-topic for tokenisation, with the custody and legal-certainty paragraphs near the end being the most compliance-relevant.

t: HKSAR Government's Inaugural Tokenised Green Bond Offering
sl: HKMA · HKSAR Government's Inaugural Tokenised Green Bond Offering (2023)
s: The HKSAR Government successfully offered a HK$800 million, one-year tokenised bond, issued as green debt under the Government Green Bond Programme, billed as the first tokenised green bond issued by any government worldwide. A four-bank syndicate distributed the bond, which was cleared and settled through the HKMA's Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) using Goldman Sachs' GS DAP(TM) tokenisation platform, with the initial issuance settled delivery-versus-payment between security tokens and HKMA-issued cash tokens on a private blockchain. The HKMA said records on that private blockchain would be the legally final record of ownership, and that CMU settlement enjoys statutory finality under Hong Kong law. The HKMA also said it would publish a paper summarising lessons learned and offering a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.
w: For a compliance head, this is a market precedent rather than a rulebook: it shows a real Hong Kong-law tokenised bond settling on-chain through the CMU with statutory finality, relevant if the bank later joins a similar deal, but it does not create any ongoing compliance duty.
k: The tokenised green bond -- HK$800 million, HKD-denominated, one-year term -- is the first tokenised bond any government has issued anywhere, and the first one that Hong Kong law governs.
para 1, p.1

Settlement ran delivery-versus-payment: security tokens stood for a beneficial interest in the bond, swapped against cash tokens standing for a claim on HKD owed by the HKMA, completed on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network.
para 3, p.1

The bond clears and settles through the HKMA's CMU, which under Hong Kong law carries statutory finality for settlement; the HKMA describes records on the private blockchain as the legally final record of ownership.
para 4, p.1
This offering was one of the pilot projects flagged in the Government's October 2022 policy paper on developing virtual assets in Hong Kong.
quote from Secretary Christopher Hui, p.1

As the Government's representative under the Green Bond Programme, the HKMA said it will publish a paper covering lessons learned, next steps, and a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.
para 8, p.1
The deal builds on Project Genesis, a joint effort the HKMA finished with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre in 2021.
quote from Eddie Yue, p.1

The bond paid a 4.05% coupon, settled 16 February 2023 (T+1), and was rated A-1+/F1+ by S&P and Fitch; Bank of China (Hong Kong), Credit Agricole CIB, Goldman Sachs and HSBC acted as joint global coordinators, lead managers and bookrunners.
Summary terms and conditions table, p.2
rg: Read the first five paragraphs and the summary terms and conditions table (p.1-2) for the substantive facts; the quoted statements from officials and bank executives (paras 6-13) are largely promotional and can be skimmed, as can the US-securities-law disclaimer at the end.

t: LCQ11: Tokenised green bonds
sl: Government · LCQ11: Tokenised green bonds (2023)
s: In a Legislative Council written reply, Hong Kong's Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury confirms the HKMA plans a pilot issuance of tokenised green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme, aimed at institutional investors and intended to test Hong Kong's legal and market infrastructure for tokenised issuance. The reply explains that tokenisation may cut issuance cost and settlement time, that HKMA will publish a project report afterwards to guide future issuers, and that the government will explore using blockchain to track green-project performance data for bondholders.
w: Early signal of the HKMA's intent to pilot tokenised bond infrastructure that a bank's markets/custody arms may later be asked to support; no current obligations arise from this reply.
k: The tokenised green bond pilot is for institutional investors only and is expected to be smaller in scale than prior green bond issuances
Reply (1)
HKMA will publish a report on the pilot after issuance to guide future issuers on the process, including issuance, settlement, coupon payment and redemption
Reply (2)
Government will separately explore blockchain-based tracking of green project performance for green bond reporting
Reply (3)
rg: Short LegCo Q&A; read in full.

t: Conclusion of discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Conclusion of discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins (2023)
s: The HKMA published its conclusion to the January 2022 discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins, summarising 58 submissions received and its response. It confirmed it will bring certain stablecoin-related activities into a mandatory licensing regime, starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins, with flexibility to scope in other structures later. Key regulated activities are governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets. Both AIs and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins, and the HKMA targeted implementation of the regime in 2023/24, with a more detailed consultation to follow.
w: Signals the HKMA's intent to bring stablecoin issuance into its regulatory perimeter with implementation expected in 2023/24; compliance should treat it as an early-warning marker for the licensing regime that later materialised, not as a source of present obligations.
k: Certain stablecoin-related activities will fall under a new mandatory licensing regime that the HKMA administers, starting with stablecoins that purport to reference one or more fiat currencies.
para 1.4, p.3

Four categories of key regulated activities: governance, issuance (issuing/creating/destroying), stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets (custody of cryptographic keys enabling access to stablecoin holdings).

A licence is required from an entity that conducts a regulated activity in Hong Kong, actively markets a regulated activity to the HK public, conducts an activity concerning a HKD-referenced stablecoin (regardless of location or marketing), or that the HKMA considers should be regulated on public-interest grounds.

Reserve assets must fully back outstanding stablecoins at all times, be high quality and high liquidity, and holders should be able to redeem at par within a reasonable period; algorithmic/arbitrage-based stabilisation will not be accepted.

Both Authorized Institutions (AIs) and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins, subject to a 'same risk, same regulation' calibration of requirements by issuer type -- the HKMA rejected an AI-only issuance requirement.

Principal business restriction applies to licensees (e.g. wallet operators must not engage in lending), but this restriction does not apply to an in-scope AI because AIs are already subject to similar or stricter deposit-taking regulation.
para 4.33(iii) and footnote 9, p.18

Tokenised deposits of AIs, closed-loop limited-purpose stablecoins, and possibly CBDCs/settlement tokens are candidates for exclusion from scope; separately, the HKMA will work out how tokenised deposits should be regulated (distinct from the stablecoin issuer question).
para 4.15 and footnote 10, p.14, 23

Local incorporation is viewed by the HKMA as highly conducive to effective supervision and enforcement (asset segregation, seizure of assets for user protection), though the HKMA said it would further evaluate alternative mitigation measures raised by respondents.

The HKMA flagged potential regulatory overlap between the proposed stablecoin regime and the SFC's VASP licensing regime and the SVF licensing regime under the PSSVFO, and said it will coordinate with other regulators to avoid arbitrage and address overlaps/gaps.

Target implementation of the stablecoin regulatory regime is 2023/24; a more detailed, granular consultation on the regime (including choice between new stand-alone legislation vs. amending existing laws) will follow before draft legislation.

Draft legislation is envisaged to define regulated/excluded structures and activities, grant HKMA powers to implement the regime, set key regulatory requirements, and give HKMA a mechanism (plus published 'guiding factors') to scope in additional stablecoin structures/activities in future.
para 5.4, p.27
rg: Read the Executive Summary (paras 1.1-1.8, p.3-6) and the HKMA's responses under each Q1-Q8 heading in Chapter 4 (p.13-26) for the substantive policy positions; skim the market-volatility narrative in Chapter 3 and Annexes 1-3 (international/comparative surveys and respondent list), which are largely background/boilerplate.

t: Conclusion of Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Conclusion of Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins (2023)
s: This paper closes out HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper, reporting 58 submissions received and setting firmer proposed parameters for the coming stablecoin licensing regime, informed by the 2022 collapse of TerraUSD and the FTX bankruptcy. It commits to a risk-based regime starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins, names governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management and wallet custody as the core licensable activities, and confirms full backing, par redemption, and a principal-business restriction (waived for authorized institutions) as key regulatory principles. It also records Hong Kong's parallel move to bring virtual asset exchanges under an SFC licensing regime from June 2023, and the October 2022 government Policy Statement on virtual asset development.
w: This shows how the TerraUSD and FTX failures directly shaped the full-backing, par-redemption and principal-business-restriction design of the regime the bank now operates under or deals with counterparties under, and confirms why authorized institutions get lighter treatment on some criteria - useful context for explaining current rules to internal stakeholders.
k: HKMA confirmed it will prioritise regulating fiat-referenced stablecoins first, while building in flexibility to bring other stablecoin structures into scope later.

Four categories of activity were identified as core to the coming licensing regime: governance of the stablecoin arrangement's rules, issuance (minting/burning), stabilisation and reserve management, and wallet custody of users' cryptographic keys.
para 1.4 table, p.4

A licence would be required by an entity conducting a regulated activity in Hong Kong, actively marketing it to the Hong Kong public, referencing the Hong Kong dollar, or which HKMA considers should be regulated on public-interest grounds.
para 1.4 table, p.4

Core proposed principles were full backing and par redemption at all times, exclusion of algorithmic/arbitrage-based stabilisation, and a principal-business restriction preventing regulated entities from straying outside their licensed activity (e.g. wallet operators barred from lending) - waived for authorized institutions given their existing prudential regulation.
para 1.4 table, p.4-5
The target implementation date for the regime was reaffirmed as 2023/24, and HKMA was still weighing new standalone legislation against amending existing law.
para 1.4 table, p.5

The May 2022 depegging of TerraUSD (then the largest algorithmic stablecoin) and Tether's brief drop to USD 0.95, plus the November 2022 FTX collapse, were cited as evidence of governance, stabilisation-mechanism and disclosure vulnerabilities that reinforced the case for regulation.

Separately, Hong Kong's AMLO was amended in December 2022 to require an SFC licence for operating a virtual asset exchange, taking effect 1 June 2023 - a parallel but distinct regime from the stablecoin issuer licensing later created by the Stablecoins Ordinance.

Consultation respondents were divided on whether a local incorporation requirement should apply to stablecoin licensees, foreshadowing the requirement that ultimately appeared in the Stablecoins Ordinance for non-bank issuers.
para 4.5(iii), p.12
rg: Read the executive summary table (para 1.4) for the proposed regime parameters and para 3.2-3.3 for the TerraUSD/FTX context; the detailed question-by-question feedback summary in Chapter 4 can be skimmed since the eventual ordinance is the authoritative source.

t: Web 3.0 in Hong Kong – from crypto to blockchain
sl: Other · Web 3.0 in Hong Kong – from crypto to… (2023)
s: This FSDC newsroom piece reports on a London panel discussion about Hong Kong's virtual asset regulation, held shortly after the 2022 crypto market turmoil. Panellists described Hong Kong moving from a voluntary 2019 licensing option for exchanges to a mandatory licence requirement restricted to professional investors, and discussed tokenisation trends among banks. It is a secondary media summary of speaker opinions, not a regulator statement.
w: Useful only as historical colour on how the mandatory VASP licensing regime (which later took effect in June 2023) was being described publicly before it existed; it is not a citable source for current rules.
k: The article recaps that Hong Kong's 2019 regime let virtual asset exchanges opt in to SFC licensing voluntarily, and only one exchange did so.
paras 4-5
It describes the then-upcoming mandatory licence requirement covering all virtual asset exchanges, limited to professional investors with no retail offering.
para 5

t: Prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures
sl: HKMA · Prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures (2022)
s: The HKMA relays the Basel Committee's final global standard on the prudential (capital) treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures, issued 16 December 2022. Cryptoassets are split into two groups: Group 1 (qualifying tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins) generally gets existing Basel risk-based capital treatment, while Group 2 (everything failing Group 1 criteria) gets more conservative treatment with limited hedging recognition and an exposure limit guardrail. The standard adds an infrastructure risk add-on for Group 1 assets and a redemption-risk test for stablecoins to qualify for Group 1. The Basel Committee set a global implementation deadline of 1 January 2025, and the HKMA states its intention to implement locally on that timetable, with industry consultation on local implementation to follow.
w: This is the capital-charge framework the bank must plan for on any cryptoasset exposure, including which exposures could qualify as lower-capital Group 1 (via the redemption-risk test for stablecoins) versus punitive Group 2 treatment, ahead of local HKMA implementation.
k: Group 1 cryptoassets (qualifying tokenised assets and stablecoins) generally receive the existing risk-based Basel capital treatment.

Group 2 cryptoassets (everything not meeting Group 1 conditions) get a more conservative capital treatment, with only limited hedging recognised and an exposure limit to cap how large Group 2 holdings can grow in a bank's portfolio.
Only stablecoins issued by supervised, regulated entities with robust redemption rights and proper governance can pass the redemption-risk test needed for Group 1 qualification.

The Basel Committee's global implementation deadline is 1 January 2025, and the HKMA intends to implement the standard locally on that timetable, consulting the industry on local implementation details in due course.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full.

t: Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns to investors

t: Passage of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022
sl: HKMA · Passage of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill… (2022)
s: The HKMA tells banks that the Legislative Council passed the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022 on 7 December 2022. The amended ordinance puts virtual-asset service providers (VASPs) under a licensing regime and sets up a two-tier registration system for dealers in precious metals and stones, plus various changes to align with FATF standards, including an updated definition of politically exposed person (PEP), a risk-based approach to former PEPs, recognition of digital ID systems for customer due diligence, and a broader definition of beneficial owner for trusts. The changes take effect on 1 June 2023, and the HKMA says it will consult banks on related changes to its AML/CFT guideline.
w: This is the legal basis for Hong Kong's mandatory VASP licensing regime, which directly shapes how the bank checks VASP counterparties going forward -- only licensed VASPs should count as compliant partners from the effective date -- and it also updated the AML/CFT Guideline the bank's own AML programme follows.

t: LCQ4: Promoting development of virtual assets market

t: An Event Study on the May 2022 Stablecoin Market Crash
sl: HKMA · An Event Study on the May 2022 Stablecoin Market… (2022)
s: This HKMA staff research memorandum examines the May 2022 collapse of the algorithmic stablecoin TerraUSD (UST) and why some other stablecoins faced less redemption pressure than others. Studying 18 stablecoins existing at the time, the authors estimate the fair value of each one's reserve assets and find that stablecoins with stronger reserve backing suffered smaller declines in market value. Crypto-collateralised stablecoins absorbed the largest shock from the Terra crash, and among those, stricter collateralisation ratios provided more protection against redemption runs.
w: This staff research explains, with data, why reserve strength and collateralisation ratios matter for stablecoin resilience -- directly relevant background if the bank is assessing counterparty or custody risk from any stablecoin exposure, including any algorithmic or crypto-collateralised stablecoin.
k: TerraUSD (UST), an algorithmic stablecoin, failed to maintain its US$1 peg in May 2022, triggering widespread crypto sell-offs across the market.
Key points, para 1
Looking across 18 stablecoins, the ones with bigger reserve backing saw, on average, smaller drops in market value during the crash.
Key points, para 2
Crypto-collateralised stablecoins were the primary shock absorbers of the Terra crash, given their role providing leverage within crypto markets, and faced extra redemption pressure as a result.
Key points, para 2

Among crypto-collateralised stablecoins, the ones with tougher lending terms (i.e., needing more collateral per coin) held up better against redemption pressure, showing the benefit of a bigger safety margin.

t: An assessment of the volatility spillover from crypto to traditional financial assets: the role of asset-backed stablecoins

s: This HKMA staff research memorandum studies whether volatility in crypto-asset markets can spill over into traditional finance through asset-backed stablecoins, focusing on Tether. It finds that when Tether adjusts its reserves, this magnifies volatility spillover from crypto assets into money-market instruments, creating a channel by which stablecoin reserve fire-sales could affect traditional markets. The authors, writing in a personal capacity, suggest regulators consider standardised reserve-asset disclosure requirements and stronger liquidity-management rules, including reserve composition restrictions and well-defined redemption rights, for asset-backed stablecoins.

t: Project mBridge: Successful CBDC project for real-value cross-border payment and foreign exchange transactions
sl: HKMA · Project mBridge: Successful CBDC project for real-value cross-border payment… (2022)
s: HKMA, together with the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre, the Bank of Thailand, the People's Bank of China's (PBoC) Digital Currency Institute, and the Central Bank of the UAE, published 'Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC'. It reports on a six-week trial moving real value across borders using central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). Twenty banks across four jurisdictions ran more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange (FX) trades worth over HK$171 million (US$22.1 million) -- the biggest cross-border CBDC trial so far. The project will keep building toward a Minimum Viable Product and, eventually, a system ready for production use.

t: Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC
sl: HKMA/SFC · Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC (2022)
s: This BIS-authored report, dated October 2022, covers the first real-value pilot of mBridge, a shared blockchain platform letting four central banks issue their own digital currencies for cross-border settlement. Twenty commercial banks from Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE moved over US$12 million of digital currency and settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades for corporate clients over six weeks in mid-2022. The report explains how the platform keeps transaction details private except to the two counterparties and their central banks, describes the legal contracts used to give the pilot legal certainty, and sets out where each participant's own bank conducted its anti-money-laundering and sanctions checks. A dedicated section covers unresolved legal questions, including how to classify the digital currency itself and who should operate the platform, based on external legal advice obtained by the project team.
w: This is the clearest evidence that mBridge, even at pilot stage, put AML/CTF and sanctions screening responsibility on each participating bank itself rather than on the platform, which is exactly the control gap a bank's compliance function would need to confirm and own before any live use. If the bank is ever approached about connecting to mBridge or a successor platform, this report is the primary source for what legal documentation, screening obligations and data-visibility limits to expect.
k: In a six-week live pilot from mid-August to late September 2022, twenty commercial banks issued over US$12 million of digital currency onto the platform and settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades worth over US$22 million, on behalf of their corporate clients.
s.1 Executive Summary, p.4

Before the pilot, participants signed three sets of legal documents: one covering each central bank's role, one setting out platform-wide rules including when a payment counts as final and irreversible, and one covering each digital currency's specific terms of use.
s.5.1 Preparation and setup, p.16

Every payment on the platform required each bank to carry out its own anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorist-financing and sanctions screening before sending or confirming a transaction; the platform itself does not run these checks.
s.6.5.2 Payment and PvP, p.30

Sensitive transaction details, such as the identities of payer and payee and the amount, are visible only to the two transacting banks and their own central banks, not to the other participating central banks or banks.
s.6.4 Privacy controls, p.28

The pilot deliberately excluded certain transaction types, such as domestic payments in a foreign digital currency, because of the risk that a jurisdiction's own currency could be displaced or controls on monetary policy weakened.
s.7.1.2 Foreign and domestic use of CBDC, p.32

External legal counsel reviewed over 200 pages of analysis across four jurisdictions on unresolved questions such as whether the digital currency should be treated legally as currency, a claim on the central bank, or a form of debt.
s.7.2 Legal and regulatory considerations, p.34

Only banks that are domestically licensed in a given jurisdiction may request new issuance or redemption of that jurisdiction's digital currency; foreign banks can hold and transact in it but not create or redeem it directly.
s.7.1.1 Measures to preserve monetary sovereignty, p.31-32

Fewer currency-exchange trades took place than simple one-way payments during the pilot, partly because pricing for currency exchange happened off the platform beforehand, adding time and complexity to each trade.
s.5.4 Key lessons, p.22

The pilot ran on a single, centralised cloud environment hosted in Hong Kong for simplicity; the project team flagged this as a data-privacy and governance point still to be revisited before wider rollout.
s.7.1.3 Data privacy and governance, p.33
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.4-5), section 5.4 Key lessons (p.22) and all of section 7 Policy, legal and regulatory considerations (p.31-34); the technical architecture chapters on consensus algorithms (p.24-30) can be skimmed.

t: e-HKD - Charting the Next Steps
sl: HKMA · e-HKD - Charting the Next Steps (2022)
s: This is the full HKMA position paper following two rounds of e-HKD market consultation (75 responses total). It summarises consultation feedback (Annexes 1-2) and sets out the HKMA's three-track plan for getting ready in case e-HKD is eventually implemented: Rail 1 builds the technology (wholesale layer first) and legal groundwork (identifying required legislative amendments for legal tender status); Rail 2 runs deep-dive application research and pilots (including Project Sela, e-wallet access pilots, DvP tokenised-securities settlement, industry engagement); Rail 3 covers eventual launch, with timeline dependent on Rails 1-2 and market developments. The HKMA notes e-HKD's traditional rationales (financial inclusion, competition, resilience) are less compelling for Hong Kong's already diversified payment market than in jurisdictions that have launched rCBDC (Bahamas, Nigeria) or piloted one (China, Eastern Caribbean).
w: No binding requirement attaches yet, but a compliance head should track this roadmap for early sight of possible bank participation (e.g. Project Sela, DvP settlement pilots) and the legislative-amendment step that will eventually create e-HKD-specific compliance obligations.
k: Rail 1 will first develop the wholesale interbank layer (expected to take at least 2-3 years to build to production grade, subject to resources) before the retail layer design, since retail design may change based on further deliberation
Rail 1 section
Early legal analysis found the current laws would not give enough certainty to support issuing a digital version of legal tender; changing the legislation would be needed.
Rail 1 section

The HKMA is inclined to give e-HKD legal tender status, meaning by law it would be a valid means of tendering payment for a debt absent contrary agreement, but merchants could not be compelled to accept it just as with existing cash
Annex 2, Q11 HKMA response

Of the retail CBDCs launched worldwide so far, only the Bahamas' Sand Dollar and Nigeria's eNaira were actually up and running, while Mainland China's e-CNY and the Eastern Caribbean's DCash remained at pilot stage; the reasons those places moved ahead (financial inclusion, competition, resilience) are assessed as less relevant to Hong Kong.
Charting the next steps section

Consultation respondents generally favoured a two-tier distribution model, an unremunerated e-HKD, offline payment support, and cross-border interoperability (including potential e-HKD/e-CNY convertibility)
Responses received section
Rail 2 pipeline includes Project Sela (cybersecurity), e-wallet app access pilots, DvP settlement of tokenised securities, and studying CBDC as an on/off-ramp for DeFi
Rail 2 section
A tiered-account structure (different transaction/holding limits and anonymity levels based on KYC level) was broadly supported by respondents to balance privacy and AML/CFT compliance
Annex 2, Section 2

t: e-HKD: A Policy and Design Perspective
sl: HKMA · e-HKD: A Policy and Design Perspective (2022)
s: This HKMA discussion paper sets out the policy and design issues in introducing e-HKD, a retail central bank digital currency. It weighs benefits such as more usable central bank money and readiness against stablecoins, against challenges such as bank funding disintermediation, cyber risk and reliance on power and networks. It sets out design choices including issuance mechanism, interoperability, privacy and legal treatment, and states three possible issuance routes, with HKMA leaning toward a 'Coins approach' run through agent banks. It stresses that no decision has yet been made on whether or when to launch e-HKD, and lists twelve questions for public and industry comment.

t: Regulatory approaches to Authorized Institutions' interface with Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers

s: The HKMA's core policy circular setting out its overall regulatory approach to banks' interface with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs), organised around three pillars: prudential supervision, AML/CFT and financial crime, and investor protection. It says the HKMA does not currently intend to stop banks taking financial exposure to VAs, provided risk controls and senior-management oversight are adequate, but expects proper due diligence, prudent exposure limits, conservative loan-to-value ratios on VA collateral, and capital set aside for residual risk. It requires banks to discuss any VA activity with the HKMA and get feedback on their risk controls before launch, and references the same-day joint circular on intermediaries' VA-related activities for investor-protection detail.

t: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
sl: HKMA/SFC · Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (2022)
s: The joint SFC/HKMA circular updating investor-protection rules for intermediaries distributing virtual-asset (VA) products, offering VA dealing services, or giving VA advice. VA-related products are treated as complex products and generally restricted to professional investors, with a mandatory virtual-asset knowledge test for others, except for a narrow set of exchange-traded VA derivatives on specified exchanges in designated jurisdictions. Intermediaries providing VA dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms, must keep client fiat and virtual-asset holdings segregated, and must not offer any financing to buy virtual assets. A six-month transition period applied from the circular's date, and intermediaries must notify the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) before starting VA-related activities.

k: VA-related products are normally complex products and, other than a limited set of exchange-traded derivatives, should only be sold to professional investors.

t: Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins (2022)
s: HKMA set out its early thinking on regulating crypto-assets and, in particular, payment-related stablecoins, and invited industry feedback by 31 March 2022. It explained why payment-related stablecoins (those pegged to fiat currency and likely to be used for payments) pose distinct monetary, financial-stability, settlement and user-protection risks compared with other crypto-assets, and proposed that any entity carrying out core stablecoin functions - issuance/redemption, reserve management, key custody, transaction validation, or fund transmission - be licensed by HKMA, incorporated in Hong Kong (a branch would not qualify), and meet prudential, governance, AML/CFT and disclosure requirements. It targeted introducing the new regime no later than 2023/24, and confirmed HKMA would issue separate guidance to banks on their crypto-asset customer interface separately from this paper. This paper is the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance.
w: Sets out the regulatory logic and specific licensable-activity list that became Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance, directly relevant to a bank's due diligence on any stablecoin issuer, custodian or reserve manager it deals with, and to any bank considering issuing or supporting a stablecoin itself.
k: HKMA proposed to prioritise regulating payment-related, asset-linked stablecoins (particularly those pegged to a single fiat currency) over algorithm-based stablecoins at the initial stage, while keeping flexibility to expand scope later.
Discussion question 1 answer, Section 5.3

Seven categories of stablecoin-related activity were proposed for licensing: issuing/destroying stablecoins, managing backing reserves, validating transactions, storing private keys, facilitating redemption, transmitting funds, and executing transactions.
Discussion question 2 answer, Section 5.3

Any entity carrying out a licensable stablecoin activity in or targeting Hong Kong must be a Hong Kong-incorporated entity holding an HKMA licence; a mere branch or office of a foreign company would not qualify.
Discussion question 5 answer, Section 5.3

Proposed requirements for licensed stablecoin arrangements include authorisation, prudential capital/liquidity rules, fit-and-proper checks on controllers and management, reserve adequacy and legal clarity of holder claims, sound risk management (including AML), redemption robustness, and disclosure to regulators and users.
Discussion question 3 answer, Section 5.3

The existing proposed VASP licensing regime (VA exchanges) does not cover most core stablecoin functions like issuance, redemption, custody and reserve management, leaving a regulatory gap this paper aims to fill.
Section 4.1
HKMA aimed to introduce the new stablecoin licensing regime no later than 2023/24.
Discussion question 8 answer, Section 5.3

Banks distributing VA funds not authorised by the SFC should target only professional investors, assess client VA knowledge, ensure suitability, and give prominent risk warnings, per the SFC's November 2018 circular referenced here.
Section 4.3
AIs intending to provide VA-related investment services must notify HKMA and SFC in advance.
Section 4.3

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Crypto-assets and stablecoins
sl: HKMA · Eddie Yue on Crypto-assets and stablecoins (2022)
s: In this article the HKMA Chief Executive sets out, for the first time in this batch, the HKMA's three-pronged approach to crypto-assets: regulating payment-related stablecoins, protecting investors dealing in crypto-assets, and managing how Authorized Institutions (AIs) interface with crypto-asset service providers. It announces same-day publication of a Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins, open for comment until 31 March 2022, targeting a new stablecoin regime no later than 2023/24. It also flags that the HKMA and SFC are jointly developing supervisory expectations on AIs' crypto-related intermediary services, and that a circular giving detailed guidance on AIs' crypto exposure will follow.

k: The HKMA adopts a 'same risk, same regulation' principle: entities and activities are regulated based on the function performed and risk posed, not the technology label used.

t: Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins

s: The HKMA announced its Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins, asking industry and the public for feedback on a proposed regulatory approach aimed at payment-related stablecoins. Responses were due by email by 31 March 2022.

k: The HKMA asked the public and industry for feedback on the Discussion Paper's regulatory approach for crypto-assets, especially payment-related stablecoins, by email to stablecoin_feedback@hkma.gov.hk.

t: Enhanced Competency Framework on Fintech | Enclosure: Guide to Enhanced Competency Framework on Fintech
sl: HKMA · Enhanced Competency Framework on Fintech (2021)
s: The HKMA's catalogue entry for its Enhanced Competency Framework (ECF) on Fintech, a training and qualification standard for bank staff working in fintech roles. It is a workforce-competency scheme, not a product or risk-management rule.

k: The ECF on Fintech includes a specialist Distributed Ledger Technology track covering DLT architecture and design, digital tokens and smart contracts, and DLT security and oversight.

t: Fintech: Metamorphosis of the financial industry - Keynote address at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2021 (Julia Leung)
sl: SFC · Fintech: Metamorphosis of the financial industry - Keynote address… (2021)
s: SFC Deputy CEO Julia Leung reviewed three years of the SFC's virtual-asset regulatory journey and previewed change. She confirmed the government had by then decided to amend anti-money laundering law to make licensing mandatory for all centralised VA trading platforms. She described growing bank and broker interest in offering virtual assets to private-bank and professional-investor clients via introducing-agent or omnibus arrangements, and said the SFC was reviewing its VA regime with HKMA, expecting to issue a joint circular. She flagged unresolved questions on whether platform-style obligations (like knowledge assessments) should extend to intermediaries who merely introduce clients to VA platforms.
w: Directly foreshadows the joint SFC/HKMA circular on intermediaries' VA-related activities that followed in January 2022, and flags that using an omnibus or introducing-agent structure to access VA platforms does not automatically avoid platform-style compliance obligations.
k: The SFC and HKMA were jointly reviewing the VA regulatory regime and expected to issue a joint circular.

t: mBridge - Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
sl: HKMA · mBridge - Building a multi CBDC platform for international… (2021)
s: This is a brochure describing the mBridge project, a multi-jurisdiction wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) platform involving the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE, supported by the BIS Innovation Hub. It lists 15 private-sector business use cases identified with 22 participating financial institutions, spanning trade settlement, tokenised bond issuance, FX transactions, and wealth-connect settlement. It reports early trial figures on international trade settlement testing and sets out an iterative roadmap from pilot toward a production-ready platform from 2022 onward.
w: Several major banks the compliance head's institution may compete with or partner with were early mBridge participants; this brochure is useful context for understanding cross-border CBDC settlement infrastructure that could eventually intersect with the bank's own payments and trade-finance business, though nothing here creates an obligation.
k: mBridge is a collaboration among the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE, supported by the BIS Innovation Hub, testing whether CBDCs can speed up and cut the cost of cross-border payments.

Twenty-two private-sector participants across the four jurisdictions -- 19 financial institutions, two banking associations and one exchange -- identified 15 potential business use cases for the platform.

Named participants proposing use cases included Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS Bank (Hong Kong), Goldman Sachs (Asia), HKEX, HSBC, Societe Generale-FORGE, Standard Chartered, and UBS, covering areas like tokenised bond settlement, programmable trade finance, and FX derivatives settlement.

Test transactions on the trial platform for international trade settlement covered four jurisdictions and 11 industries, with a combined tested value including 10 billion Thai baht, 1 billion RMB, 2 billion HKD and 2 billion AED.
The roadmap moves from the 2019 Inthanon-LionRock proof-of-concept, through the Q4 2021 mBridge trial platform, to a pilot minimum viable product and a production-ready system from 2022 onward.
Implementation considerations flagged for the next phase include a minimum viable legal framework, legal governance, and policy and regulatory compliance requirements.
rg: Read pages 2-3 for the platform overview and page 7 for the roadmap; the use-case list on pages 4-5 can be skimmed for named participants only.

t: Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force
sl: HKMA · Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force (2021)
s: A routine HKMA relay of the latest FATF high-risk/increased-monitoring jurisdiction lists and plenary outcomes, telling banks to keep applying enhanced due diligence to Iran and North Korea and to note the updated monitored-jurisdictions list. It also flags that in October 2021 the FATF issued revised risk-based guidance on virtual assets and VASPs, covering how the FATF rules apply to banks engaging in VA activity.

t: e-HKD: A technical perspective – Request for Comments
sl: HKMA · e-HKD: A technical perspective – Request for Comments (2021)
s: This is a technical discussion paper, prepared with the BIS Innovation Hub, exploring possible architectures for a Hong Kong retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD), part of a wider e-HKD feasibility study alongside a separate legal and policy study. It proposes a two-tier model in which the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD at a wholesale layer while commercial banks distribute it at a retail layer, and it sets out seven open research problems (privacy, interoperability, performance, cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, and technology-enabled features). It explicitly states the design is not a blueprint or a decision on e-HKD, only a basis for further dialogue, and invited written comment by 31 December 2021.
w: This is a non-binding, now-superseded technical research paper, but it shows the HKMA's early thinking that any future e-HKD design would still require banks to run standard KYC/AML onboarding and would preserve some transaction traceability for compliance purposes -- relevant background if the bank's payments or treasury teams engage with later e-HKD pilots.
k: The HKMA's CBDC research runs on two tracks: wholesale CBDC work that became Project mBridge, and this separate retail CBDC (e-HKD) track begun in June 2021.

The paper proposes a two-tier architecture: a wholesale system where the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD, and a retail system where commercial banks distribute and circulate it or a CBDC-backed e-money form.
Executive Summary, point 3
The design is explicitly not a blueprint for e-HKD and does not represent a decision on which distribution model will be used.
Executive Summary, point 4

Seven open problem statements are listed for public comment: privacy, interoperability, performance/scalability, cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, and technology-enabled functional capabilities.

Comments on the proposed architecture, including security modelling and new use-case ideas, were invited by email by 31 December 2021.
Executive Summary, point 5
The compliance problem statement specifically calls for exploring how computing methods can support AML/CFT regulatory compliance goals within an e-HKD system.
Table 1, item 5

The paper's safety design principles state that a CBDC system should be compliance-friendly, supporting compliance with AML/CFT and sanctions regulations, though full technology-enforced traceability is not presented as a fixed requirement.
s.4.1 Safety (Compliance-friendly), p.19
Onboarding of retail e-HKD users would need to fulfil KYC/AML rules, and pre-registration is described as desirable to support that compliance.
The paper builds on the BIS Innovation Hub's Project Aurum, which is separately developing a basic prototype implementing parts of the architecture described here.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Technical Whitepaper on Retail Central Bank Digital Currency

s: This short press release announces publication of the HKMA's first technical whitepaper on a possible retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD), prepared jointly with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre. It describes the whitepaper as exploring technical design options, including a privacy-preserving traceability approach, and invites academic and industry comment. It sets a target of an initial HKMA view on e-HKD feasibility by mid-2022. The full technical content is in the attached whitepaper, summarised separately.

k: The whitepaper is described as the first of its kind among central banks to include a technical design allowing transaction traceability while preserving user privacy.
para 2
The HKMA aims to form an initial view on the feasibility of issuing e-HKD by around mid-2022.
para 2

para 2

t: Joint research on multiple central bank digital currency (CBDC) shows potential for speeding up cross-border payments and reducing costs

s: The HKMA, together with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre, the Bank of Thailand, the PBC's Digital Currency Institute, and the Central Bank of the UAE, published the report 'Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments', presenting interim findings of the mBridge project. The enhanced prototype can manage CBDC liquidity, monitor flows and balances, enhance transaction privacy, and automate compliance functions, with potential to substantially speed up and reduce the cost of cross-border transfers compared to correspondent banking.

t: Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
sl: HKMA/SFC · Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for… (2021)
s: This September 2021 report covers the second phase of the joint central bank blockchain project, rebuilt on a new technology base and expanded beyond the original Thailand-Hong Kong pairing, and records the point at which the project brought in mainland China and the UAE and was renamed mBridge. It reports that the upgraded prototype cut cross-border transfer times from days to seconds and could lower several cost components tied to using correspondent banks. It sets out three guiding principles the group adopted going forward: doing no harm to other currencies, complying with each jurisdiction's laws including anti-money-laundering rules, and staying interoperable with existing systems. It also describes a new governance structure with a steering committee and four specialist subcommittees, including one dedicated to legal issues chaired by the Hong Kong authority, and lists a work plan of legal, policy and technical gaps still to be closed.
w: This is the report where the project explicitly commits to complying with local anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing law and sets up a dedicated legal workstream, which is the clearest early signal that any bank later connecting to mBridge would face jurisdiction-specific AML/CFT and legal-certainty requirements rather than a purely technical integration. It remains background rather than a current instrument, since the platform has since moved on to the pilot and further stages covered in the later reports.
k: The prototype moved from days-long settlement to a matter of seconds and pointed to potential cost savings compared with routing payments through a chain of correspondent banks.
Executive Summary, p.7
With mainland China's central bank digital currency institute and the UAE's central bank joining in February 2021, the project was renamed from Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge and entered a third phase.
Executive Summary, p.7

The group adopted three guiding principles going forward: not undermining other currencies' monetary control, complying with each jurisdiction's laws including anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing rules, and staying compatible with existing payment systems.
s.4.1 (principles), p.52-53
A legal subcommittee, chaired by the Hong Kong authority, was set up to coordinate the project's legal paperwork and to examine legal and regulatory issues tied to each proposed use case.
s.4.2.3 Legal sub-committee, p.55

s.5 Conclusion and next steps, p.58

The forward work plan explicitly includes building features so the platform meets each jurisdiction's own regulatory and reporting rules, and designing the legal contracts that will govern participation.
s.4.3 Roadmap, p.56

t: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset platforms
sl: SFC · Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset platforms (2021)
s: The SFC flags that Binance is offering so-called stock tokens elsewhere and worries these could reach Hong Kong investors. No Binance entity holds an SFC licence. The SFC's view is that these tokens, which track the price of real overseas shares in fractional form, are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law, so selling or promoting them here would need a licence or an exemption. It warns that unregulated platforms may not verify that the tokens are genuinely backed, and that investors could struggle to recover money if the platform fails.
w: Warns that no Binance entity is SFC-licensed and that unlicensed 'stock token' platforms may be operating illegally in Hong Kong -- relevant to compliance mainly as a name to screen out of any client referral, custody or counterparty relationship.
k: No Binance group entity is licensed to carry out any regulated activity in Hong Kong.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening remarks at HKAB Fintech Seminar: Next Phase of Hong Kong's Fintech Journey – 'Fintech 2025'
sl: HKMA · Opening remarks at HKAB Fintech Seminar: Next Phase of… (2021)
s: This speech by an HKMA Deputy Chief Executive launched the Fintech 2025 strategy, a four-part plan to push banks toward full digitalisation, build data infrastructure, grow fintech talent, and expand sandbox funding. One strand covers central bank digital currency (CBDC) work: continuing wholesale CBDC research with the Bank of Thailand and starting a new study into a retail CBDC for Hong Kong, later named e-HKD. No virtual-asset or stablecoin rules are announced here; the speech is a strategy launch, not a binding instrument.

t: HKMA unveils "Fintech 2025" strategy
sl: HKMA · HKMA unveils "Fintech 2025" strategy (2021)
s: HKMA launched its Fintech 2025 strategy, a five-year plan to push banks to full digital adoption. t: The HKMA Unveils "Fintech 2025" Strategy

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Enhance Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Regulation in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Enhance Anti-Money Laundering… (2021)
s: Published by FSTB in May 2021, this paper concludes a late-2020/early-2021 consultation and confirms the government would proceed with a licensing regime for virtual asset service providers (VASPs, essentially exchanges) under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, plus a separate registration regime for dealers in precious metals and stones. It set the design that was later enacted: SFC as licensing authority, professional-investor-only trading, a 180-day transition window, and specific criminal and civil sanctions. This regime has since taken effect and been elaborated by SFC guidelines, so this paper is now historical background rather than a current rulebook.
w: This is the design document behind today's VASP/VATP licensing regime that any exchange the bank deals with (for custody, trading, or referral) must hold, so it is a useful reference for understanding why VATPs are currently professional-investor-only by default and what licensing gaps mean for due diligence, even though the live rulebook is now the AMLO as amended plus SFC guidelines.
k: Anyone operating a virtual asset exchange in Hong Kong would need an SFC licence as a VASP, and the exchange definition catches any platform that takes custody or control of client money or virtual assets at any point.
Peer-to-peer platforms that only post buy/sell listings without ever holding client funds or assets fall outside the VASP licensing definition.
para 2.5, p.5
A licensed VASP could initially only serve professional investors, despite over 40% of respondents wanting retail access; the government kept the restriction given the sector's risk and volatility.

VASPs would need either to be incorporated in Hong Kong or to hold Companies Ordinance registration as a non-Hong-Kong company here, and to keep a permanent local place of business, giving the SFC a local entity to supervise.
Applicants and at least two designated responsible officers must pass a fit-and-proper test covering past convictions, compliance history, experience and financial integrity.
A 180-day transition period was set after the regime commenced, letting existing operators keep running while their licence application was processed.
Marketing a virtual asset trading service to the Hong Kong public without a VASP licence, from Hong Kong or elsewhere, would be prohibited.

Maximum proposed criminal penalties included a HKD 5 million fine and 7 years' imprisonment for operating unlicensed, plus lower fines and 2-year terms for false statements, AML/CFT non-compliance, or fraudulent misrepresentation to induce a trade.
rg: Read Chapter 2 (VASP proposals, pp.4-15) in full; Chapter 3 covers precious-metals dealers and can be skipped as not digital-asset relevant; Chapter 5 (Conclusions, p.27) gives the implementation timeline.

t: Joint statement on Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC) Bridge Project
sl: HKMA · Joint statement on Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC)… (2021)
s: HKMA announced that the UAE central bank and the People's Bank of China's Digital Currency Institute were joining a cross-border central bank digital currency (CBDC) project with Hong Kong and Thailand, renamed the Multiple CBDC (m-CBDC) Bridge, supported by the BIS Innovation Hub in Hong Kong. The project would build a proof-of-concept using distributed ledger technology to let central banks settle real-time cross-border foreign-exchange payments around the clock, aiming to cut cost and complexity in cross-border transfers.
w: Early-stage wholesale CBDC infrastructure project; not yet operational for banks, but worth tracking as a potential future cross-border settlement rail.

t: SFC licenses first virtual asset trading platform
sl: SFC · SFC licenses first virtual asset trading platform (2020)
s: The SFC announced that Hong Kong now has its first SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP), granted under a voluntary opt-in scheme. The licence covers two regulated activities: dealing in securities (Type 1) and running automated trading services (Type 7). Only professional investors may use the platform, and it must follow the Terms and Conditions written for VATP Operators, which echo rules already used for securities brokers and automated trading venues. This grant follows the SFC's Position Paper of 6 November 2019, which first set up the framework. The release also notes that, separately, the government had opened a November 2020 consultation on anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing rules, proposing that the SFC oversee every centralised virtual-asset exchange, even ones trading only non-security tokens.
w: This marks the first working SFC-licensed VATP. When checking whether a trading-platform counterparty is properly licensed, compliance can confirm it holds Type 1 and Type 7 licences and follows the professional-investor-only limit described here.
k: The licensed platform may serve professional investors only, matching the definition used in the SFO's Professional Investor Rules.
Note 1, p.1
The platform is licensed for two regulated activities under the SFO: dealing in securities (Type 1) and providing automated trading services (Type 7).
Note 1, p.1
As a licence condition, the platform must follow the Terms and Conditions written for VATP Operators.
Note 1, p.1
At this point, SFC rules reach only platforms that trade at least one security token; platforms dealing solely in non-security tokens stay outside SFC jurisdiction and remain unregulated by the SFC.
body para 2, p.1

The government, in a November 2020 consultation, proposed new legislation that would let the SFC oversee every centralised virtual-asset exchange, even ones that trade only non-security tokens; feedback was due by 31 January 2021.

t: Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
sl: SFC · Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (2020)
s: This SFC document sets out detailed, binding Terms and Conditions imposed as a licensing condition on virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operators licensed under the voluntary opt-in regime (Types 1 and 7). It covers financial soundness, operations and token admission due diligence, market manipulation prevention, client dealing (KYC, suitability, disclosure, contract notes), custody of client assets (trust structure via an Associated Entity, cold storage, private key management, insurance), risk management, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors, AML/CFT, and ongoing reporting obligations. It applies only to platforms serving professional investors and offering at least one security token.
w: This document does not bind the bank directly, but its 98% cold-storage and Hong Kong-key-storage baseline is the origin of the custody standard a compliance head should expect any VATP counterparty, including a bank-affiliated one, to still be measured against in substance.
k: A Platform Operator should hold, in Hong Kong at all times, sufficiently liquid own assets (such as cash, deposits, treasury bills or certificates of deposit, but not virtual assets) worth no less than a year's actual running costs.
para 3.1, p.5
A Platform Operator and its Associated Entity are expected to hold client assets so that at least 98% sit in cold storage, capping hot-wallet holdings at 2%.
Under the Platform Operator's key-management controls, cryptographic seeds and private keys for client assets are kept within Hong Kong.
para 7.6(e), p.22
An insurance policy should be maintained covering client virtual assets in hot storage (full coverage) and cold storage (substantial coverage, e.g. 95%).
A Platform Operator should not offer clients any financial accommodation (e.g. margin) to acquire virtual assets.
para 4.8, p.7
A Platform Operator should not trade for its own account or make markets on a proprietary basis.
A client counts as having sufficient knowledge of virtual assets once they have carried out five or more virtual-asset transactions in the preceding three years.
para 6.7, p.11

Records should generally be kept for at least seven years; certain records (contract notes, receipts, audit logs) for at least two years, and system design documentation for two years after the system is retired.
A Platform Operator is expected to tell the SFC within seven business days of a planned change to its scope of services, controlling persons, or authorisation status.

A token that qualifies as a 'security' can only be admitted for trading if it is backed by assets, approved or registered with a comparable overseas regulator, and has a track record of at least 12 months since issuance.
para 4.3(i), p.6
rg: Focus on Part IV (token admission), Part VI (KYC/suitability/disclosure), Part VII (custody -- the 98% cold storage and key management rules), and Part XIII (AML/CFT); skim Schedule 1's list of cross-referenced Codes and Guidelines.

t: A New Trend for Fintech - Cross-border Payment
sl: HKMA · A New Trend for Fintech - Cross-border Payment (2020)
s: This 2020 HKMA Insight article by the then Chief Executive discusses cross-border payment inefficiencies and Hong Kong's initiatives to address them, including the Faster Payment System, the joint blockchain-based CBDC research with the Bank of Thailand, and early technical discussions with the People's Bank of China on piloting cross-border use of e-CNY (digital renminbi). It is commentary, not a rule.
w: This documents the earliest public signal of a Hong Kong/e-CNY cross-border pilot, background relevant to CBDC-related product and payments-infrastructure planning, though it creates no compliance obligation.
k: The HKMA and Bank of Thailand's blockchain CBDC research had entered a second stage exploring specific business applications and scaling the platform to three or more participating CBDCs.

The HKMA and the PBOC's Digital Currency Institute were discussing and preparing for a technical pilot to use e-CNY for cross-border payments between Hong Kong and the Mainland, with no launch timetable yet set.
closing para on e-CNY

s: SFC CEO Ashley Alder announced that the government had that day proposed a new mandatory licensing regime under anti-money laundering law for all virtual asset trading platforms, closing the gap left by the 2019 opt-in framework, which only caught platforms that chose to list at least one security-type token. Going forward all Hong Kong VA platforms would fall under either the existing opt-in regime or the new mandatory regime, with the same standards. He also confirmed that security tokens already fall under existing securities law for both primary distribution and secondary trading.
w: Marks the policy pivot from voluntary to mandatory VATP licensing in Hong Kong, the direct ancestor of the licensing regime a bank must check counterparties against today.

It is a policy-launch speech, not a rule, and has no other virtual-asset content.

t: Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in Cross-Border Payments
sl: HKMA/SFC · Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in… (2020)
s: This is the joint report, produced together by the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand, on the first phase of their shared blockchain experiment for cross-border payments, published January 2020. It describes a working prototype, built with technology partner R3, that lets participating Thai and Hong Kong banks move funds and do foreign-exchange deals directly with each other rather than through a chain of correspondent banks. The report says the prototype cut settlement layers and supported same-time payment-and-FX settlement, while also trying to build in local regulatory compliance checks. It closes by naming unresolved legal, regulatory and operational gaps that would need further work before any real-world use. This is the earliest, now-superseded phase of a project family that later grew into mBridge.
w: This is a superseded, proof-of-concept-stage report with no live obligations for the bank today, but it is the documented starting point of the technology lineage now running as mBridge and Ensemble, so it is useful background if due diligence questions come up about how mature those later, live pilots really are. It also shows early on that regulators flagged AML/compliance and legal-certainty gaps as open problems, not solved ones, which remains a live theme in the later reports.
k: The prototype bridged Thailand's and Hong Kong's own blockchain payment networks so that participating banks could transfer funds and swap currencies directly, cutting out extra intermediary banks.
s.01 Executive Summary
Ten commercial banks took part in total, eight based in Thailand and two in Hong Kong, working alongside the two central banks and blockchain vendor R3.
s.01 Executive Summary
The prototype was designed to let a currency swap and its matching payment settle together, so neither side of the trade completes without the other.
s.01 Executive Summary
The design tried to build local rulebook checks into the payment flow itself, alongside features to help banks manage their foreign-currency liquidity across the two markets.
s.01 Executive Summary
The report itself flags that legal and regulatory questions, along with some operational and technology limits, were not yet resolved and were left for the next phase of the project.
s.07 Conclusion
The authors suggest the next step is to reshape the model so it fits each jurisdiction's existing rules and lines up with international standards before it could be used for real transactions.
s.07 Conclusion
rg: Read the Executive Summary (p.9) and the Conclusion (p.58); skip the 60-page technical walkthrough of liquidity mechanics and the glossary/appendix on Project Inthanon and LionRock history, which are background detail only.

t: Managing ML/TF Risks Associated with Virtual Assets (VAs) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)
sl: HKMA · Managing ML/TF Risks Associated with Virtual Assets (VAs) and… (2019)
s: This circular formally replaces the 2014 virtual-commodity letters and updates HKMA guidance to match the FATF's 2019 rules on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells banks to apply a risk-based approach when banking VASPs, doing extra due diligence proportionate to risk, including understanding the VASP's business, checking if it is licensed or registered, and assessing its anti-money-laundering controls. It also says banks must run a money-laundering risk assessment before launching any new VA-linked product.
w: This circular is the direct predecessor of the AML/CFT due-diligence checklist still used today for onboarding and monitoring virtual-asset-service-provider customers, so it is a foundational reference for VASP counterparty due-diligence procedures.
k: Banks should assess and differentiate the money-laundering risk of each VASP customer individually rather than applying one blanket approach, since VASP business models vary widely.
Extra due diligence on a VASP customer should include understanding its business, checking its licensing/registration status, and assessing its own anti-money-laundering controls.
Before launching any new banking or investment product linked to virtual assets, a bank should carry out a money-laundering risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks found.
This circular replaces the two 2014 letters on virtual commodities.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full, note the supersession line on p.2.

t: Managing ML/TF risks associated with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs)
sl: HKMA · Managing ML/TF risks associated with virtual assets (VAs) and… (2019)
s: This circular, addressed to all Stored Value Facility (SVF) licensees, passes on FATF's June 2019 update to Recommendation 15 and its Risk-Based-Approach guidance on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells SVF licensees to apply extra, risk-based due diligence before establishing a business relationship with a VASP, including checking whether the VASP is licensed or registered and AML/CFT-supervised, and to run an ML/TF risk assessment before launching any new VA-related product. It signals that more VASPs would become licensed in Hong Kong and elsewhere as FATF-aligned regimes took hold.
w: This is an early, direct HKMA instruction that any bank-affiliated SVF licensee must treat VASP counterparties as a distinct AML/CFT due-diligence category, which is the template later intermediary and custody guidance builds on.
k: SVF licensees must apply a risk-based approach when starting or maintaining a relationship with a VASP, tailoring due diligence to that VASP's individual risk rather than a one-size-fits-all check.
p.1, para 4

Due diligence on a VASP counterparty should cover understanding its business, checking from public information whether it is licensed/registered and AML/CFT-supervised, and assessing its AML/CFT controls, scaled to the assessed risk.
p.2, para 1

Before rolling out any new VA-related product or service, an SVF licensee must first carry out an ML/TF risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks identified, consistent with paragraph 2.11 of the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline for SVF licensees.
p.2, para 2
SVF licensees are expected to keep monitoring international and local VASP developments and apply a risk-based approach on an ongoing basis, not just at onboarding.
p.2, closing para
