t: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: In this 2019 position paper, the SFC set up a voluntary licence path (Types 1 and 7) for a centralised platform that trades at least one security token, placing licensed platforms inside the SFC's regulatory sandbox for close oversight. The SFC said it had no legal power over platforms that only trade non-security tokens, so many venues could stay unregulated, but it judged that regulating this subset served the public good while broader legislation was pending. The paper lays out licence conditions, and Appendix 1 gives the complete terms and conditions for platform operators, covering custody, know-your-customer (KYC) checks, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) controls, market monitoring, accounting, risk management, and conflicts of interest.
w: Even though this paper is now superseded, it set the original custody and insurance benchmarks -- 98% cold storage, trust-held client assets, insured custody -- that compliance teams can still use to check how well a virtual-asset platform counterparty protects client assets.
k: Under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), only 'securities' or 'futures contracts' fall under SFC authority, so a platform trading only non-security tokens sits outside the SFC's power to license or supervise it.
para 4, p.1-2
To fall under SFC jurisdiction and need a Type 1 and Type 7 licence, an operator must run a centralised online trading platform based in Hong Kong and list at least one security token.
para 32, p.7

para 33, p.7

t: SFC issues warnings on virtual asset futures contracts
sl: SFC · SFC issues warnings on virtual asset futures contracts (2019)
s: The SFC warned that virtual-asset futures contracts (for example on Bitcoin) are high-risk because the underlying assets are volatile, hard to value, and traded on largely unregulated venues, some of which have changed trading rules mid-contract or halted trades to investors' detriment. It said any Hong Kong platform offering such futures without a licence may breach the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), and separately such contracts could count as unlawful gambling under the Gambling Ordinance unless expressly authorised. The SFC stated it had not licensed any such platform and, given the risk profile, said it would be unlikely to do so. It reminded investors that breaching the SFO or Gambling Ordinance carries criminal penalties, and it excluded from the warning certain US-regulated Bitcoin futures already authorised for automated trading services (ATS) purposes in Hong Kong.
w: Confirms that unlicensed VA-futures venues carry both SFO licensing risk and a possible illegal-gambling characterisation in Hong Kong — a relevant screening flag if the bank's customers reference such platforms or if the bank considers any related product referencing VA derivatives.
k: Offering VA futures trading in Hong Kong without an SFO licence or authorisation may itself be an offence.
para beginning 'In Hong Kong, any trading platforms or persons...'
Depending on structure, VA futures contracts can also be treated as contracts for differences, making them potentially unlawful gambling unless separately authorised.
para on Gambling Ordinance definition
As of this warning the SFC had not licensed or authorised anyone to offer or trade VA futures contracts in Hong Kong, and said a grant was unlikely given the risk profile.
para 'The SFC has not licensed...'
US-regulated Bitcoin futures already authorised for ATS purposes and covered by a 2017 circular to licensed corporations and registered institutions are excluded from this warning.
footnote 1
rg: Read the two risk paragraphs and the SFO/Gambling Ordinance paragraphs; skip the footnote detail on the 2017 ATS exclusion unless relevant to a specific product.

t: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: The SFC finalised its opt-in licensing framework for centralised virtual asset trading platforms: a platform only falls under SFC jurisdiction once it lists at least one security-type token, but once caught, all of its virtual-asset business (security and non-security tokens alike) must sit in one SFC-licensed entity holding Type 1 (dealing) and Type 7 (automated trading services) licences. The attached Terms and Conditions set detailed, legally binding operating rules covering custody (98% cold storage, key management, insurance), KYC and suitability, AML/CFT, market surveillance, conflicts of interest, record-keeping and SFC notification duties. Services are restricted to professional investors only. This framework was the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's later mandatory VATP licensing regime.
w: This is the core rulebook a bank must benchmark any Hong Kong VATP counterparty against for custody, AML, KYC and governance standards, even though it was later superseded by mandatory licensing; the specific numeric benchmarks (98% cold storage, insurance levels, 7-year record-keeping) remain the industry reference points cited in later regimes.
k: A platform only becomes subject to SFC licensing once it offers at least one security-type token; a platform trading only non-security tokens stays outside SFC jurisdiction entirely.
All of a licensed platform's virtual-asset trading activity marketed to or conducted in Hong Kong must be run through one licensed legal entity, so the SFC can oversee the whole business.

Client virtual assets must be held on trust through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity, with 98% kept in cold storage and no more than 2% in hot wallets.
Terms and Conditions para 7.1, 7.5(c)
Seeds and private keys for client assets must be generated and stored in Hong Kong, with distributed backups and strict internal access controls to prevent any single person controlling a full key.
Terms and Conditions para 7.6
An insurance policy must cover client virtual assets in hot storage in full and in cold storage substantially (SFC's benchmark example is 95%), at all times.
Terms and Conditions para 7.17
Platform operators must only serve professional investors, and must assess and document each client's virtual-asset knowledge before onboarding, or provide training first.
Terms and Conditions para 6.4, 6.7-6.8

Platform operators must run written AML/CFT systems, apply enhanced due diligence to tainted wallet addresses, mixing services and high-anonymity assets, and unmask or reject clients using masked IP addresses (e.g. VPNs) where needed.

Operators must notify the SFC of material non-compliance, system failures, and various operational changes, generally within seven business days or immediately depending on the item, and file monthly business reports.

A licensed platform operator should not trade for its own book or make markets on a proprietary basis, and must have written policies restricting and monitoring employees' personal dealing in virtual assets.

Platform operators cannot offer clients financing to buy virtual assets, and cannot offer or trade virtual asset futures or related derivatives at all.
Terms and Conditions para 4.8-4.9

s: SFC CEO Ashley Alder announced, in this speech, the launch of the SFC's new opt-in licensing framework for virtual asset trading platforms, alongside a separate investor-warning statement on VA futures. He explained the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, why the SFC chose an opt-in route rather than waiting for new legislation, and the framework's built-in limits: it only catches a platform once it lists one security-type token, so platforms trading only non-security tokens stay unregulated. t: SFC adopts new approach to virtual asset trading platforms
sl: SFC · SFC adopts new approach to virtual asset trading platforms (2019)
s: This press release announces the SFC's 6 November 2019 Position Paper, 'Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms,' moving from the conceptual November 2018 framework to an actual licensing regime. Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7). Licence conditions require serving professional investors only, sufficient client knowledge of virtual assets, strict criteria for admitting virtual assets, and placement in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close supervision. The SFC states it still has no power to license or supervise platforms trading only non-security tokens. A companion statement warns investors about unregulated virtual asset futures contracts.
w: This is the historical bridge from the 2018 conceptual framework to actual VATP licensing. A compliance head only needs it to understand where today's custody and liquidity rules came from, since the Position Paper itself has since been superseded.
k: Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7 regulated activities).
