Terms and Conditions, para 7.5(c), p.21-22
Insurance must fully cover virtual assets held in hot storage, and cover most of those in cold storage (for example, 95%) at all times.
Terms and Conditions, para 7.17, p.25-26
Seeds and private keys for client virtual assets must be kept physically in Hong Kong.
Terms and Conditions, para 7.6(e), p.23
A Platform Operator must hold liquid financial resources equal to at least 12 months of operating expenses.
Terms and Conditions, para 3.1, p.6
The SFC has no power to license or supervise a platform that trades only non-security virtual assets or tokens, since those do not count as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO.
Position Paper, para 4, p.1
A Platform Operator must not trade on its own account or make markets for itself, and must not offer leverage for clients to buy virtual assets, nor trade virtual asset futures or derivatives.
Terms and Conditions, paras 4.8-4.9, 10.2-10.3
Only security tokens that are backed by assets, approved or registered with comparable regulators, and have a 12-month track record after issuance should be allowed for trading.
Position Paper, para 80(i), p.14
Licensed Platform Operators sit in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close, intensive supervision, including monthly reporting.
Position Paper, paras 10, 85, p.2, p.15
rg: Read the press release for the headline shift; then Position Paper Parts I and III (paras 1-12, 30-44) for the regulatory rationale and licensing regime, and skim the numbered Terms and Conditions sections (custody VII, risk mgmt VIII, cybersecurity IX, AML XIII) for the operative standards -- Schedule 1's list of applicable Codes/Guidelines can be skipped.

t: Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations which Manage Portfolios that Invest in Virtual Assets
sl: SFC · Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations which Manage Portfolios… (2019)
s: This short circular announces that the proforma standard Terms and Conditions for 'Virtual Asset Fund Managers' -- licensed corporations managing or planning to manage portfolios with a stated virtual asset investment objective, or intending to invest 10% or more of GAV in virtual assets, as first announced in the 1 November 2018 Statement -- are now published on the SFC website and will be imposed on all such managers as licensing conditions, subject to minor firm-specific variations.
w: Confirms operationalisation of the Nov 2018 virtual asset portfolio manager framework via a published, standard proforma terms and conditions document -- the actual legal text a bank's Type 9-licensed asset management arm would be bound by if managing virtual asset portfolios.
k: The proforma Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Fund Managers, referenced in the 1 November 2018 Statement, are now published and available on the SFC website
The SFC will apply this proforma as a standard licensing condition on every Virtual Asset Fund Manager, subject only to minor firm-specific variations
rg: One-page announcement; the substantive terms and conditions are in a separate linked PDF not included in this document's text (see footnote URL), so this record only covers the announcement.

t: LCQ15: Application of blockchain technology
sl: Government · LCQ15: Application of blockchain technology (2019)
s: A Legislative Council written reply describing early government use of blockchain, including the bank-consortium trade-finance platform eTradeConnect, a cross-border link being planned with Singapore, and pilot blockchain projects in four government departments. It also reports Innovation and Technology Fund support for 18 blockchain/DLT research projects and various training statistics. No digital-asset regulatory content is discussed; the focus is public-sector blockchain adoption, not virtual assets.
w: Background context on eTradeConnect, the trade-finance DLT platform some banks already participate in; not itself a compliance-driving document.
k: eTradeConnect, a 12-bank blockchain trade-finance platform facilitated by HKMA, was still at an early operational stage in mid-2019.
reply (1)
HKMA and the Monetary Authority of Singapore were working to connect eTradeConnect with Singapore's trade platform via a 'Global Trade Connectivity Network'.
reply (1)
The Innovation and Technology Fund had backed 18 blockchain/DLT projects worth about HK$67.2 million over the prior three years.
reply (4)
rg: Skim only; general blockchain-in-government background, not virtual-asset regulation.

t: LCQ20: Regulation of virtual asset investment activities
sl: Government · LCQ20: Regulation of virtual asset investment activities (2019)
s: A Legislative Council written question-and-answer covering police enforcement statistics on virtual-asset fraud and money laundering, whether virtual-asset goods like mining rigs fall under trade description law, how profits tax applies to VA transactions, and the government's plan to keep monitoring VA regulation. The government confirmed VA transactions are already taxable under ordinary profits-tax rules and that police handled hundreds of VA-related crime reports in 2018.
w: Illustrates that as of 2019 there was still no dedicated VA licensing law - taxation and enforcement relied on general statutes - useful context for how far the regime has since moved.
k: Police recorded 324 virtual-asset-related crime reports in 2018, up from 50 in 2016 and 67 in 2017 (Bitcoin-only figures for those years).
reply (1)
Existing profits tax rules apply equally to virtual-asset transactions; there is no VA-specific tax regime.
reply (3)-(5)
The government said the SFC and HKMA would keep studying whether to increase regulation of virtual-asset activities.
reply (6)
rg: Skim; mainly of historical/statistical interest, no compliance obligations for banks.

t: Circular to intermediaries Statement on Security Token Offerings
sl: SFC · intermediaries Statement on Security Token Offerings (2019)
s: This circular transmits the SFC's 28 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings (STOs), which reminds market participants of legal and regulatory requirements for STOs. It confirms Security Tokens are likely 'securities' under the SFO, so marketing/distribution requires Type 1 licensing, and treats Security Tokens as 'complex products' subject to enhanced investor protection under the Code of Conduct para 5.5 (effective July 2019). It imposes selling restrictions (professional investors only), due diligence duties, and client disclosure requirements similar to the November 2018 virtual asset fund circular, and requires intermediaries to discuss STO activities with the SFC beforehand.
w: This 2019 circular binds SFC-licensed corporations, not the bank as an AI. A compliance head's interest is counterparty due diligence if security tokens are distributed through a group LC, since STOs are automatically treated as complex products requiring professional-investor-only marketing.
k: Security Tokens are likely to be 'securities' under the SFO and therefore subject to Hong Kong securities laws
Marketing/distributing Security Tokens requires Type 1 (dealing in securities) licensing/registration unless exempt; unlicensed activity is a criminal offence

Security Tokens are treated as 'complex products' under the Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms and Code of Conduct para 5.5 (effective July 2019), triggering additional investor protection measures
Intermediaries marketing/distributing Security Tokens must be licensed for Type 1 and should only offer them to professional investors
(A) Selling restrictions, p.1
Intermediaries should conduct due diligence on the STO issuer's background, financial soundness, and the rights attached to backing assets, and scrutinise whitepapers/marketing materials
(B) Due diligence, p.1-2
Intermediaries are told to consult the SFC in advance of any STO-related activity.
p.2, footnote 5
rg: Read the 2-page attached Statement in full; the transmitting circular itself is a 1-line cover note.

t: Statement on Security Token Offerings
sl: SFC · Statement on Security Token Offerings (2019)
s: The SFC reminded firms that security token offerings (STOs) - digital tokens structured like traditional securities and backed by real assets or revenue rights - are almost always 'securities' under Hong Kong law. Anyone marketing or distributing them therefore needs a Type 1 dealing licence, must treat them as complex products, and must do proper due diligence on the issuer and the token's backing before offering them, normally only to professional investors. The statement was later superseded by a November 2023 circular.
w: Sets the baseline classification that most tokenised-asset offerings a bank might be asked to distribute or facilitate are treated as securities requiring full licensing and suitability compliance, not a lighter VA-specific regime.
k: Security tokens are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law, so distributing them needs a Type 1 licence.
para 4-5
Firms distributing security tokens must apply existing suitability rules and treat the tokens as complex products with extra investor-protection steps.
para 6
Firms must do due diligence covering the issuer's and management's soundness and the rights attached to the backing assets, including scrutinising the whitepaper.
para (B)
Firms are expected to talk to the SFC before starting any STO-related activity.
para (footnote 5 / final para under selling restrictions)
rg: Short document; read in full. Note it is formally superseded by a 2 Nov 2023 circular, so treat as background/history rather than current guidance.

t: BCBS Statement on Crypto-Assets
sl: HKMA · BCBS Statement on Crypto-Assets (2019)
s: The HKMA relays a March 2019 Basel Committee statement setting out prudential expectations for banks' crypto-asset exposures. It says crypto-assets do not reliably act as money, are not legal tender and are not backed by government, and that growth in crypto trading platforms could raise financial-stability and bank-risk concerns. The HKMA tells banks to take note of the Basel statement and, if they plan crypto-related activities, to discuss this with the HKMA and show they have proper systems and controls in place.
w: This is an early, direct statement that the HKMA expects prior discussion before a bank takes on crypto-asset exposure, a prior-consultation expectation that recurs across every later HKMA virtual-asset circular in this batch.
k: Crypto-assets do not reliably work as money, per the Basel Committee's view, and no government or public authority stands behind them.
A bank planning to engage in crypto-asset activities should discuss this with the HKMA in advance and demonstrate it has adequate systems and controls to manage the related risks.
rg: Two-page circular; read in full.

t: Circular to intermediaries Distribution of virtual asset funds
sl: SFC · intermediaries Distribution of virtual asset funds (2018)
s: This circular sets expected standards for SFC-licensed intermediaries (Type 1/Type 9) distributing virtual asset funds. It confirms distribution of a fund investing in virtual assets triggers Type 1 licensing regardless of whether the underlying assets are 'securities'. For funds not authorised by the SFC with more than 10% GAV in virtual assets, it imposes selling restrictions (professional investors only, knowledge assessment, concentration limits), due diligence duties on the fund/manager/counterparties, and mandatory client risk disclosures. The document itself states it was superseded and updated by a circular dated 28 January 2022.
w: This circular is superseded, but for a compliance head it is the direct ancestor of today's VA-fund distribution controls (professional-investor-only sale, knowledge test, concentration limits, counterparty due diligence), useful mainly to confirm which of those requirements have since been tightened or replaced.
k: Distribution of a virtual asset fund in Hong Kong requires Type 1 licensing/registration regardless of whether the virtual assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'
p.1 (Background section)
For unauthorised virtual asset funds with stated VA objective or >10% GAV in virtual assets, intermediaries should only target professional investors and assess client knowledge unless institutional
Intermediaries should ensure aggregate client investment in unauthorised virtual asset funds is reasonable relative to net worth, to avoid concentration risk
Intermediaries should conduct due diligence on the fund manager, the fund, and counterparties (custodians/exchanges) before distribution
Custody arrangement of fund assets across exchanges/custodians/hot/cold storage should be understood as part of due diligence

Intermediaries should provide prominent warning statements to clients on volatility, manipulation, lack of secondary markets, unregulated custodians, counterparty risk, hot-wallet loss risk, and cyber risk
Failure to comply may affect fitness and properness and result in disciplinary action
rg: Read the banner notice on p.1 first (supersession), then sections (A)-(C); skip footnote definitions unless needed for precision.

t: SFC sets out new regulatory approach for virtual assets
sl: SFC · SFC sets out new regulatory approach for virtual assets (2018)
s: This press release announces the same-day Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolio managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators. It explains that firms managing or distributing virtual asset funds will face new licensing conditions from the SFC, and that the SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to test whether platform operators can be brought under supervision and eventual licensing. It quotes CEO Ashley Alder on investor protection goals and the sandbox pathway.
w: This is the SFC's founding 2018 policy statement; it does not bind the bank directly but explains the professional-investor-only starting point and sandbox concept that later hardened into the licensing regimes the bank's counterparties operate under.
k: SFC will impose licensing conditions on firms managing or intending to manage portfolios investing in virtual assets, regardless of whether the assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'
para 2, p.1
Within the SFC Regulatory Sandbox, the SFC will test whether trading platforms dealing in virtual assets could be brought under a licensing regime.
para 5, p.1
If found appropriate, the SFC would grant a licence and place platform operators under close supervision; alternatively it could decide no licence should be granted
para 6, p.1
Many virtual assets do not meet the SFO definition of 'securities'/'futures contracts', so managing funds solely investing in such assets is not itself a regulated activity
Notes, p.1
rg: Short release; read in full, then cross-reference the full Statement circular for operative detail.

t: Fintech: Meeting the regulatory challenges - Keynote speech at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2018
sl: SFC · Fintech: Meeting the regulatory challenges - Keynote speech at… (2018)
s: In this speech the SFC's then-CEO previewed the SFC's first structured virtual-asset framework: new conduct standards for fund managers and distributors dealing in crypto assets, and an opt-in sandbox pathway for exploring regulation of virtual asset trading platforms. It explains the SFC's reasoning for why it could only reach parts of the crypto market given the legal definition of 'securities'.
w: This speech is the origin point for the fund-manager/distributor conduct standards and the VATP sandbox-to-licensing pathway that later hardened into today's SFC regime; useful for compliance to understand why certain thresholds (like the 10% portfolio trigger) and the professional-investor-only starting point exist.
k: SFC-supervised managers putting more than 10% of a mixed portfolio into virtual assets would need to meet new standards, initially limited to professional investors only.
'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5
Firms distributing funds with crypto exposure, already required to be SFC-registered/licensed brokers, would face new specific guidance on distribution standards for such funds.
'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5
VATP regulation would start as an opt-in sandbox: interested platforms would explore a conceptual framework with the SFC, with no formal licence granted during that sandbox stage.
'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.5-6

The SFC's jurisdiction is legally limited to virtual assets that qualify as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO; assets and platforms outside that definition fell outside its regulatory perimeter at the time.
'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' section, p.4
Sandbox-stage platforms would be expected to serve professional investors only and meet standards at least as high as existing automated trading services the SFC already supervises.
'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.6
rg: Read 'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' through 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' (p.4-6); the opening remarks on general Fintech regulation (p.1-3) are less relevant to digital assets specifically.

t: Circular to intermediaries Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
sl: SFC · intermediaries Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios… (2018)
s: This landmark 1 November 2018 SFC circular transmits the accompanying Policy Statement, which for the first time sets out a full regulatory approach covering managers and distributors of virtual asset portfolios and funds, and a conceptual (opt-in) framework exploring whether virtual asset trading platform operators might in future be regulated, to be tested via the SFC Regulatory Sandbox. It brought Type 9 and Type 1 licensed firms managing or distributing funds investing 10%+ GAV in non-securities virtual assets under licensing-condition-based oversight, and proposed core principles for a future licensed platform operator regime (single legal entity, professional-investors-only, 98% cold storage expectation, no leverage/derivatives, 12-month ICO token trading restriction).
w: For a compliance head, this 2018 statement is historical scaffolding: it establishes where the now-standard VATP custody and professional-investor terms originated, but creates no obligation on the bank itself (status: historical/superseded).
k: Firms managing portfolios with a stated VA investment objective or intending to invest 10%+ GAV in virtual assets must be licensed/registered and will have SFC standard terms and conditions imposed via licensing conditions
Statement, Section I(a), p.4-5
Investment in virtual asset portfolios under the terms and conditions is limited to professional investors, as that term is defined in the SFO.
Statement, 'Type of investors and disclosure', p.5
A licensed corporation that holds non-SF virtual assets for portfolios it manages must keep at least $3 million in liquid capital, or a higher variable amount if that applies.
Statement, 'Liquid capital', p.6-7
A prospective licensed Platform Operator must run all of its virtual-asset trading business (Relevant Activities) through one single company holding an SFC licence.
Appendix 2, Core principle (1), p.3
A Platform Operator should provide services only to professional investors
Appendix 2, Core principle (3), p.4
A Platform Operator should only admit ICO Tokens for trading at least 12 months after ICO completion or when the project starts generating profit, whichever is earlier
Appendix 2, Core principle (4), p.4
Transactions must be pre-funded; no margin financing, leverage, or virtual-asset futures/derivatives may be offered by a Platform Operator
Appendix 2, Core principle (5), p.4
A Platform Operator is expected to keep most client virtual assets not needed on short notice -- for example 98% -- in cold storage.
Appendix 2, Terms and conditions (11), p.11
A Platform Operator should take out insurance providing full coverage for hot-storage assets and substantial coverage (e.g. 95%) for cold-storage assets
Appendix 2, Terms and conditions (2), p.7-8
The SFC's approach was an opt-in Sandbox exploratory stage; no licence would be granted initially, and the SFC could ultimately decide not to regulate platforms at all
Statement, Section II, p.6-7
At this exploratory stage the SFC would not consider licensing platform operators trading virtual assets that are 'futures contracts' or 'structured products'
Appendix 2, footnote 4, p.2
rg: Read the Statement (pages 1-7) in full for the policy framework, then Appendix 1 (portfolio manager terms) and Appendix 2 (platform operator core principles, pages 3-4) closely; the detailed AML/CFT and admission-criteria terms and conditions lists (Appendix 2 items 4-12) can be skimmed for specifics once the core principles are understood.

t: Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
sl: SFC · Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers,… (2018)
s: The SFC set out how it would bring virtual asset (VA) fund managers and fund distributors into its licensing net, since most VAs are not captured by the legal definition of 'securities' or 'futures contracts'. It listed the investor-protection risks it saw in VAs (valuation, custody, market integrity, money laundering, fraud) and introduced standard licensing terms for managers running VA portfolios. Separately it opened a conceptual, non-binding sandbox exploration of whether VA trading platforms could one day be licensed. This statement is the origin of the SFC's opt-in VA regulatory approach later formalised for platforms in 2019.
w: This is the founding document of Hong Kong's opt-in VA regime and explains why, pre-2023, most VA trading platforms a bank might deal with were unregulated by design. It also set the licensing-notification habit (tell the SFC before touching VA portfolios) that persisted into later regimes.
k: A firm that distributes a fund investing in virtual assets in Hong Kong needs a Type 1 dealing licence and must follow existing suitability rules.
Section I(b)
A licensed asset manager whose portfolio puts 10% or more of gross asset value into non-security virtual assets is treated as managing a VA portfolio and gets extra licensing conditions.
footnote 6, Section I(a)(i)
Firms already managing or planning to manage any VA portfolio must tell the SFC, even below the 10% threshold.
Section I(a)(iii), footnote 9
If a firm will not accept the SFC's proposed terms and conditions, its licence application is refused, or an existing VA portfolio must be wound down.
Section I(a)(iii)
VA portfolios may only be sold to professional investors, with a de minimis carve-out.
Section I(a)(ii)
The SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to watch selected VA trading platform operators operate live before deciding whether platforms can be licensed at all.
Section II
rg: Read Section I in full for the manager/distributor rules; skim the risk-factor list (Valuation, Cybersecurity, etc.) as background; Section II is superseded by the 2019 position paper.

t: False News Report Claiming HKMA’s Investment in Crypto Products
sl: HKMA · False News Report Claiming HKMA’s Investment in Crypto Products (2018)
s: A fabricated news item, attributed to an international news agency, claimed the HKMA had put money into crypto products through a dedicated trading venue. The HKMA rejects this and says it has no holdings and no intention to acquire any. It again points victims of any related fraud to the police.
w: Shows fake HKMA-endorsement scams using crypto as bait predate the licensing regime; a recurring pattern a bank should recognise when advising customers.
k: HKMA denies the claim that it invested in crypto products via a trading platform.
para 1
HKMA says it has no current plans to invest in crypto or related assets.
para 1
Members of the public who believe they were scammed should contact the police.
para 2
rg: Short; read in full.

t: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Keynote Speech at Treasury Markets Summit 2018: “Crypto-assets and Money”
sl: HKMA · Keynote Speech at Treasury Markets Summit 2018: “Crypto-assets and… (2018)
s: In this 2018 keynote the then Deputy Chief Executive sets out the HKMA's early public position that crypto-assets such as Bitcoin fail all three classic tests of money -- medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account -- and should therefore be called crypto-assets, not crypto-currencies. He walks through the Financial Stability Board's early view that crypto-assets were not yet a systemic risk but needed monitoring, flags money-laundering and investor-protection gaps on unregulated trading platforms, and references a 2014 HKMA circular reminding banks to apply KYC/AML controls when dealing with crypto-assets. He closes by noting HKMA research into DLT trade finance and an early, cautious look at central bank digital currency (CBDC).
w: This is the HKMA's earliest public articulation of not treating crypto-assets as money, and its reminder that ordinary KYC/AML duties apply whenever the bank deals with crypto-assets or clients connected to them, which remains the baseline expectation behind all later, more detailed guidance.
k: The speech concludes Bitcoin-style crypto-assets do not meet the medium-of-exchange, store-of-value or unit-of-account tests of money, mainly because of slow, costly transactions and extreme price volatility.
paras (a)-(c) analysis, mid-speech

It reports the Financial Stability Board's contemporaneous assessment that crypto-assets were not yet a material threat to global financial stability given their small size, but that ongoing monitoring was warranted.
para on FSB assessment

It says anonymous, cross-border transfer of crypto-assets makes it hard for banks and regulated firms to meet KYC and source-of-funds requirements, and recalls that the HKMA issued a circular in 2014 telling banks to apply KYC/AML controls to crypto-asset dealings.
para on illicit-activities risk
It flags that most crypto-asset trading happens on unregulated platforms, creating gaps in investor protection and exposure to market manipulation and platform security failures.
para on investor protection/market integrity
The speech confirms the HKMA and Hong Kong banks were about to launch a DLT-based digital trade finance platform, plus a bilateral DLT link with Singapore.
para (d) on DLT applications
It discloses that the HKMA was studying the technical feasibility of a wholesale central bank digital currency, describing the work as still early-stage.
para (f) on CBDC
rg: Read the three-part money-attributes analysis and the three risk categories (financial stability, illicit activity, investor protection); the DLT and CBDC closing remarks are brief context and can be skimmed.

t: Speech by FS at "Innovative Blockchain-based Remittance Solution to Enhance Financial Inclusion" press conference (English only) (with photo/video)
sl: Government · Speech by FS at "Innovative Blockchain-based Remittance Solution to… (2018)
s: The Financial Secretary's remarks launching a blockchain-based Alipay remittance pilot to the Philippines, used to showcase HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox and the growth of the stored value facility (SVF) e-wallet market following the 2015 Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.
w: Background only: shows how HKMA used the sandbox mechanism for blockchain-based payments/remittance before any dedicated virtual-asset licensing regime existed; not a source of current obligations.
k: The HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox had, by mid-2018, supported 22 new technology products/services through to market launch over two years.
Speech body, p.1
SVF account numbers rose 15.4% year-on-year to 46.7 million by end-2017, with transaction value up 27.7% to over HK$38 billion.
Speech body, p.1
The Faster Payment System (FPS), launching September 2018, would connect banks and SVF operators for real-time transfers.
Speech body, p.1
rg: Skim; mostly promotional remarks with a few statistics of historical interest.

t: LCQ5: Issuance of cryptocurrency
sl: Government · LCQ5: Issuance of cryptocurrency (2018)
s: A 2018 LegCo written reply summarising SFC ICO/crypto enforcement actions to date (letters to exchanges/issuers, a Bitcoin-futures licensing reminder), reconfirming the September 2017 ICO securities test, and stating the HKMA had no plan to issue a retail central bank digital currency at that time given Hong Kong's already efficient payments infrastructure.
w: Historical confirmation of the SFC's early enforcement posture and reasoning against a retail CBDC; largely superseded by e-HKD work since, but useful as trajectory context for how the regime escalated from warnings toward licensing.
k: In February 2018 the SFC sent letters to cryptocurrency exchanges and ICO issuers connected to Hong Kong, warning against trading unlicensed securities-type tokens; most complied by delisting tokens or ceasing HK offers.
Reply (1), p.1

The SFC's December 2017 reminder treated dealing in, or relaying/routing orders for, Bitcoin futures contracts as a regulated activity requiring an SFC licence, regardless of where the business is based.
Reply (1), p.1

The HKMA stated it had no plan at that stage to issue a central bank digital currency, given Hong Kong's already efficient payment infrastructure, but would keep monitoring international developments.
Reply (3), p.2
rg: Read replies (1) and (3); reply (2) on offshore digital-currency hub ambitions is less relevant to compliance.

t: A Golden Opportunity for Hong Kong’s Bond Market
sl: HKMA · A Golden Opportunity for Hong Kong’s Bond Market (2018)
s: This is a 2018 HKMA Insight article by the then Deputy Chief Executive on why Hong Kong should keep developing its conventional bond market, alongside its equity and loan markets. It covers the government's new Pilot Bond Grant Scheme, tax incentives, the CMU settlement system, Bond Connect, and a planned government green-bond programme. It contains no mention of virtual assets, tokenisation, stablecoins or DLT. It is commentary, not a rule or supervisory statement.
w: This has no digital-asset content and creates no obligation; a compliance head can treat it purely as historical policy background on conventional bond-market development, unrelated to the digital-asset mandate.
k: The piece describes a new grant scheme and expanded tax exemptions announced in the 2018-19 Budget meant to attract more corporate bond issuance to Hong Kong.
para on Budget measures, p.1 (mid-page)
It explains that the Central Moneymarkets Unit, the HKMA's clearing and settlement utility for debt securities, held about HK$2 trillion of securities and had around 200 members at the time.
para on CMU, p.1
It announces a planned Green Bond Issuance Programme with a HK$100 billion government borrowing ceiling, with the HKMA running the offering and promotion.
para on green finance, p.1
rg: Not essential reading for a digital-assets compliance function; skip unless researching the HKMA's general capital-markets-development history.

t: Crypto product alleged to be launched by the HKMA
sl: HKMA · Crypto product alleged to be launched by the HKMA (2018)
s: The HKMA responds to a public query about a rumoured crypto investment product supposedly launched by the regulator itself. It states plainly that it has never started, and will never start, such a scheme, and that crypto investment products sit outside its supervisory scope. Anyone who thinks they have been defrauded is told to report to the police.
w: A minor early data point that impersonation of the HKMA for crypto scams is a recurring problem long before the VA regime existed.
k: HKMA denies ever launching or planning to launch a crypto investment product for the public.
para 1
HKMA says such crypto products are not something it regulates or supervises.
para 1
Suspected fraud victims are directed to the police's Commercial Crime Bureau.
para 2
rg: One short paragraph; read in full, nothing to skip.

t: Circular on BCBS Sound Practices Implications of Fintech Developments for Banks and Bank Supervisors
sl: HKMA · BCBS Sound Practices Implications of Fintech Developments for Banks… (2018)
s: The HKMA forwards a February 2018 Basel Committee paper on how fintech may reshape banking, without adding Hong Kong-specific rules. It flags that new technologies such as artificial intelligence, distributed ledger technology and open banking-style interfaces could create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks. Senior management is expected to assess this strategic risk and, for locally incorporated banks, bring the assessment to the board. The HKMA says it had already begun talking to major banks' senior management about their fintech plans.
w: It is background policy tone-setting rather than a rule, but it is the document that first put fintech (including DLT) strategic-risk assessment on the board's plate, a theme that later hardens into specific HKMA supervisory expectations.
k: Distributed ledger technology and other fintech tools may create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks for banks, alongside opportunities.
Bank senior management is expected to assess the strategic risk fintech poses to their institution and build a monitoring plan.
For locally incorporated banks, that strategic-risk assessment should go to the board of directors.
rg: Two-page letter; read fully, it is short.

t: SFC warns of cryptocurrency risks
sl: SFC · SFC warns of cryptocurrency risks (2018)
s: This press release reports that the SFC sent warning letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges connected to Hong Kong, advising them not to trade cryptocurrencies that are 'securities' without a licence, and separately wrote to seven ICO issuers. Most recipients confirmed compliance or ceased relevant activities. The SFC restates that it may lack jurisdiction where there is no Hong Kong nexus or where products are not 'securities'/'futures contracts', but can refer fraud cases to police. It warns investors of volatility, hacking and fraud risk.
w: As Head of Compliance, this is background only: it shows the jurisdictional gap the 2023 VATP licensing regime was built to close, and is not itself a source of any current bank obligation.
k: SFC sent letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges in or connected to Hong Kong warning against trading 'securities'-type cryptocurrencies without a licence
para 2, p.1
Most exchanges confirmed no trading of such cryptocurrencies or took rectification measures (e.g., delisting)
para 3, p.1
SFC also wrote to seven ICO issuers; most confirmed compliance or ceased offering tokens to HK investors
para 4, p.1
SFC may lack jurisdiction over exchanges/issuers with no Hong Kong nexus or not dealing in 'securities'/'futures contracts'
para 8 (Notes area), p.1
Where fraud is suspected, the SFC may refer cases to the Police
para 8, p.1
rg: Read in full; short release; the notes at the end explain the jurisdictional nexus limitation.

t: Public education campaign on risks associated with initial coin offerings and "cryptocurrencies" jointly launched by FSTB and Investor Education Centre (with photo)
sl: FSTB · Public education campaign on risks associated with initial coin… (2018)
s: This announces a joint FSTB/Investor Education Centre (a subsidiary of the SFC) public-education campaign warning retail investors about ICO and 'cryptocurrency' risks, using MTR ads, TV/radio spots and the Chin Family investor-education website.
w: This is a retail investor-education initiative, not a rule; relevant to the bank mainly as a reminder that regulators expect firms to reinforce, not undercut, this risk messaging when marketing crypto-linked products to retail clients.
k: The campaign's core message is that cryptocurrencies are volatile, unbacked virtual commodities, not real currencies, and unsuitable for everyone.
Quote from IEC Chairman, p.1
rg: Short release; read in full.

t: SFC issues reminder on cryptocurrency-related products and derivatives
sl: SFC · SFC issues reminder on cryptocurrency-related products and derivatives (2017)
s: This press release announces the SFC's 11 December 2017 circular cautioning investors about Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products, and reminding financial service providers of licensing requirements when targeting Hong Kong customers. It quotes SFC officials warning that unlicensed order routing may be a criminal offence and that risks of volatility and illiquidity may be magnified by leverage. It restates the licensing categories (Types 1, 2, 5, 9) triggered by various Bitcoin futures activities.
w: Public-facing companion to the same-day circular; shows the SFC's early public messaging tone on crypto derivatives that set the stage for later formal guidance.
k: Dealing in or routing orders for Bitcoin futures contracts for Hong Kong investors requires an SFC licence regardless of where the business is located
para 2, p.1
SFC quotes: parties routing orders without a licence may be committing a criminal offence
para 3 (quote), p.1
Client assets have in the past been taken through theft or misappropriation from crypto exchanges, some of which later failed.
para 4, p.1
rg: Short press release; read in full alongside circular 17EC79 issued same day.

t: Circular to Licensed Corporations and Registered Institutions on Bitcoin futures contracts and cryptocurrency-related investment products
sl: SFC · related investment products (2017)
s: This circular reminds SFC licensees and registered institutions of the legal and regulatory requirements applicable to Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products. It explains that Bitcoin futures traded on regulated exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO, so dealing, advising or fund marketing/management activities relating to them trigger Type 1, 2, 5 or 9 licensing requirements. It also notes some cryptocurrency products may separately be 'securities'. It closes with a warning to investors about risks of unregulated exchanges.
w: As an RI, the bank must map any Bitcoin-futures-linked dealing, advisory or fund activity onto the correct SFO licence category and suitability rules before offering it, and must not route client orders to SFC-unauthorised exchanges.
k: Bitcoin futures traded on SFC-authorised exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO even though the underlying asset is unregulated
Dealing in Bitcoin futures, including relaying/routing orders, requires a Type 2 licence unless exempt
The SFC expects intermediaries to strictly observe the suitability requirement (Code of Conduct para 5.2) and the conduct requirements under paras 5.1A and 5.3
para referencing Code paras 5.1A, 5.2, 5.3, p.1
Marketing a fund investing in Bitcoin futures is normally Type 1; managing such a fund may be Type 9; advising may be Type 5
A party providing regulated-activity services relating to Bitcoin futures needs a licence regardless of location, so long as it targets the Hong Kong public
Other cryptocurrency-related products (options, swaps, CFDs) may be 'securities' under the SFO, triggering licensing, conduct and authorisation requirements
Engaging in these activities without a licence/authorisation may be a criminal offence under the SFO
rg: Read the full 2-page circular; footnotes provide detail on regulated activity definitions but are optional.

t: LCQ15: Regulation of offering and trading of digital tokens
sl: Government · LCQ15: Regulation of offering and trading of digital tokens (2017)
s: A 2017 LegCo written reply restating the SFC's newly issued ICO statement and the government's early position: digital tokens are not currencies, ICO regulation varies globally, and existing AML/CFT laws apply to virtual-commodity businesses even without a dedicated crypto regime. It also states that virtual commodities were not seen as posing a systemic risk to Hong Kong at that time.
w: Historical confirmation that AML/CFT duties toward virtual-commodity counterparties predate and are separate from the later VATP licensing regime; useful only as background trajectory context now.
k: The government reiterated that digital tokens are a type of virtual commodity, not currency, and are not guaranteed by any issuer.
Reply para 1, p.1
AML/CFT statutory customer due-diligence and record-keeping duties applied to financial institutions dealing with virtual-commodity operators even without crypto-specific rules.
Reply para 3, p.1
At the time, virtual commodities were judged unlikely to pose a systemic risk to Hong Kong's financial system given their limited circulation as a means of payment.
Reply, closing paragraph, p.1
rg: Read the reply's middle paragraphs on AML/CFT and systemic-risk assessment; skip the preamble restating the question.

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology - Annex
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology - Annex (2017)
s: This is a compilation of seven third-party contributions annexed to HKMA's 2017 Whitepaper 2.0, each written by a different outside firm or academic: proof-of-concept write-ups on trade finance (Deloitte) and digital identity (ASTRI), a mortgage-loan case study (Bank of China Hong Kong), a governance framework called 'six control principles' (Deloitte), a security paper (PwC), a legal-issues note (the Law Society of Hong Kong), and an academic paper on blockchain liability. As background material contributed by outside experts rather than HKMA's own position, it is of reference value only and predates Hong Kong's current virtual-asset and stablecoin regimes.
w: This is outside-expert commentary annexed to a 2017 HKMA paper, not HKMA's own regulatory position; its main current use is as background on the governance-model choices (consortium vs joint venture vs statutory body) a bank faces when joining a shared DLT platform with other institutions.
k: Deloitte's framework names governance, law/regulation, and technical standards as the three factors most likely to determine whether banks can adopt private DLT platforms at scale.
Annex D, sec 1, p.39

Three governance structures for bank DLT consortia are compared: a consortium (no separate legal entity, decisions by consensus), a joint venture (separate legal entity, faster decision-making), and a statutory organisation set up and funded by government.
Annex D, sec 1.1, p.39-41

Deloitte estimates industry-wide potential savings from blockchain use in areas like transaction monitoring and account onboarding, citing a Goldman Sachs 2016 estimate of roughly $2 billion in operational savings for the banking sector.
Annex D, sec 1.1.1, p.40-41

PwC's security contribution flags confidentiality of on-ledger information, network scalability/availability, and cryptographic key security as the main technical risk areas DLT must manage to meet accepted security standards.
Annex E, intro, p.57

The Law Society of Hong Kong's legal note discusses whether personal data should be stored directly on a DLT ledger or only as a pointer/hash to an off-ledger database, given the difficulty of deleting data once written to an immutable ledger.
Annex F, 'Data protection', p.75

An academic paper (Zetzsche, Buckley, Arner) warns that DLT projects run by multiple banks could be treated by courts as joint ventures, spreading legal liability across all participating owners and operators of the shared ledger.
Annex G, abstract, p.98

The Bank of China (Hong Kong) mortgage-loan proof of concept illustrates how property valuation, ownership verification and mortgage-count checks could be run on a shared DLT platform between a bank, valuers and the Land Registry.
Annex C, p.33 onward
rg: If time is limited, read Annex D (governance models, pp.38-56) and skim Annex F/G for legal framing; the Trade Finance, Digital Identity and Mortgage Loan proof-of-concept annexes (A-C) are illustrative case studies rather than compliance guidance.

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology (2017)
s: This is HKMA's second whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), following its 2016 whitepaper, and was released around HKMA Fintech Day in October 2017. It updates the earlier technology overview, then works through compliance issues (AML/CFT, systemic risk, technology risk, reporting, governance and legal issues) that a bank should think about when deploying DLT. As of this review it carries only historical/reference value: it predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset licensing regime, its stablecoin regime, and HKMA's later DLT circular, but its governance and key-management principles were echoed almost unchanged in the 2025 study.
w: Although superseded in substance by HKMA's later DLT circular and 2025 study, this whitepaper is the origin of governance and key-management expectations (HSM, multi-signature, key recovery agents) that HKMA continued to apply; it is useful background for understanding why those expectations exist.
k: AML/CFT rules are not disapplied for DLT; a bank using a permissioned DLT platform must still design customer-onboarding and transaction-monitoring controls that satisfy its existing AML/CFT obligations, including those under the AML ordinance for Hong Kong financial institutions.

Using an unpermissioned (public, anonymous-participant) DLT platform for mainstream banking is flagged as carrying substantial money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk because participant anonymity is unresolved.

Deploying DLT for outsourced or cloud-based functions triggers HKMA's existing Supervisory Policy Manual modules, naming Outsourcing (SA-2), General Principles for Technology Risk Management (TM-G-1) and Business Continuity Planning (TM-G-2).

Regulators or auditors could in principle be given direct, near-real-time access to DLT ledger data through a 'supervisory node'; institutions should consider this possibility in solution design and related agreements.

Three governance models are set out for permissioned DLT platforms shared between banks: a consortium, a joint venture, and a statutory organisation, each with different cost, flexibility and control trade-offs.

New members joining a shared DLT platform should go through AML-aligned due diligence, a cybersecurity/internal-control check, and sign a binding end-user agreement, with ongoing monitoring and re-certification after onboarding.

Key management (authentication and access control) and smart contracts are singled out as the two areas needing the most further work, recommending hardware security modules, multiple signatures, and key revocation/recovery agents.

Concentrating on a small number of third-party DLT service providers raises outsourcing concentration risk that could become systemic if a widely-used provider fails; banks should prepare contingency/recovery plans with their providers.

The Hong Kong Electronic Transactions Ordinance gives digital signatures the same legal status as handwritten ones for most purposes, but excludes certain categories such as assignments and mortgages, which a bank should check before relying on DLT signatures for those document types.
rg: Read Chapter 5 (Compliance Issues, pp.25-29) and Chapter 6 (Governance and Control, pp.29-40) for the compliance content; skip Chapter 4's technology-platform survey (Hyperledger, Corda, Bitcoin, Ethereum comparisons).

t: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology (2017)
s: This is a technical annex to the HKMA's second DLT whitepaper, made up of seven contributed papers from banks, consultants, a research institute and lawyers rather than from the HKMA itself. It records the outcome of five 2017 proof-of-concept projects on trade finance and digital identity done with five banks, a live mortgage-valuation platform BOCHK built afterwards, and separate think pieces on blockchain governance models, network security, Hong Kong data-privacy law, and legal liability when something goes wrong on a shared ledger. It is descriptive and educational, aimed at helping banks weigh up DLT adoption; it sets no rules and creates no obligations. Much of the technical detail (choice of protocol, consensus thresholds, cloud hosting) is now dated.
w: This is HKMA-hosted but externally-authored background reading rather than supervisory guidance, so it creates no obligations; its main value for a compliance head today is the still-relevant reasoning on DLT governance models, key-management risk, PDPO exposure, and third-party liability that later HKMA custody and tokenisation expectations build on.
k: Five Hong Kong banks and Deloitte ran a proof-of-concept trade-finance DLT platform, built on a private fork of Ethereum, to share purchase-order, shipment and invoice status data and cut duplicate financing fraud.
Annex A, s.1-2, p.5-9
The pilot's own estimate was that banks could cut trade-finance operating costs by roughly 15% to 60% by removing manual reconciliation and forged-document risk.
Annex A, s.3.4, p.11

Deloitte set out three possible ways to govern a shared bank DLT network -- an informal working group, a jointly-funded private company, or a hybrid body with government involvement -- each with different tradeoffs on speed of decisions versus IP ownership.
Annex A, s.3.5, p.11-15

ASTRI's digital-identity pilot let a client be onboarded once by one bank, with only cryptographic hashes of the KYC documents (not the documents themselves) shared on the ledger so a second bank could confirm authenticity without collecting the paperwork again.
Annex B, s.1-2, p.21-24

BOCHK's live mortgage-valuation platform, built on the earlier pilot, treats the network as workable once at least two-thirds of its nodes are online, and relies on a rolling node-to-node backup instead of a separate disaster-recovery site.

BOCHK found that day-to-day governance -- patching, onboarding new members, agreeing who is obliged to act as another node's backup -- needed a designated central coordinator even though the ledger itself has no single owner.

Deloitte's control-principles paper frames DLT adoption around three linked themes banks should address together: choice of governance model, the legal/regulatory environment (including whether smart contracts are enforceable), and technical standards.
Annex D, s.1, p.39

Because writing to a blockchain requires a transaction signed with a private key, the paper flags Hardware Security Modules for key generation and storage as a necessary control, alongside the usual network credentials for read access.
Annex D, s.2.1, p.45

Deloitte recommends keeping personal or commercially sensitive data off-chain and putting only a minimal, permissioned set of fields on the ledger itself, with data-retention and key-destruction plans built in from the start.
Annex D, s.1.2, p.42-43

The Law Society's contribution concludes Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance still applies to DLT data even when only a hash is stored, if the transaction details let someone work out who the parties are.
Annex F, Data protection s.1, p.74-75

It also flags that moving data outside Hong Kong over a DLT network engages the (then not-yet-commenced) cross-border transfer restriction in the Ordinance, and that written consent from the data subject is the most workable way to comply.
Annex F, s.2, p.76-77

The academic liability paper (Zetzsche, Buckley, Arner), not PwC, cites well-known losses on public crypto networks -- the Mt.Gox and Bitfinex exchange thefts and the Parity wallet bug -- as evidence that distributed ledgers do not by themselves remove custody and legal risk.
Annex G, Introduction, p.99
rg: Skip the diagrams and vendor-specific architecture detail; read Annex A s.3.4-3.5 (governance options), Annex D s.1-2 (control principles, key management) and Annex F/G (data privacy and liability) for the parts that still inform current custody and governance thinking.

t: Statement on initial coin offerings
sl: SFC · Statement on initial coin offerings (2017)
s: The SFC's founding statement establishing that digital tokens issued in an ICO can be 'securities' under the Securities and Futures Ordinance depending on their features, for example if they carry share-like, debt-like, or collective-investment-scheme-like rights. Anyone dealing in, advising on, or managing funds in such tokens needs an SFC licence regardless of location, if targeting the Hong Kong public.
w: This remains the foundational test compliance uses to decide whether a given token is a 'security' under Hong Kong law, which in turn decides whether dealing, advising, or fund activity around it needs an SFC licence.
k: Tokens giving shareholder-like rights (dividends, surplus on winding up) may be treated as 'shares' under the SFO.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Tokens acknowledging a debt with fixed repayment or interest may be treated as a 'debenture'.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Pooled token proceeds invested for a share of returns may be treated as an interest in a 'collective investment scheme', also a form of security.
'Offering of securities' section, p.1
Dealing in, advising on, or managing/marketing a fund in tokens that are securities is a regulated activity requiring an SFC licence, wherever the firm is based, if it targets the Hong Kong public.
'Engaging in regulated activities' section, p.1
The SFC flags that ICO tokens' anonymity creates inherent money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk and points licensed firms back to its 2014 AML circular on virtual commodities.
'Cautionary statement' section, p.2
rg: Read the whole (short) statement; the footnotes give the exact SFO definitions used for 'shares', 'debenture' and 'collective investment scheme'.

t: LCQ16: Application of blockchain technology
sl: Government · LCQ16: Application of blockchain technology (2017)
s: This is a 2017 Legislative Council written reply describing the government's early, exploratory stance on blockchain: possible public-service uses, an HKMA proof-of-concept study, and confirmation that Hong Kong had no targeted rules for 'virtual commodities' like Bitcoin at that time. It also confirms an early-stage HKMA study into a wholesale central bank digital currency.
w: This is a historical marker showing how far the regime has moved since 2017; useful only for understanding the starting point of HK's digital-asset policy trajectory, not for any current obligation.
k: The government said Hong Kong had no rules specifically for virtual commodities, treating them as unbacked and not legal tender.
Reply (3), p.1
The HKMA had begun a first-phase study, with three note-issuing banks and others, into central bank digital currency for wholesale interbank and securities settlement use.
Reply (3), p.1
No government department had a concrete plan to use blockchain for public services like tax filing or land registration at that time.
Reply (1), p.1
rg: Read reply part (3) only, which is the crypto/CBDC-relevant answer; parts (1),(2),(4),(5) concern general e-government blockchain use and are not digital-asset regulatory content.

t: Whitepaper On Distributed Ledger Technology
sl: HKMA · Whitepaper On Distributed Ledger Technology (2016)
s: This is HKMA's first whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), issued 11 November 2016 at HKMA Fintech Day. It introduces DLT's technical building blocks, then walks through operational, identity-theft and conduct risks and early regulatory-compliance questions, before covering security, privacy, legal considerations and two bank-led proof-of-concept projects (mortgage-loan application and trade finance). At the time, HKMA stated that DLT compliance with regulatory requirements remained largely unexplored, and it treats the paper as a starting point for further study rather than settled guidance. As of this review it is historical background: it predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset and stablecoin licensing regimes.
w: This is the founding document behind HKMA's later DLT and custody-related expectations (cold storage of keys, AML/KYC on DLT platforms, data-privacy handling); it is useful only as background since HKMA's 2024 circular and 2025 study now state its own current expectations.
k: DLT platforms could be misused for money laundering, illegal-goods payments or receiving ransom payments if a platform lacks Know-Your-Client (KYC) checks and transaction monitoring.

Owners of DLT-recorded assets are responsible for safeguarding their own private keys; HKMA notes that 'cold storage' (keeping keys offline, e.g. on a hardware security token) gives better protection than online key storage.

HKMA states that, at the time of writing, regulators had issued little formal guidance on DLT and it remained unclear whether a traditional regulatory approach could adequately address DLT's risks and legal issues.

In permissioned DLT networks, member identities can be kept private from other members through pseudonymous transaction credentials, with only authorised auditors able to link a credential back to a real identity.

Under Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance, personal data placed on a DLT ledger must still be properly notified to, and consented by, customers, and kept no longer than necessary — which is hard to reconcile with DLT's immutability; the paper suggests deleting an encryption key rather than the record itself as a workaround.
sec 10, 'Legal implications in relation to data privacy', p.55-56

Because an unpermissioned DLT network has no central administrator, HKMA flags that it may be hard for a harmed participant to identify anyone legally accountable for a loss caused by a coding defect.
sec 10, 'Litigation and legal disputes', p.56

A five-bank working group (Bank of China Hong Kong, Bank of East Asia, Hang Seng Bank, HSBC, Standard Chartered) ran a trade-finance DLT proof of concept to test whether DLT could cut duplicate-financing fraud in trade finance.
Annex, trade finance PoC intro (also summarised at sec 11.2)
rg: Read section 8 (Risk Management and Regulatory Compliance, pp.44-47) and section 10 (Legal considerations, pp.54-57) for the compliance content; the technology chapters (sections 4 and 6) are a generic 2016-era primer and can be skipped.

t: Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities
sl: HKMA · Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities (2014)
s: A short follow-up letter to banks after press reports of more virtual-commodity exchanges appearing in Hong Kong. It repeats the January 2014 warning and reminds banks that filing a suspicious-transaction report with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies equally to virtual-commodity-related dealings. It also points banks to a government public warning on virtual commodities issued in March 2014, and gives named HKMA contacts for questions.
w: It shows the HKMA reinforcing, only months later, that the January 2014 controls were meant to be applied continuously, not just at onboarding, and that statutory suspicious-transaction reporting was already in scope for crypto-linked activity a decade before licensing regimes existed.
k: Banks should keep applying stronger due diligence on customers who run or use virtual-commodity businesses, since the full picture of a customer's activity may only emerge after the account is already open.
The statutory duty to report suspected money laundering or terrorist financing to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies just as much to virtual-commodity dealings as to any other business.
Banks should stay on top of official warnings and news about virtual commodities, including the government's March 2014 public alert.
rg: One-page follow-up; read in full, skip nothing.

t: Risks associated with virtual commodities
sl: HKMA · Risks associated with virtual commodities (2014)
s: The HKMA's Banking Regulatory Document Repository (BRDR) catalogue page for a short letter sent to all banks in January 2014 about Bitcoin-type virtual commodities. The letter warns banks to be careful about money-laundering risk when dealing with firms that run virtual-commodity schemes. It tells banks to check that such customers have solid anti-money-laundering controls before opening or keeping an account for them. It also says a bank must tell the HKMA before launching any product linked to a virtual commodity. This circular was later replaced by a 2019 letter on virtual assets.
w: This is the founding document in Hong Kong's crypto oversight of banks: it set the first prior-notification expectation and the customer due-diligence mindset that every later HKMA virtual-asset circular builds on, even though it has since been superseded.
k: Banks must step up vigilance before starting or continuing a relationship with a customer that runs a virtual-commodity exchange, brokerage or transfer service.
para 1, p.1
Banks should weigh whether the operator of a virtual-commodity scheme already has real anti-money-laundering controls when judging the money-laundering risk of that customer.
para 1, p.1
Before offering any new product tied to a virtual commodity, a bank should notify and discuss it with the HKMA.
para 2, p.1-2
rg: Read the one-page attachment in full; the catalogue page itself is navigation boilerplate.

t: Stablecoin Review Tribunal
sl: FSTB · Stablecoin Review Tribunal
s: This is FSTB's short webpage on the Stablecoin Review Tribunal, an appeal body created under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) to hear challenges to certain HKMA decisions on stablecoin issuer licensing. It names the current chairman and six members, whose term runs from 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2028, and explains that an aggrieved party has 30 days to lodge a review request after an HKMA decision. This confirms the ordinance and its appeal mechanism are already operating, not merely proposed.
w: Confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance appeal mechanism is live with a sitting Tribunal, which is relevant if the bank itself becomes a licensed FRS issuer or needs to understand a stablecoin counterparty's recourse against an adverse HKMA decision.
k: The Tribunal reviews specified HKMA decisions made under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656).
para 1
A person aggrieved by a qualifying HKMA decision has 30 days from the decision to refer it to the Tribunal for review, or longer if the Tribunal allows.
para 3
The Tribunal only convenes when needed, not on a fixed schedule.
para 3
rg: The whole page is short (under 40 lines); read it in full.

t: Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB) — HKPF
sl: Other · Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB) — HKPF
s: This is a short description page for the Hong Kong Police Force's Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB), which investigates cyber and technology crime, does computer forensics, and coordinates with other agencies. It contains no digital-asset-specific policy content.
w: This is the police unit that would investigate crypto-related fraud or hacking affecting the bank's customers; it is background context rather than a source of obligations.
k: CSTCB has treated combating technology crime as an operational priority since 2012, covering public awareness, inter-agency cooperation, and proactive investigation.
Body text, p.1
rg: Whole page is short; no skipping needed.

t: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong
sl: FSTB · Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory…
s: This is the FSTB webpage index for the joint FSTB/HKMA public consultation on licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers, linking to the December 2023 consultation paper and the July 2024 consultation conclusions paper. Both linked documents are analysed as separate registry entries below. The underlying consultation fed into the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656), which has since come into force, so this consultation stage is now historical.
w: Use this only as a pointer; the compliance-relevant content sits in the two attached documents in this package.
k: The page is purely a links index to the two substantive PDFs; it carries no independent regulatory content.
whole page
rg: No independent content to read; go straight to the consultation paper and conclusions paper.

t: HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
sl: HKEX · HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
s: This is HKEX's own webpage for its Virtual Asset Index Series, covering the same Bitcoin/Ether reference index and daily reference rate as the companion brochure in this batch, with added detail: an FAQ on how constituent exchanges are chosen (rated AA or A by an Exchange Benchmark Report, licensed and regulated, offering USD trading pairs), semi-annual constituent review, and oversight by an Index Oversight Committee. It names CCData as the index administrator. It is exchange product/marketing content, not a regulatory publication.
w: Gives the governance mechanics behind HKEX's crypto reference prices (constituent-exchange vetting, oversight committee) that a bank would want to understand before relying on the index for product settlement, but it is product literature, not an SFC-recognised benchmark standard in itself.
k: Constituent exchanges must be rated 'AA' or 'A' in the latest two Exchange Benchmark Reports, be licensed and regulated, and offer USD direct trading pairs to be eligible.
FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'
The top five eligible exchanges by rating become constituents, reviewed every six months (June and December), with an extra quarterly review in March and September if fewer than five qualify.
FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'
An Index Oversight Committee, including HKEX and the index administrator, oversees index maintenance and must endorse any methodology changes.
FAQ, 'What kind of oversight'
CCData, described as a UK-registered benchmark administrator, calculates and administers the index series for HKEX.
'Methodology Overview' section
rg: Read the 'About the Index Series' and FAQ sections; skip the long HKEX site-navigation menu that makes up most of the fetched page.

t: MPFA — no dedicated virtual-asset statement located
sl: Other · MPFA — no dedicated virtual-asset statement located
s: This is the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority's homepage, captured in Chinese, showing routine MPF administration news items (fund prices, savings rates, chairman's blog). It contains no virtual-asset, stablecoin or tokenisation content.
w: Confirms the MPFA currently has no published digital-asset-specific guidance for the bank's retirement-scheme business to track; nothing to action here.
k: The page is general MPF scheme administration content and mentions no digital-asset topic.
Homepage news list
rg: No action needed; this page has no digital-asset content.

t: IRD: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page
sl: IRD · IRD: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page
s: This IRD webpage explains Hong Kong's plan to adopt the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), a global tax-transparency standard for crypto-asset transactions. It sets out who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what must be reported, and the timeline for new legislation. It links the enabling bill and OECD guidance material as attachments.
w: If the bank or an affiliate deals in crypto-asset exchange or transfer services for customers, it may itself become an RCASP with new registration, due-diligence and 6-year record-keeping duties from 2027; compliance should also flag this framework when assessing crypto-asset-linked counterparties and clients.
k: Hong Kong plans its first automatic exchange of CARF tax data with partner jurisdictions in 2028, conditional on the domestic law being ready by 2026.
Overview section, p.1
The enabling bill was gazetted 22 May 2026 and had its First Reading in LegCo on 3 June 2026.
Overview section, p.1

Subject to the Bill's passage, CARF duties (registration, due diligence, reporting) are due to start 1 January 2027 for firms meeting HK's nexus tests; the related amended Common Reporting Standard duties are due to start 1 January 2028. As of this review the Bill has had only its First Reading and is not yet enacted.
Overview section, p.1

A business counts as an RCASP if it runs exchange services between crypto and fiat, between different crypto-assets, or operates a trading platform for customers, including as principal or intermediary.
'Individuals and entities subject to...' section, p.2
An entity can be caught by HK's nexus rules through tax residence, incorporation, place of management, or having a branch or regular place of business in HK.
'Nexus rules' section, p.3

Under the proposed Amendment Bill, RCASPs caught by the nexus rules would need to sign up for an account on the future CARF Portal no later than 31 January in the calendar year after they first satisfy a nexus test, whether or not they have anything to report for that year.
'Reporting portal and mandatory registration' section, p.4

The proposed Amendment Bill would require RCASPs to retain due-diligence and reporting records for six years from the date the related CARF return was due, and this record-keeping duty continues even after the entity dissolves, falling on whoever was a director at the time.
'Record keeping requirements' section, p.4

In the Amendment Bill, the Government proposes penalties for RCASP offences, including an administrative (civil) penalty track as an alternative to prosecution, with a right of appeal to the Board of Review.
'Penalty provisions' section, p.5
rg: Read the Overview and 'Individuals and entities subject to...' sections first to check RCASP status; skip the multilingual navigation boilerplate at the top.

t: Hong Kong Police Force — Press Release listing (JPEX case updates, incl. 16 charged Nov 2025)
sl: Other · Hong Kong Police Force — Press Release listing
s: This is the Hong Kong Police Force's general press-release index page (a year/month archive of all police press releases, crime, traffic, missing persons, etc). The fetched page shows only navigation and archive controls, not the substantive text of any specific JPEX release.
w: The JPEX collapse remains a live enforcement matter; compliance should track the individual charge announcements on this index (not captured here) for AML/fraud red flags relevant to counterparty due diligence, but this listing page itself carries no facts to summarise.
k: The page is an archive index of police press releases by month/year, not a single press release with substantive content.
Archive/filter controls, p.1
rg: Not useful as fetched; a specific JPEX press release URL would need to be fetched separately for substance.
